summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4, visited the grocery shop of the respondent and took a sample of Lal mirchi powder from the groceries of the appellant. The Public Analyst found that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirchi was adulterated. The High Court, however, acquitted the respondent on the ground that the evidence by way of a public analyst 's report did not satisfy the requirement of the definition of "adulterated article of food contained in section 2(1)(f) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "or is otherwise unfit for human consumption" is residuary provision which would apply to a case not covered by or falling squarely within the clauses preceding it. [470F] Dhanraj 's case was largely based on the circumstances that the standard of quality and purity was not prescribed in respect of cashew nuts. The adjectives "filthy", "putrid" "disgusting" "decomposed", "rotten". "insect infested" refer to the quality of the article and furnish the indicia for presuming the article to be unfit for life. [471G H] Dhan Raj vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. 2. The words "or was otherwise unfit" in section2(1) (f) are disjunctively.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption under para 3(2) could not be drawn against him because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn. HELD : (i) The presumption under paragraph 3(1) could only be drawn if there is something intrinsically wrong with that evidence. The total circumstances in the case show that the appellant was in fact carrying on agricultural operations. He produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution. But sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there because storage has reference to business as a dealers and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case, the appellant produced receipts from oral evidence that he was an agriculturist and that his brother cultivation was also grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. Therefore, the presumption is not drawn against the appellant. [90 D E] (ii) The High court erred in holding that the words 'carrying on the business ' in the context of the Act postulate a course of conduct and continuity of transactions. The conclusion must be upheld. [91 F G] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , followed.

The appellant was a monthly tenant in respect of certain premises. He had been paying rent regularly from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, and continued to pay rent regularly till the end of the year provided for in the lease. The respondent instituted a suit against the appellant for ejectment of a lessee on the ground that he was a tenant from month 'to month under the provisions of the . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the view that the notice to quit was defective and inoperative as the notice had been defective. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellant was not entitled to a decree in his favour because he was in possession of the land belonging to the respondent with the permission of the Receiver who represented the plaintiff 's estate. He was therefore entitled to be ejected from the land as a trespasser and the suit was maintainable. (ii)The mere fact that the parties might have intended to create a lease for another year, did not make it a tenancy from month lo month under s. 106, Transfer of property Act, Transfer Of Property Act. The terms of the lease were clear and unambiguous and could not be read in isolation. The question whether the rent was created by payment and acceptance of rent by the Receiver was one for the purpose of section 116, Transfer or Property Act and the mere fact of payment did not affect the validity of the notice under s, 106 of the Act. (iii)The appellant had no authority to receive them. The suit was therefore governed by the provisions Of section 107 of the Indian Evidence Act.

The appellant assessee, a firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn, filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722/ from the defendants, M/s. D.N.G.S. and Smt. Budh Prakash, who were partners in the firm. During the course of proceedings in the suit, the plaintiff obtained summons to produce certain documents relating to assessment of an assessee under section 137 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer, to whom the summons was issued, sent the record to the Income tax Department for the purpose of making a reference under section 138(1)(b) of the Act, and after considering the objections of the assessee, held that the said record was privileged under section 139(1) (b). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal. In further appeals by the assessee the High Court held that since the documents, records, etc., were filed by an assessee or a third party after April 1, 1964 in respect of assessment years 1964 65 onwards, no right, privilege, obligation or liability could be said to have been acquired, accrued or incurred prior to April 1. 1964, and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under section 140(1), was not removed by the IncomeTax Authorities. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the appellant assessee that after the repeal of section 137, by Act V of 1964, there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production of documents filed by the assesseee before the income tax authorities after April I, 1964. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The finality which has been attached to the order if the Commissioner under section 136(1 (b) is applicable only in cases where application is made to the Commissioner by a party or any other person for receiving documents or information. Section 138(2) of 1961 Act provides that a person can make an application to the Commis sioner in the prescribed form and also to his decision in this behalf shall be final and shall not be called in question in any court of law. The provisions of section 139 (1)(a) and (b), therefore, are applicable to cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person, other than a court of Law by a judicial order. [561E F] 2.

The plaintiff appellant was the widow of one Mammotty. The father of Mammottty executed a gift in favour of his minor daughter in law by which she bequeathed her properties to her mother. The gift was confirmed by the mother who had been in possession of the property as guardian of the minor and remained in possession till the date of the execution of the gift deed. In other words, the widow gifted the properties to the appellant 's father. The appellant filed a suit for partition and possession of his property which was decreed by the trial court. On appeal the High Court held that the gift was void as it had not been made in contemplation of death of Mamman and as such no question of delivery of possession was necessary in a suit to be filed against Mammothty under the Muhammadan Law. The High Court further held that a gift by the husband to his minor son could have been completed by delivery of the properties, that even if the gift had not become final by delivery, the donee could have made a declaration of gift and take possession on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift from his minor child even though her father be living; that even under the Guardian and Wards Act, the husband can claim to the property in his hands as guardian specially when he is unautho rised. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf for the appellant that (1) the gift in the present case was a valid gift and (2) the respondent had not completed the gift within the meaning of section 12(4)(iv) of the Muhammadans Act, and as the deed also records the fact that possession was given to one of the stated guardians of the respondent, the High court should have refused to go into the question whether the gift made by Mammots was void. HELD : (1 ) The gift in question was a proper gift and complete. [553 B] (2)(a) The donor must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. Exceptions to these strict rules which are well recognised are gifts by the wife to the husband and by the father to his daughter. [554 C D] (b) There is no evidence that Mammats were guardian of any property in existence. The fact that Mamman was living at the time of the gifted in the house of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut, does not make him a guardian. [555 E F] (c) There can be no question that there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammen and to transfer the property to the donee. If the property is with the donor he must depart from it and the donee must enter upon possession. The strict rule of Muhammadan law about giving possession to one or the other of the parents is not a condition of its validity in certain cases. One such case is gift by a husband to the minor son and the donor, where there is gift to a minor who has no guardian of her property in continuance. In such cases the benefit to the father and to the mother cannot be given to the wife. [557 F G] (3) The rule about possession is relaxed in certain circumstances.

The Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of Hindu religious and charitable institutions and endowments in the State of Madras. The Act provided for the establishment of a committee to make its report to the Government of the State. Section 76(1) provides that the trustee of every religious institution shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments, Madras issued notices to the respondents who were trustees of the Venkataramana temple at Mulki, District South Kanara, for payment of contributions to the temple. The respondents challenged the validity of the demand on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 76(2) of the Act and therefore the demand was premature. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63, 64, 65 and 89 were ultra vires the State Legislature. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the provisions of the Madras Hindu religious & Charitable Endowment Act, 1950, which were in fact enacted at a time when several different kinds of services were intended to be rendered and the court had no jurisdiction to make rules under section 100(1)(b) of that Act. HELD : (i) The High Courts erred in not examining the question whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to he collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be performed. [923 B C] (ii) The rules under the Act have to be general. And such rules were in substance framed and were in operation. Therefore, the High Court erred in holding that appropriate rules were not in existence at the time when the demand for contribution was made. [936 D E] (iii) The order passed by the High court upholding the claim of the respondent temple on this part of the case must be set aside.

The appellant alleged that the notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the , to show cause against the alleged liability to be punished under section 15. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondents that no appeal lies to this Court under section 19 of the Act from an order issuing notice as nothing yet has been decided by the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proceeding is not barred, and therefore, the preliminary objection raised on behalf of the respondents was well founded. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide any question. This Court has to see whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of the High Courts or not. The proceedings are initiated under section 18 by issuance of a notice. Thereafter there may be many interlocutory orders passed in the said proceeding by theHigh Court. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to this court as a matter of right from each and every such order made by the Calcutta High Court, if the order has been made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. No appeal can lie as a matters of right under section19. [512 B C] (2) The proceedings is initiated under s.17 by issuance, of a show cause notice and thereafter there may he many interlocutory applications made to this High Court under s 19. A final order, surely will be appealable. [511 E F] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court ; , referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted and convicted for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 6 (1 A) of the Act was not applicable to a case of a later amending Act inserting new provisions in an earlier Act, for where an earlier statute was amended by a later Act, it could not be said that the earlier Act applied, incorporated or referred to. The earlier Act did not indicate any intention different from that envisaged by the said section. The section does not prohibit the possession of wireless apparatus. The word " text" in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another, it amends the subject or script of it, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. The Legislature did not intend to give it any legislative effect but to excise dead matter from the statute book. Secretary of State for India in Council vs Hindusthan Co operative Insurance Society Ltd., ; , referred to and distinguished. Held, further, that the word " printed" in section 6 A of the Indian Telegraphs Act was comprehensive enough to take in a wireless telegraphic apparatus and imposing a more severe punishment. The words are comprehensive enough and the Legislature did so in the present case. Secretary, of State, for India vs Manager, Caledonian Press Chakravartti, C.A. No.

The appellant, who was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930, instituted two suits against the respondents for recovery of moneys due in respect of the Hatchita and the promissory notes executed by her. The suit was decreed on the basis of a compromise dated 23rd July, 1933, and the decree was confirmed on appeal by the High Court. In execution proceedings under section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, the properties mentioned in Schedule Ka were sold and they were purchased ostensibly by the two decreeholders. The appellant contended that the properties described in Schedules Ka and Kha were not liable to be partitioned after the coming into force of the new instalment decrees and that the respondents were entitled to have the two compromise decrees reopened and on the passing of new instalments, the appellant was entitled to get the properties set off against the decretal dues thus ascertained by instalments. Held, that the appellant had been rightly assessed under section36(2)(c) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act and the reliefs which the Court was competent to grant in terms of that section were not wiped out and the parties were not relegated to their rights and liabilities under the original cause of action (i) The suit for recovery was therefore barred by limitation. Renula Chandra vs Manmatha, , followed. Held further, that in a proceeding under section 37 of the Act the court has not only the right but is under a duty to make an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decreeholder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b) of section 36.

The respondent, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 as arrears of rent and interest on the ground that the said amount had been paid by him to the firm in respect of certain transactions in gold and silver effected by the firm as well as by the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant could not apply under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure for that rule could not be applied to a case where there was no decree at the date of the assignment of the property and the term "decree holder" could not cover a party who had become entitled to the benefit of the decree as soon as it was passed. The High Court also held that in view of the provisions of Order XXI rule 16, the respondent could not claim to come under O. XXI, r. 16 of C.P.C. for that Rule could not have been applied to him because he had not filed a suit on the date when the decree was passed and therefore the application made by him prior to the coming into force of the equitable principle that the right, title and interest of the respondent in the decree passed in his favour were transferred by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order 21, rule. The appellant contended that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for execution as the respondent had not made an application under O XXI, Rule 16 of 0. XXI. r. 11(2)(j) and therefore, the application was barred by limitation. Held: (i) The respondent could have applied under Order 21 rule 16 only against the assignment in question which was subsequently obtained by the assignment. The transfer in writing of a decree that may be passed in future may not amount to an transfer of the original decree but it is only when the execution is made and the application is made to the Court which passed it, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee of the order of transfer invalid or inoperative. (ii) The High Courts have held that under O, XXI, R. 16, C. P.C., the respondent was entitled to execute the decree in his own favour and that the application under Order I, r., 11(1), C.p. 325, C., P. 325 and C.I.T. Bombay vs Macklin & Co. (A.I .R. , referred to. (iii) The transfer of or an agreement to transfer a decree does not make two applications one for recording the assignment and another for executing the decree. The respondent cannot claim to be a transferee in the absence of an assignment in the writing executed by the transferor in writing. (iv) The application under 0. 21, r, 16, is not a fresh application and the respondent cannot seek to invoke the provisions Of O. 21 r. I, C P. 326, C D. R., as he had made the transfer on the 25th April, 1951.

The respondent, a manufacturer of steel doors and door leaves, was fabricating steel doors, windows, etc. and making no separate charges for the service. The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. On appeal the Deputy Commissioner confirmed the order. The High Court in reference, however, held that there was a stipulation for payment of price for services rendered by the respondent "volunted and fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl edge and that the price of the supplied but not the charge for service was taxable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the contract entered into by the Respondent was a works contract, and the amount received by the appellant was not taxable; (2) in undertaking to install or fix these units or articles the sellers did not enter into a works contracts merely because they undertook to install and for the articles sold. HELD: (i) The object of the Respondent being to enter into "a works contract" it was one for sale of materials or is a contract for service. [516 B] (ii) The contract in question in this case was of the second variety. Counsel for the respondent contended that the terms of the tender were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and that it was only upon the "fixing" of the windows as stipulated required special technical skill. If the windows were not properly "fixed", the contract would not be complete and the Respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [511 C D] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the appellant had agreed to and did supply the windows but not to supply them. The contract was of a second variety, and was one completed by the manufacturer. The amenities were to be rendered under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution of the works of sale. [506 E] (iv) The construction of the building was an integral part of the premises and the appellant could not claimed the amount stipulated to be payable to it.[517 G] (v) The respondent had agreed that the amenities were provided for the completion of the erection of the walls intended to be used for offices of the Accountant General. The appellant had not paid the charge or charges for service, but had made a specific provision for passing of property in the materials supplied by the res pondent.

The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla were found to be the same person. On November 16, 1967 Shankerlal representing himself to be a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar with a conspiracy to arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then agreed, would be sent through Shankar Lal. On the following day, Shankar Lal brought one Saheb Jaman Khan alongwith him to Ram Avla and introduced Saheb Jamn Khan as agent of M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. The prosecution case against the accused was that he had entered into a conspiracy with one Shanker Lal to cheat the complainant and to cheat him. The complaint was filed on November 15, 1967. The trial court convicted the accused under section 420 read with section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced him to pay Rs.38/ per day as penalty. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence but acquitted the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the case against him was quashed by the High court in a revision petition under section 439 Cr. P.C., the order of the High COurt was not vitiated because no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the trial court had been made out and there was no cogent reason for interference. HELD: (i) The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwala respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. [279 D] (ii) There is no cogent grounds for interference in the judgment.

The petitioner, an All India Institute of Medical Sciences, was a public utility service run by the Indian Railways. He had been running a commuter in the State of Kerala and had been awarded a compensation of Rs.22 crores for his services. The petitioner alleged that he had suffered loss on account of defective bridges and heavy rains and murders and had pointed out that the Railways had improved and in 1982, as many as 27233 unmanned level crossings were provided mostly on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. He also claimed compensation for the services rendered by the I.T.O. to make periodical inspection of carriages, engines etc., during the period ending March 31, 1983 and also for the removal of defects in the rolling stock and required gadgets, etc. The respondent authorities were of the view that the petitioner had failed to comply with the constitutional provisions and that he was guilty of misconduct and negligence in the discharge of his duty, engines, tracks, etc., and that the Indian Railway Act, 1890, has prescribed several safety measures for improvement and improvement of railway work particularly at accident prone spots. The respondents filed a counter affidavit stating that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined by the Chief Medical Officer who had reported that the accidents were serious in nature and that they were problems of law and order, maintenance of which was an obligation of the State Governments. The Court directed the Union Government to file a counter affidavits before the Court. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the report of the accident Enquiry Committee was not examined by this Court; that the Central Board of the Railway had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter and that there were nearly 12000 people who had been injured during the incident; that there was no negligence on the part of the Railways in providing adequate facilities and creating an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Union Government should be free to collect the entire operational cost which would include the interest on the capital outlay out of the national exchequer. It is of paramount importance that every citizen must get involved in the determined march to resurrect the society and subordinate his will and passion to the primordial necessity of order in social life. All the wrecks on either side of the stream of time, all the waves of the great cities and all the nations that have passed away all are a warning that no nation founded upon injustice can stand. [723D E] 2. The Railways are a public sector undertaking run by an Indian Railways and are providing the lifeline and link throughout the length and breadth of the country. The Railway Administration is a Public utility Undertaking. There is at present a general agreement among the lawyers that the price policy of such a public corporation should neither make a loss nor a profit after meeting all capital charges and this is expressed by covering all costs or breaking even though they are frivolous and unprepared for. [700H; 700A B] 3. The Indian Constitution has definitely rejected the authoritarian form of Government and directed the State to bring about an egalitarian social order through the rule of law. It was not a mere technical agreement among lawyers but only in a sense of the matter. The court is concerned with the policy of the Government and it is for the Court to decide what should be done by the Union of India and its instrumentalities. [621C D] 4. The Ministry of Home Affairs has been given the power to deal With the situation, and take an action which will be a challenge to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. If necessary, it shall set up a high powered body to quickly handle the many faced problems standing in the way.

The appellants were holders of jagirs. The jagirs Abolition Act, 1953 was enacted to provide for the restoration of an appeal against the Collector 's award and for certain other purposes. Section 13(2) provides that any jagirdar entitled to compensation under section 11 or 12 shall, on or before the 31st day of July 1958 apply in writing to the Collector for determining the amount of compensation payable to him under the said section. The appellants filed applications for restoration of their jagirs which were dismissed by the Tribunal but the appeals were allowed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals had become final and conclusive, the appeals should be allowed as they were prevented from appearing at the hearing of the appeals. HELD: (i) The Tribunal has no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing. [143 B] (ii) Section 14(2), which provides that "any jagirdar entitled under section II or 12 to compensation shall, if he has not appeared either in the appeal, or through an agent or pleader when the Appeal or application was called for hear ment, be given notice and opportunity of being heard before the order for restorancdings. [144 C D] (iii) The words "decide it on merits" in section 17(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act mean "decided ex parte". On a consideration of the language of section 17 (1), the Tribunal has jurisdiction to dismiss the appeal for noncompliance with article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 20. [145 E F] (iv) The expression "decides it on merit" in Section 17(2)(a) does not include in its scope and ambit an application for restoration under Regulation 20, but in Regulation 20 the expression used is "decided Ex parte".

The appellant was the Mahant of a temple in Madhya Pradesh. He had three sons, one of whom was a wealthy person and the other a Hindu. The first appellant was appointed as the manager of the temple by the Board of Trustees. The second appellant was also appointed a Receiver for the management of the affairs of the deity. The appellant 's case was that he had committed several breaches of trust by transferring trust properties to the deities in the temple and that he was not entitled to any proprietary interest in the property. The trial court held that there was no dedication of the village as claimed by the appellant and that the village Telibandha was dedicated absolutely to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy, and that consequently it was a public religious trust. On appeal the High Court set aside the decree holding that the dedication was valid and that it was not satisfied that the endowment had been made by the members of the family with the intention of transferring the trust properties and that there were no restrictions on the alienation in the matter of the trust. The High Court further held that the appellant 'was not entitled under section 92 of the Code to succeed, that the property was given in full ownership to Shri Ramchandra as the Manager and trustee of the Temple and that therefore the village was dedicated to the deity and that a Commissioner would be appointed later on to enquire into the alienations made by him. On a reference made by this Court, it was held that: (1) the dedication of village Telia Dasi was not valid; (2) the use of words "from the profits and income of Mouza Teligana" in the translation of the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 showed that only a portion of the income was intended to be used and that supports the presumption arising from the use. of the word "Malik". The High court accordingly set aside its judgment and decree and directed the trial Court to dispose of the appeal after giving an opportunity to the parties to decide whether the award of the panchas was proper or not, and (3) the appellant had committed breach of trust as a trustee of his village. Held:(1) that the word 'Malik ' in section 92 is used in the widest sense and includes all rights and interests of ownership in the donee. The fact that the suit is stated to be dismissed as compromised and the compromise appears to have been in accordance with the terms of the compromise would not make any difference. (2)(a) The word "Milkiyat" in section 2(1)(d) of the Madhya Pradesh Zamindari Abolition Act, 1908, means "from a person who is entitled to do so". (b) The words "Mouza Teliatia" in that section mean "from an profits and gains. " In other words, the word has been used in connection with the maintenance of the public trust and it cannot be said that the use was not from the profits or income of a person. (c) The fact, therefore, that Ramsaran Lal had only a life interest in his property and did not make an absolute dedication of it to the appellant could not affect the force or validity of the absolute nature of the dedication. (3)(a).

The appellants were the President of a High Court and Chairman, Action Committee of the High Court described as contemner No. 2 was actively associated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers he was guilty of contempt. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had not considered the contemners guilty of criminal contempt and that the Judges of the Division Bench were guilty of contumacious conduct, and that they should have punished the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language used by them was unfortunate. [602C] 2. The judgment of the Allahabad High Court in a contempt case is set aside and the proceedings are quashed. [ 602D] 3. The matter becomes clear when the High court said "we do not propose to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumacious act of which we have adjudged them guilty though we express no opinion that they were responsible for the passing off the resolution. [ 603E F] 4. The contempt is a matter of regret and cannot be passed in that manner. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty, the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. It was the duty to protect our dignity and decided not to punish contemner No 2 for contempt. [600F] 5. The Judges of Division Bench are guilty of wilful conduct and the High courts gave them the ground that they had committed contempt as contemner NO. 1. They rightly said that contemners Nos 1 &2 were guilty and punished for contempt as they did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion.

The respondents Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into an agreement with the four brothers for partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge under section 14 of the , praying for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in order to return the award to enable them to present it before the sub Registrar for registration. On the question whether the award had been presented within time as required by section 25 read with section 23 of the . HELD: (1) The award was made on 28th January, 1978 and it was presented for registration to the Sub Registrar on 25th November, 1983. Section 23 of , provides that if owing to urgent necessity or unavoidable accident, any document executed, or copy of a decree or order made is not presented for registra tion till after the expiration of the time prescribed, the Registrar, in cases where the delay in presentation does not exceed four months, may direct that on pay ment of a fine not exceeding ten times the amount of the proper registration fee such document shall be accepted for registration and the Registrar may order the same to be heard when the injunction order was vacated. [123B C] (2) The provisions of section 15 of the are applicable in this case, as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely, 28th of January 1978 to 24th November 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down in section 15 read together. [124D E] (3) Section 25(1) of the provides that any application for such direction may be lodged with a Sub Registrar. who shall forward the same within fifteen days from the date of its execution to the Registrar. Therefore, the cumulative effect of sections 23 and 25 read together is that total period of eight months is available for registration if the conditions are fulfilled. [125E F] (4) The High Court was wrong in holding that the only period which should be included was from 26th July 1978 till 20th December, 1982. Therefore the cumulative consequence of sections 3 and 25 of the is that the total period for eight months was available for regu larisation if the condition are fulfilled, and no arbitrator could be compelled to disobey the order of the court and if in compliance or obedience with Court 's injunction, he could not take back the award from the custody of the Court to take any further steps for its registration then it cannot be said that he has failed to get the award registered as the law required. [126A B] (5) The order made by the court directing the arbitrators to keep the award within the custody and to pay a fine, not exceeding 10 times the proper registrable amount, is set aside. [127B C].

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting. The appellant contended that under section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, there was no prohibition against a contract of sub letting, but it was urged that the provisions of section 15 were not applicable to contracts between the landlord and tenant and therefore the respondent could not succeed in enforcing the agreement which recognised sub letting but he asked the Court to enforce the right of eviction which flows directly from an infraction of a provision of the Act. Held, that the appellant was entitled to claim protection under section 13(1)(e) of the . The provisions of the section were applicable only to contracts entered into by the landlord with the tenant and not to agreements between the parties. The provisions in section 15 are based on public policy and it has been held that if public policy demands it even an equal participant in the bargain, it is unenforceable as being in contravention of the express provision of section 14(1) of Act. The maxim "failure of a statutory right" is not applicable in this case because the respondent was asked to enforce his rights under the statute and the appellant could not evict him under section 14 (1)(a). The respondent had failed to do so and the suit for eviction was not maintainable. The suit was therefore not brought within the purview of the protection of section 13 (1) (e) and the High Court was right in holding that the tenancy by the respondent had been terminated by the appellant and he could not be evicted under section 10(1).

The appellant, a candidate for selection to the post of Junior Engineer in the respondent University, was selected and appointed as a result of an interview held by some members of the Board. The final list of candidates recommended by the examiners was published on June 30, 1990. In the meanwhile, the marks awarded to the respondent were reduced from the marks initially obtained by him. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court in a writ petition filed in the High court against non declaration of the results and the High Courts directed the Board to take expeditious action to declare the result of the examination within the specified time. The High Court directed the State Government to take steps to declare results of the examinees and the Board was directed to take effective steps to declaring the results of all the candidates. Aggrieved by the order, the appellant filed a writ appeal in this Court against the judgment of the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The examination standing committee of the respondent Board itself had no power to take decision on behalf of the appellant. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, the Standing Committee did not record any reason in support of its conclusion that the examines/recommendations were done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardians and that the subject/subjects in which fabrication was committed belong to him or her. [890C] 1:3 The High Courts have to consider whether the conclusions reached by the Board can be fairly supported by evidence on record, then the High courts have no jurisdiction to quash the order merely because the conclusion reached by them is perverse and cannot be sustained. [800D] 1st Respondent has not been given any opportunity of showing cause as required by clause (2) of Article 311 unless such opportunity was dispensed with by the Governor acting under the provisos (b) and (c) to that clause. The Board did not discharge its duty, on the other hand, the Board had presumed that fabrication was done at its behest. [900E] 2:1.2 The High court has no jurisdiction under article 226 to quash a decision of the quasi judicial authority or the Standing committee or the Enquiry Officer unless such an opportunity is dispensed with. The findings of the Single Judge are based on no evidence and there is no room for any distinction between what is found by the evidence and what is held as a positive face.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence punishable under section 5(2) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special judge convicted them and sentenced them to three months rigorous imprisonment each. On appeal by the State the High Court reduced the sentence on the ground that section 5 (2) of the Act was not applicable to the facts. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the offence as defined in cl. (d) of a. 165 Of the Indian Railways Act, was one committed by a person who had no authority to make an arrest and therefore the charge under section 6 read with section 116 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was unsustainable. Held, that the offences committed were less grave and call only for lenient or nominal sentences. The offence as contemplated by cl. 2 Of the , was one punishable under s 5(1) of that Act and under sub section (2), it was made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The words "corrupt or illegal means" in cls. (a) to (d), cl. 3, cl. 4 Of the Code, refer to a motive or reward for doing or forbearing to do something showing favour or disfavour to any person or for inducing such con duct by the exercise of personal influence. The word "obtains" is used in sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (d). The words 'corrupt ' are intended to cover criminal breach of trust by a public servant and the wording takes colour from the sub clause. In one sense this is no doubt true but it does not follow that there is no overlapping of offences. The definition of "obtain" in cl., 2 Of section 165 Of Indian Penal code, is used as a means of criminal force or punishment for doing something showing favor or disfawing to any one. To put it differently, the ingredients of the two offences are common, no doubt, but to go further and the police authorities themselves supply the money to be given as a bribe, severe condemnation of the method is merited, as in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh and another vs The State of Vindhya Pradesh, [1954] S.C.R. 1069, followed.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368/ . The respondent bank resisted the claim on the ground that it had agreed to grant cash credit facility to the surety and since the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods, the surety was discharged. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the appellant Bank in not paying the entire amount and that as the contract was independent it could not be discharged. On appeal by the respondent bank, the High Court held that the surety had agreed and had in fact pledged 5,000 tins of oil tins and that the security of pledged goods was lost on account of negligence of the Bank. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that in view of clauses 5, 7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee, Ext. 31, even if it is found as a fact that negligence of creditor bank was responsible for the loss of security of the pledged goods, yet the surety would not be absolved from his liability under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant Bank had agreed that cash credit facilities should be given to the sureties and in case the creditor failed to do so, the sureties would be discharged from his obligation as surety if the creditors have put it out of their power to hand over to the appellant the means of recouping himself by the security given by the principal. [928C] 1.2 The appellant was the plaintiff and its suit was decreed by the trial court, i.e., the Court of first instance. The appellant had made an application that in compliance with the decree made by the Trial Court he had paid the entire sum and he should not be exposed to second round of litigation for restitution of the amount and this Court should give a direction to the Bank as part of this judgment that the amount be returned with interest at current rate to the respondent surety. [936F G] 1:3 The appellant bank was entitled to restitution. It would stand disposed of accordingly. [830C D] 2.1 In view of the clauses 5 and 7 of the Letter of Guarantee, the appellant is entitled to recover from the surety a sum which was collected from the sureties on a mere demand.

The appellant was the holder of a jagir village in Berar. He was granted a jagir to the respondent No. 1, who was the proprietor of a village in the State of Bombay. The respondent No 1 filed a suit for possession of the "patelki inam" lands which were not his "poli inam" within the meaning of section 3 of the Patels and Patwaris (Abolition) Act, 1927. The appellant contended that the lands were granted to him by the Government as he was not entitled to hold them free from any liability under the Act. Held, that the grant was a mere grant of office with emoluments in the shape of Inamlands and was not a service grant. The grant was made by the jagirdar of the jagir and not by the sovereign authority. The holder of the Jagir was entitled as of right to a share in the emoluments. The land had been given to his ancestors in lieu of patelki huq and it should be taken into consideration for determining the proportions in which they shall share in them. The lands were given to the appellant by way of emoluments for the office of patels. The High Court was right in holding that the grants were not a grant of land revenue but were made by an order passed by the revenue authorities in respect of the matters mentioned therein and no right was given to a member of the family of the patel to claim a share therein. Raja Jagannath vs Raje Vinayakrao, (1923) L.R. 46 I.A. 222, referred to.

The respondent, who was the father of two respondents, died in 1955 leaving behind his widow and three daughters. The appellant 's mother died on March 22, 1955 leaving a will whereby she transferred certain properties to the respondent. The respondent claimed that the entire property held by her husband as well as the joint family property should be assessed under the Madras Hindu Law as it stood prior to the coming into force of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1937. The trial court held that neither the said evidence nor the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third of the said estate was sufficient to sustain the claim for partition. On appeal the High Court reversed this decision holding that the respondent 's family was in Madras till about 1930 when its members were shifted to Madras and thereafter in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, and as a large part of the property had been settled by the Bombay High Court in Madras, it should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. The question for consideration was whether the Hindu law applicable to the Madras estate was applicable to Cutchi Memons governed by the Madras Estate (Abolition) Act of 1937. Held, that the Hindu Law applicable to cutchi Memon and not to the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, is clear from section 3 of the Act which provides that any cutchi memor shall be deemed to have been governed by that law as to stridhan. The definition of joint family in section 2(14) of the Indian , includes a person who had attained the age of majority and was at the time a resident in British India, but has not been proved affirmatively that he had ever adopted as part of his customary law the Hindu system of Settlemen in Madras and Bangalore. The Hindu Law of inheritance is applicable to all persons governed by it and the rule of devolution of property by survivorship is applicable only to matters of succession and inheritance. The fact that a cutchi members who proceeded either from Cutch or from Bombay to Madras, and who, it was not proved before him and never had been proved negatively that they had ever been adopted as parts of their customary law does not affect the validity of the rule as to coparcenary property. The rule of succession is applicable even where a single and undivided family has merged into one. In the present case, the respondent was governed by Hindu Law and the custom prevailing in Madras was not extended at first to the Civil Station area in Bangalore, but later to the civil station area in Mysore. The High Court had rightly held that the rule applied as its section 2 did not make the Mahomedan law applicable in all matters relating to Muslims nor did it abrogate the custom and usage in respect of matters other than those specified in section 3.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants did not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which were manufactured in the mills were liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also did not deny their liability to pay excise duty in respect of yarn which is obtained on an intermediate stages in the Mill. The Central Board of Excise, by its order dated 20th February, 1982, directed that "use of goods in manufacture of another commodity even within the place/premises specified in rule 9(1) of the Rules will be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises immediately before such consumption or utilisation". The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. During the pendency of the writ petition, the Central Board issued a circular dated September 24, 1980 purporting to interpret rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, and directed that the use of the goods in which is produced at an intermediary stage in mill of a factory would be liable to pay duty on its removal from any place where they are produced, cured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto. The High Court held that the retrospective effect given by section S(1)(a) will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the expression "place of removal" in rule 173(1), as defined therein, does not contemplate only removal from a place where the excisable goods are produced; (ii) the words "place or premises appurtenant to such factory" do not contemplate any deemed removal but a physical and actual removal of the property from the place of manufacture as envisaged by rules 9 & 49 of Central Excise Act; (iii) the notification issued under rule 9 of the Cen tral Excise Rules was ultra vires the provision of clause (b) of sub section (4) of section 4 of the Finance Act, 1982. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression " place of removal", as defined in Rule 173(2), does not mean only removal but also removal within such place and premises appurtenant thereof for captive consumption or use it is called. Thus if a commodity which is manufactured in such place is brought within the factory, will be removed from that place or Premises immediately before that consumption or utilization. Therefore, in view of section 3A of the , the taxing event under section 3 of the Excise Act is the production or manufacture of goods and not removal. [707C D] 2. The words " place" in Rule 9(i) are used in the context of the end product. It must be admitted that prima facie rule 9 does not show that it also covers a case of integrated, continuous and uninterrupted process of manufacture producing a commodity at an independent stage of such process for the manufacture of an end product or commodity. [077D E] 3. The definition of "place" in section 2(1A) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 is that the goods obtained at any place or place or any Premises appurtenant thereto, but also removed or utilised for the purpose of payment of duty are made in a factory which is required to be removed within the meaning of Rule 174 of the rules. [087E F] 4. The Explanation to rule 9 and rule 49 of Cen tional Excise Rules clearly indicates that if a unit is taken outside the factory it will be removal, but rule 9 cannot be interpreted in the light of provisions of the Explanation to sub rule (2) of Rule 9. [807G H] 5.

The petitioner, a holder of a permit issued under Chapter IVA of the , to ply a stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasians Shambhaoli Babugarh Jadol Jahangirabad route in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed his objections to the scheme and the State Transport Undertaking submitted its objection to it along with several others. After considering the objections, the State Government passed an order under section 68 C of the Act directing that the scheme published under section68 C should be implemented by 21.5.1979. The State Transport Undertakings filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order and the High court dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by him since the jurisdiction of the civil courts was impliedly barred. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 69 D) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the hearing authority from proceeding with the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. Whenever statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction is vested in the Civil Court. The civil courts jurisdiction must be held to be excluded insofar as the merits to the case is concerned. If jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil court has jurisdiction only to examine whether the provisions of the Statute have not been complied with or the tribunal had or had not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. In cases of the present nature where invariably reliance is placed by the private operators on Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, a writ Petition lies before the High Courts. [544C D] H. C. Narayanappa and Ors. vs The State of Mysore and Ors., ; at page 753; H.C.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was charged with having committed an offence under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5 (1)(d) of that Act. The prosecution case was that the appellant had no child of his own and wanted to adopt a child. The appellant asked for a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . The appellant offered a bribe to the girl and the girl was handed over to the appellant who took her with him. The girl was then handed over by the appellant to the police station. The Police Inspector, Nathaniel and his wife gave evidence in regard to the proceedings. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 5 of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs 5001 or in default to undergo further period of six months under section 6(2). On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The order of sanction was bad in law as all the relevant papers and materials were not placed before the D.I.G. Police but were kept before the police officer. The order did not show that the accused person had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act or for showing or forbidding to show in the exercise of his official functions favour or disfavour to any per son. In other words, the appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as public servant and extorted money from Russel Nathanite and his marriage with the girl child. (ii) The High Court erred in holding that the order of sanctioning a prima facie case was bad. When a public servants is charged under section 165A of the Indian Penal code or section 5, it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing, or procuring an official act, it was not necessary for the court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act. The High Courts were therefore in error in holding the appellant guilty of grave abuse of his position and obtaining for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. Mahesh Prasad vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , followed. (iii)The order of the sanction in that case was based on the evidence of a public officer who was expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and to uphold the maintenance of law. But the High Court did not record any finding that or the accused Public servant was incapable of doing anything which would interfere with the maintenance 'of law.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The sanction was given by the Chief Commercial Superintendent of the Eastern Railway who had been authorised to deal with the case in a court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 (2) Of the Act. The appellant contended that the sanction was not a valid sanction as it was not issued by the General Manager of the railway, and that the prosecution was barred by section 6 of the Act, because, the sanction given in this case was not one for the prosecution of the appellant. Held, that the sanctioning authority was competent to grant the sanction under section 6(c) of Prevention of ' Corruption Act. Section 6(C) of that Act provides that no sanction shall be granted unless it is shown that the offence or 5 (1) A.I.R. 1952 Cal. 829, followed. The fact that a complaint was made against the appellant in respect of the same transaction did not prove that he merely put his signature on a ready made sanction presented by the police. The sanctioning authority had to consider the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction accorded by him was not valid. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1948) L.R 75 I.A. 30, referred to. Held further, that in granting the certificate under section 4(2), the sanctioning court had no power to grant it. The only point which had been argued before the High Court was whether the sanction granted in this ease was a valid one and whether the sanctioning officer was competent or not to grant such sanction. Gokul Chand Dwarkadis Morark vs The State, A. I. R. 1952 All. 827, approved.

The appellant was the holder of life interest in the property. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the tenant on the ground that the building is bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The tenancy was admitted by the tenants there was also no question with regard to validity of the notice of eviction. The trial court held that the requirement of the landlord bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the appellate authority holding that the landlord had no right to ask for eviction of his tenant on grounds of demolition and re construction. Allowing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard tO the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. On the other hand, the Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act. [275E F] M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, ; , followed. The Act with regardto two different tenancies though in the same premises one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purpose is not maintainable. [276F] M. Balakrishna & Ors. vs M. Granite & Co., ; , referred to. In the instant case, the tenancy was admittedly held by the tenant for more than a life interest and hence the landlord could not evict the tenants on these grounds. The Rent Controller had no power under section 14(1)(b) of the Act to evict the tenant from two different premises.

The respondent decree holder obtained a decree against the appellant in respect of certain trees. The decree holder filed execution proceedings under section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 for recovery of possession of the land. The executing court held that after the coming into force of the Act what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. This decision was affirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the respondent decree holders had not acquired any interest in the land, the right of trees of the groves could not be proceeded against. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The position taken by the executing court as well as the execution court is that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the , and vested in the State free from all encumbrances. This means that "grove land" and an "intermediary 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the "land". Section 18(1)(a) of Act provides that an "initial" 's grove" is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari right. After these clear words of the enactment, the rights in land are deemed as parts of "land." [510C D] 2. The definition of intermediary 's sir and Khudkasht means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such. This mean that "agrove" and grove land are equated. groves arc equated and printer lands. After the coming in force of Act, the what could then be sold is the right to vest. [511D E] 3. The mere fact that trees and grove land are equivalent and grotes are on lamics collections of tree land cannot be upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench).

The first appellant Subran was charged with an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and each of them was convicted for an offence under Section 326/149 I.P.C. and each one of them were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. The prosecution case was that all the six accused persons were armed with weapons like chopper, iron rod, cycle chain and lathis. They were charged with offences punishable under Sections 302, 324, 323, 324 read with Section 149 I. P.C., but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On an appeal by the State, the conviction and sentence were set aside. The High Court acquitted two of the accused persons. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) all the 6 accused except the first accused caused injuries with a chopper; (ii) all other accused could not be convicted for the offence under section 326/34 I.p.C.; and (iii) the appellants 2 to 4 were convicted only under Section 325/149, I.e., 302/149 and 324/149. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention to cause murder of Suku was not proved by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt. [92B] 2.1 There is no evidence that all these accused had shared common intention with each other. It is the cumulative effect of all the injuries which resulted in the death of the deceased and the other accused, besides appellant No. 1. [93C D] 2(a) The intention of causing murder of the Suku by Subran, Subran and Preman appellants 2 and 3 was clear from the evidence of PW4, who had been believed by both the courts below and with which finding we have no reason to differ, all the four appellants had caused those injuries. It was not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by the first appellant with the chopper were either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused by him, sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of Suhu. [94F G] 2.(b) The High court failed to draw the distinction between an offence u/s 302 I.PC. and 300 I.A.C.[92D] 2 (c) There was no evidence on record to show that all of the four accused had contributed to the common intention of committing the crime. [95F G; 96G] 3.1 The intention, to cause the bodily injury of the second appellant and the role assigned to him by the Prosecution was doubted by both sides. It could not therefore be said that all other two accused had acted in furtherance of the common object of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause his death. [96H; 97A] 3.(a) There is a distinction between offence uptodate and an offence within the meaning of section 141 I. PC. [97B C] (b) In the trial court all the accused except one were individually involved in the assault, and the death was caused due to multiple injuries. What offence can then be said to have been committed by the four convicted persons is not a matter which is in doubt. From the ocular evidence read with the medical evidence it stands established that the injury on the appellant was inflicted by all the 4 appellants and that the death had occurred due to receipt of multiple injuries, and what offence can be said so is the common purpose of the two accused persons for committing murder of one of the victims. [98F G]. (c ) The intention in the present case to cause an injury of murder was not established by the evidence on the record. There were no injuries having been inflicted on him by all of them and that he had not been charged for the substantive offence of murder under section 302 I P.P., and they were therefore liable for the said offence.

The assessee, a non resident company, was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. The assessee claimed that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis alone and accordingly brought to tax the royalty amount disclosed. In the returns filed by the assessee, the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs. 9,25,257 but claimed that this amount was maintained in its books of account for the relevant years. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the return filed by it. The appellant 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. In respect of its Indian income, it did not include the royalty income of Rs 9,26,257. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that even though the Indian company had credited to the assessee in its account books for the years 1967 68 and 1968 69, it was maintained accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile system in the past years. On a reference made at the instance of the Revenue, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, it is contended that even if the Indian Companies had credited the amount in the account books of the Indian companies, it could not have been said to have received the royalty amounts only when it received the same in U.K. The High Court held that the assessee was maintaining accounts on Cash basis and since it did rot actually receive the amount, there was no receipt until it was received by it in U, K. In this view of the matter, it must be held that in the circumstances of the case, the method of accounting adopted by the appellant for the assessment years 1967 69 and 196869 was really irrelevant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question referred did not really arise in the facts and circumstances of this case and need not have to be answered. [105A] 2.1 In the instant case, it cannot be said that the credit entry made in the accounts of the assessee is a bogus or a mere make believe entry. The fact that the Indian Bank had credited its account in the books of Indian Company does not amount to receipt of income by the assesseee. [106B] 2:2 In the present case, there is no doubt that the appellant was maintaining the accounts on the cash basis in U K. The accounting year in question was the calendar year. There was no evidence that the Income Tax officer made any particular method of account to have been mercantile, that the amount was not received by the assesses and was therefore taxable and that it is immaterial when did it actually receive it in the U. K. [107C D] 2 :3 The High court was right in answering the question in favour of the revenue. [108D E] 2I2 In this case, on facts of this ease, the appellant had been filing its accounts regularly and again for the two subsequent years. There is no evidence to show that the income tax officer made a false account in respect of the assessment year 1967 68 or 1968 69. The accounts were not found to be maintained by the Income tax Officer. Therefore, it would have been possible for the assessee to raise the contention relating to the method adopted by him, though such income had accrued in U and K. It would immediately be evident that this was not the basis put forward by the Revenue before the High court. [109E F] 2l3 In the circumstances, the Tribunal should have made the assessment on the amounts disclosed in the returns relating to assessment years 1966 68 and 1969 69.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 34 for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars, from the evidence of an accomplice, that he had a liaison with his wife, and that the knife was used by him as a wrestler and that he was responsible for the murder. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was unsustainable. The evidence of the approver was sufficient to convict the appellant. The statement of the co accused was no corroboration of the accomplice 's story because the knife had been got prepared by accused No. 1 and the appellant had a torch and two others who were unarmed. The appellant had no motive for committing the murder, as he had no direct or direct relationship with his deceased wife. The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an approver was unsustainable, the law being that there should be corroboration of his story because of the fact that the accomplice made a confessional statement to his brother. Bhuboni Sahu vs King (A.I.R. , re Rajagopal, A.I.,R. and Bhubani Sahu vs The King, , referred to. In re Rajagopal (A I.R, and re Rajagopal , approved. The combined effect of sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act is that there must be corroboration in the evidence Of an accomplice. It cannot be doubted that under section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of the witness may not be illegal, but the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence on the sole ground that it is within their legal province to convict upon such unconfirmed evidence.

The appellant was a servant of the State Electricity Board constituted under the . He was charged with having committed offences by obtaining loans from the Corporation. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted him under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On appeal the High Court acquitted the appellant but confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal Code and therefore he could not be deemed to be a public Servant within the definition of section 2(1)(d); (ii) the High court had erred in holding that the appellant could not have been deemed to have been a public servants within the ambit of section 3, because (i ) the appellant had been performing only routine clerical duties and cannot be treated as an officer within the purview of cl. 12; and (iii) the conviction was bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD: (1)(a) The officers and servants of the Board are deemed to function in pursuance of any of the provisions Of the . Therefore, the appellant is not a Public servant within section 21(9), cl. 13 of the Act. [690 B] (b) The word 'officer ' in section 21 cl. 2(l) of Indian Penal code means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. He is either himself armed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so The decision in Reg vs Ramajirao Jivbaji, ; , referred to. (2) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 2, cl., (12).

The appellant was convicted under r. 125(9) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ in default further rigorous imprisonment. He was also convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1962. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him by the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Mehkar. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: Rule 141 (2) does not matter because section 43 of the Rules requires the rules to be conclusive proof that he was so informed; but a failure to comply with sub r. (1) shall not preclude proof by other means that he had information of the order, (ii) The rule contemplates that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid, they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation. [273 G H] In the instant case, r.141(2), is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). Section 3 gives very wide powers to the Collector to seize stocks but does not enable the Court to forfeit the juar. The rule must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that Sia was not aware of the date on which he had gone to the police station and that he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High court was dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal in his favour. There are certain important considerations which lend weight to the view of the trial court that it was unsafe to convict Sia on the ground that he knew the accused prior to or at the time of the occurrence. [626 D E] (2) The fact that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107. A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the crime, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not sufficient if an act on the part of the accused is shown to have been done in pursuance of the conspiracy. [625 E F] (3) The mere proof that the offence charged could have been tried without the participation of the other accused would not necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of accused 2 under section 307 read with s.34, Indian penal Code. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of them on the basis of constructive liability. HELD : (i) It is well settled that common intention within the meaning of section 114 of the Evidence Act implied a pre arranged plan and the criminal act was done pursuant to the prearranged plan. The said plan may also develop on the spot during the course of the commission of the offence; but the crucial circumstance is that the said plan must precede the act constituting the offence. If that be so, before a court can convict a person under section 34 read withs.34 of the Indian Penal code, it should come to a definite conclusion that the accused had a prior concert with one or more other persons named or unnamed, for committing the said offence. A Court cannot obviously make out a case for the prosecution which is not disclosed either in the charge or in regard to which there is no basis in the evidence. There must be some foundation in the Evidence that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission Of the offence and if there is such a basis the case will be covered by the third illustration. [684 D F] (ii) The High court gave conflicting findings on the evidence adduced in the case. It did not take into account the impact of section 34 on different situations. The judgment of the High Court cannot stand. [685 E F] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed.
