The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron ore, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of duty on the ground that the goods were undervalued and that the rate of duty was higher than the rate applicable to the goods. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had no fundamental right to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the material change in section 15(1)(b) of the Act was only the substitution of the words "the rate of excise duty" and tariff valuation if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner has no fundamental rights as such to clear any goods imported without payment of duties in accordance with the law. [626C] 2.1 It is not permissible for the Court to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of the fundamental right. Whenever a person complains and claims that there was a violation of law, it does not automatically involve breach of fundamental right for the enforcement of which alone Article 32 of the Constitution is attracted. [625D] 2:2 The facts of this case show that the peti tioner as such has no right to ' clear any ' goods imported after payment of duty in accordance With the law and therefore, it is not possible to entertain on these averments of the Article 32. [526C D] Prakash Cotton Mills (P) Ltd. vs B. Sen & Ors., [1979] 2 SCR 1142; Prakash Cotton mills (P.) Ltd. V. State of Uttar Pradesh, ; and Prakash Cotton Mill (Pvt.) Ltd., vs Bamnantine, ; , referred to.

The appellant, who was the managing director of a company which was in liquidation, applied for a decree against the respondent for partition of his joint family property and possession of his separate share. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court held that the debt was not avyavaharika as there was no evidence to support the finding of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the debt in question was not an accretion to the creditors of the father and therefore, the debt could only be challenged on proof of the debt of the son; (2) the liability of the sons was not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the share of his sons but on the principle of independent coparti tional rights in the sons which were not immoral or illegal; (3) the claim for partition was not a bona fide one and as such the suit was not maintainable. HELD : (i) The liability of a father to discharge debts of the deceased father is not dependent on the father who has no power to sell his share of the property but on principle of pious obligation imposed on the sons under the Mitakshara law. [557 B] (ii) The debt of a Hindu father is an incident of birth, giving to the sons vested right in the coparcenary property and the remedy of the adopted son is to prove in appropriate proceedings taken by them the illegal or immoral purpose of the debts and partition cannot relieve the sons of their pious obligation or their shares of their liability to be sold or be a means of reducing the efficacy of the attachment or impair the rights of the creditor. [558 C D] (iii) The legal position is that even after partition, the sons could not claim any right in respect of the properties which were allotted to them on partition and the property was sold and the purchaser bought it intending to be the whole coparcenary estate, the presence of the two sons coupled with the attachment itself would not make the joint family estate liable for the debts of their father. [559 E F] (iv) The right of the mother to alienate for payment of personal debt is ended by partition in severalty and therefore the liability to discharge the debts does not arise on proof by the sons or the immoral obligation imposed upon them under the statute. [560 G H] (v) The position of a son who is liable to pay his share in the joint property as to what passes to the auction purchaser is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale, what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser intended to buy and did buy and what he paid for. [561 G H; 561 A] (vi) The words di right, title and interest " occurring in section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code have the same connotation as they had in the corresponding words used in the Code of Civil Procedure existing at the time the Bombay Act was enacted. Therefore, where a pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and the suit is brought on the record and the sale proceeds are to be paid off, there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the attached property. All that results from partition is that the right of father to make an application for partition operated as severance of status takes place pending the execution proceedings because the pious obligation of the appellants to discharge their debts of his father which were never tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious duty imposed on them by the Mitakshara Law.

The petitioners, who were the members of the Bar Association and the Additional Chief Secretary to the Government of Delhi, filed a complaint against them before the Metropolitan Magistrate alleging that they had committed offences punishable under section 178 I.P.C. The learned Magistrate after recording their statements in the case, passed an order directing the filing of the complaints and criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Committee. The petitioners challenged the aforesaid orders by way of writ petitions before this Court contending that the provisions of sections 8 B and 8 C of the Act were not applicable to those witnesses falling under section 8 B of the . Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order passed on 29th June 1988 is set aside and the petitioners are quashed and they are discharged from the Committee as per law. [521D] 1.2 The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B of the Delhi Administration and its police officers. Taking into consideration all the aspects of the case it is obvious that the Committee should not have in the circumstances of the present case directed the filing the complaints, and the criminal proceedings started against the Petitioners before the committee. [525E] 1:3. The Committee shall have considered the question whether the persons were entitled as persons under section8 B of Delhi Administration to be treat as persons covered by section8B of Delhi Police Act, 1980 before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end of inquiry. If the Committee had found that the petitioners was covered under section 9 B then perhaps they would not have been asked to get in the witnessbox for being examined till their end of the inquiry. [511B C] 1 :4. The committee should have consider whether the Petitioners were entitled, as persons, governed by Section 8B, before asking the petitioners to get the witnesses examined for being re examined. If they otherwise satisfied it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by s.8 B. [51F] 2. The inquiry of the Committee directing the filling up of the complaint and criminal proceeding initiated against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under Section 178 I P.C., is not contemplated under section 6B of that Act. It is enough if at any stage the Commission considers it necessary, to inquire whether the complainants were entitled or not to be considered as persons bound by section 9B. [52G H] 3. The action of the committee in asking them for being crossexamined at the end Of the inquiry appears to be discriminatory. Merely non issue of notices to them under section 10 B ought not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8. The issue of such a notice is not envisaged under section 7B of Act. [53H; 54A] 4. The procedure prescribed by the Act for dealing with certain incidents which took place on the 15th January 1988, was not followed. Therefore, the Committee could not have taken into consideration the other aspects of this case.

The Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, were framed under section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Act, 1959. The rules provided that a lump sum payment shall be made in lump sum of which the amount shall be fixed by the State Government from time to time by notification in the official gazette. The petitioners who were partners of a firm, challenged the validity of the Rules and contended that the tax was not laid upon them as they had been assessed to tax on fares and freights but upon "fares and freight" which were different entities and in support of their contention it was urged that the Act did not provide for the levy of lump sum. Held, that the provisions of the Act and the notification issued thereunder were valid and the rules and the notifications were valid. The expression "paying to a lump sums" in section 3(1) of the said Act means payment made in lieu of payment of the tax calculated on actual fares and the freights are fixed by competent authority under the Act, and that it does not cease to be a tax on passengers and goods. The words "pay" and "taxes" used both in Rules 8 and 8 A and the expression "payable" show that the amount of lump sums must be, if lump sum payments are made in respect of actual fares or freights. The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers and the tax is payable. The word "pay ' shows that the election to pay a lump amount is with the taxpayer who may choose one method of payment or the other. The charge of tax calculated by the amount paid on actual fare and freight is not a tax but a tax for purposes which are subordinate and from which they must take their colour and meaning. The distinction between "pay", "tax" and 'taxes attributable to routes outside the State, is that where the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan, it would lead to anomalies if the amount charged be the same in every case.

The appellant was a private limited company. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on the respondents, who were sought to be retrenched in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. The workmen demanded a revision of wages on the one hand and higher wages on other. The Labour Court, after examining the evidence led before it, held that the reasons stated in the notice were not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and, therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The High Court also awarded full back wages to the workmen as back wages. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from the day on which they were sought lo be retrenched; (2) the non supply of raw materials or reciles for the livehood could not be a mere pretext or rust to toring the workmen, by depriving the them of the basic right of livelihood, and (3) the failure to pay the full back Wages did not amount to unfair labour practice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Labour Law 's interpretation is intended to give relief to a workman who has no bargaining power, but it is not to be arbitrary, vague or fanciful but legal and regular. [571C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant is making profit. A statement of account certified by the Chartered Accountants of the company dated 25th July, 1978 shows that the appellant has been making profit since 1976 77. The unit is, therefore looking up. It has started making profits. The industry is looking up and it has started raising profits. [572F] 1:3. In the present case, there was no material on record to show whether the Managing Director had made any sacrifice; whether his salary and perks have been adversely affected; whether the managerial coterie has reduced some expenses on itself.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge for committing murder of his wife. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the confessional statement made by the accused to the police regarding the father of the boy was inadmissible in evidence and no oral evidence in respect of that confession could be relied upon. HELD : (i) It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender are not specially empowered during the investigation of a case. The discovery and the arrest of an accused person is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation. [434 B] (ii) The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house of the accused. It is not necessary to dilate upon this aspect of the matter because it is not possible for higher class magistrates to practically abrogate the safeguards created in section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [427 C] (iii) The confession made by an accused before a second class magistrate was inadmissible under section 164, Cr. P.C., and no such evidence could be led at the trial. [534 D E] (iv) The High Courts were not justified in holding that the confession recorded during the course investigation of the case cannot be deemed to be devoid of force. It was also not necessary for the High Court to dilate on this aspect. [ 428 C] Nazir Ahmed vs State of Delhi, ; , referred to. (v) The statement made to a magistrate under section 161 Cr.P.C. is admissible in evidence. The accused may have a natural affection for the child and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi deceased from him without the child. It cannot be said that the accused was not aware of the murder of Churi. [416 D] (vi) The fact that the statement made before the magistrate was admissible during investigation did not affect the guilt of the appellant. The confession was inadmissible and no evidence had been adduced to show that anyone noticed the accused at the film show. [414 E F] (vii) The plea of the respondent that he had gone to see film shows that the persons with whom he sat at the time of occurrence were seen were not examined as a witness. The statement of the person who was present at the scene of occurrence was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 Cr. It could be used for contradicting the evidence given by him.

The plaintiff sued the defendant for a sum of Rs. 80,507/ with interest at 6 per cent from the date of the mortgage and future costs. The defendants contended that the suit was barred by section 43 Of the Transfer of Property Act, as it was not instituted within three years of the date on which the mortgage was created. Held, that the plaintiff had no right to sue for a half of the amount due under the mortgage from the dates of the mortgages and the only remedy available was by way of suit for recovery of the balance of the property. The provisions Of section 43 of the Transfer Of Property Act did not apply to a mortgage and the suit must be dismissed as barred by limitation. Held further, that in view of the provisions of the Limitation Act, the plaintiff 's suit must fail. Section 82 of the Indian Contract Act does not deal with mortgages but only deals with the rights which are payable under them. The words "the mortgagor who redeems and directs that in the absence of a contract to the contrary he shall be reduced to Rs. 2,000/ . " In the present case the plaintiff was entitled to claim interest on the amount of Rs., 80,057/ with costs. Held also, that section 43 did not deal expressly with mortgages. The suit was therefore time barred by time. The question whether a mortgage is inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs 40,253 11 10 with interest against each defendant.

The appellants, who were unsuccessful in the Public Works Department, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that they had been selected for the post of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) by the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 7 of the Karnataka State Service Rules, 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% of the total marks was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 If the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of tho total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellants were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [497C D] 1.2 The selection for appointment to the post was made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation thereof. [498D E] 1:3 The Rules are clear in violation ly in the instant case. There is no allegations of any mala fides in the matters of the appellants ' appointment. However the Rules were clearly in contravention of the decision of this court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C.R. 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State, ; , referred to. 1.4 The Rules were not in existence.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 302 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the fateful day, the deceased came to his house and informed him that his wife had been murdered by him. On 14th July, 1982, he started giving reli gious discomfort to his wife. He tried to make his followers believe that he had seen God and if they followed him and his preachings, they too could see God. The deceased was taken out of the room of the Collectorate and was chased by P.W.2. On the same day, P.Ws. 3 and 4 were also arrested. The appellants were put on trial along with other accused persons for offences under sections 302 readwith section 120 B of the I.P.C. The Trial Court acquitted all the accused except the appellant No. 1. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State against the acquittal of the appellants. In this appeal, it was contended that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence that the deceased was beaten up badly after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bomb burst and that he was falsely implicated in the murder case. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this Court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , the confes sion of a Co accused is neither substantive evidence nor substantive evidence and therefore, would not be admissible against the other accused person at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. [408B C] 1.2 The confession was voluntary and truthful. It was true that a set of witnesses who were present when the bombs were fired at the deceased, were not examined in the case. Obviously, when Yadav was beaten upto the police station, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in the fight. It is true as argued by Mr. Jai Narain for the State that it is difficult to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413C D] Kashmira singh vs State Of Madhya Pradesh ; , followed. 1:3. The confession is not admissible against other accused in the present case. The conviction of the appellant under section 3 of the Explosive Substance Act and the sentence as awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court are set aside. [414D] Kashrik Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; ; KashmiraSingh vs State, ; and Kashmira Kaur vs State (Delhi Administration), ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson Private Limited. The last of the companies was governed by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the workmen were paid dearness allowance on different scales depending upon the rates prevailing in comparable concerns. The appellant company claimed that the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance should be applied to the industry and that if an employee was dismissed or discharged for misconduct which caused financial loss to the employer, gratuity should be paid to him. The Tribunal held that the workmen cum region was entitled to dearness allowance at a certain rate and that the company had failed to make the comparison between the employers and employees of different categories of employees with which the Tribunal had compared the appellant 's concerns. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant company could not be said to have committed an error in applying the industry ' cum region test for fixing wage scales and dearness allowances. The award relating to wages and Dearness allowance was therefore justified on the ground that it paid scant regard to the exemplars filed before it and did not care to make comparison with the total wage packet of comparable concerns and thus arrived at a just figure for basic wage, for each category of factory workmen. (ii)The Tribunal had no where considered what would be the total wages packet in fixing wages, and dearness and other subordinate staff were concerned. The tribunal was right when making comparisons took into account the total pay packet in fixed concerns and also taking into account its trend in that region. (iii)The award relating back to the appellant for the reason that it had not considered the total salary packet in comparable concern was justified.

The appellants filed a suit against the mortgagees for redemption of certain mortgaged property. The mortgagors pleaded that they were the legal representatives of one of the brothers and that the mortgage was not binding on them and that as the mortgagees had failed to pay the amount due under the mortgages, the mortgagees could not claim redemption of the mortgage. The trial court held that the Rajinama executed by the mortgagees did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property and that it was a complete relinquishment of his interest but as regards an undivided interest in the property he had no right to redeem the mortgage on the ground that the appellants were agriculturists, that they could not acquire title by adverse possession. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the respondents did not come up to this Court and that there was sufficient evidence on record to show that the mortgagees were the manager and karta of the joint family and that in the matter of passing the RajInama he had acted as Karta and the appellants could not be said to have entered into possession of the property pursuant to the usufructuary mortgage. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that there could be no question of limitation on the date of the passing of the Raj In the Letters Patent Appeals. The Rajinma passed by Shiddappa did not affect the right of an occupancy tenant as he had not entered into a written agreement to become the registered occupant and his name was not recorded in the register of relinquishment. Khiarajmal vs Daim (1904) L. R. 32 Ind. App. Cas. 1, relied on.

The respondent, a company, was an accessory anti not a part of the typewriter. The respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry 2 of the Schedule to the Act, but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed under the Notification and (2) ribbon was an integral part of a typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon papers did not contain any technical or doubt as to the contents of the schedule to the Notification but a specialized article used by the respondent in printing and supplying the goods from its head office at Kanpur which was used for obtaining prints and trenches. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% prescribed under Entry 2, List II of the Seventh Schedule to. the Act was challenged by the appellant before the High Court. The High Court held that the carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that the ribbon is a part and parcel of the type writer and grows abundantly along the Nile river in Egypt, and that it is used for writing. printing or drawing on, for wrapping things in, for covering the interior of wails etc., and therefore taxed the turn over of carbon papers for the aforesaid period. The appellant contended before this Court that carbon Paper does not lose their character as 'paper ' even after having been subjected to Chemical processes and hence taxable at the point of first sale. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact that the word 'paper" forms part of an denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [841E] 2. It is clear from the definition of "paper" in the Act that in popular parlance, the word "paper " is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used to bear, writing or printing or for packing, or for drawing on or for decorating, or cover ing the walls. [850F] 3. The word ' paper ' in the common parlance or in the com plaint in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i.e., making replica tions on the side of the Nioghta factured by coating the tissue paper with a thermo set, cannot properly be described as paper. [851C] 4. The fact that word ' Paper ' forms part and is derived from the name of reedy plant papyrus and grow sorrows, does not necessarily mean paper which is so used for printing, writing, or printing, or to packing or for making on or, for deco sion or covering the walls, [850E] 5. The very same question with which we are here confronted came up for decision before the Bombay High Court in State of Mysore vs Kores (India) Ltd., ; , referred to.

The respondents were employed in the appellant Mills at Amroha. The respondents were employees of the appellant Mill at Amroha and the mills at Bulandshahr. They were retrenched by the appellant on the ground that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under Standing order No. 1, but the Labour Union, who was a party to the dispute, raised an industrial dispute and made its award holding that the management had no right to transfer the respondents 1 to 4 to the new factory and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. The appellant contended that the right to have the respondents ' services transferred to another factory was implicit in every contract of service and as such the respondent could not be transferred to a new concern, and that the appellant was not entitled to any of these amenities. Held, that the employer had no power under Standing Orders No. I to transfer his employees to a newly created one of the ordinary incidents of service in the Bank. The employer in the present case has no such right. Mary (Anamalai Plantation) Workman 's Union vs Seliparai Estate, ; , followed. In the instant case, the respondents had been employed in a business or concern and the question that arose was whether the appellant had the right of transfer to another place where he chooses to start his business subsequent to the date of his employment. Mary, (Ananamalai plantation) workman 'S, Memp & Co., Ltd., vs Ali Hasan, A.I.R. 1950 All. 816 and Mary, , referred to.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. In 1965, the special contribution was to be made by the respondent employer under section 73 of the . The respondent company was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the Act until the provisions were enforced in the area where the appellant 's factory was situated. The appellant company challenged the liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA of the , before the High Court, which held that the contribution payable under Chapter IV A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant Company. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contributions payable under Ch. V A were not a fee but a tax and therefore, the Act does not contemplate rendering of service or conferment of an benefit to be quid pro vised for payment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit clauses are extended should alone make contributions and thereby help to set up a corporation. [1094C] 2.1 The object is to make appropriate provisions for securing the right to work, to education and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of any undeserved want, to make legitimacy or not at all. The payment of contribution by an employer towards premium (what else is it ?) of an employee 's compulsory insurance under the falls directly within entries 23 and 24 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [ 1094D E] 2:2.1 There is no reason to brand or stamp the contribution as a tax or fee in order to seek to legitimise it. Legitimacy need not be sought fictionally from Entry 97 of List I, but simultaneously with the power entrusted in respect of entries 23 & 24 of list III. Even if the charge is to be construed as a fee as the High court has done, it appears to be justifiable on that basis too. [1194F G] Basant Kumar vs E. S.I. Corporation, ; , referred to.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that they have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a longer period. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [620C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This Court in spite of the fact that the petitioners are being paid their daily wages in spite thereof, they have not been paid the minimum wage for equal work. [625D E] 3. The petitioners are included therein. They are included in the category of temporary workmen and payment of regular wages on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regularly workmen. [650E F] 4. The question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. The Court directed that all the 63 daily rated workers including the 54 petitioners mentioned in the Annexure R V to the counter affidavit together with Annexure RV thereto be given the benefit of the voluntary retirement scheme framed by respondent No. 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues.

The plaintiffs claimed to have purchased the entire property as transferees from the National Agency Co operative Bank Ltd., who had been impleaded as defendants. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court upheld the title of the plaintiffs to the share in the property. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the sale in execution of a mortgage decree obtained by the National agency Co operative bank was valid and extended to the entire interest in the mortgaged property and (ii) even if the transfer was not effective, the suit was liable to be dismissed. HELD : (i)(a) The question whether an alienation is a benami or not must depend on the facts of each case. It is well settled that a sale by a person who has no right to bring a suit or rather has a vested interest in it cannot affect the title to the extent of 16 as share belonging to him. [211 B] (b) The mere fact that the property was not the subject matter of the mortgage decree does not make it a joint owner. A sale by one who has got himself or mediately, the entire estate is not an ostensible owner of the entire Estate in view of section 3 of the Crown Grants Act, 1895. [212 C] (c) The fact that a person has no interest in any such property is immaterial and cannot be ignored at any stage of proceedings until in this Court. It may be pointed out that the question whether a sale is benami or a mere personal bar against the plaintiff in the first suit and that the cause of action on which the suit is laid and the present suit title suit 18 of 1943 are not relevant for deciding the question as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on record. [213 D] (d) The plea of the defendants based on the ground that they had acquired from several co sharers through the Pir Baksh, was not pressed before the trial Court and the trial Judge held that the sale by the plaintiff was not binding on him as the ostensible owner. [214 E] (e) The suit in the present case was based on title of a co sharer who had no right in questioning the validity of the transaction. It was also contended that the defendants were entitled to a decree for declaration that they were the sole proprietor of the Tea Estate and that as the plaintiff had failed to prove his rights under the purchase from Pirbaksh, the sale was not liable to any relief. [216 F] (f) The contention that the suit in execution was barred by section 16 or section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, was also not pressed.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions judge for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction but on a reference under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court held that the trial had not been vitiated by any irregularity or misdirection in the case and set aside the convictions and sentences passed against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the omission to comply with the provisions of sections 173(4), 207A and 207A of the Criminal Procedure Code, had caused prejudice to the accused; (2) the failure to comply did not vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudiced in their defence. HELD : (i) The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more severe effect than the omission which was curable by reference to section 537(a) of the code. [292 B] (ii) The failure to do so did not affect the trial and consequently ipso facto, a fresh trial became necessary irrespective of whether or not the accused had shown any prejudice. [293 C] (iii) The absence of compliance with the provi sions of section 173(3) of Code of criminal Procedure was fatal to the prosecution case. [294 E] (iv) The defect in the evidence could not be cured by reference only to section 540 of the Cr. P.C., and it was not necessary for the trial court to find out whether the provisions aforesaid were complied with. [295 G] (v) The non compliance with those provisions had necessarily, result in re opening the proceedings and trials which may have been concluded long ago. [296 D] (vi) The mere irregularity in the police investigation and the omission of the investigating officer to fully comply with section 173 did not render the entire proceedings and subsequent trial void. [297 G] Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor, A.I.R. , referred to.

The appellant Municipality was constituted under the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901. The respondent Municipality had been consulted and it was found that the water of some of the wells in the surrounding area was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluent being discharged through the existing channels. The appellant filed an application before the Special Officer under section 153A(1) of the Bombay district Municipal Act for permission to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluents from the factory of the respondent Municipality. The Special Officer rejected the application on the ground that the respondent had carried out similar tests and that the appellant was not satisfied with the report of the Special officer. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of section 153 A(1)(a) were not applicable to the case as the permission to carry on the effluent in question was granted by the Municipality only after issuing a notice to the respondent municipality and after hearing the appellant, it held that the Municipal Corporation had no jurisdiction to issue the notice. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Special officer had wrongly decided that lie could not go into the question whether the nuisance in question existed. [398 D] (ii) The provisions of sections 153A and 153B of the Act are not applicable because the person to whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence of the nuisance. The purpose of section153A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence or a nuisance which was purely a matter for the subjective satis faction of the municipality. [399 E] (iii) The power conferred on the Municipality by section 153B is to be exercised in a capricious manner. If the person concerned objects to the notice and the requisition contained therein absolutely the objection is in substance to the issue of the notice itself, which means he objects to, the declaration of the public shall be made within the subjective conclu sion of the Municipal Council.

The appellant was charged with the offence of theft of railway stores. The prosecution case was that the appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods and that he had not offered any satisfactory evidence of possession of goods. On the strength of some information received on 28th July 1964, that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police, searched the premises of the motor transport company at Lucknow and found that the said stolen railway Property was being used for his own use or were intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The appellant pleaded guilty and contended that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The trial court found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the prosecution must prove that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration and that the article was not only the property belonging to a railway administration but also those which were intended for use in the constructions, operation of a Railway Stores. The evidence in the case did not establish that the items seized were Railway stores within section 2 of the Act. The mere description of the articles as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 3(2) of that Act. There was no evidence before the courts to prove that they were railway property within the definition of section. The only description of goods as new was sufficient to show that they belonged to a Railway Administration. The fact that the seized stolen railway properties were being used by a railway administrate and that they had been used for the construction or operation of the railway cannot be established.

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she did not carry on the business with her till date of her death. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent tenant on the ground that she had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent landlord was the tenant and as such the respondent was entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. On appeal, the High Court held that since the appellants had not carried on the 'business with her as family business in the demised property, they were not enti tled to the benefit of the amended definition of tenant under the Act. The High Court also held that the appellant was entitled only to the protection of the amendment of the definition of 'tenant ' under the Rent Acts and that the legal representatives did not acquire any right to remain in possession of the premises. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the lease hold rights of the tenanted premises were heritable and the heirs of the deceased tenant were entitled to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under section 13(1)(a) of the Act, and that since they had not been evicted from the demised shop, the tenancy thereto was heritable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent landlord after termination of the contractual tenancy of the tenant is entitled to continue to remain as a statutory tenant under sub section (1) of section 13. [108G] 2. The term 'tenant" in Section 3(vii)(a), means a person by whom the rent is, or but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any accommodation and includes any person occupying the accommodation as a sub tenant, and also any person continuing in possession after the termination of his tenancy in his favour otherwise than under the provisions of the Rent Act. [109B] 3. The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs or the heirs in respect of commercial tenancies on the death of the sub tenant after termination, does not indicate that the legislature intended that the heirs should be deemed to have acquired the protection under the statute. [110C D] 4. In case of commercial premises governed by the Rent Laws Act, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard tO tenancy. It may also be borne in mind that in case of a commercial premises the heirs are entitled to succeed, not only to his business but also to his tenan cy rights under the rent Act which protects the heirs from ejectment except in accordance with the provisions contained in the Rent Control Acts and the other Rent Acts continue to enjoy. [111D E] 5. The Legislature has neither intended nor in the absence of any provision restricting the heritability of the commercial tenancies not with standing the determination of the statutory tenancy will devolve on the heirs, in accordance therewith, and no order or decree for eviction shall be passed against the tenant unless any such ground is established to the satisfaction of the Court. [112F G] 6.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund Scheme to all its workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The employees have to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not be covered by the same scheme under the Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Provident Fund. The Board has made no effort at all to analyse the balance sheet of the Board to show the actual results of its working. It has made a no effort to work out the financial implications of its order. It had made no efforts to workout the financial implication of its own employer. It is true that in the year ending March 1969 Board 's gross profits amounted to Rs. 305.12 lakhs and it had been continuously rising from Rs. 59.39 lakhs in 1961. The appellant Board has also made no attempt at all lo explain the actual result of its work. It was contended on behalf of the workmen that this would impose additional financial liabilities which the Board would not be able to bear. Therefore, the main question for consideration by the Tribunal was whether there should be a contributory provident fund scheme on the basis of basic wage or total wages. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Provident Fund is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the respondent Board. That is why the Tribunal has dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [47 D E] 2. The Tribunal has dealing with the matters in a thoroughly arbitrary manner. It does not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the respondent, the interest should be taken into account before the profits could be ascertained. Even with regard to the deprecia tion reserve the provisions of section 68 may have to he taken into consideration.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected the application holding that the appellant had been impotently incapable of having sexual relations with the respondent. In appeal, the High Court held that the wife had been suffering from mental cruelty with a view to deprive her of her legitimate right to live with her husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of the maintenance. The High Court also rejected the contention of the appellant that it was not necessary for the respondent to discharge the marital obligations, and dismissed the application filed by the respondent for maintenance. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the husband had been found to be impotency and was therefore unable to perform his marital duties; (2) the wife was not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live in her husband 's house; and (3) the respondent had been subjected to mental cruelty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have taken a contrary view and have not noticed that the main object and interpretation of the second proviso to sub section (3), of section 125, is to provide an effective and summary remedy to provide for appropriate food, clothing and lodging for a wife. [707B] 1.2 In order to find out whether the husband was justified in refusing to live alongwith her husband, the Court has to consider the grounds on which the wife refuses to live. The ground of impotence which had been held by the High Courts as vague and irrelevant is not only for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. [608C D] 1:3. In order that a wife may refuse to live, she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. Apart from the various decisions referred to above, there is a direct English decision on the point. [700D] 1I2 In the instant case, the husband has very rightly pointed out as follows: (1 ) The concept of cruelty is the same whether it is a criminal case or a civil case; (ii) The High court had taken into consideration all the relevant factors and the setting, object and understanding of the proviso to section 125(3), which was introduced with the clear object of providing an effective remedy to providing for appropriate maintenance, clothing or lodging for the wife. This alteration gives rise to a serious doubt as to the effect of the first proviso to subsection (3). [708D E] 1l3 In the present case, it is not disputed that the husband did not have any intention on the part of the husband to inflict that cruelty, she would be entitled to maintain her husband according to his means. The wife had also been subjected by the Magistrate to severe mental cruelty and the High court was therefore right in refusing maintenance to the respondent under section 127 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973. [079F G] 1?4 In the circumstances, it would be pusillanimous to ignore such a valuable safeguard which has been provided by the legislature to a neglected wife. The expression "difference between Sunni Muslim rites" and "woman" is not purely illustrative and self explanatory. It is only when the husband is willing and unable, to discharge her marital obligations that would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a just ground for refusing to go with the husband. [1099B C] 1.(i) The expression 'different Sunni Sunni Muslims ' in section 125 Cr. P.C. clearly means to give a clear instance of circumstances which may be treated as a just grounds for refusal of the wife to live at according to her means.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the city of Bhavnagar. The first respondent Union of India, the Municipal Committee of the appellant 's factory, filed a suit for possession of the said plot on the ground that the structure in question had been constructed by the appellant and that the structures were occupied by the State Government and that consequently the appellant was not entitled to recover possession of such land. The trial court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the suit property till 7th July 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of Saurashtra to the State Public Works Department of the State of Saurashtra. The High Court allowed the appeal of the Union of india and dismissed the suit for recovery of possession. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Article 65 of the Constitution is applicable in this case as the suit was filed on 3rd March 1964 and that on the finding of the Trial Court in favour of the plaintiff on the question of title in respect of 'Parade Ground ', and in the absence of specific plea of adverse possession in his writ petition, the trial court 's decree should have been confirmed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The suit was for possession based on title to a plot based on the title to it but the right to execute the sale deed in respect thereof was transferred or vested in the Municipalities concerned. It amounts conferring an authority or authorising the Municipalities to execute sale deeds in respect o f those lands situated within the Municipality, which should normally have been done by the Government. The subsequent correspondance and orders of the government also show that the Government had corrected themselves in their communication dated 6th May, 1952 and stated that the claim of the plaintiffs that the lands were vested in Bhavnagar Municipality was erroneous and that it was not open to the appellant to rely on the principle that possession follows title. [231E F] 2. The fact that the suit itself is for possession basing on title and the plaintiff have not proved title, does not make any distinction and it refers to only lands and not buildings. It refers to merely lands and buildings. In the instant case, the suit had been filed on March 7, 1964 and the suit has not been shown as a transfer of title. The plaintiff has not proved possession. [232G H] 3. The question whether the plaintiff was handed back by the Union or the State to the Government to reconsider the entire case and decide it is not necessary for the defendant to plead or prove adverse possession. It is only in the present case, that the title itself should have be vested in them. Since a number of Municipalities made representation to the government to reconsider its entire case, and decided that the right of the state to sell plots of land given under Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January 1948 by the plaintiff to the defendant Government only on 7th March, 1952, it is clear that the document was evidence against the Municipality in so far as it treated the properties as belonging to the Defence Department of Government of India and that its right to sell such lands of the Govern ment was with the Government concerned. [230B C] 4. The claim of title itself is not a transfer or an authority to them. The other documents relied on by the defendant in support of his contention that the possession of land was also not taken by the Municipali ties at any time. It does not give a right to the plaintiff. In this case not only there is evidence to show that physical possession was with defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title had been handed over to the Municipality. [229C D] 5.

The appellant was a Class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the Special Judge, Ajmer, for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal against that conviction but on a certificate granted by the High Court under article 134 (1) (c) of the Constitution it held that the appellant accepted Rs. 150 from Nanak Singh as and by way of illegal gratification and did not commit an offence within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal code. The appellant contended that he was an officer in the service or pay of Government and was performing a public duty and therefore, was liable to be convicted under section 420 Indian Penal. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was illegal and the appeal must fail. The offence of criminal misconduct was committed by the appellant as a public servant within the terms of section 2(9) Of the Indian penal Code and he was not an officer of the Government within the definition of that term in section 21 (9). The appellant was, therefore, rightly convicted under the Act. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed. The question whether a person is an officer or not has to be decided by the Court coming to the conclusion that a person was not in the employ of the government and could not be said to have been an officer within the term of section 6(9). In the present case, the appellant had been convicted under sections 5(i)(d), 6(1) and 7 of Act 11 of 1947 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months. The conviction was therefore illegal.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga, with a building constructed thereon. The auction was held by the department and the sale was notified for June 14,1977. The Collector, Patiala, by his order dated January 16, 1976 issued a proclamation prohibiting transfer or creation of a charge by the Respondent of his halfshare in an immoveable property consisting Khewat NO. 374. The respondent filed a civil suit against the State of Punjab and the appellant for permanent injuction restraining the Government and the Collectrate from auction ing his half shares. The trial court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The High Court, however, allowed the second appeal by the State. Allowing the Appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that a property is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree. [847C] 2. Section 61 of the code provides for the mode and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the said Act and the sales which were notified were not exempt from attachment and sold under section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent injunction with regard to the portion in whose favour the respondent was residing. [884D E] 3. Section 59 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides for mode and method of recovery of arrear of revenue and declares what properties are liable to he attached and sold in execution thereof. The opening words of sub section (I) of section 60 are "the following property is also liable to attach and sale" The opening word of sub sec tion (1) of Section 60 is "the same as the property which is liable" in the said sub secion. [854E F] 4. Section 62 of the Cr. P.C. provides that the following properties shall not be liable to attached or sold, namely: (a) one main residential house and other buildings attached to it; (b) a building used by him for his residence and occupied by him; (c) a shop constructed thereon; and (d) any building constructed in execution over which such a decree is passed. [864G H] 5. Section 63 of the Act provides that where property is so liable to an attachment and sell in execution, of a money decree, it shall be attached or sale in the execution of such a debt and the said clause (ccc) provides as follows: "The following properties are hereby liable to seizure and sale under section 68 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, while the liquor shops are situated in village Bamgga. with a build ing thereon. " [851C D] 6. Section 58 of the C.P.C., provides that when property is sold by public auction or auction or re lute or re tained or re structed or re stored in execution to be, and sold, in execution fir ly, the Court shall issue a permanent inju nate injunction with regards to the property sought to be recovered. [871D E; 848A] 7. Section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act provides for a mode and agency of attachment and sales and sale. The said section is in express terms applicable thereto. So far as the said act is concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery to recover arrears of Revenue under the said enactment.

The Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20,000 to the appellant. The Special Deputy Collec tor determined the value of the lands passing on the death of Rashid in 1963 and fixed the compensation at Rs.20,000. This award was received by the heirs of Rashid on whom the estate of Rashid devolved in equal shares. On appeal, the High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands which had been undervalued in the original assessment and as such property (meaning lands) chargeable to estate duty had escaped assessment to duty, it was not liable to be re assessed. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High court erred in holding that there were no two separate rights one a right to receive compensation and other a right of claim for further compensation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the notice issued under s.59(a) of the Act was valid. [337B] 2.1 The High court was right that there are no two different rights one as a right and property had not been correctly valued in the Original assessment proceedings inasmuch as the lands were lost to the estate by reason of the acquisition of their lands under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. [330C D] 2:2 In the instant case, the assessments made by the Special Deputy collector were for the years 1954 to 1960 and the value was determined on the basis that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate. The lands had vested in the Government long prior to the death and therefore it was merely a right which could not be elevated to the status of an asset or property and as a result of acquisition of his lands under section 18 of the Land Acquisi tion Act, the appellant had only one right which was to receive the compensation for the said lands at their market value on the date of the relevant notifications. [328D E] 2I2 In view of the provisions of section 59 and the fact that the lands in question could not have been valued at an earlier point of time, the notice under s,59(b) was issued by the respondent on the wrong assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to estate because the lands had become liable to estate tax. [326E F] 3.1 In the present case, it is clear that the assessments were made in the year 1958 and the same had escaped assess ment to duty. The Revenue will pay the costs of the appeal to the assessee. [324G H] 3:2. The notice under section 59(a), would have been issued on the assumption that the respondent had acquired any surplus land which was an inchoate right which can not be enlarged to the position of an assets or property. [325A B] 3I3. In the case of a right acquired by a person, who has taken voluntary action and declared his intention to acquire such a thing on the happening of his death, the estimated value can never be below the figure quantified by the Collector because under section 25(1) or the Land acquisition Act, Civil Court cannot award any amount below that awarded by the collector. [322C D; 322A] 3l4. The respondent is really seeking to change his opinion about the valuation of lands acquired and not a case of mistake apparent from the record. [323D] 3i. The Collector had no objection to this course and, therefore, the respondent himself did not estimate the market value of these lands on the relevant date. [ 322F] 3ii. The contention that the land was not acquired as it was in existence when the Collector made his award, is without substance. [320G] 3iii. The proper valuation for the purpose of section 61(a)(1) is to be determined by the assessing authority as on the dates of death of the deceased. It is, therefore.

The appellant, a member of the Cooperative Society, was elected as Director of the Bank on 18.8.1986. His election was not called in question by the Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Nagpur, on the ground that he had defaulted in payment of certain loan instalments on 21.10.86. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the said order was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court holding that section 73FF(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank (Amendment) Act, 1960 and Rule 71(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Rules, 1986 were not applicable to him. The Division Bench held that the appellant ' s election was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant"s election as a Director of a bank and that procedure having not been followed the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 78(1). Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the Act such as in section 78 (1) which deals with disqualification for membership. Under sub section (2) of section 73F, a person shall cease to be a member if he is so disqualified by or under any other provision of this Act. Section 77(1), which deals regarding disqualification for members of a committee, provides that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section(1 ) shall cease lo be a Member of the Committee and his seat deemed to have fallen vacant. The fact that he has been disqualified to continue as Director or creasing to be Director on account of his having committed default does not detract from special, would apply, because the appellant was in arrear in respect of instalments on the date of his election and till 21. 10.1986 i.e. both prior and anterior to his election on 18th August 1986. [682B C] 2.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's services were terminated by giving full opportunity to defend himself. On the conclusion of the enquiry, the State Govt. issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which quashed the order of the government 's reducing the pension by 50% and directed the State government to reconsider the question of reduction of pension by fifty per cent. The High Court held that the State Govern ment had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice on attaining 58 years. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government has power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [188B] 1.2 In the present case, the purpose of the inquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent "s pension". The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. It appears that the attention of the High court was not drawn to these Rules. Therefore, the Government has no authority to initiate any proceedings against Respondent. [189C D] 1:3. The State Government had power to reducing or withhold the pension granted to the Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service and after completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government Servant depend upon the good conduct of the Govern ment servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable lo a Government employee for misconduct, which he might have committed whilst in service or after completion thereof. [190E F] 1 :4. The Government had no power to initiate proceedings against respondent as it was not competent to initiate action against the State servant even though his retirement was found guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or After the completion of the service, the order passed by the State Gov ernment is set aside and quashed.

The appellants were the tenants of certain premises in the town. The respondent landlord applied for permission to sue him under section 3(1) of the West Bengal (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for ejectment of the appellants on the ground that they had applied for the permission to institute a suit against them. The appellants contended that the permission was not valid in law because the permission granted by the Commissioner was invalid in law; but the High Court held that the appellants were entitled to apply under section 6(2) of Act II of 1947, and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the jurisdiction conferred on the State Government by section 7 F of the Act was very wide and as such the bar created by the relevant provisions of the said Act excluding the jurisdiction of the civil courts could not operate in cases where the plea raised before the civil court goes to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order was a nullity. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the application for permission was invalid. [560 C] (ii)The bar created under section 7 G of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Act II Of 1947 is very wide. As the appellants had not raised any objection to the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate, the High court was in error in coming to the conclu sions that the same limitation must be imported in construing (a) the provisions of section 3 (4) and (5). [560 E] (iii)The power conferred on a State Government under section 4 is very limited. The power conferred by section 3 is very narrow. As it must be held that a party can move the Commissioner under section 5(2), he has to satisfy the Court that the District Magis trate has acted illegally or with material irregularity, and that would give him the jurisdiction to exercise his revisional power. [561 G] (iv)The High Court had no doubt that the provisions Of sections 3 (3) and 16 of the Calcutta Act II, 1947 were clear and unambiguous and they indicated that the High Courts in exercising their powers under section 13(4) had not intended that before a District Magistrate grants permission to file a suit to bring a suit, he should issue notice to the party affected by the order. [562 E] The power given by section 4 (3), is very broad and unambiguous. It must be read as meaning that the Civil Courts which have jurisdiction to deal with civil causes can exercise their powers in cases of this kind.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, physically assaulted his wife and her children. The respondent filed an application before the High Court for quashing the proceedings on the ground that the President of India had no jurisdiction to make this reference as he was not happy with his appointment as a Member of the State Public Service Commis sion. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant could not have been prosecuted under section 3(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for having committed gross misconduct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the report of the Commission was not in accordance with law and (ii) the High court had no power to examine the evidence recorded by it instead of being made by a Magistrate or a Munsif. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of reference is set aside and the case remitted to the High COurt for disposal on merits after giving an opportunity to the respondent to defend himself. [645D] 2. The report of a Commission is not a part of its own procedure. It is open to the Court in the first instance, to consider whether there was a conspiracy to involve his client falsely or that there were reasons for so involving him. If the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed no grievance can be made that the facts which establish the charge of misbehaviour are found by the highest court of the land and not by the lowest. [643E F] 3. The evidence in this case is not such as to justify the High Courts ' decision on a reference under article 317(1) of Constitution. It will have to be read in the latter order in order to enable this Court to pass proper orders in the interest of justice. [641A B] 4. The power of the President to make a reference to this court under article 318 is not subject to any limitation or restriction on the exercise of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. It can be exercised after the Supreme court has on inquiry reported that the allegations made against the respondent are false and motivated. [651C D] 5. The question whether the respondent should make a false allegation that he was slapped, courting trouble and involving her own status and respectability depends upon the will of this Court. If a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove their case that the charge is false and actuated, it is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme Courts. [661D] 6. The court may write to the Registrar of the High Commission for extension of time. The Court may write such a letter as it ought to be. No person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court will be examined or cross examined as a witness, except with the leave of this court. [671E] 7. The Supreme Court is not pronouncing on the question whether a particular piece of evidence which is bound to limit or otherwise affect the inherent powers of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process of the court. It would be impossible to accept that the Supreme Bench will be reluctant to entertain an examination and examine witnesses who have filed affidavits before this Court, and indeed, section 146(3) of Evidence Act specifically permits the cross examination of a witness in order that he may be summoned or requested by the Judge to attend his Court for the purpose of cross examination. [681G H] 8. The observations made by this Court in Union of India vs R.M. Sharma, ; , referred to.

The appellants were the deity installed in the temple. The temple was a public trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and, therefore, was to be governed by the Act. The respondent Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa, filed an appeal against the decision of the Subordinate Judge. The High Court reversed the decision holding that the temple and the deity were private temples within the meaning of section 4(2) of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the endowment being a public one, the deity was not a public body or a public institution within the definition of section 2(a) of that Act and therefore, the temple was not an "public" one. HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that it was a circumstance which could be spelt out and held that the dedication to the temple by members of the public was of a private nature. [837 B] (ii) The essential distinction between a private and a public endowment is that while a public or a private endowment is not capable of holding property and the property dedicated to the public must be vested in the beneficiaries and the income from the property is used for the maintenance and support of the family of the founder. [829 C] (iii) The mere fact that members of a Hindu public are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members of such public had a right to worship in the Temple. [828 D] (iv) The question whether a religious endowment is of a purely private nature or of a statutory character, depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. [827 E] (v) The fact that the manager of the temple is not debarred from entering into the temple for the purpose of worship does not make any difference because the temple itself is not a private one capable of being held property and therefore the mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the endowment. Indeed if it is found that the worship by the members is as of right, that may be a circumstance where the evidence shows that there was provision for a scheme to be framed by associating the members with the members. [826 G H] (vi) The position in law is that the mere fact of worship will not determine whether the user of the Temple by members is of private or public nature. It may be that the main object of the dedication cannot be ascertained, the question whether the use of the deity by members, of the community is as a matter of right or a religious character, has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is not necessary for the Court to decide whether the usage and management of the property are of a Private nature. The essential features of a Public trust are that while the endowment is lost by the founder, the endowment must be deemed to have been made by a person who has no issue and who after installation of the idol, is entitled to take over the management. [825 G H; 836 A B] Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji vs S.P. Das, ; , referred to. (vii) The temple is a public temple and it was built up by the founders of the worship of the deities. This clearly establishes that the intention of the founder was to dedicate their properties and install the deity in the temples.

The appellant Bank originally known as Bharat Bank Ltd. agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. The agreement provided that all powers hereby granted were and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorneys against the bills were made or made hereafter. The appellant was authorised to sue for recovery of and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaL repatriated Bank Ltd., Jabalpur. On July 19, 1948, the power of attorney recited that the appellant had no right to attach it. The respondent filed objections under section 47 of the Indian Contract Act before the Sub Divisional Magistrate who held that the appel lant was the assignee of the bill and decreed the suit.
