The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no equitable assignment. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The law on the subject admits of no doubt. In Palmer vs Carey, , it is necessary to bear in mind that there is an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. The power of Attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill. [777 E F] (ii) In view of the power conferred upon the appellant to receive all monies due or to become due to Malhotra in respect of pending or future contracts with Government authorities, the powers of attorney coupled with endorsement on bills dated July19, 1948 were a clear engage ment by the borrower to pay him. [778 F G] Palmer 's case, approved. (iii) The High court was in error in holding that there could be no equitable assign ion. In view Of the power given to the appellant under section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act, the order of attorney having been made by the appellant, the High Court was in a wrong way and therefore the appeal must fail.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and was assessed to income tax in respect of that assessment year. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary had to be considered as his salary as defined in section 17(1) (iv). The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, HELD: The receipt of Rs. 27948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered a salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(3)(ii) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income Tax under the head "income from other source" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. In computing the taxable income, the receipt of an interest on any investment is a gain made by the investor and therefore the same is exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17 (3) (ii). [445 D E] The respondent was not represented before this Court. It was not shown that the assessee had any interest on the securities. The income from the other sources was brought to tax under section 56. Therefore, the question is what is meant by "profits in lieu" of salary".

The Bihar Act, in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cow or buffalo, is valid. The Act provides for the establishment of a committee to make recommendations on the method of selection of cattle of animals of the species of bovine cattle. Section 3(1) of the Act provides that no person shall slaughter a cow without a licence from the appropriate authority mentioned in section 4 and section 6 of the said Act or any other law for the time being in force or in any usage to the contrary. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Acts on the ground, inter alia, (1) that the impugned Acts were not violative of article 19(1)(g) of their Constitution as they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 19(i)(g), 21 and 22 of the Constitution; (2) that sections 3(3) and 4 of the Bihar Act were ultra vires the State Legislature and (3) that section 3(4) was violative of the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19 (1)(f) of our Constitution. Held, that the provisions of the impugned Act infringed articles 19 (i)(d), 21, 22 and 23 of the constitution and are not void under article 13(2). The Act is a law relating to the slaughter and does not infringe the rights of the petitioners under article 19. The provisions of sections 3 and 4 are not violative Of article 19 and are therefore void. The Bihar Act is constitutionally valid in so insofar as it prohibited the slaughter by the impugned acts of the butchers (Kasais) of a cow or cow, and the slaughter animals which are useful for human consumption cannot be supported as reasonable under article 21. The restrictions imposed on the slaughter must not be arbitrary or excessive. The restriction must not only be reasonable but also valid. It is well settled that the power to regulate the slaughter is subject to the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on the exercise of the power. The impugned Acts are not unconstitutional as they violate articles 14, 19(l)(g). The provisions in the Bihar Acts show that the restrictions imposed by them were reasonable and valid. There was no violation of any fundamental right under article 31 (1), (g) or (vi) of Part III of the Constitu tion. The ban on slaughter of animals above a specified age may not be justified as it is not reasonable within the meaning of article 21, but only reasonable. The State of Bombay vs R. M. section Kasais, ; , referred to.

The respondent was a clerk in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service by an order dated January 31, 1956, and on his appeal to the High Court he was informed that the order of suspension had been revoked by the relevant authorities under the provisions of the . The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High court challenging the orders of suspension and termination of his services. The High Court held that the Standing Orders did not apply to him, but only applied to Standing Orders No. 2(a) and (b), and that the respondent was not an employee within the meaning of the Standing Order No. 1. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellant had committed a breach of the statutory provision in section 30 of the local Act in the sense that no Standing Orders had been made in respect of the respondent and his service had been terminated in accordance with Standing Order NO. 18 which provided for penalties for misconduct. The Standing Orders were not therefore subject to any other provisions of law, and the words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental musters ' account" in Standing Order 2(b) should be read as " whose name and ticket number is included in a departmental muster 's case". The respondent was an employee of the appellant Company and not of a workman. The respondent had no ticket for the purpose of the standing Orders, and he was not therefore an employee under the Standing order No. I.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the year 1961, was carrying on the business of manufacturing controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The claim was resisted by the company on the ground that the Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained for each unit and separate profit and Loss account was maintained for every unit. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project could not be treated as separate establishments because under the Act, a Company is an establishment which has been in existence for a long period and has been paying its employees, controlled or managed by persons other than companies. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that merely because Alloy steel Project is owned, controlled and run by a person or body other than the company or body of individuals, it cannot be said that it is an 'establishment ' within the meaning of section 16(1). [633 B C] (2) The expression "establishment" in the definition of "establishment " has been used in the Act to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . In the present case, the Company, Hindustan Steel Ltd., had a number of undertakings, separate accounts were kept for each separate undertaking. The annual reports for three years were produced before the Tribunal and they clearly indicated that separate balance sheet was prepared for each of the units. [634 C D] (3) The word "establishment ' in section 16 is used to indicate some other establishment for purposes of section 3(1) of the Act. It is, therefore, quite clear that the Tribunal went wrong in ignoring the fact that separate accounts and profit & loss account were kept by the Head Office. [534 E F] (4) The only exception has been made in the case of workmen of the head office where no separate profit & Loss was worked out and the bonus was paid on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. The only exceptions have been in the present ease, namely, workmen of Head Office where no different accounts were filed before the Tribu nal and the evidence of the Company 's witness Umapada Chakraborty, but is also admitted by Suprakash Kanjilal, the only witness examined on behalf of the workmen.

The respondent assessee is a sugar mill in Karnataka raising similar question of law. The State Government issued a notification under Section 3 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1974 exempting from the operation of the Act and the State Boards from all the provisions of the said Act. The cess was levied on the ground that it fell under item 15 of Schedule I to the Act. In respect of the assessment year 1982 83, the respondent assessee claimed exemption from payment of cess from the sugar factories on the grounds that this industry falls under item No. 15 of the Schedule I of the Cess Act and as such the levy and collection of cess was not justified. The Assessing Authority held that the sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 as "processing of animal or vegetable products" and accordingly levied cess from its factory on the basis that this activity fell under Item 15 of schedule I to The Cess Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that sugar manufacturing industries would fall under item 68 as " processing of animal products industry". The State Board of Revenue in revision set aside the order of the Assessing Authority and directed the Assessing Authorities to take appropriate action for recovery of cess. The High Court also took a similar view holding that sugar manufacture would come under Entry 15 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that sugar industry would fall within Entry No.15 and therefore, the levy of cess could not be said to be an industry within Entry 14 of the schedule I. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Cess is a fiscal enactment, as is held by this Court in Member Secretary, Andhra Pradesh State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd., [1963] Supp. 2 SCR 79. The levy and recovery of Cess is on water consumed by persons carrying on the industries specified in Schedule I. The Act does not contain vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. It was also of the view that sugar factories would fall squarely within Entry 68 of Schedule 1 as processing agricultural products industry would be covered by Entry 15. [532C D] 2.1 The Cess act is a taxing statute, as it is held in the context in which the word 'vegetable ' is used in Entry 15 'veg et tory of agricultural or processed food products ' and that is to say product of or made of or out of vegetable. [525D E] 2:2 The term 'vegee ' has been defined in various statutes, including manufac ture, manmade for food, such as peas, beans, melting, salting, smoking, peeling or filleting or any other method of processing which the authority made by notification in the official Gazette specified in this behalf. [500F G] 2(a) The term "vegetables" is defined in Entry No 15 as follows: "to include any plant but in common parlance it is understood as referring to any kind of plant life or plant product, including a part of such plant, as prepared for market or the table. It would be used in connection with agriculture and manufacture without adequate treatment. [51B C] (b) The word 'crylon ' has not been defined. In the context of processing it is not necessary to produce a commodity which may lead to production of any new article. The term is used as a neces sary for understanding, producing or making something. It is not possible to conclude sugar cane as vegetable. The word "vegor" has been used in contra distinction to the word "animal". [528C D; 526D] (c) The expression 'veetable product ' means product of a kind of animal that is produced by or is made of, for tablet.

The respondent, an Advocate, filed an application before the Rent Controller for eviction of the appellant 's tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who contended that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds that he requires the premises bona fide for the purposes of carrying out his profession. The Rent Controller held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for carrying on the profession as a advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction. In revision, the High Court affirmed the decision of the Rent Control Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression business occurring in Section 10 (3)(a)(i) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of the advocate. [14 E] 1.2 In a broad sense it is taken to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of livlihood or profit. In a narrow sense it may be confined to commercial activity. It is confined to business carried on by an Advocate but not section 10 (1) (c) only. [15 E] 2. The expression 'business ' in Section10(3)(a)(ii) is intended to include a practice of business within its meaning. [16 F G] 1:4. In the context of the Madhya Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, section 10(1) provides for the eviction by a tenant where the landlord of a residential building requires it for his own occupation. Section 10 sub section (3)(b) provides that a tenant shall not be evicted whether in execution of a decree or otherwise except in accordance with the provisions of Sections 10, 12 and 13. [17 G H] 1 5. The word 'business occurring in section 10 of the Act is used to include 'business as understood in one Act with reference to their use in another Act; more so, if the two Acts in which the same word is used are not cognate Acts. Neither the meaning nor the definition of the term in one statute affords a guide to the construction of the same term in another statute and the sense in which that term has been understood in the several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which it appears. [18 C D] 1 6. The words 'business" and 'profession ' are used in the definition in section 2(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings, (Lease & Eviction) Act, 1950. [19 G H; 20 A] 7.

The respondent, a limited company, was the creditor of M/s. India Supplies Ltd., and the appellant in the year 1942, filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 with interest at 6 per cent from time to time. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding that the respondent deposited the sum of Rs 4 lakhs with the appellant and also held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the use of the word " deposit" in the roznamcha, entry No. 30 of the entry showed that the amount was deposited with the respondent 's money; (ii) there were disputes between the partners of the firms and the respondent regarding the payment of the money to M/S India Supplies; (iii) the appellant had no ordinary loan of Rs4 lakhs from the respondent; and (iv) the respondent had not examined himself and did not examine himself. HELD: (i). The High Court was correct in decreeing the suit. [578 D] (ii). The mere fact that money in specie was not paid would not be destructive of deposit. The relationship between the parties, the surrounding circumstances at the time of the transaction, the pecuniary position of the appellant are all overwhelming features to taluqa tion. [579 E] Nawab Major Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , referred to. (iii). The respondent acted as bankers and the money was paid by the appellant. The mere circumstance that money was not given would not make it a case of deposit of the amount. [580 G] (iv). The fact that the money in question was deposited at the same time as the rest of the writing did not show how the parties treated and understood their financial dealings. It is precisely because of the then inability of India Supplies to repay the money immediately. It was precisely because the respondent demanded the money by a letter dated 27 April 1953 (exhibit 7) from the appellant, and ultimately the appellant 's claim for return of the said amount was rejected by the trial court.

The petitioner was detained by an order of the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, dated February 28, 1986 under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to his detention. The grounds of detention were served on him on March 27, 1986 and he was produced before the Advisory Board constituted by the Central Government on April 22, 1986. On March 23, 1987, the petitioner was taken into custody and was produced at the time of hearing. On February 20, 1987 the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate passed an order under section 11(1)(a) of COFEPOSA directing that the detenu be detained until further orders on the ground that he had been prejudiced in making an effective representation to the Board against his detention in the absence of the summons issued under section 108 of the Customs Act. The petitioner challenged the order of detention by a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The fact that the appellant is in custody when the order was made and produced before him cannot take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making the order. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining author ity was aware of the fact that he was already in custody and yet he was sub jecting the order or that he being sub jected in detention, the appeal is pending and in re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention and the principle enunciated by this decision must apply but where the offences in respect of which the detenu is accused are so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that these affect continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby jeo pardise the security of the State, then sub jection to other conditions being fulfilled, a man being in detention would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention.

The petitioners are working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The casual labour consists of unskilled, skilled or skilled workers, who have not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more. They were engaged by the Union of India to do the work of the last ten years as casual labour on continuous basis. As an alternative to regular absorption they were denied the benefits of the interim relief. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the denial of the benefits claimed. The respondents contested the writ petitions and contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour, the wages paid to them are very low and far less than the minimum pay payable under the pay scales applicable to regular employees may be effected as is at present available to casual labourers working in different departments. The Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Union to pay to the petitioners same salary and allowances and other benefits as were being enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The Union of india, however, contended that the State cannot deny at least the minimum wages in the pay scale of regular employees on the ground that they are being paid wages far less. Allowing the writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to corresponding Dearness Allowance and Addl. Dearness Allowance if any, payable thereon. whatever other benefits which are now being enjoyed in the Postal and Telegraph Department. Is it for paying them lower wages? Then it amounts to exploitation of labour. [606C D] 1.2 In Dhirendra Chamoli and Another vs State of U.P., this Court has taken almost a similar view with regard to the employees working in the Nehru Yuvak Kendras who were considered to be performing the same duties as Class IV employees. The said decision is being repeatedly observed by those, who are in charge of economic affairs of the countries in different parts of the world that as far as possible security of work should be assured to the employee so that they may contribute to the maximisation of production. It is again for this reason that managements and the Government agencies in particular should not allow workers to remain idle. [066G H; 609A] 1:3 The petitioners have not been regularly recruited but many of them have been working continuously for more than one year in the Department and some of them are rendering service which is being rendered by regular employees doing the same type of work. There are several types of work such as road making, railway construction, house building, irrigation projects, communications etc. which have to be undertaken on a large scale. Development in these types of activities (even though they do not involve much foreign exchange) is not keeping pace with the needs of society. [076E F] 1st petitioner has not been regular recruited but some of the petitioners have been rendering service for nearly ten years. They are rendering services to many as casual workers, for a long period is not a wise policy. It may be that the casual labourers have agreed to work on such low wages. That he has done because he has no other choice. It was poverty that has driven him to that State. The Government should be a model employer. [086G] 2.1 In the instant case, the classification of employees into regularly recruited employees and casual labour for the purpose of paying less than their minimum pay is equally untenable. There is clearly no justification for doing so. Such a classification is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It has been made in order to avoid fair wages and equal wages for equal work. [096H; 609B] 2:2 The petitioners, therefore, are entitled for corresponding Dearness allowance and Addl., Dearness Allowance, if any. whatever may be poverty that they have driven them to that state. The State cannot take advantage of its dominant position, and compel any worker to work even as a casual labourer on starving wages. It will not be an empty formality.

The assessee, who was a partner of an assessee firm, had sold his house to another person. The Income tax Officer included the value of the house in his return for the assessment year 1945 46 and assessed him on it for the said assessment year. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income tax officer was not competent to issue a notice under section 34(1) of the Act, because, he had failed to give a notice as required by section 34 (2). The Tribunal, however, rejected his contention and the High Court upheld the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The assessee could not be allowed to raise any question of law in this Court under article 136 of the Constitution. [448 C] Under section 22(1), the Income tax Act, 1922, is a complete code providing for the filing of returns and the assessment can be completed within one year of the date of service of notice under sub section (1) or sub section(2). But if the return filed on January 5, 1950, was no return at all, then the conditions under the first subsection of section 34 are satisfied. [449 D] The assessee had not made a full return as required under section 22 (3), and therefore, the period during which action could be taken was the extended one of eight years. [453 E] In the present case, the notice under s.23(2) was issued on January 4, 1950. The notice under that section was valid in law. [454 F G] The notice was valid only for a year and not for a return of income which showed no assessable income.

The first petitioner, a registered Central Trade Union, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi. The second petitioner, who was a registered central trade union, challenged the Circular dated 23 8 1982 ( Annexure A) on the ground that it violated the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act 1970, as amended by the N.B.S. & Co. (Amendment) Act, 1970, and the N .B. Series being a self contained code, the circular was ultra vires section 9 of the Act unless it was so read as to be in harmony with the provisions of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the Circular is to neutralise and dis criminate the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. [855C] 1.2 In the instant case, the object of Circular is not to neutralize and disengage any officer of the Bank to be appointed by the Central Government as the true representative of the employees. The object is to give the Board a truly representative character so as to reflect the genuine interests of all persons specified under section 9 as well as the larger and wider interest of national economy as postulated in Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43A of the Constitution. [862E F] 1:3. In the light of the rival contentions, it is clear that the object is not only to neutralises and disenchance the employees but also to reduce the choice of their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govern ment to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employees, and, if necessary, to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. [861F G] 1 :4. The Circular dated March 23, 1982 (Annexure B) is ultra vires the Act and the Scheme and it is null and void and of no effect. [863G H] 1 5. The transfer cases are directed to be conducted in a manner as specified in the Scheme. The scheme in effect postulates all appointments to be by nomi nation. In other words, the Central Govt. has a discretion to avoid election even where election is appropriate and feasible in respect of a particular category of persons. [864A B] 1 6. The Central Government must in this regard act in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India for it is the latter that has the necessary expertise and intimate knowledge in the field of banking, finance and other connected matters. The Act does not contemplate a manage ment unmindful of the true and legitimate interest of the employee. [854C D] 7.

The appellant assessee was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Tribunal declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The power to stay is incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. [67D] (ii) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribunal with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers, fully effective. In the present case, the Appellate Tribunals were given the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal before the Tribunal. [69F] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had the power to impose penalty as incidental or ancillary to it. [70G H] (iv) The Appellate Tribunals must be held to have the power under section 254(1) with widest amplitude, and have in some cases been held similar to and identical with those of the powers of an appellate court under the Civil Procedure Code. [71A B] (v) The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is not a court but it exercises judicial powers. [72F G] (vi) The provisions of section 255(5) do not expressly confer a power on the Income Tax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee. The right of appeal is a substantive right and the questions of fact and law are at large and are open to review by the Appellate Authority. [73G H; 74A] (vii) The Tribunal must be hold to have been the power in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. A certain apprehension may legitimately arise in the minds of authorities administering the Act that if the Appellate tribunals proceed to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the appellate Tribunals. [74E F] (viii) The right to appeal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matters of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It wilt only be when a strong prima facie case is made out that the Tribunal will consider whether to stay the recovery proceedings and on what conditions and the stay will be granted in most deserving and appropriate cases where the Tribunal was satisfied that the entire purpose of the appeal will be frustrated or rendered nugatory by allowing the recovery proceed ings to continue during the pendin g of the Appeal.

The respondent was appointed a constable in the U. P. Police Force and on his appointment he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and in May 1952, he was posted as Station Officer. On September 16, 1952, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement on the report that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of dishonesty and therefore the order was invalid. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High Courts in India have not expressed their opinion on the other questions raised and argued before them. In view of that finding the departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the appellant in regard whereof the respondent had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the Police Regulations. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries did not affect the validity of the order. (ii) The departmental inquiry is only a continuation of the enquiry and the departmental trial was validly held. If so, the question is whether para 486 would govern the present case or it would fall out side its scope. (iii) The fact whether in the meantime the police receives further complaints, or that it would fail within the express terms of para 487(2), does not affect either the question whether substantially the subject matter of the departmental proceedings and the department is the same.

The appellant was appointed to supertime grade II in the Super time grade II of the Indian Medical Education Service. He was promoted as a Professor in the Specialists 'Silicon Hospital, and transferred to the said hospital on July 17, 1978. The promotion of respondents 4 to 24 was challenged by the appellant before the High Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. A Single Judge of the High court allowed the petition holding that the promotion of respondent 4 to super time grade 11 was in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules and that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion as he was not qualified for being promoted to super Time grade II. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal preferred by the State. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appointment of respondents four persons in super time scale II was made by way or through a proper channel and (ii) the Government had acted mala fide in issuing the promotion order to the appellant at Simla instead of making an unspecified Specialists. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of promoting service into five different categories is to promote departmental candidates from amongst those who qualify for the same as provided for in rule 8(3). It is clear that when a post is created in a certain grade, category or cadre and it is to be filled in by promotion, that would only be from amongst persons belonging to Specialists Grade II. [53E] 1.2 The object is to encourage posts in the service into a specified post which means specified in the speciality in which a need has been felt from amongst the members of the specialists ' grade belonging to that speciality and in order of their inter se seniority a promotion could be given. In passing a contention, it is not open to him to urge that the post at Willingdon Hospital alone must have been filled by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But it was very much possible for him to contend that whenever unspecified specialists were appointed on a particular grade, it could be filled up in either by promotion. [54F G] 1:3 The object being to encourage post of manningdon hospital at Willeddon, speciality and to promote the defence services, it must be held that whenever an unsadhent is created, a post in converted to a specified grade which means a specified higher post in the same speciality. [55G] 1 :4 The object was to encourage the post of a specialists cadre at Willningdons speciality and not to create posts for upward promotion service rendered as probationer. [56A B] 1 5.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about agrarian reform. The object of the Act was to provide for the ceiling on land ownership and for matters connected therewith. Section 19B provides that where a person is in possession and has no interest in any land acquired by him exceeding in the permissible area, he shall within the period prescribed, furnish to the Collector a return indicating the permissible areas he desires to retain. The Act was amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High Court had upheld certain patterns of alienations and acquisitions. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the land inherited by them and later transferred to their sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1962 which prohibited the acquisition of land by inheritance in excess of permissible area. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Land Reforms Act are intended to give some time to the heir to ascertain the assets he has inherited, make the choice of his reserved area which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. A processual facility cannot be converted into an opportunity to pervert and to thwart the substantive object of law. After all courts, faced with special case situations, have 'creatively ' to interpret legislation. The Courts are 'finishers, refiners and polishers of legislation which comes to them in a state requiring varying degrees of further. processing ', said Donaldson J., in Corocraft Ltd. vs Pan American Airways Inc., ; , referred to. 2. Section 10A of the Pepsu Security of land Tenures Act 1953 provides that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest of gift, the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible limit. Indeed section 19 B had to be enacted because the High Courts took the view that area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 could not be regarded as paper tiger, agrarian reform and assumed social values. [632C D] 3.

The appellants were the sons of one B, who was the eldest among the five sons of B. The respondents claimed that the property in suit originally belonged to B and the estate was divided into three categories: (i) his father 's share in the Zamindari; (ii) his brother 's interest in the estate; and (iii) his mother 's son 's family properties. The trial court held that the respondent had acquired occupancy rights in the lands and that the appellants were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i ) the State Government had acted in exercise of the power conferred by section 3 of the Act and therefore the order of the Governor recognising Dayaram as Zamindar was not binding; (2) the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding the mutation was erroneous because no suit challenging the decision was instituted within two months from the date of the order, and (3) the decree of the Trial court was not barred by the decision in the present case. HELD : (i). The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded to the appellants. [334 B] (ii). The order of Governor dated August 30, 1951 declaring that Dayaram as a Zamindar had become the estate in favour of the respondent was binding on the appellants and that it was open to the Governor to select one of the two members of the family related to the last holder in the same degree even though he was senior in age. [336 C] (iii). The decision of Governor did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to determine competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3. The order was in the form of a memorandum addressed to the Deputy Commissioner, Chanda, who had been authorised to make his adjudication. [328 D] (iv). The Collector 's order was not open to challenge under article 226 of the Constitution. [330 G] (v) The High Courts were in error on the face of the terms of section 35(7) of the , which provides that the payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State Govern ment from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary rights, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect Of such rights to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the appellant was in arrears of rent from 1st September, 1964 and also on the grounds that the appellants were in arrears. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenants were in arrear of rent for more than six months. On appeal the appellate court confirmed the decree. In an application under article 227 of the Constitution the High Court held that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) and (b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 did not apply to the suit. The appellants contended that they had raised dispute about the standard rent by their letters dated 17 November 1966 and 19 December 1966 and therefore there was a dispute as to standard rent and the provisions in section 11(4) (b), of the Act were applicable. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that since the appellants had not complied with the provisions of section 12 (3) of Act, they could raise the dispute as they raised dispute regarding standard rent or permitted increases. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was in continuation of the tenancy and the notice terminating the tenancy was dated 1st December 1956 and therefore the period of one month after service of the notice under section 12 had expired. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have not agreed with the view of the Gujarat High Court in Ambalal 's case. [633 B] (2) In the present case the appellants did not raise any dispute regarding the standard and the non existence of the dispute was also not disputed. The provisions in sections 12(4)(a) & (b). of the said Act deal with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of the suit disputing the rent. [625 C D] Ambalals ' case, ; , followed. (3 ) The Bombay High Court has not agreed on the question whether the provisions relating to standard and rent or permitting increases in rent are attracted. [726 B] Amalal vs Badaldas, Bom. L.R. 67 I.A. 129; Ambalala Pannalal vs Gajanan Vithoba Bobhate & Anr., ; and Ambalai 's Case, referred to. (4) The provisions of the section are applicable only to suits in arrears and not to suits for recovery. [526 C D]. Ambalaram vs Badal Das, Bom, L. R. , followed; Amalala vs Badal R. Pannalal, Bom., L. J.

The respondent company was a limited company incorporated in Canada, and its shareholders were the directors of the respondent company. The Aluminium Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in India with effect from December 31, 1939, and in exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of respondent company, one of whom was a director of the Aluminium Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the Respondent company. One of these directors was Mr. L. G. Bash and the other directors had between them during the chargeable accounting periods ending December 31st, 1941, to 1943. The question for determination in this Court was whether the directors were entitled to be regarded as a company the directors whereof had a controlling interest therein. Held, that the Aluminium Limited was a subsidiary of the Indian Company and was not liable to tax under section 2(21) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, as amended by the Finance Act, 1951, read with section 66(1) of that Act. The shares in question which give the controlling interest are neither held by Mr.L. Gibby & Sons Ltd., nor were they subject directly or indirectly to his will and ordering and, therefore, he cannot apply either of the tests mentioned above. Commissioners of Inland Revenue vs Jamed Hodgkinson (Salford) Ltd., applied. Commissioner of Income tax vs Bipin Silk Mills Ltd., , approved.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st November, 1956 he was allotted to the new State of Karnataka with effect from 1st October 1957. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore, was abolished by the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. On 21st November 1972, some person junior to him were promoted as Assistant Engineer Grade II on their being found guilty of misconduct. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. On 22nd November, 1972, the Board framed Recruitment and Promotion Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December, 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I division clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their acquiring higher qualification and for promotion. On 31st October, 1957, some others junior to respondent were reverted as he had not passed the examination. The Respondent made several representation one such representations being on 25th December 1969. On 23rd January, 1970, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The Single Judge dismissed it and the Division Bench held that the writ petition could not be thrown out on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in view of the later Resolution dated 5th January,1970, it was no longer open to the Board to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court found that the earlier resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the question of seniority and was therefore not applicable to the respondents.

The petitioner, a widow of one of the deceased son of the petitioner, was taken from his home in police custody on January 1, 1987 by respondent No. 6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Station, Bishalgarh, for the investigation of an offence under section 379 I.P.C., which was registered at 8 P.M. on January 2, 1987. The petitioner was arrested on February 1,1987 by respondent Nos. 6 to 8 and his dead body was recovered from the railway track. The case against the petitioner was that she had died in police service on March 1, 1988 due to multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police lock up after he had escaped from police custody. In her petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for compensation for contravention of fundamental rights to life, it was contended that the death of her son occurred as a result of injuries inflicted by him while she was in judicial custody at the Police Outpost and his death was unnatural. The State of Orissa and its officers were also impleaded as respondents in the writ petition. The High Court rejected the contention of the respondents and dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the investigation into the matter and evidence led by the prosecution witnesses was wholly inadmissible; (ii) the failure of the State to take the right of redressal under Article 21 of the Constitu tion was confined only to a specific case of custodial death but not of death of the victim; (iii) the High Court had erred in holding that the responsibility of the state for the safety of the life of the victims was not established and that the petitioner could have been relegated to the ordinary remedy of a suit if his claim to compensation was factually controversial; and (iv) the State should pay a sum of Rs.1,50,000 to the petitioner and a sum which would be more than Rs.10,000 in lieu of compensation for violation of fundamental right guaranteed under Article 22(2). Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The defence of "sovereign immunity" in article 21 is not available to the State and in fairness to Mr. Adverting to the grant of relief to the petitioners for violation or infringement of their constitutional rights, it does so under the public law by way of penalising the wrongdoer and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. [608C D] 2. The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental right under article 32 or 226 of the constitution. [508D] 3. The Supreme Court has the power to award monetary compensation for breach of fundamental freedoms under Article 19(1) (g), in an action based on tort. It is a sound policy to punish the wrongdoers and fixing their liability for public wrongs resulting from the contravention of the fundamental freedom guaranteed by article 21 of our Constitution. The payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by way or restitution, even though it may be available as a defence in private law for damages for the tortuous act of its servants. [596D E] 4.

The petitioner was convicted by the Chief Justice of India for committing an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed his petition for commutation of sentence on the ground that he had not been informed of the application made by him asking for a similar permission. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press unless in the first instance the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be interview. [1187B] (2) The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of death. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for the Court to say that the two prisoners are ready and willing to he interviewed. [1108C] (3) The petition is dismissed. [1087D] (4) If in any given case there are weighty reasons for doing so, which we expect will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore the petitioner should not be allowed to interview the two convicts. [1018E F] (5) The Court cannot overlook that the petitioner has already been asked for permission for interview by the Superintendent of Jail. No material has been shown either that they are not willing to appear and, indeed, if it were to appear that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be heard, it would have been impossible for them to pass an order directing that the petitioners should be allowed.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. On January 20, 1950 the appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. On August 26, 1950, the respondent moved an application requesting for damages from the Receiver and the appellant prayed that the receiver be appointed as Receiver. The trial court decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but the High Court dismissed it on June 29, 1970. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor court. The surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District Judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Thus, by virtue of section 150, the Subordinate judge was entitled to exercise the same power in the matter of the enforcement of the bond as the District judge himself. [359 B C] (2) Under the terms of the surety bond, the appellant rendered itself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the Court. Therefore, the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver could be executed against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the terms thereof.

The appellants who were dealers in food grains, supplied wheat to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants and rejected the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. In appeal the Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of the U .P. Act, 1948. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge. The appellants appealed to this Court with special leave. HELD : (i) Under section 4 of the Uttar Pradesh Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959, the occupier of a sugar factory had to buy sugarcane from cane growers in conformity with the directions issued under the Act and the purchase order was not made in pursuance thereof. The power of the occupier to sell goods is conferred on him by the Control Order. Under section 21 of the Act the occupier may, by a written order require any person holding stock of iron or steel, acquired by him otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of clause 4 to sell the whole or any part of the stock to such person or class of persons and on such terms and conditions as may be specified in the Order. The State Government was competent under section 21 to impose tax purchases of sugarcane for use, consumption or sale in a sugar mill. [677 E F] (ii) Under the Act, the owner of a factory had a right to sell to the State Government 50% of the wheat held by him at the commencement of the Order and thereafter 50% Of the wheat sold was to be delivered by the dealer to the purchaser. The sale price was fixed by the State Govt. and the appellant was bound to deliver 50 per cent of the quantity of wheat purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of Order. [678 F G] (iii) Under clause 5 of the Control order, the State Govern ment had power to tax purchases in respect of goods specified in Schedule I. The appellant could not claim that the supplies were not sold as required by the order. The High Court was wrong in holding that the sales were made without any authority of law and that the transactions were not exigible to tax under section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act. [679 G H] (iv) Under cl. 5, the appellant could authorise a producer or stockholder to dispose of wheat from the dealer. If the cane grower made an offer, the factory was to take delivery on his behalf. The sugar cane growers were not given any option to sell it at the controlled rate. The Cane Commissioner had no option but to purchase 50 per centum of the sugar purchased by the appellant every day. [680 G H; 681 A] (v) Under r. 5(1), the occupier could only sell to a person declared entitled to the value of goods, which was determined or determinable in accordance therewith, or that he had no power to enter into a contract with the dealer for sale. The purchase of sugar by the appel lant was not a sale within section 2 (h) and the Sales Tax Authorities were therefore justified in imposing sales tax on the turnover of the appellant resulting from those transactions to sales tax under r. 7.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him and he was informed that he was not to be taken at the place before the Advisory Board within three weeks from the date of detention. He was also not so released. The Advisory Board made its report on September 26, 1986. It found that the appellant was in jail for a longer period than three months and that there was no sufficient cause for such detention. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the second order of detention dated August 7, 1986 contending that there had been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) of the Constitution and therefore the appellant 's detention was illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Advisory Boards constituted under the Act were not competent to make a subsequent detention order under the . In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there has been a violation of the Constitutional protection afforded to him by article 21(4). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedure under the Gujarat Act and the statute have been complied with before the date on which the detention order was made. [209B] 2.1 In habeas corpus proceedings, it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statu tions have been fulfilled before the day of hearing and therefore, the detention should be upheld. The substantive requirements are, there fore, to be strictly complied with if any value is to be attached to the liberty of the subject and the Constitution al rights guaranteed to him in that regard. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to he made within three months, it would be no answer to saying that the report though not obtained within three month, was obtained before the hearing of the case. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it will be not answer to that question. [208C D] 2:2 In a habeas corpus proceeding, it cannot be made imperative to read down so as to enable the constitutional rights guaranteed under article 22 (4) to be complied with.

The petitioner, a student of the respondent University, was established Vaidyas in Rajkot. He had intervened between them and the respondent. The respondent applied for filing an award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (the Act). A notice was issued to him by the petitioner under section 18 of the Act calling upon him to appear before the arbitrator, who made his award on 18th January, 1977. The application was converted into a Special Civil Suit No 84 of 1977. In the meantime, the respondent applied to the Court for filing the award and obtained an order from the trial court that he had torn off the award, and therefore, the petitioner was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objection and held that the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the Award, and that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and he had taken the responsibility. He also observed that the petitioner had taken a responsibility. Thereafter, the High Court dismissed the revision application filed by the respondent against the order of the trial Judge raising almost all the disputes which had been raised by the parties in this civil revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the dispute to arbitration, and the entire onus of soling the dispute had become highly technical accompanied by unending prolixity at every stage providing a legal trap to the unwary. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did. [538C] 2.1 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, the petition is allowed and the order passed by the High court is set aside. [540D] 2(a) The High court was right that on this aspect the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. The special leave petition fails and is accordingly dismissed. [541F] 2.(b) The petitioner is entitled to raise the question of limitation in his civil revision petition. The question had come up for consideration before the Judicial Committee in Rajah Amir Hassan Khan vs Sheo Baksh Singh, ; , where all the relevant authorities on this point have been discussed. But in the light Of the facts, and circumstances, it was not necessary that they should have exercised their jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. [543F] 3(a). The High Courts were right in doing so. It was not relevant according to the Judicial Committees, if the parties had agreed to refer a dispute to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award; secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter addressed to the arbitrator wherein it was stated that both of them had appointed him as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them. The award was signed by all the parties and also their respective advocates. This, in our opinion, is not relevant for the purpose of section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code. [544F G] 3.2 In the instant case, there was nothing on record to indicate that they decided to refer to arbitration of dispute to an arbitrator. The agreement was executed by both parties about which there was neither factual dispute nor any inability of the Judge concerned. In this connection reference may be made to the observations of this Court in several cases. [546G H] 3:3. The conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties have agreed to referred the disputes in writing to the arbitra tion of the said named arbitrator, and this agreement was also done twice.

The appellant, a sub mortgagee of the respondent 's property, instituted a suit for recovery of money on the ground that the mortgage was not in execution and that the decree holder had become the successors in interest of the mortgagors. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the judgment debtor having made special request to the decreeholder for an amicable settlement of the properties, the decree holders were protected by sub section (5) of section 36 of the Act. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent as a bona fide assignee was not entitled to value of the mortgage money and that he had no right to receive it from the original mortgagor. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The question whether a sub mortga tion is or is not an absolute interest depends upon the sufficiency of the right assigned to enable the sub mortgagee to sue the original owner for the proceeds of the sale debt, that is, whether there is privity of estate between the landlord and the mortgagee. If the mortgage could operate as an assign ment of the entire interest of a mortgagor in the lease, the mortgagee would be liable by privity of Estate for the burdens of the lease. If on the other hand it operated only as a partial assignment of the mortgagor 's interest, no such result would follow. [586 H; 586 A B] The question as to the nature of the rights transferred to a sub tenant under his sub mortgage was considered in Promode Kumar Roy vsRupees One Pada Bhattacharjee, (1901) L.R. 59 I.A. 594 and R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala vs The Union of India, ; , referred to.

The appellant was the karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided by metes and bounds in 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 and A 2 there was a disruption of the joint family and a severance of the Joint status between the members. In 1954, he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint Hindu Family. In 1950, he sold the properties to the respondents. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court dis missed the suit on the ground that the transfers were made by the respondents under exhibit A I and A2. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree in O.S. No. 62/54 but held that the transfer was valid and the subsequent severance of joint status was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers and the two deeds though ostensibly sale deeds were in reality gift deeds. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The properties sold by the appellant were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras School of Mitakshara law by which Venkatacharyulu was governed he had no power to make a gift of the coparcenary properties, the two documents being in reality gifts. [46 D] (ii) The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h) of the . [47 C] Balo vs Parbati, I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of Naga Pradesh, filed a petition under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for the recovery of certain amounts due to her husband from the Life Insurance Corporation of India (for short, the L.I.C.) during the period 1958 to 1960. The L. I.C. did not revoke the order of attachment in spite of the notice under section226(3). The Ll.C., however, issued a notice under Section 226(2) of Income Tax, 1961 on May 21, 1972 to the appellant stating that the policy had been absolutely assigned to her as admitted by the LlC and so she was not entitled to any interest for the period during which it was restrained from making the payment on account of the L1.C 's notice under sub section (3) thereof. The appellant contended that the LI. C. should have made double payment of Rs.34,1570/ by the policy which matured on 14th December 1975 much earlier to the date of the death of her husband and that the said amount had become due only from the L2.12.75. The respondent contended that in view of the express concession made by the appellant that no part of the said sum was due to the L3rd and that she was entitled to interest on the basis of its failure to discharge the statutory obligation of making the requisite statement on oath under section 22(3)(vi) of Act, the notice issued under section writ(3), 1961 could not be treated as having been served upon the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not liable to pay any interest on L2nd December 1975 and that it was entitled only to interest for a period of 9 years from the date on which it became restrained from taking the payment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) The LIlC had already deposited the amount in terms of the policy with the I.I.,C. and there fore the LO.I had been rightly directed to make the necessary statement on her behalf; (2) The liability for payment of interest has been correctly fastened on the appellant by the IL.I,C. The notice under s.22(3 ) of the Act was issued by the l.l.c. to the respondent and not to the I .I.T.O. as contemplated by section 244(vi) read with section 22 (4) of that Act; (3 ) The L1I.c., therefore, did not extend the benefit of section 244 to the 1st respondent. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The notice issued by l.Il. C., was in fact made without any statement on behalfof the L I.lC. [114D] (ii) The appellant 's action did not amount to discharge of statutory obliga tion under section 21(3); (iii) The I.L.C had no power to make payment of such interest as was payable in respect of the first two years. [115E F] (iv) The respondent 's failure to pay the L 1.l C.I./70, Income Tax dues did not disentitle her from claiming any interest under section 244 (3). [116G H] (v) The High COurt was right in holding that it had no jurisdiction to make a payment of the interest on a notice issued to the lI.lO.C.; and that there was no question of revoca tion of the liability of the II.I/I.L., in these circumstances, by the 1.1. The liability of L.lI.A. was not governed by section 246(3.) of the Indian Income Tax. Act, 1922.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the said properties on the ground that the appellant had not been in possession of them and that the suit was barred by limitation under section 116A of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the period of 30 days prescribed for filing the appeal was not applicable to the case as it was filed beyond the period prescribed for an appeal under the Limitation Act. On appeal the High Court held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time and dismissed the suit. In this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that (i) the first part of section 29(2) of the Limitation act did not apply to an appeal filed under the Indian Law; (ii) the second part of the section did not prescribe any period of limitation for an application under the Code of Civil Procedure and (iii) the words "where any special or local law prescribes a period of time different from that prescribed therefor by the First Schedule" occurring in the first limb of sub section (2) would also apply to a case where the first Part of the Act does not prescribe a period within which an appeal lay; and (iv) the third part of Section 29(1) was independent of the first, part reading "for the purpose of determining any period Of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special, or local laws" as being wide enough to include a suit, Appeal or application under a special or a local law which is of a type similar to that prescribed by the first schedule. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The second part reading section 29 (2), of the Code, in so far as it provides for an exhaustive and exclusive code of limitation, makes it clear that the procedure applicable in an appeal against an order made by a civil court under section 98 of the Civil Procedure Code is that prescribed in the First schedule to the Limitation Acts. [166F G] (2)(a) The first part reading 'for the purposes of computing any period or limitation prescribed ' for any suits, appeal and application by a special law makes it plain that the general provisions of the , are excluded from the operation of the second parts of section 12(2). [167G H] (b) The expression "appeal" in article 156 of the First Part means an appeal governed by the Code or the General Clauses Act, which is a special statute. It does not mean a revision under the Civil procedure Code.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate, Mathura under section 76 of the (Act) on the ground that the power to fix any area as a bus stand was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76(2)(r) of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix places for the bus stand/halting place '. It further observed that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get down and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as one of the bus routes. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authori ty has passed the impugned orders in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area in question. That appears to be so from the order passed by District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of the Town Area Committee. [717D] 2. The District Magi trate has passed an order in question without prejudice to its providing a bus service for anybody who chooses to use it voluntarily and to such person being required to pay for such use. [700E F] 3. Section 76 of Act empowers the State Government to make rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and the fees, if any, which may be charged for their use. Section 77(2) (r) provides that no person incharge of a motor bus plying for hire shall for the purpose of taking up or setting down passengers, park or stop his bus anywhere within the limits of the municipal ity except at the Municipal Bus Stand. The other bye laws provided for a levy of a fee of Re. 1 for every 8 hours or part thereof in respect of the use of the Bus stand by such buses and for the issue of a permit on such payment. [617F H] 4. Section 68(2), (r ) of the , empowers the Regional Authority to specify places within the limit of any municipality notified area, town area or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where alone public service vehicles or any specified class or classes of public service vehicle and/or goods vehicles may stand indefinite ly or for such period as may be specified or public service Vehicles may stop for a longer time than is necessary for the taking up and setting down of passengers. [72B C] 5. Section 73 of the provides that the Regional Officer shall not in any manner interfere with the exercise of the power conferred under sub section (1) of section 68 of the .

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the . The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961 Sub Inspector of Food and Supplies Department was present at Smalkha Barrier along with Head Constable, who was driving a truck. On the way the truck was intercepted by the police and the driver was found carrying 75 bags of paddy. The truck was seized from the truck as also the bags of rice. It was alleged that the consignment of paddy was booked from Lakerkotla on October 18, 1961 by Qimat Rai on behalf of M/s Sawan Ram Chiranji Lal. The consignee of the paddy was Messrs Devi Dayal Brij Lal of Delhi. The consignor of the rice was Messrs. Sawan Singh and others. The goods were seized under a permit issued by the State Government. The respondent was convicted for an offence under section 3(1) of the , but acquitted on appeal, the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence imposed upon him. On appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export. HELD : (i) The fact that the truck with the loaded paddy was seized at Samalkha Barriers which is 32 miles from Delhi does not affect the possibility of an attempt to commit a crime. [665 D] (ii) There is no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence punishable. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under s 7 of . The conviction and sentences imposed upon them are set aside.

The Sassoons entered into a contract with the Sassoon for the supply of their Managing Agency to Messrs Agarwals and they were assessed to income tax on the basis that they had earned the commission in the hands of the Sassoon Agencies. The Sassoosons agreed to transfer their managing agency to M/s Agarwals at the same rate as the Managing Agency Agreement and the transfer was made by the Sasawall Agencies to the respective transferees. The transferors were to be paid the remuneration for the period of actual services rendered by them to the company and the portions of the remuneration or commission which were earned by the companies during that period. The managing agency agreement provided that the remuneration payable to the Sasseosons would be the income accruing to them in the chargeable accounting period, but that the company would not be entitled to any commission or remuneration for such remuneration. The company was assessed to tax on its own income and the company claimed that the managing agency commission was earned by it as a result of the agreement between the Sasomans and M/S Agarwals. Held, that the transaction in question was one of the Managing Agents of the respondent company and not of the managing agents of the company. The Managing Agency Agreements were independent contracts and the remuneration received by the respondent from the companies under the managing Agency Agreement could be taxed only as income accruing directly to the respondent and not as a part of it. Held further, that in computing the taxable income of the assessee the profits and gains of the whole year must be taken into account. The agreement was independent of the business of the Company and was the source of the income. The mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source or character of income. Held also, that on the facts of the case it could not be said that the commission received by M/ s Agarwals from the Companies under the agreement was income accruing in the course of the year and therefore the profits of the firm were liable to tax.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A statement made by a witness within the meaning of section 157 of the Evidence Act should be in the first instance fully established. [90 D] (2) It is not necessary that the statement must be proved beyond doubt. The probative value of an admission or confession does not depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece of evidence it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. This proof in the case of oral admission or a confession does no depend upon the communication to other than they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. [91 E F] (3) The High Courts have consistently accepted the circumstantial evidence adduced in the ease and have held that the word "statement" used in section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "sthing that is said". [92 G H] Pakala Narayana vs R. , referred to. (4) The evidence of an admit ted or not, as it stands at the first occasion, fully established that the accused must have committed the murder. No other reasonable hypothesis was or could be suggested. [92 F] Pakla Narayana vs ranthi Narayana, A.I.R. 1959 S.C.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. He was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973. The appellant submitted his reply on december 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The said order was challenged in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court.
