In appeal to this Court it was contended that Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Service Regulation, 1976 is ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution and that the rule is ultra rites of Article 14 of The Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 5 is ultra vivour of Article14 of the Constitu tion. [225B] 2. Rule 9 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services of a permanent employee by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. It was not the contention therein that the Rule was capable of two constructions. It is settled law that there is a presumption of constitutionality of the rule. The Court ought not to interpret the statutory provisions, unless compelled by their language, in such a manner as would involve its unconstitutionality, since the legislature of the Rule making authority is presumed to enact a law which does not contravene or violate the constitutional provisions. Therefore, there is no valid opportunity to interpret Rule 5. [226C D] 3. The rule is valid and it cannot be said that the language in Rule 5 would be capable of both interpretation.

The appellant State issued a notice on February 3, 1970 inviting tenders for the grant of li cial rights for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. The appellant was declared an elected candidate and his name was entered in the prescribed register and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. On February 3. 1970 the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the bid at the auction was not approved by the State Government as required under section 22(1) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State Govern ment had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collector after it had been duly constituted in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the notification dated February 3 1970 issued under section 29(2)(b) of Bihar and Bihar Excise Act 1915, was invalid as the authorities for fixing the procedure under the amended section 29 (2)(a) had not been specified, the Government had no authority to issue such a notice; (ii) the State had no jurisdiction to direct the withholding and re auctioning of the licenses and that the appellant was entitled to license under sub section (2) of section 22 by virtue of section 6(a) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29 of the Act has been amended with retrospective effect and it is not open to the State Legislature to enact such a law. [723D] 2. Section 22(i) provides that no grantee of a privilege shall exercise the same "unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or the Excise Commissioner". The High Courts have held that section 6 (a) does not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and naked power" in determining the amount payable under sub s.(1) to the extent it is sought to be done by the order dated August 19, 1970. [788E F] 3. Section 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 has been given retrospective effect from April 16, 1971. The State Government had issued a special order under section 9(2) for grant of licences for the retail vend of country liquor. It was not open either to the Government or the specified authority to determine the sufficiency of the amount which was payable under section 5(1). [724F] 4. Section 6 (b) does no doubt confer power on the State legislature to enact a regulatory measure and consequently, the effect of section 7 is that thereby the Legislature has the exclusive right or privilege to manufacture, store and sell liquor and to grant that right to its license holders on payment of consideration with such conditions and restrictions for its regulation as may be necessary in the public interest. [789G H] 5. The Government had the exclusive power to regulate the manufacture and sale of country spirit. It is not a privilege of a citizen of the State to sell intoxicating liquors by retail, but only to the Central Government. [784C D] 6. Section 7(a), (b), (c) and (d) of s.22 of the Orissa Excise (Second Amendment) Act, 1970 are ultra vires the Act. The impugned judgment is set aside and writ petitions Nos. O.J.C. 2091 of 1972 are allowed, the judgment of the High court dated April 16. 1971 is set at naught. [783G H; 784A] 7. Section 8(1)(b), which has been inserted with retrospective operation, does not empower the State Govt. to accept payment of a sum in excess of the quota fixed under section 28(1), and it has expressly provided that no grant shall be made by the Government on payment.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 302 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 19th December 1967 one of the accused, a friend of deceased Narendra and his wife, had gone to Bombay for his business in the manufacture of medicines. The Manager of the said house searched the house of the appellant and recovered a cycle from him. The appellant was further charged with having committed theft of articles in the house. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 120 B read with sections 302, 454 and 201 of the I.P.C. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder and that the evidence of the deceased was not corroborated by the evidence against him. HELD: (i) The appellant had been rightly convicted under section 201 read with s.120B of I. P.C., [619 A] (ii) There was no motive for the appellant to commit theft. The evidence of PW 2 that he and his son were seen alive by Kewal Ram, owner of the betel shop on 26th December, 1967, is not corroborated in material particulars. The High Court found that there were no corroboration in regard to the crime. [620 B] (iii) There is no corroboration as to the actual complicity in the crime with the crime and the evidence must confirm that part of the testimony which suggests that the crime was committed by the accused. If a witness says that the accused and he stole the sheep and he put the skins in a certain place, the discovery of the skins would not corroborate the evidence. [625 E] (iv) The High court found that the death of Narendra and the theft were proved beyond doubt. There was also no corroboration to the evidence regarding the crime as well as the common intention by way of a pre conceived plan to murder Narendra. The nature of corroboration is that it is confirmatory evidence and it may consist of the evidence in material details to connect the accused with the time. When it is said that the corroborative evidence must implicate or tend to connect an accused with his crime, the court must satisfy that there is nothing inherently impossible in evidence. The rule as to corroboration is based on the reasoning that there must be sufficient corroborative evidence in materials particulars to connect a person with the commission of crime. In the present case, the evidence washerman and not that of a woman who had been fair skin and wore khaki shorts and white shirt. [613 E F] (v) The evidence on record did not establish any infirmity in the evidence which connected the murder of Narendra. It was also found that he was seen alive when the crime took place. The identification of the cycle by accused No. 2 was as a result of a statement by accused NO. 2. The name of accused No 3 was found in the note book of Takali 's shop. The shirt and chain were identified by the witness. [512 G H] (vi) There were no corroborative evidence to connect accused No 1 with murder. The recovery of the stolen articles from his house was not challenged in cross examination. It is obvious that the identity of the articles recovered from the house was doubtful. The identity of accused NO 3 could not be established by circumstantial evidence. In view of the fact that there had been no corroboration, the conviction of appellant No. 1 under section 2(g) of the Evidence Act must be set aside and he acquitted.

The appellant was the owner of a Hindu undivided family. He had been granted a sanction to the draft scheme under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 (Bombay Act No. 1 of 1954) for the purpose of acquiring his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. yard. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2 per sq., by his order dated November 4, 1971. On appeal, the Town Planning officer held that the appeal was not maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of the Town planning Officer on matters dealt with by him in his order. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Gujarat High Court which dismissed the same holding that the Act does not provide for an appeal against a decision by the Town Plan officer on matters dealing with by the parties and that the provisions of sections 32, 33 and 34 have a direct bearing on the question of appealability of the town planning scheme. The High Court held that section 32(1) provides an appeal only to the Town planner who is given a plot in the final scheme and not to the final plot holder. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Town Commis sioner 's decision was appealable under clause (viii) or clause (xiii) of section 32 (1); (ii) the Act specifies a principle of compensation, and (iii) the High Court erred in holding that enactment of a rule determining compensation payable to an owner for loss of land has to be determined on the basis of market value of the land on the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating the compensation payable by persons interested in the scheme estimated on the market value on the dates of the declaration of the intention to making a scheme, and section 64 (1) prescribes an additional amount of loss to be paid to an owners of land who are injuriously affected by the making of a town planning Scheme. [92F] 2. The object of determining compensation is to make provision for estima tion or adjustment of price of land of which the owner was deprived by the scheme estimate on the valuation of the lands under section 66. Section 73 provides that the owner shall, after notice given by him, pay to the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the par ties. The rate of interest is fixed at 6 per cent per annum. [93G H] 3. The provisions of Ss. 32 and 34 are intended to provide for estimations of compensation payable in respect of any property acquired under a scheme estimated at its market value and the net amount of such loss shall be payable to the owner by "the local authority" in cash, or in any other way, as may from time to time be agreed on by the party". The rate is fixed on the assumption that the scheme has been completed on that basis. [94H; 95A] 4. Section 64(1)(f) provides that where the owner or person interested in a land is not given a reconstituted plot, he shall be allotted to another person and the lands needed for public purposes may be earmarked for those purposes. Under section 65(2), the compensation is determined on an annual basis. The amount of compensation is payable on the value of a plot used by the owner for the purposes of the scheme. [95F G] 5. Section 66 provides that in determining the amount of compensa tion to be awarded for land acquired under that Act, the damage sustained by the "person interested" shall be determined after taking into account the improvements contemplated in the Scheme. The increment is a principle applicable to all cases in which by virtue of operation of the Act a person is deprived of his property whether in whole or in part.

The appellant was the brother of his grand son, who died in 1934 leaving two daughters. The widow filed a suit for partition of land according to her share and for mesne profits. The appellant contended that the daughters were entitled to their lands taking into account the provisions of the will to select their respective shares and that the appellant was entitled to the lands taking them as his son. Held, that the testator 's heirs had no right to make a selection in respect of the properties which they were entitled. The testator 'had only an option to select the land to be given to each son and therefore there could not be any question of the legatees making the selection. Narayanasami Gramani vs Hindle, Mad. 981, approved. Narayana Krishna Moideen vs Hinde, Mad 980, referred to. The will was a will by which the testator appointed his brother as guardian of his minor daughters as well as his foster son as also two other sons. The question whether the legate were entitled under the will was one for election to the Court and not for the daughters to make the selection, but only for the daughter to make it clear that the intention of the testator was clearly to select her son and not to appoint a third person to make selection. The nomination of the appellant did not amount to an appointment by the legatee under the Will to select his nearest heir.

The appellant, a widow of one B, filed a suit for joint possession over the land in dispute. The respondents contested the suit and pleaded that the defendants were in separate occupation of the land or plots in dispute and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to any share out of the produce and, therefore, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. The District Judge decreed the plaintiff 's suit for a joint possession of the lands in dispute but the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in law in holding that there had been no evidence on record to prove that the appellant was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the respondents assured the plaintiff that her name shall be entered in the record during consolidation proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court erred in Law in holding the suit was barred by section 49 of the Act. [867D] 2. The possession of B apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of his sons as co sharers would be deemed in law to be the possession thereof. [886E] 3. In the instant case, the High Courts had held that the possession was not given by the defendants because they were co sharer of plaintiff 'S ' and the respondents had absolutely any concern with the appellant giving her an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. [876G] 4. The fact remains that the District Judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during consolidation operation either by the respondents or somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. In this connection, the District Court found as follows: (1) The possession was never given to the plaintiff by the defendant, as the defendants had no concern in the rent and profits of the suit land of a co shar holder; (2) the plaintiff has not been informed about the consolidation proceedings and was assured by the plaintiff. [877B] 5. In view of the clear decision of this Court in Subha Singh vs Mahendra Singh & Ors., this Court is clearly wrong in holding on the basis of title, the courts will not easily infer a bar of suit to establish the title of the parties. [878E F] 6. The plaintiff ' s claim was that she had practised fraud on her by giving her another son, who had also sirdari tenants under them, how could the sirdars be removed from the land of one of the co shar holders leaving the defendants alone so that the plots were re allotted to them. It is well settled that unless there is an express provision barring a suit on the strength of title the courts would not easily inferred a bar to sue the other co sharars. [879F G] 7. The contention that after the chakbandi was completed under the U .P. consolidation of Holdings Rules, 1953, the suit is barred by Section 49 of that Act cannot be accepted. [881A B] 8.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Haryana. The first respondent filed an affidavit in support of the petition stating that he had been appointed Deputy Prime Ministers and that the oath administered to him as Deputy Prime Minis ters was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution. The petitioner also stated that he was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to the petitioner. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Ministry. [219G H] 2. The prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. This Court in Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , held that the prescribed oath must be divided amongst the Ministers and the description of the Prime Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Chief Secretary, along with his other submis sions, but the description as longas the other Ministers are required to take. He has no power of the President to make the affirmation. [319H; 319A B] 3. The practice which has been followed by this Court in the case of Virjiram Ram Sutle vs Nathellan Bhavadia and Ors., , is that the form prescribed in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of Article 75(4) is only for a Minister of the Union and there can be no separate form even for the Prime Ministers.

The appellant, a company which was carrying on the business of running and maintaining work, stopped work in the factory on 1st November, 1948, and closed it on that day. The dispute between the workmen and their employers was referred to the Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) (c) of the , for adjudication. The Tribunal held that there could be little doubt that the stoppage of work by the night shift workers on the night of 1st Nov., 1948, was a strike and therefore an illegal strike. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the action of the workers on 1 st November, 1949 fell within the definition of "strike" in section 2(q) of The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as it stood prior to its coming into force of the Factories Act, and the dispute was not a strike which could be said to be an illegal lock. Held, further, that on a proper construction of section 49 B (1) 29 222 of the Act, the action taken by the workers in the night intervening 1st December, 1948 and 31st November 1948, fell within that definition. The closure of the factory was not an illegal strikes and the workers were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under the said section inasmuch as they would have otherwise got under the rules. Held further, also that the strike was not illegal on account of the lock in the continuity of their service by the stoppage. The strike was a lock which was in accordance with the provisions of Ch. IV A of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, and it was an illegal closure.

The appellant, actor, was charged with offences under section 292 I.P.C., for having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors. The prosecution alleged that the famous picture was misleadingly foul and he had arrived at the scene of offence. The Magistrate after examining some witnesses, took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused under section 79 I. P.C. The appellant contended before the High Court that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the Act, there is a justification for its display thereafter and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 of the Penal Code, the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals are liberally certificated. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been certified by the Central Board of Film Censor and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious was a valid certificate under section 80 of the Code. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under the provisions of the Constitution and once the special law polices the area it is pro tanto out of bounds for the general law. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 does not come down to the ground that the certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 I.p.C.[515D E] 1.2 The High Courts in their judgment have taken the view that the facts stated in the complaint prima facie attract the offence under Section 292 I P. C., and therefore, the Court cannot legally sustain the displaying public exhibition. [516F G] 2.1 In the instant case, the prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. It is alsoXthogly wrong to hold that once the Special law policed the area, it is not to be regarded as an offence. [525F G; 526B] 2:2 The trial Court when itars the matter may be suitably apprised of its certificate under Section 5A(1A) and, in the light of our observations, it fills the bill under section79 it is right for the court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. [25G H; 26A] 2 :3 The trial courts when it theyars the cases may be properly apprised of their public duty, shall not play to the gallery; nor shall it restrain aesthetic expression and progressive art through obsolete norms and grandma inhibitions when the world is wheeling forward to glimpse the beauty of Creation in its myriad manifestations and liberal horizons. [26C D] 2 .4 The trial Courts when it comes under their jurisdiction and on an application made and pursued in good faith, sanctions the public exhibiting public exhibition the producer and connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 80 does not apply to the case groundless and gracefully enlarged to promote a riot of sensual display.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an Advocate on the ground that he had suffered from a acute shortage of work. The petitioner challenged the power of the Government under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court. The High Court declined to dispense with his personal appearance and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Government Pleader was not a party to the writ petition, (ii) the Advocate General had no locus standi to file an affidavit; (iii) the State Government was in error in holding that the Government pleader was not entitled to seek or cling out any other remedy; and (iv) the High Courts were wrong in holding the petitioner guilty of gross negligence of fee and mayhemence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Court is not exception. Since the rules stand, he has a number of other duties to discharge. [766D] 2. The Government Pleader is only an ordinary litigant and is not bound to encourage monopoly within the profession. It vests no sole control on one Government pleader over others and Government is perfectly free to put a particular Government pleader in charge of particular cases. Each one is a Government pleader under section 2(7) Code of Civil Procedure. It is heartening to notice that the State is expected to fight and win its cases and sheer patronage is misuse of power. [764D E] 3. The State, appreciating the need for a Government lawyer, should engage competent lawyers without hunting for political partisans regardless of capability. Public offices and Government Pleadership are both important stages in a developing society controlled by the politics of skill and enjoying a legal monopoly. [753G H] 4. The practice of a Government advocate is not to be concealed conspiracies with 'effete, aristocratic, protective color, arrival, sabotage, p 37, if they are opposed affectionately or indirectly. [774A B] 5. The Supreme Court has power under article 136 of the Constitu tion to interfere with the order and subvert the rule of law itself. After all, a government Pleader and in a sense, every member of the legal profession has a higher dedication to the people. [773C D] 6. The court is expected not to sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number or pleader on its behalf for the sake of convenience. [763D] 7. The very judicial journey vindicates the short and ill defined functions covered much that later would crystallize out into new, specialised occupations. [765E] 7(i) The Government pleader is more than an advocate for a litigant. He holds a public office. It has no exception. [761G H; 761A B]. (ii). The State Government and other public sector undertakings have been given the right to appoint any person who has a crowd of cases to be conducted, their engagements in court proceedings even as any client, who has already been convicted by the court for contempt of court is a dignified renunciation of office. [762C D]. (iii). The Government Pleaders and Assistant Government Pleader are appointed according to administrative rules of the State. They have to perform their duties with reasonable promptitude and efficiency in the administration. [759E] (iv).

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Mills held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the bank and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by the shareholders. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., which was a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50 per share and the shares were allotted at a lesser rate. The respondent No. 1, who was a Public limited company, filed an application under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the issue of bonus shares on the ground that the release by the Mills of the shares of its shareholders amounted to distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income of the seven appellants and of other shareholders of their company as dividend on the footing that the releasing by the mills was dividend within the definition of that expression in section 2 (6A). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the distribution of the right to apply for the shares had a market value of Rs 100 per share but the shares could not be distributed amongst the shareholders as dividend within that meaning. In reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the appellants. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The definition of "Dividend", in section2(6 A), is a distributive share of the profits or income of a company given to its shareholders. When the Legislature by section 2, (6 A) sought to define the expression "dispute" it added to the normal meaning of the expression several other categories of receipts which may not otherwise be included therein. By the definition in section 3(6a), "drugend" means dividend as normally understood and includes in its connotation several other receipts set out in the definition. The word "d Undivided ' is defined in section 617 of the Companies Act, 1913, as inclusive of various items and exclusive of certain others which it is not necessary to set out for the purpose of this appeal. [588 E F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the distributed by the appellants amounted to a distribution of dividend within its ordinary meaning.

The appellant was defeated. The election petitioner filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent, the returned candidate, on the ground that the names of the witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present in Court without any order of the Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that except the appellant, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the appellant was recorded, the Court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidates; and thereafter, the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the parties. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf the appellant that (1) the purpose of section 87(1) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 must satisfy the requirements of section 83 and 84 of the Act, and (2) the Court must ascertain how far sub rule (3) would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1A of Order XVI. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The scheme of the various provisions of the , is that after the court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list of witnesses with the gist of evidence of each witness in the Court within the time prescribed by sub rule(1). But where the party would be in a position to produce its witnesses without the assistance of the court, it can do so under Rule 1 A of Order XVIII. [532C D] (b) The purpose of the Rules is to provide for the examination of witnesses within the period prescribed under sub rule 1 of Rule 1 of order XVI and Rule 22 of the High Court Rules would not have omitted to mention that only those witnesses kept present could be examine whose names are mentioned in a list prepared by subrule (1). [533E] (c) The consequence is that where the witness summoned either to give evidence or to produce documents fails to attend or to do so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings, the court on being satisfied of the service as provided therein and is further satisfied that the person has without lawful excuse failed to honour the summons, the trial as provided in sub rule 2 of Order XVII would be a proclamation requiring him to attend to give his evidence or produce documents without applying for summons under Rule I. If it was implicit in Rule IA that it only enables the party to examine only those persons whose names were mentioned in that list, the person who wanted to produce the witnesses could not be allowed to do such witness on the date of hearing and the court cannot decline to examine the witness unless the Court proposes to act under the proviso to sub rule.(1) or (2).

The appellant, a teacher of the Intermediate College, was appointed on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay of Rs. 550 1200. The appointment order stated that he had assumed charge of the post of Principal and he had convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on April 12, 1981. The appellant submitted his application for appointment to the post. The Manager of the College informed him that as per the communication received by him from the Manager of his college, he had been appointed as Principal and that he has convened an emergency meeting of its staff to consider his suitability for appointment. The manager of the college wrote to the Manager that since the appellant was not willing to hold the post, he should be given one year 's notice. The management did not pay any salary to the appellant though he functioned as Principal. The Management did not make any reference to the fact that the order contained in the radiogram was communicated to the manager of his College. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the date on which appellant was appointed as principal, the Committee of Management had no power to make appointment and therefore the appointment of the appel lant could not be invalidated, and that in any case once appointment was made, the appointment would be valid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The order dated April 7, 1981 contained in Annexure P.B.I. is not in dispute. [975C] 1.2 In view of the finding that sub section (4) of section 9 did confer power on the Committee to make appointments, the order became effective only with effect from April 27, 1981 and the appointment was therefore valid. The resolution dated May 1, 1981 which has been extracted above clearly shows that on April 7 1981 the order contains an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions. [ 975D] 1:3. The power to appoint is conferred by the regulations.

The respondent, a textile mill, was assessed to sales tax on the ground that it had wrongly escaped assessment. The Sales Tax officer rejected the contention of the respondent and held that the goods were not the "end product" within the meaning of the Act so that the appellate authority could go into the whole evidence and decide disputed questions of fact. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court was right in not interfering with the decision of the taxing authorities at this stage. The taxing authorities had the power to decide the question before them either rightly or wrongly. The High Court could not interfere under article 226 of the Constitution on the grounds that no disputed questions arose. The respondent was entitled to a writ of certiorari as it was the stage reached by this product in the process of manufacture of fabrication of a "textile" which should decide the questions satisfactorily and decided disputed questions. The State of Rajasthan vs M/s. Delhi Cloth Mills Co., Ltd., ; , referred to. The definition of "textiles" given in the Oxford Dictionary is "a textile". It must acquire a body and a texture. Presumably it is more than that. But against pushing this point of view, the High Courts were right in holding that the taxing authority had committed error apparent on the face of record. The interpretation of the word "totton" given by the Delhi Cloth Mill was correct. The context in which the entry occurs shows that it is meant for "toollen fabrics". The term fabric has a wide meaning and its first meaning given in tile Oxford Dictionary, is: "A textile fabric" means any kind of cloth". It is true that the term fabric had a wide connotation. Its first meaning was that the tyre fabric should be a fabric or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. A sample of the tyre cord fabric was actually produced before the assessing authority and it became the raw material for the tailors ' manufacture. The fact that the tyres cord fabric may be so well established a category of rayon "fabric" does not appear to give the exact meaning of "feel". It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "tyre cord fabric" and an evaluation of opinion of experts on the subject.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising out of the said incident was referred to Labour Court, Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered a reference under section 10(1)(c) of the , and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. The appellant contended that it would be difficult for him to attend the labour court regularly at Dhanbad and that transfer of the case from the Labour Court to the Labour court, Patna should have given an opportunity to the management before transferring the case to the labour Court, Patna. The Management contested the petition contending that no reasons were stated for passing the order. The High Court did not agree with the contention and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no reason was given for passing an order transferring the cases from one Tribunal to another without hearing the parties, and that the Government had withdrawn the pending case from Labour Court Dhanbad and transferred it to another Labour Court at Patna. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that the government was misled by the representation of the workman. [297G] 1.2 In workman of Punjab State vs Labour Court; , ; , the Calcutta High Court had expressed the view that for application of rules of natural justice the classification of functions as quasi judicial is not necessary. The principles of natural Justice are fundamental in the concept inherent in the exercise of a judicial power. [298H] 1:3. In work man of Punjab Chheharta vs Varty, ; , referred to. 1.4. The principle of natural justi fication is that in a democratic set up, the fairness of procedure should be fair and not arbitrarily or capriciously. [300A B] 1.(i) It is a rule to ensure the vast power in the modern state is not abused but properly exercised. The doctrine of natural law is flexible and it is intended for improving the quality of government by ensuring that the statutory authority arrives at a just decision either in promoting the interest or affecting the rights of persons. To use the time hallowed phrase "that justice should not only be done but be seen to be done" is the essence of fairness equally applicable to administrative authorities. [301C D] (ii) The doctrine has been evolved by this Court as a result of which the concept of natural right is virtually a fundamental principle of good administration. It is intended to protect the interests of the people and to ensure that there should be just and fair decision. [302E F] 1(iii) The principles are fundamental principles of good management. They are fundamental rights. They have been recognised as alternatives to "natural justice" without drawing any distinction. There is no right to any party to have any question decided by a particu lar forum. An arbitrary exercise of power and the decision must be based on objective considerations. [304G] 2.1 In workmen of Punjab Act, 1961, there are two High Courts decisions in which the expression "judicial review" has been defined as an appellate authority. The Court held that for purposes of application of these provisions of the Act, a classification of function as quasi administrative is not essential to the fairness in action and discretionary executive justice cannot degenerate into unilateral injustice. [305B] 2(i) In work men 's case, this court had expressed its view that the principles of " natural justice" know how the principles are implied by the duty to act fairly and fairly. The requirement of acting judicially in essence is nothing but a requirement to act justly and fairly and not arbitrary or capricically. [306C] 2.(ii) In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the cases pending against the Labour Commissioner, Dhanbad and transfer it to the High Court Patna.

The appellant company was the manager of a hotel and its workmen were the Chief Commissioner, Delhi. The dispute between the appellant and its employees related to the payment of bonus to them. The company contended that the reference was incompetent as two grounds had been urged in support of it; one was that the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and the other was that there was no dispute between it and its workers, and the second ground was that no notice of dismissal had been given to the workmen. Held, that the question whether the reference is incompetent was a mere technicality upon technicality, for the union not being a living person can only be served through some officer or servant of a trade union connected with, or by any other workman employed in the industry in which the workman is employed. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy (A.I.R. , approved. State Of Madras vs V. C.P. Sarathi, A.I R. and State of Madura vs C P Sarathy, A I R. , referred to. Held further that the dispute was not a mere legal one and the reference did not become incompetent merely because it was mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the dispute. The nature of the dispute is also specified in the terms of reference. State vs C, P.S. Sarthy, A,I R., , referred only to the dismissal etc. of particular workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi, and not on any other union.

The appellant imported a part of the engines mentioned in Heading No. 8406, and claimed benefit of Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 2 8 1976 as amended by Notification No, 281 C. Ex., dated 1 9 1976. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the said Notification. The Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appel lant. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the imported parts of the engine or engines mentioned under Heading No 84.06 were exempt from payment of duty as provided in the Notification. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Notification grants exemption in part from payment to a certain extent of the customs duty. [225B] 2.1 The Notification does not mention 'parts thereof '. Non mention of 'part ' in Heading 84.07 is excluded from the benefit under the Notification.[226C D] 2(a) The Notification will apply to parts of engines mentioned thereunder, and not to Parts thereof. [227D] 2.(b) The intention of the Notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of engine, mentioned under heading No.84.06, will get the benefit thereof. The words 'partes thereof ' are excluded from Heading No., 84.05. [226F G] 2 (c) The notification will apply only to parts in respect of which the exemption is claimed, and also to 'part parts thereof. In other words, the Notification will not apply to the parts. [228G] 2:2. The intention is clear that the part of a engines, mentioned in heading No.,84.07, will got the benefit Of exemption under the notification irrespective of the fact that they or any or some of them have already been included under Heading NO. 84.04 or under any other Heading. Therefore, even if bushings are the same as bearings, still they would come within the purview of the notification provided they are parts of such engines mentioned. [229B C] 2 :3. The expression 'part of the Engine ' occurring in Heading NO., 8406 not only contemplates the engine and engines, but also the parts thereof.[230D E] 2 4. The contention that the article referred to in paragraph 2 of column (2) of the Table must be all the parts or any of some of the parts, of the cage or engines in question, is without any force. [230E F] 5. The notification would apply to part of engines, which must be only all the part constituting the engine, or engines, and it also mentions the parts which are not so constituted. [231F G].

The right of management was divided between the two sons each taking six months ' share in the offerings made by their father and the son. The first defendant was a Mujawar and was receiving the offerings by right of inheritance. After his death, the plaintiffs 1 and 2 were entitled to 3/4th share each. The second defendant was also entitled to one half share each in the profits of the Dargah. The plaintiffs filed a suit against the defendants for declaration that they were entitled only to the property of the said Dargah. According to the plaintiffs, the said property belonged to their father who had two sons and one daughter. The trial court decreed the suit and in appeal, the High Court held that the courts below proceeded on an erroneous assumption that the Courts below proceeded upon an erroneous conclusion as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster has been established. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts proceeded on a wrong assumption that if really the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by limitation, all the rights had become extinguished; (ii) the defendants were entitled under section 14(1)(c) to have their own management of the suit Dargah and (iii) the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathina Bee had lost their right by ouster. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Courts committed a serious error in reversing the finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the basis of judgment and decree given in Suit No. 116 of 1909 and on the ground that Fathita Bee was a co sharer in the right of the offerings in the Dargah and that the plaintiffs were entitled in the rights to perform the duties of Mujawar of the respondent Dargah. [525F G] 2. The appellants and their counsel Shri Tarkunde have drawn attention to paragraph 19 of the written statement filed by the respondents in the suit which is totally lacking in the particulars and thus apart from the want of evidence, there was no proper pleading of ouster in the present case. There is no proper pleadings of ouster as such in the instant case. [526G] 3. The Trial Court had proceeded on erroneous assumption and held ouster on a correct basis. It cannot be said that the High court was right in holding that the rights were not entitled to any right of ownership or possession in the respondent 's Dargah. It is an admitted case of the parties that the appellants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not enti tled to any share in their management or offerings in their offerings. [25H; 26A] 4. The respondents are entitled to have the manage ment of the appellant Dargah from 17th to 30th June and 1st to 13th July in the year 1990 and 18th to 31st June and 30th to 14th July, in the next year. To be more precise the plaintiffs would be entitled to having their right of possession or offerings of the plaintiffs of Fila Bee or the plaintiffs. [26D E] 5. The suit was not barred by section 14 (1)(C) of the . [27F G].

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was charged with house rent allowance for 10 months and dearness allowance. The first respondent contended that the house rent allowances were not wages within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the , as it was not payable to an employee who occupied Government quarters or to those to whom accommodation had been offered by the Government but who had refused it, and that therefore the claim for house rent was allowed by the Authority. The Authority held that the first respondent 's house rent could not be said to be "wages" within the definition of "wages". On appeal the Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Authority and directed the Authority to pay house rent at certain specified rates. The appellant contended that (i) the terms of the contract between the parties included the rule of " Rates" as defined in section 2 (vi) and therefore the position in law was that there was no absolute right in the first respond ent to claim the house allowance; (ii) the rules which must be included in the terms Of the contract were inconsistent with some of the terms thereof, and (iii) the rule did not make it unconditional and absolute in terms. Held, that the rule laid down by the Railway Board was inconsistent with any provision of the Act and was not ultra vires the Government 's right to claim house rent. The definition of 'wages ' contained in section 3(i) of Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, includes "any bonus or other additional remuneration of the nature referred to in sections 7 and 11 as well". Section 7 of the said Act prohibits an employee from entering into such a contract as has the effect of depriving him of his vested rights. The rule does not make any distinction between a house rent and any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee; otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages.

The detenu was detained under the . The grounds of detention were served on him. He filed a writ petition in this Court challenging his detention mainly on the ground that he had been denied an opportunity to make an effective representation against his detention. This was dismissed by a single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the detenu that (i) the grounds of the detention were as elaborate as possible and that the supply of copies of all the relevant documents had not been supplied to him; (ii) the supply was conclusions drawn from facts and not matters of detail or any other matter which is not referred to or relied upon in the grounds; and (iii) the detenu 's representation dated March 24, 1980 was considered by the Advisory Board constituted under section 3(1) of the . Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus mechanically refused as desired by the Collector, to supply the copies. [351 D] 2. The detenu had asked for copies of the full text of those statements. It was on receiving a direction from the Central Government that the copies were supplied. On account of this chill indifference and arbitrary refusal, the detenu, who had applied for copies on February 18, 1980, could get the same only on March 27, 1980 i.e., after more than one month. Thus there was unreasonable delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the detenus. [352 E F] 3. The mere fact that the grounds were not supplied to the detenu with reasonable expedition to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest, did not absolve the detaining authority from its constitutional responsibility to supply all the basic facts and materials relied upon or referred to in those "grounds" to the detenue, and it was on this short ground that there was inordinate delay of nearly three weeks. [353 G] 4. The failure to apply its mind vitiates the order of detention. [354 A B] Khudiram Das vs State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant State filed a joint appeal against the acquittal of several accused persons, and the High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by the sections was against the maintainability of a joint appeals by the State against an order acquitting several accused person. The question for determination in this appeal was whether several accused were acquitted by the trial court, and if the High court rejected the appeal without going into the merits. HELD : (i) Section 419 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not in terms cover the case of an appeal by the state against several accused. [878 C] (ii) The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Courts by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C. and r. 6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. [873 D] (iii) Section 417 which provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal empowers the State Government to direct the public prosecutor in any case to present an appeal from an order of acquittal. This section also does not appear to indicate any bar or prohibition against presentation of a Joint appeal against several persons acquitted in a ease. [874 E] (iv) The High Court was wrong in holding that the joint appeal by several accused was incompetent. [872 G] (v) Section 418 of the code on which the High is said to have been made applicable, does not contemplate a joint application for a joint hearing by all the accused persons jointly tried and acquitted by a common order, but if an appeal against more than one accused person is competent, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in India and in the former Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The income of the assessee from the said business was not liable to be taxed by reason of section 25(3) of the Act. The Income tax Officer accepted the fact that the entire profits of the foreign business came to be assessed in the hands of the appellant under the 1918 Act and it was also charged under the 1922 Act read with the appropriate Finance Act, resulting in double taxation in respect of the income for the year 1921 22. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3) Of the 1922 Income tax Rules, 1922. On a reference made by the High Court, the High court held that the foreign income could be deemed to have been charged under section 3 of the 1918 act only when there was an assessment to tax on the foreign profits and there was no tax on such income. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the appellant was entitled to the relief under s 25(4) of 1922 Act except for the income received from the house properties in Malaya which was discontinued in the year of account, and that the income derived by the assessee in respect his activity styled foreign business was liable to tax under the provisions of the 1922 act. HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that section 25 of the Income tax 1961 Act was applicable even if the person assessed under that Act was different from the person who claims relief under that section provided the former was the predecessor in interest of such person in relation to the business. [910 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , followed. (ii) The income derived from foreign business is not liable under the 1961 Act because the assessee received the entire profit of the Indian business at Penang, and Kambar. Therefore, the assessee is entitled to both parts of relief contemplated under section 2(2)(a) of that Act in respect Of the foreign 'business in British India and the income from the foreign firm which was discontinuance in the previous year of accounts. [936 D] (iii) The question whether the foreign company was liable under section 5(3), of the 1961 Income tax is not relevant to the present case because, the income was received by the appellant as a receipt under section 6 of the earlier Act. [981 E] Commissioner Of Income tax vs sectionV.R., M. Palanappa Chettiar & Ors., , followed and applied. (iv) The assessee was entitled only to relief in respect the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign partner which was continued under different heads only for the purpose of computation of the total income. By virtue of the provisions Of the 1918 Income tax 1922 Act, the charge was made on the receipt of income in British Indian and as the income had been discontinued in 1955, it must be taken to be impliedly over ruled by the recent decision of this Court in Commissioner of Incometax, Madras V. section V R.M., Palaniappan Chettiar & Others, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R, 912.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of a capital project. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959, on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, to determine whether the supplies of bricks were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supplies were not sales and that the supply was for the best quality and in strict accordance with the specification and price specifications. The respondent appealed to the Tribunal which held that supplies of brick bats were sales and works contract and therefore, the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department was a sale or works contracts. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction contemplated by the Contract entered into between the applicant and the Public Work Department of Government was a works contract, and not a works contracts and therefore the transaction was a contract of sale and not works contract; and that as the contract was for sale or work contract it had to be handed over back to the Government after manufacturing of the brick work is completed. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a contract for sale and the works contract is not a Works Contract. The appellant is liable to sales tax. [165G] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. 2.1 The contract entered between the appellant and the public works department of the Govern ment was a transaction of sale of bricks and not work contract. There was no contract for the sale of brickbats. The Government in its overall interest and anxiety for general welfare could insist on compliance with certain beneficial legal measures. It could also insist on certain terms which will ensure efficient production of the material. provision against subletting when the land was given free by Government is also understandable. All the features do not negate the concept of a contract. [166H; 167A] Chandra Mohan Gosain 's case, ; referred to and all the features did not negate tile concept of contract of sales of bricks that are ultimately manufactured. The true test in this ease is whether in making the contract to brick produced was transferred as a chattel for consideration and we are clearly of opinion that this has taken place in this appeal. [167D E] Chandra Bhushan Gosain & Ors. vs State Of Bihar, ; , distinguished.

The President of India promulgated the Emergency Commission on March 25, 1971 under Article 352 of the Constitution. The President issued a proclamation of emergency on March 3, 1977 in exercise of powers conferred by sub clause (a) of clause (2) of article 352 of Constitution of India. Clause (1) of Article 352 was substituted for the original clause (c) of that Article which was later amended by the Constitution (Amendment) Act, 1976. Clause 2 of the said Article provided that if the President was satisfied that a grave emergency existed whereby the security of India was threatened, whether by war or external disturbance, he might by proclamation make a declaration to that effect. Clause 3 of the Emergency Com mission on March 31, 1971 provided that the period of five years in relation to the then House of the People shall be extended for a period of one year "on such terms and conditions as may be determined by the President. The petitioner who was an assessee under the Income tax Act, 1961, challenged the validity of the proclamation of Emergency on the ground that the duration of the House of People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of emergency was in force under Article 356 of the constitution of India and since the proclamation had ceased to be in force on March 1, 1971, the President 's assent was not obtained. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proclamation was valid and that the validity could not be questioned by any subsequent proclamation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the two Proclamations of Emergency were validly issued under Article 359 of the Constitu tion and since they had been duly revoked by the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament, the validity cannot be challenged. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proclamation of the emergency was not in force when the House was dissolved or dissolution of the Legislative Assembly of India or the Speaker of the Assembly of States or the House or the Assembly thereof. [445C] 2. The effect of the Proclamation of Emergency had been that the security and the report of the proceedings of Parliament were duly revoked. The Lok Sabha Debates and the Rajya Sabha Debates contain the proceedings in the Legislative Council of Parliament and the State Legislatures gave them ample publicity. The reports of the Proceedings of Parliament are widely circulated. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament. [454E F] 3. The publication in the official Gazette of the Bills of Parliament is not a sine qua non for giving such publicity. It is open to him to publish a notification issued by him under Article 174(2) or article 356 of Constitution, as the case may be. [453G H] 4. The two Pro clamations are kept in force by virtue of the resolutions of both Houses. The Bills of the Houses of the Parliament and of the State Legislature established under any laws for the time being in force in a Province or in the State. [452H; 453A B] 5.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the authorities. The High Court held that the property was a public temple within the meaning of Madras Act II of 1927, and that the suit was not maintainable under section 84(2) of the Madras Act 11 of 1927. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the question whether the property in dispute was a private or a public trust could have no market value and therefore was incapable of valuation. HELD: The High court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that the properties were private or public temple. [156 B] (a) The question whether a private property is incapable of valued depends upon the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property is the private property of the family capable of alienation, the High Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to them the property belonged to the Thoguluva family capable Of alienation. [157 C] (b) The appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit is the public temple and not a public Temple as held by the High court. The question for consideration is whether the High Courts were right in holding that the land in question belonged to Thoguva family or was a Public temple. The appellant had also relied on the observations made in the judgment of this Court in the case of G. R. 155, which are not applicable to the present case. [158 D E] (c) The High Courts have proceeded on the basis that the disputed property belonged exclusively to the family and it was incapable for valuation. But as observed earlier the appellant ' s claim was that he had in his possession municipal receipts showing the property tax paid to the Madurai Municipality. According to him, property tax for the half year ending September 30, 1950 was Rs. 94 0 6 and for the first time it was increased to Rs. 1,672.32nP in 1961. If that be so, capitalising that value at twenty times the annual rental value would come to more than Rs. 20,000/ .

The appellant, a non gazetted employee of the respondent company, was appointed as a clerk in a clerical staff. On an application made by him under section 33 of the Factories Act, 1948, the Industrial Tribunal granted him the relief claimed by him. The appellant contended that the practice started by the appellant of re employing retired persons should be discontinued and that the said practice was being followed in many cases and that it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffinition of its employees. Held, that the appellant 's grievance against the direction in the award that as a result of the demand made by the respondents, the appellant should be paid wages in lieu of the workmen who were entitled to look forward was not justified under the Act. The fact that the re employed persons had made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant could have no bearing on the point. The question whether the practice of employing retired person was a matter which was within the discretion of the Tribunal and the appellant could not be blamed on that account; but there were some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored. The history of the relations between the parties coupled with the prevailing practice in the comparable concerns in the region strongly supports the view taken by the Tribunal that in the appellant company it was an implied condition of service that in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, a provision for tiffs should be made in that behalf. The result is that the question posed by the respondent 's demand must be considered.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Bank of India 's Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, the respondent applied for transfer of the money from the Reserve Bank of lndia to the Reserve bank. The Union of India claimed immunity from attachment of the cheques on the ground that they represented provident fund money long before they were attached and hence they were not immune from attachment. The Central Government rejected their claim holding that the money was immune from attach. The respondent thereupon applied for removal of attachment on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that they represent provident fund moneys which by section 3 of the , was immunefrom attachment; (2) that the Union of lstia had no interest in maintaining an application for removal and the attachment was illegal as it was not made out to his credit in the Provident Funds. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1)(a) The Union 's claim that they were immune from attached under section 3 was not barred from attachment because the Union had no interests in maintaining the application for removing attachment. [32 B] (b) The respondent 's case was a trustee for the subscriber of the amount standing to his account as the agent of the Railway Administration and not as the first intimation at Liverpool by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of the Bank. [33 C D] (c) The Central Govern ment had no right in maintaining application for remove ing attachment. But the Union 'of India was a Trustee for the subscribers of the moneys which were converted into sterling and were transmitted by the ReserveBank to Browne, the money remained at the disposal of the railway Administration. [34 E F] (d) The Bank was in respect of the provident fund amount on retirement. The Reserve Bank was the agent. of the Railways Administration for conversion of the amounts into sterling. The debt was discharged as soon as the money became payable. The payment was required either under the first information report or under section 60(1)(k) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [35 G] (e) The High Courts were in error in holding that money in the hands of the Reserve Officer of the appellant had ceased to be provident fund and was liable to be attached. [36 C D].

The appellant was employed as a pump operator in the respondent company. He was charged with misconduct of misappropriation and misappropriation of certain amount paid to him by the company without damning, as distinguished from dismissing him for misconduct. The management found that the appellant had failed to prove his guilt and dismissed him for mis conduct. The Labour Court held that the termination of services of the appellant was illegal and therefore the respondent was not guilty of any misconduct. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of dismissal but on a further appeal by the Management, the High Court held in favour of the management. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the termination was legal and immune to judicial interference; (ii) the respondent had lost confidence in the employee; (iii) the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the Labour court; and (iv) the appellant has merit on merits. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in setting aside the impugned order of the Labour 'Court. [497G] 2.1 The respondent workman was an intolerable person undesirable to be retained for misconduct as a colourable exercise of power by the management and the appellant could not have any merit on that score. [498A B] 3.2 In the instant case, the termination order was not bona fide. The termination was in accordance with the provisions of the Standing Orders. The respondent had not dis closed the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968. Further after 1968, the appellant remained silent and did not even file a counter affidavit. Therefore, the management could not be said to have lost confidence on the appellant. [501C D] 3(i) In the present case, there was no specious attempt by the employer that he had lost faith in the appellant 's employee. The appellant had not been given any notice with regard to the dismissal of his union activities. There is only the ipse dixit of the employer and that the Labour Courts have the power to interfere and set matters fight. [500D E] (ii). In the absence of a clear allegation of mala fides, unfair labour practice or victimisation, the Court cannot shut out the finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point. The findings of the trial Court are not vitiated either in law or in fact. The order of termination is therefore illegal and liable to be set aside. [ 500E F] (iii). In a reasonable case of a confidential or responsible post being misused or a sensitive or strategic position being abused, it may be a high risk to keep the employee, once suspicion has started and a disciplinary action cannot be forced on the master. There, a termination simpliciter may be bowli with due care and caution. If the management, to cover up the inability to establish by an enquiry, illegitimately but ingeniously passes an innocent looking order of terminating the services, terminates his service even though he might have only a good word for his employees. The power of the Court to go behind the language of the order is preserved and must be exercised by the employee objectively in good faith which means honestly with due regard and ' prudence.

The petitioner, a retired Government employee, was appointed as an Assistant Surgeon in the District Hospital. On 21st April, 1986, he was posted at the Campus of the hospital. He was transferred to Delhi where he was on deputation and continued to work as such till his discharge. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the transfer order contending that the victims of this medical mishap were not given any opportunity of being heard and that the doctors, who had been allowed to go back immediately after the operations, had been injured in the hospital by the doctors. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the patients were entitled to get a fixed percentage of the scale possible and evolve proper guide lines for the conduct of eye camps. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the guidelines laid down by the Union Government on 9th February, 1988 had been violated as the doctors were allowed to hold free eye camps in the hospitals and that they were not entitled to claim any additional payment. Dismissing the writ Petition, HELD: 1. The Revised norms issued by the union Government on September 8, 1986 have been updated and revised. [234D] 2.1 The Revised guidelines dated 9th2, 1988 with the suggested modifications are these: (a) The doctors should be given some monitary relief by the State Government; (b) the doctors should also be afforded some monaster in emergency; (c) the medical treatment should be provided to the patients with attraction of the improved facilities and the destitute, sub ject to the condi tions for the health implicit in standards; and (d) the further question whether in such cases of mass use, a pre test for safety and purity of the article was necessary and whether failure to do so would be action able. [235E F] 2.(a) It is not correct to say that the State should provide some mono ry relief by way of restitution or action for negligence on the part of the doctors or others against whom the existing schemes now in force in the State, their cases shall be considered for such benefit. The State would indeed be willing to render help to the victims within the constraints of its resources. [236F] (b). The guidelines issued by Union Government are not intended to ensure the protection of the patients who are generally drawn from the poorer and less affluent section of society or whether any further guide lines would require to be evolved. After the institution of these proceedings Central Government, in the wake of reports of mishaps in 'Eye Camps ', constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of the Union Health Minister with six members, who were present at the meeting, to re examine and updated the existing guidelines or evolve fresh ones. The Committee considered the issues and recommended modifications. [237H; 238A] (c). The recommendations made by the sub committee are these. [238D] (d).

The appellant No. 1, a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1984, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly in March 1983 and elected to be a member of the Samiti from the very inception. The appellant No 1 filed an election petition before the High Court challenging the action taken by the respondent No. 2 on the ground that the election was vitiated because of the dissolution of the Society declared and declared as a result of which the President of the Samities had been elected. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned Act and the Rules framed thereunder were passed in contravention of the provisions of the Bidhan (Constitu tion) Order, 1984 inasmuch as it was passed on 17.7.83 after the passing of the Act and that a fresh Government came into existence in the Samiti in exercise of his powers under section 16(G) of the said Act. The appellants have come to this Court by way of special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant No 2 that since the election had been brought about by the President amendment, the impugned order could not be granted and fixed 13.8.84 as the date for showing cause. On behalf of respondent No 1 it was submitted that the procedure stated in the Act was followed and the Chief Minister of Assam was the ex officio Chairman of the Committee appointed under section 3 of the Bihar Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (taking over of Management and Control) Act,1984. It is further contended that since there was mismanagement, delay in examination and results, it was because of that that the President could not have been allowed to function as the ex Vice Chancellor. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned Act is silent and although as quoted above it talks of being temporary measure but it talks about being temporary act, it continues and even as stated above there appears to be no intention of the State Government to restore the body back to its elected bodies and office bearers, despite the fact that the Court has not expressed any opinion on this question. [175F] 2. The Act and Rules framed under the Act taking over the management of the Rashtra bhasha prachar Samiti could not therefore be accepted to be in accordance with the Constitution. Apart from this it is also clear that although when the Act talks of a temporary measure in fact, the Act does not provide for as to how when the temporary measures come to an end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalika would be restored.

The respondents were married to one of the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal, a resident of Asansol in Bengal. The appellants filed a suit for a declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940 executed by her was void and inoperative under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the marriage was settled at Deoghar and the terms which were settled between the parties were: (a) that Sumitra Devi would arrange for the gift of four houses at Asanso in favour of her daughter as her share on partition; (b) that the gift was collusive, fraudulent and without consideration; and (c) that there was no compelling reasons for the High Court to differ from the appreciation of the oral evidence by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the proper finding should have been that Sumitra had made a "sankalpa" at Deotoli and that such a gift was not binding on the reversioners, as she had only a life interest in the corpus of her husband 's property and there was nothing in law which would justify the inference that the gifts were made by the widow of the deceased husband. HELD: (i) The High Courts have held that there is no evidence to show that the possession of the houses in question was made over to Kamala Devi before the death of Ram Kishori Lai, that the widow respondents could not get a declaration which they had asked for. [477 D] (ii) There was no consideration nor any discussion of the texts bearing on the question whether there was an agreement or arrangement between the par ties in respect of the two houses. The evidence showed that the parties had made an oral gift of 4 houses at Deopoli and during the lifetime of her father, the appellant 's daughter in law was a full owner of the house. [476 E F] (iii) There is no consideration or discussion of any texts bearing upon the question as to whether there were any such oral gift. The fact that one of them had become indebted cannot take away the power of the father to make such a provision.

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly.
