The first respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices as alleged by the appellant and that the proceedings were taken ex parte against him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej Singh had been clearly proved. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh was guilty and not guilty of having committed any corrupt practice as alleged in his election petition. [419G] (2) The result is that the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Kaur had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. Tej Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of the respondent would have gone to the appellant (Ahsan Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered. [416D E] (3) The conclusion is irresistible that can he arrived at on a short point because, in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, the High Court was justified in holding that Tej singh had actually made an application for setting aside the election. Therefore, the irresistible conclusion that could be arrived is that Shri Tej Singh has actually paid the posters for the poster which were prepared at his behest and Rup Lai was not collecting with the Printing of the poster.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was defeated in the legislative assembly election held in 1982. The Chief Minister of the State filed an application for contempt against the respondent, who was then the Chief Minister, alleging that one Shri Devinder Sharma, a forest officer, had been prosecuted and convicted under section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1982, by the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with the due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the application on the ground that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. The High Court dismissed the application holding that there was no punishment imposed on the respondent by the appellant, and discharged the rule neces sary. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when the High Courts do not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High court does not exercise its jurisdic tion or power to punish for contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the High Curt is to punish a person who has been punished for contempt of itself. [893C] 2.1 In considering a question whether the alleged contemner is guilty of contempt or not, the court may look into the materials produced before it and, if necessary, examines witnesses and, thereafter, passes an order either acquitting or punishing him for contempt.[893D] 2:2 A contempt is a matter between the court and the alleged offender. Any person who moves the machinery of the court for contempt only brings to the notice of the Court certain facts constituting contempt of court. After furnishing such information he may still assist the court but it must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the Court and the contemnor. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature in not conferring any right on the petitioner for contempt, and as there is no exercise of jurisdiction or power by the Court to punish able for contempt it is difficult to say that the High COurt has exercised its jurisdiction or powers to punish the for contempt [894E F] 2 :3. The power of the Supreme Court is to impose a punishment for contempt on the contemnor or by acquitting him. It is true that in considering a matter whether the allegation is guilty or not the court, hears the parties and considers the materials placed before it, and if necessary examines them, the materials produce before it. If necessary, examination of witnesses and thereafter passes an Order either acquitting the contemnor, or acquitting him for Contempt. When the HighCourt acquits the contemnor after hearing the parties, and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the order does so also in the exercise of its jurisdiction as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution. [889F H] 3:4.

The appellant was the daughter of one V. R. who died in March, 1941. The widow filed a suit for possession on the ground that she had become a tenant by forfeiture of rent and also agreed to pay the agreed rent in monthly instalments. The trial court granted a decree for ejectment against V.R. on the grounds (1) that she was entitled to the whole compensation money as the tenant 's rights had ceased by forfeiture; (2) that the notice under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, was not necessary for terminating the lease in suit and (3) that there was no forfeiture because no rent was fixed in respect of the suit property. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statutory provisions of section 111 (g) as well as section 114 were not applicable to leases executed prior to the coming into force of the . HELD : (i) The provision as to notice for determining a lease for non payment of rent was not based upon any principle of justice, equity or good conscience. It is one thing to decide what is the true meaning of the language contained in an Act of Parliament. It has to be decided by itself, the delay, the conduct of the parties and the difficulties to which the landlord is put should be weighed against the tenant. This was the view taken by the Madras High Court in Tatya Savla Sudrik vs Yeshwanta Kondiba Mulay (I.L.R, , distinguished. (ii) The provisions as to notices for determining the lease for bona fide requirement of a tenant would not be based on any principle or rule of equity and good conscience which must govern even agricultural leases. [1023 B C] (iii) In the present case the appellant was a recalcitrant tenant and is a habitual defaulter. Rent has been in arrears at times for six years, at other times for three years and at other time for four years and so on, and every time the landlord had to file a suit in ejectment which was always resisted on false defences. [1123 C D] (iv) The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of his own wrong and plead relief against forfeiture on every occasion particularly when he was warned by the Court of appeal on a previous occasion. [1102 B] (v) In view of the fact that the tenant is a recalci nationless defaulter, the provisions of the Rent Act are not applicable in this case.

The appellant, a union called Kymanna Pradhan and others, was dismissed from service by the management on 13.9.1968. The Management served a notice on the management to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against them for the alleged misconduct committed by them. The respondents filed their reply denying the charges levelled against them. They also stated that while they were working as casual workers in the appellant 's factory, the Management had decided to terminate the strike without giving any reason and that since the workmen had gone on strike without 14 days ' prior notice, they could not be removed from service. The management served a charge sheet dated 3.10.1968 on the respondents in which four common charges were levelled against all of them. In addition to the charges, three separate charges were also framed against two of them in addition to one of them being found guilty by the Enquiry Officer. The appellant challenged the aforesaid charges before the High Court by way of a Writ Petition. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that the enquiry was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the respondents and that there was no second opportu nity for the same. In appeal, the Division Bench confirmed the order of the single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The real question that arises in these appeals is whether when paragraph 3 of the Standing Order No. 17 provides for second opportunity being given to a workman to showcause against the proposed punishment of dismissal after he has been found guilty or the opportunity spoken of is the opportunity to meet the charges in the domestic inquiry ? [368C D] 1.2 The word 'opportunity ' in clause (a) of O.B.I. Rules means a unilateral obligation on concerned authority or the officer to give due consideration to the gravity of the misconduct and the previous record of the delinquent in awarding the maximum punishment. It is true that the Arbitrator has undoubtedly taken the view that the opportunity agreed to by him was not called from the 'accused ' which suggests that he had been guilty of misconduct. But, in the context of certain modification sought to be made in a Standing Order requiring a second show cause notice this Court does not mean that a Standing order may not provide for it but unless the Standing order provides for it. either expressly or by necessary implication no inquiry which is otherwise fair and valid will be vitiated by non affording of such second opportunity. [368E F] Hamdard Dawakhana vs Badri Das & Ors., ; , applied. In the instant case, the Arbitrator had undoubtedly taken into consideration the proper construction to be placed on Standing Order NO. 17 by the Arbitrator or the High court and that last part deals only with the punishment of dismissing and for that punishment alone makes a special provision that no order awarding that punishment will be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity to a workmen to offer his explanation. [369E F; 371A] Hamad Dawakhan vs Badri Dass & Ors. ; , referred to.

The appellant was the owner of a portion of land leased by incompetent persons to the competent persons. The lease deed purported to be a lease deed executed in favour of incompetent persons. In the suit filed by the respondents, the appellant contended that he was himself the owner and had not actually transferred possession of the land to the respondent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the benefit of section 7D would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible entry. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section7D. Allowing the appeals by special leave, HELD: 1. The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to person whose posses sion had a legal origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe it to be the property of the Government. [114E F] 2. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7A must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case, the finding of fact entered by the High court is that the appel lant had come into possession of his lands by trespass. His plea before the Courts below was that he had come to possess the lands by encroachment or forcible and unlawful entry. He respondents are prepared to pay to the appellant a sum of Rs.50,000 as ex gratia payment in full and final settlement of whatever claims the appellant may have towards the value of the rubber trees standing in plots. A, B and C or in any other respect. [115G H] 3. The finding of the High Courts is that there was no benefit to the respondents and the appellant had come in possession of these lands by encroached upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The High Court was therefore in error in holding that he could not be entitled to protection of Section 7D.

The appellant was convicted under Section 135(b) (ii) of the . He was convicted and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appellant had not produced evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. His case rested on his bare assertions in a written statement. Of course no one had come forward to state or allege that the goods found, in the circumstances stated above, were smuggled into India without payment of duty. The appellant 's explanation was that he had not given any evidence to prove that his Sub tenants had place in India and that there had been misdeclaration of the goods. [541 D E] In a written state ment it is immaterial whether the goods are legally brought into India or brought into the country without payment. [542 F G] The appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. It was immaterial that the appellant was found in possession of the offending goods on 21 4 1967 there was some evidence to enable the courts below to come to the conclusion that the gold must have been known to the appellant to be imported even if he had been not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty, and his case rested entirely on his mere assertions in the written statement which was filed on 30 10 1968. [543 G H] The State of Punjab vs Gian Chand & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants were the Presidents of a registered association which was dissolved and the members of the Association were joined as respondents. The Association was formed in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and its members were not entitled to any share in the profits made on the sale of yarn. The appellants filed a suit for accounts and claimed that they had been guilty of an illegal association with the object of carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further claimed that the suit was maintainable under section 4 Of the Rewa Act, as it was not registered as a company under the Rewa state Companies Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 69(3)(a) of , are mandatory and must be read in the light of the provisions of that section. [776 D] (ii) Under section 69 (3) of a State Companies, Act, the persons in possession of such money is entitled to keep it in his pocket. If money is paid by A to B to be applied by him for some illegal purpose, it is competent for A to require B to hand back the money if B has not already parted with it and the illegal purpose has not been carried out. [777 E F] (iii) The suit was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts. Therefore, the appellants had no right to claim any share on the sales of yarn dealings and transactions.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 54 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C., for quashing the proceedings against them on the ground that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognisance of the offences and issuing summons. The High Court quashed the proceedings holding that the complaint was barred by sec. 210(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the High Courts were not competent to take cognizance of an offence under section 9(1), read with sec. 50(l) of Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1974 and that the offences envisaged by secs. 9(i) and (ii) of Chapter IV of the Act are the same or substantially the same as Sec. 429 IPC and that after due investigation and police had filed a final report that no offence was made out and that initiation of any fresh proceedings against respondents would be impermissible. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not committed any error in taking cognizance of offences under sec. 51 read with Sec. 50 (l) and section 50(1). [467C] 1.2 The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act ' in section 56 of the Indian Penal Code, merely imports the idea that nature of the thing is "a series of complex biotic communities of which a man is an interdependent part" and that it should not be given to a part to tresspass and diminish the whole. [467D] 1:3. The expression 'any act ' in sec. 56, read with s. 50, (l), p. 469, clearly means any allegation made orally or in writing to a Magistrate. [468F] 1st respondent is a person who is an accused in a case under sec tion 9(I) read with Section 50(2) of Act on the one hand and the investigation by the police is in progress in relation to same offence, i.e., the one on which the allegation has been made. The offences are not the same. [466D] 2.1 In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence. It must constitute a different offence or omission might constitute an offi cial offence under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. [470E F] 2:2 The proviso to Section 56 has also a familiar ring and is a facet of the fundamental right enshrined in Article 20(2). A protection against a second or multiple punishment for the same offence technical complexities aside, including a protection against re prosecution after conviction and a protection from double or multiple punishments for the similar offence. But where an act or an omission constitutes an offence, under two or more enactments, then the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be liable under either of those enactment, but should not he liable to pay twice for thesame offence.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that he had committed a breach of his liberty by indulging in his activities in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order, and was released on bail. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that: (1) the provisions of section 439 Cr. P.C. should be construed liberally so as to ensure that the 'bailee ' does not flee justice; and (2) the High Court under section 439 Criminal Procedure Code, enlarge the petitioner on bail, should have been within its power to reject a surety because he or his estate is situated in a different district or State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law is being followed by the courts not only for juvenile justice but also for a large number of other minorities and distant densely minorities who are to be given bail. [343G] 2.1 In order to secure release on his own bond, the court must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deter mination for releasing the petitioner. [344A B] 2:2 The law, not the money tag, must be read 'bail ' to mean that it popularly docs, and lexically and in American Jurisprudence is stated to Mean, viz., a generic expression used to describe judicial release from custodia. [346C D] 2I1 In the instant case, the petitioner was rightly convicted for offences under section 307 I. P .C. and sentenced on his application for bail. He could not be released on his personal bond without sureties. [347D E] 2l2 The High Courts have been in error in imposing the sentence of death on him. [349G] 3.1 There is no definition of bail given to a court under section 437 Cr.P C. and the expression 'bail" has been defined as including only cases of release with sureties. In the present case, there was an ambiguity because even if the petitioner had not been found guilty, he would have been appearance at the appointed place. [348H; 349A] 3:2. The petitioner could not have been convicted on his bail in a sum of Rs. An application for his release on the basis of his own undertaking to appear before the court in a personal bond was filed in this Court. [350B] 3(a) There is nothing in section 439, Cr. Procedure Code or in any other provisions of the Criminal Procedure, which shows that the Code indicates no limitation based on sureties. Counsel for the State agreed that this is so. The counsel for the respondent contended that the petitioner 's application for release on bail was not maintainable because he had not filed a personal affidavit and that the court had no power to grant bail. This contention is not tenable. [351B] (b) There was no definition in section 437, Cr., Procedure Code which shows the nature of bail. In order that an accused may be released under the section, the Court must always have the judicial process. The judicial system is a kind of social justice and indigent persons are entitled to get equal justice under law. [352C] (c) There are many considerations which weigh with the court while deciding whether in socialist republic, with social justice as its hallmark, monetary superstition, not other relevant considerations like family ties, roots in the community, membership of stable organization, should prevail for bail bonds to ensure the 's 's presence.

The assessee, a registered firm, had at various places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee to include in the computation of capital invested for the purpose of section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but the Income tax Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment order and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. The High Court declined to require the Tribunal, on the view that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from non inclusion by the Income Tax Officer in the assessment in question of the income of Eastle 's and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Tribunal in coming to its conclusion, was a relevant factor. The Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner and held that the findings of the Income. tax Officer were one of facts as it had been based on inference arising out of the non inclusion of the amount advanced to 'Castle. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Courts in India have jurisdiction to call upon the Tribunal for the opinion of the High court whether the question of law arises and the High, Court being approached by the aggrieved party within the period of limitation prescribed, is not satisfied about the correctness of the decision of the appellate Tribunal refusing to state a case for the reasons that no question of fact arose and the finding on matters of appreciation of evidence cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was appointed as a party to the writ petition filed by him. The Minister was directed to file his affidavit. In the writ peti tion filed by the appellant, he stated that he had not been impleaded as a respondent. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding that the Minister concerned should file an affidavit in regard to allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The Minister concerned is the Minister responsible for the decision of the High Court directing that the minister be impleaded as respondent. [972 B] (2) The High Courts were in error in directing that a Minister should file his personal affidavit. [963 C] (3) The direction for impleading of the Minister as a necessary party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made against him and thus, to afford an opportunity to the parties and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter. [952 D] (4) The Secretary of the Department should file affidavit in respect of allegations made by the Minister himself. [943 C D] In the instant case, the High Courts had not committed any error in direct ing that the Ministers concerned should be impleaded. [ 943 E] (5) The order passed by the Governor was set aside and the Minister was impleaded as the party.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application for recovery of arrears of rent under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1924, was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala Cantonment, on January 7, 1960. The respondent contended that the provisions of the Act and Rules were not applicable to him as he had committed a breach of the provisions contained in the lease. The trial court held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to recover the arrears of the rent due under a lease. On appeal the High Court held that (i) the rent was payable by the respondent under the lease, and (ii) the notice issued by the appellant under section 256(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not amount to a claimable by the Board under the Act or the Rules made thereunder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (a) the words "rent" in section 259 were added by the 1954 Amendment, and therefore, the provisions Of section 259 could not be applied to a simple case of money due to the Board on a contract of lease; (b) the word rent had been used in the context of a lease between the Board and the tenant; (c) the expression "rent was not intended to include any sum paid by the lessee under an express provision of the statute, and that therefore, it could not apply to a mere suit for recovery.

The appellant was terminated from service on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. At the instance of the appellant the Government referred to the Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court/Tribunal/Industrial Disputes, which held that the appellant was not a "workman" and therefore, the reference was incompetent. The Labour Court also held that there was no evidence under section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act to prove the fact of misconduct. In appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that since the appellant had been employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company, his services were illegal but dismissed the application only on the grounds that the was not applica tion in the nature of workmen 's case. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal on the nature and circumstances of the case is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. [474F] 2.1 A long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. In the instant case, the Tribunal found that the appel lant was not an "workman". The finding is therefore not sustainable. [473G H] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah shell Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, ; ; DS.Nagraj vs labour officer, Kamal & Ors., ; ; G.Sivarathin Chemicals and Chemicals Ltd. vs Burmahu Shell Management and staff; , , referred to. 2.2 The finding that the termination of the appell lant from service was illegal but not treated as precedent is a subsequent enactment and it cannot be treated as a precedent. [475B C] 3. In view of the fact that a long period o f over 16 year had passed, it would he unjust to Leave the appellant with no remedy at present. [476D E] 4. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The respondent Company was a Government lessee under the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Samvat 1999. On the expiry of the lease period, the respondent company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Additional Collector dismissed the suit holding that the land in question was held by the Company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The High Court confirmed the order of the Additional Collector. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant State it was contended that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant and that the company was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the M .P. land Revenue Code 1959. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [179F] 2. The order of Additional Collector is set aside. The findings of the subordinate authorities are set aside and the order passed by the Additional Collec tor is restored. [180G] 3. The respondent company was a person holding the land from the State Government. This is so whether or not the Company is deemed to be holding over under the old lease or holding, upon termination of that lease under and in terms of the fresh conditions agreed upon between the parties to enable the Company to remain in possession of the land as a lessee. [181A] 4. The Company has been successful in showing that the respondent Company never acquired the status of a Gair Maurusi tenant in respect of the lands in question at any time prior to the coming into force of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007. The fact that large amounts are due and payable by the company as rent and that rents have remained unpaid for a period far in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due, is not liable to be questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amount are due, and payable, by the respondent as rent. [182B C] 5. The appeal by the State is allowed with costs throughout.

The Kerala Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for the acquisition of any land in an estate. The object of the Act was to provide that the surplus land should be acquired or held under personal cultivation of the holder, and to provide a machinery for compensation for the property so acquired. Section 47 of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1965 provided that the provisions of the Principal Act shall apply to the lands acquired and held by any person through inheritance, request, gift, family settlement, purchase lease or otherwise, together with the lands in his personal cultivation at the time of such acquisition. The State Government amended the principal Act by adding a proviso to article 31 A providing for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent. The Amendment Act provided that no property shall be compulsorily acquired or requisitioned save for a public purpose and save by authority of law which provides for compensation in respect of the interest of the owner, compensation shall not be less than the market price of the lands if such land be within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. The petitioners challenged the validity of section 47 of Act 13 of 1965 on the ground that it was inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution and that the impugned Act was void as it contravened article 31 B of the Constitu tion. Held, that the expression "law in force" in article 31A of the constitution is not a law in force when the State legislature was formed but until the power is exercised by the Legislature to issue an appropriate notification, the provisions Of Ch. IV could not be deemed to be law in existence unless it was brought into operation by legislative enactment or by the exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation. The theory of a statute being "in operation in a constitutional sense" though it is not in fact in operation has no application. Held further, that section 47(1) of the , which provided for payment of compensation at a rate which was less than that originally fixed under the Act and the guarantee of the second proviso to Article 31 A of the Consti tution, is on that account infringed article 14 of the Con stitution. The right to compensation which is not less than tho market value under any laws providing for the acquisi tion by the state of any estate in an Estate in the personal cultivation or the right to possession of any property owned or controlled by the Government cannot be limited only in the constitutional sense and not in the sense of its actual operativeness. Held also, that article 31(A) was a law relating to "acquisition" within the meaning of article 31 (2) of Constitution and the compensation determined merely at 15 times the market rate fixed under section 47 was on that count inapplicable to the landholders who challenged the constitutional validity of the impugned provisions.

The widow of her husband, who had inherited the property from his widow, was in possession of the same by adverse possession against the widow. She died in 1924 leaving a son, the widow, and a daughter, the respondent. The widow filed a suit for partition of the properties on the ground that the widow had acquired a title by adverse Possession against her. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the reversioners could not claim possession so long as the widow was alive. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the widow could not make a surrender of the property during her lifetime without any valid extinction by any act of surrender; and (2) the respondent had no interest in the property which she could convey under the Hindu law. HELD: The widow 's estate was in fact acquired by adverse posses sion against her, and the widow became entitled to recover possession from the widow or his spiritual benefit. [355 E] The widow, when he takes the estate on surrender, takes it subject to the interest already created. A surrender is a voluntary act of self effacement by the widow and she is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. [356 F G] In the present case, the reversioners had not acquired any title from the respondent but only from her husband who had acquired title by reason of a subsequent voluntary act on the part of the widow; and the reversioners were entitled to possession at once. The right of the reversioner was not affected by the surrender as it was purely voluntary act. [357 B C] Per Sarkar, J. (dissenting) The widow had no absolute rights in her estate and could not be surrendered to the reversioners. [358 E F] Per Hidayatullah, J: There is no warrant in Hindu law for the proposition that in case of alienation by a Hindu widow of his property without any legal necessity, or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by personal benefit against her the interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the reversioner, the surrender must take it subject only to such prior interest. [359 F G; 360 A] Per Subba Rao, J., (disposing of the appeal) The right to surrender by a widow of the husband 's property without legal necessity or in her case of an stranger acquiring possession against her will is not an absolute estate but an estate liable to be defeated on the happening of certain events which in Hindu Law cause extinction of the estate. In the instant case, there was no warrant for the position that in the present ease the widow obtained a decree for partition against the appellant and the respondent, who were the reversioners, had acquired the property by adverse title against her and the appellant had therefore acquired the right to possession. [360 F G]. Per Subba, J (dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The Hindu law is that in cases of alienation of property by a female owner of her property without sufficient necessity or lawful authority, she can be dispossessed only by her own act of transfer against her husband. [361 A] (b) In the case before us no equitable considerations at all arise. The rule that in ease of alienations by a male owner of his estate without any justifying necessity or, in the absence of legal necessity and not as a mere device to share the estate with the reversioner is not merely a device to transfer her property but also an estate which stands in itself dependent upon the widow ' s title to her interest. The exception to this rule is that if the effect of surrender, as explained above, is to destroy the widow "s estate in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death", there is no reason why the reversioner should not subject to any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover Possession of the lands from her.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Uttar Pradesh as a limited company. The Cotton Mills Company Ltd. had acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each. On February 15, 1984 the appellant became the Chairman and Managing Director of the Cotton Mills company. In 1970, the Cotton Mill Company filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 before the High Court for winding up of the appellant company. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polytex Company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver under section 169 of the Act and therefore, there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the cotton Mills Company suffered any diminution or curtailment in its rights as a shareholder in respect of the shares so attached. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the special general meeting was not validly called because the Cotton Textile Company had not become paralysed and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares held by the other requisitionists would not have been eligible to requisition the meeting. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the Cotton Textiles Company could not be treated as the holder of the office of Receiver in view of section 153A of the deal with the contract of pledge and that the power of the company and its directors to deal with property comprised in the appointment (both property subject to a floating charge and property subject only to a fixed charge) except under certain circumstances, was not sufficient to take away the right of the cotton mills Company to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under section 170 of the Income tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of winding up is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of Receiver under the Land Revenue Act. [887C] 2.1 The power to wind up a company is not absolute and it can be exercised only when there is no other creditor of the pawner had any right to take over the shares. [889D] 2(a) The power conferred by section 169 (1) (a) (b) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 has no effect on the voting rights of the Textile Mills Company. It is also significant that the Directors of the polytex company who what that a Receiver had been appointed in respect thereof, have not been excluded from consideration. [879E] 2.(b) The resolution of the Board of Directors of a company which has not been duly approved by the Central Government under section 18AA (1)(a) of Industries ( Development and Regulation ) Act, 1950 takes over six industrial units of the textile mills Company held by it at the time of deposit of the requisition. [877F] 2 (c) The Cotton Textile Mills Co. Ltd.

The petitioners, who were plaintiffs in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, filed a suit for declaration that they were owners in possession of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat contested the suit and raised preliminary objections that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. The Trial Court framed an issues relating to the maintainability of the suits. The petitioners filed revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court because the land in question was shamlat deh and it had been vested in it. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. Section 13 of Punjab Village common Lands (Regulations) Act 1961 provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any property is or is not shamlat land vested or deemed to have been vested under the Act. The Act was amended by the Punjab Act No. 18 of 1961 which came into force on April 1, 1961 and section 13A provides that any person claiming right, title or interest therein may submit to the Collector within such time as may be prescribed, a statement of his claim in writing and signed and verified in the prescribed manner and that the Collector shall have jurisdic tion to decide such claim in such manner as may he prescribed. Any person or a Panchayat aggrieved by an order of the Collector made under sub section (1) may within sixty days from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the Commissioner in such form as may prescribed. The Commissioner may after hearing the appeal, confirm, very or reverse the order appealed against and may pass such order as he deems fit. [835C D] 2. Section 11 of the Act provides that a person claiming a right, titles or interest shall be deemed to be a public servant under the Punjab Panchayat Act, 1951 or claims that any land has not so vested in a Panchayat under the provisions of the village community or a part thereof or for common purposes of the villages; and (b) to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act. [883D] 3. Section 12 of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation), (Amendment) Act 1976 provides that an application for a declaration that land is not ' shamlat ' shall be made in favour of any land holder, and that any lands have not so vest in the Panchayat may submit it to the collector within such period as may from time to time be prescribed. [873E] 4. Section 14 of the Land Acquisition Act provides for a right to claim, title and interest in certain lands vested or acquired by a Panchayat. The appellants cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration, that the land was shamilat deh. They had, however, questioned the correctness of entries in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit property. [877F] 5. Section 15 of the U.P. Village Common lands (Regulation). (Amendment), Act 1976 provided that any persons claiming right title or interests in any land vested under this section including streets, lanes, playgrounds, schools, drinking wells, or ponds within abadi deh or gorah deh shall be entitled to question it in such a manner as might be prescribed; and the Collector may after considering the question whether the property in question is shamlat or not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat or not.

The respondent Board, a public limited company, had been in the business of supplying electricity to its consumers. The Electricity Board demanded interest on the amount payable by it under the provisions of the Orissa State Electricity Board General Conditions of Supply Act, 1948. The Board challenged the demand on the ground that the Electricity Board was not obliged to pay interest on such deposit and also for supply of energy to the consumers. It was contended that the Board had no power to charge interest on a deposit made by it in terms of the agreement between the consumer and the Board. The High Court held that the electricity board was entitled to adjust its tariffs against the security deposit as the Board was bound to pay surcharge at 18%. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Electricity Supply Act was not applicable to the supply made by the Board; and (ii) the Board has a statutory right under section 49(1)(f) to charge the interest on security deposit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The electricity supply is a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. The billing time taken by the Electricity Department is to the advantage of the consumer. Since the amount is held as security, it represents the moneys of the Electricity Boards. [262D] 2. The supply of electricity by the appellant is to be made under proviso (a) to section 49 of the Act. The conditions of supply are such that it represents a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer, and also a security deposit for payment or satisfaction of any money (for example, the Board may not encash the amount in a bank and therefore the determination of three months is arbitrary. [263F G] 3. The question whether interest should be paid on the security deposits or advance consumption deposit or satisfaction thereof depends upon the financial position of the licensee which is to he conducted in a particular manner as well as on the amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19 (1) (f). [263G H] 4. The nature of consumption deposit is such that the same has direct bearing to the level of supply in consumption of electricity. The revision in the form of an additional security deposit with interest at the rate of 3 per cent was made in January 1987. Nor again, could the Board withhold payment of interest on it from the date of the deposit at the rates of 12% per annum. [264A B] 5. The appellant is required to deposit with the Board a sum in cash equivalent to estimated three months consumption charges. In case the amount was not paid within four months, the appellant would be liable to pay simple interest at 6% per month for non payment of bills within the stipulated period. [265C D] 6. The rate of interest is fixed on the basis of the actual and character of a security deposits. It is not in dispute that the appellant has been given a right to adjust the tariffs for the purpose of Board 's finance. The rates are for consumption of energy estimated for a period of approximately three months. In one sense, the consumption security deposit represents only a part which is paid to the consumer on the bills being raised from the consumer to secure the Board against default in payment of the interest. [267E F] 7. The demand of interest by the respondent is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. It stands to reason that if there is a revision in rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in it and this is sought to be achieved by the relevant law.

The petitioners, who were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre, were promoted to the posts of Assistant Directors or Deputy Director. The petitioners challenged the promotion orders on the ground that they were not competent to do so and that the same special pay which was granted to them under the Recruitment Rules was not being paid to them. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Indian Telecommunication Service Officers who are working in the Telephone Research Centre are being given Special Pay of Rs. 300 Rs. 200 and Rs. 150 per month in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Directors and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.11.1973. [1011C D] 2.2 The Indian Telegraph Service Officers, who are functioning in the telephone Research Centre were being given special Pay of RS. 300 per month. They are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is not deputation allowance. It was paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the telecommuni cation Research Centre. The Special Pay is not being given to a few graduate engineers recruited specifically for TRC when the qualifications, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and transferred officials and that they have to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition tO their scale of pay which is the same. [1001D E] 2:3 The Indian Telephone Research Institute is engaged in the research and development Centre and is being given a special Pay in lieu of Special pay in addition lo their scale. The transfer officers who are selected by the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition examination need to be given Special pay. It does not mean that persons who are directly recruited and working in tho centre are inferior to those who enter the centre by transfer. It cannot be said that persons appointed to the post of Assistant Director, regarding whom the petitioners belong, are not given any special Pay.

The appellant, a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, was employed as a mourshi in a Mill. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him under section 7 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, and the employer dismissed his third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965. The Labour Court held that the charges leveled against him were proved, but did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approach the Labour Court and directed reinstatement of the third respondent. On appeal by the appellant, the State Industrial Court confirmed the order of the Labour court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the third Respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not require compliance with the said provisions and (2) the finding of the Tribunal was perverse, because (a) the second respondent had failed before the Labour 'Court to comply, with the provision of law, in that it did not comply with section 42 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1 ) The scheme of Chapter VIII is that a Labour Court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by paragraph A. Paragraph B thereof gives the Labour Courts the power to try offenses punishable under the Act and cognizance of such offenses. An employee desiring a change in respect of matters covered by section 42 (1), or an employee desiring to a change of his own administrative, supervisory or technical capacity drawing basic pay (excluding allowances) exceeding five hundred rupees per month, irrespective of the amount of pay drawn by him, which the State Government may, by noti fication in the Official Gazette, specify in this behalf. [738 C D] (2)(a) The scheme is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour Commissioner. A Labour Court has a creature of statute and it can only exercise such jurisdiction as the statute confers on it. If there are certain pre conditions to the exercise of its jurisdiction, it must refuse to entertain any such application unless such pre conditions are first complied with. [38 B C] (b) The Scheme of Chapter X headed "changes". Clause D of section 78(1) which later became a part of the definition in section 2(18) of that Act, provided for an agreement between the parties regarding "change" and registration of the memorandum thereof by the Registrar. Under section 44 A a memorandum of agreement arrived at is to be forwarded by either party to the Registrar by registered post and an agreement which is registered under section 44 is to come into operation as laid down in section 45. The territorial jurisdiction of Labour Courts extends to local areas for which they are constituted under section 77. [37 C D, 38 F] (c) The provisions of sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 relating to termination of employment including notice to be given by the employer and employee and punishment of dismissal, removal or discharge for misconduct, suspension etc., are not applicable to the case. [39 G H] (d) The Labour Courts are a creature Of the statute and they can only have such jurisdiction which is conferred on it under section 78. An appeal lies to the Industrial Court against the decision of a Labour court in respect oof a matter falling under clause (a). [40 D E] (e) The High Court was wrong in holding that the Labour Act is applicable to limited area within the meaning of section 3(18).

The appellants filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 for eviction on the ground that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company. The respondents contested the application contending that the appellants had formed a partnership, as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created and the respondents were liable to vacate the premises on 31st July, 1971. The Rent Controller held that the respondents are the successors of the original lessor company and the legal representatives of late S.M. Ganguli who had executed a lease for 20 years in favour of one S. M. Ganguli, who on his death was succeeded by his legal representatives. The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the grounds that they are the successor in interest as a sub tenant under the lease after due attornment and were liable for eviction after the expiry of the period of lease on 31 7 1971. They also stated that the heirs of late s M Ganguli had formed an partnership, and the appellants were not liable to eviction. The trial court held that they have been the successorsin interest of lessor company, and therefore, were not entitled to evict them under section 11 of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the Judicial Commissioner agreed with the findings of the trial court on merits and concluded that in absence of a month 's notice under section 13(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsif. The High Court also held that since the respondents had failed to seek extension of the term of tenancy, they were not bound by the terms of the lease deed and hence the entire proceeding was mis conceived.

The appellant, a registered society, filed a suit for an immovable property through its then Secretary. The suit was later transferred to the court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1, Jaipur City where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami who was elected. The trial court allowed the application holding that the appellant had not been elected as Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. The High Court, however, held that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the trial court had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected Secretary and that the Trial Court had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting withdrawal of the Suit under its inherent power, and that since the case had been remanded for reconsideration of the evidence on merits, the application filed by the appellant under section 14 1 of C.P.C. was not competent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the suit had been transferred to a prayer purported to have been made on behalf of the plaintiff does not make it an independent power of every court to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. [236B] 2.1 In the instant case, the trial Court had vacated its previous order regarding satisfaction of decree on the ground that the same was obtained by the judgment debtor 's fraud on the court. The courts below were, therefore, not right in holding that there was no jurisdiction under section 16 1 of Code of C., [236C D] Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483; Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalil Kavonia, 27 Madras Law Jour 238; Viliakatha Raman vsVayalil Kochu, 27 Mad. 483; Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil and Others, AIR 1923 Pat 483; D.S. Nakara vs Vyalikathnam, AIR 1924 Patna 483, referred to. 2.2 In the exercise of inherent power under section15 1 of Civil Proce dure Code of civil Procedure a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it.

The appellant was the accused No. 1 before the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, and was charged with having committed an offence punishable under section 7 read with section 4 of the Ordinance read with sections 5 and 6 of the Defence of India Act, 1946. The trial ended in conviction and sentence of imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 8,000 each. On appeal by the appellant the High Court agreed with his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Ordinance promulgated under the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the Government of India Ordinance, 1946, was not in operation at the date when the offence was committed by the accused and (2) the ordinance had been promulgated after the emergency was declared to have ended on April 1, 1946; and (3) the Act was not applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir as it stood prior to its enactment. HELD : (1)(a) The Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940, and April 1. 1946, the date on which the offence in question was committed, was a perpetual one and continued in operation until it was repealed. [645 B] (b) The emergency under which the Governor of India was invested with the power to make laws is distinct and distinct from and must not be confused with the emergency which occasioned the pawing of the Act and the clear effect of the words of the statute on section 72 is that Ordinances promulgated under that subsection during the currency of the Emergency were to continue in force until it is repealed. The Ordinance was therefore a perpetual piece of temporary legislation intended to meet an emergency. [643 C] (c) The Emergency Provisions which were promulgated by the Governor were not applicable in the present case because they continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India, though the Ordinance had been passed before April 1., 1946, and the Ordinance in so far as it was not extended to the territory of India. [641 D] (d) The words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" in section 72 were omitted from section 72 during the pendency of the emergency and were not synonymous with the Emergency which occasioned a contingency. The emergency on the happening of which an Ordinance can be promulgated is separate and distinct and different from and cannot be equated with the contingency contemplated by section 72. [651 D F] (e) The provisions of section 72 with the omitted words restored to their original position after April 1,. 1946, while determining the duration of the Ordinances which had been enacted between June 28, 1940 and April I, 1946 were not limited to the space for not more then six months. [661 E G] (f) The effect of section 7 of the Indian , as it originally stood in regard to Ordinance No. III of 1946 was that Ordinances issued by the Government in exercise of the power conferred upon him under section 73 of the 9th Schedule of the Govern ment of India Acts, 1946 and 1949, were to be deemed to have been in force on July 11, 1953, when the emergency had ceased.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that death sentence should be reduced to life imprisonment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of Code of criminal procedure 1973. [1072B] 1.2 In the instant case, the High Court was justified in affirming the death sentence imposed on the appellants. [ 1073C] 1:3. The question whether the death penalty should be awarded or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each particular case. It is well settled that the test to be applied by the court is 'special reasons ' necessary for imposing death penalty must relate, not to the crime as such but to the criminal. [1172E F] 1I2 In this case, there was no reason to differ from the view expressed in Rajendra Prasad 's case. The opinion of the High Courts cannot be said to have been correctly accepted by the High court. [1273G H] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. 1.3 The question of abolition of capital punishment is a difficult and controversial subject, long and hotly debated and it has evoked during the past two decades strong conflicting views on the subject. It would be impermissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence of death should be substituted by a sentence of imprisonment for life. [1373G] Rajendra Kumar 's Case, ; and Rajendra Prasad Singh 's cases, referred to. 1I3 The instant case is not one where the HighCourt has exercised its jurisdiction under section 354 (3) Cr. P.C., 1973, but has merely directed that the sentence should not be reduced. [1473H] Rajendra Prashad vs State, ; ; and Murder Reference No.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Clerk in the erstwhile Punjab State. He was compulsorily retired on 30th September, 1953. His case was that he had been exonerated of the allegations and imputations made against him on each occasion. The High Court refused to grant special leave to appeal to this Court. In appeal to the Supreme Court it was contended for the appellant that the State Government had not given a reasonable opportunity to produce nine witnesses in his defence with some documents, and that the High Court had considered at some length all relevant questions raised by the appellant. HELD: (i) The High court had given its judgment eight months after it had been passed. It was not possible for the High court to see whether the exclusion of evidence was justified or not. [583 E] (ii) The State Government could have made a revocation of special leave under article 136 of the Constitution after hearing arguments of the appellant and delivery of a judgment. But this could not stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully inquired into by officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. [584 F] (iii) The question whether the appellant was given a fair opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. [585 F] Smt Ujjam Bai vs State of & Anr., ; , referred to. (iv) The appellant was not given any opportunity to meet a new case and there was no reason for the first respondent to have failed to do so.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. The appellants contended that their contracts were identical, and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. The High Court held that the contract between the appellants and the M/s. T.K. Wadeyar was integrally connected with the contract entered into by the appellants with their foreign buyers and that the contracts were different. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contracts between the appellant and the foreign buyers are different contracts and it is the S.T.,C. which entered into independent contracts with their other foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. Under the contracts between a foreign buyer and the S .T. C. the merchants were required to bring the goods on board the ship. The foreign buyers were required by the foreign buyer to fulfil F. O.B., contract with a foreign seller. This Court in M/S. Binani Bros. vs Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Bangalore, [1975] Supp. S.C R. 169 held that there was no privity of contract between S. T., and the appellant. The contracts were separate and independent and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export of manga ness. [444B C] 1.2 In the instant case, the contracts entered into directly between the respondent and the appellants were two separate and distinct contracts and there was a privity of agreement between the M &TC. There could not be two contracts and the contract was integrically connected with each other. The contract between a merchant and S.t.B, which entered in the independent contracts, was one and indivisible contract of sale. [445E F] 2.1 In the case of a contract between an assessee and the seller, the M would be liable to pay tax on the foreign seller 's turnover. The movement of goods from the appellant to the importer is completely separate from the transit pursuant to the export sale (See Serajuddin etc. vs State of Orissa, [1976] Supp SCR 169; Serajul Chand Rataria vs Bhuwalka Brothers Ltd., ; and Seraju Chand Ratari vs Bhuawalka Brothers, ; , referred to. 2.2 The contract in the instant cases was integrating the goods with the foreign sellers from the S,T.c. which they were not parties to the S 'T.P.T .and that the movement of the goods and export was an unconditional appropriation which passes the property. This is not because of any peculiarity of F.o.B contracts but because in this type of contract the seller ' s duty is to deliver the goods F.0.B,, once they are on board, the seller has delivered them to the buyer and it was natural that they should thereafter be at the buyer 's risk. [ 445C D] 2:3 The law is this. It has to be found out whether the contracts in the present case between the merchants and the Corporation are integrated contracts in tho course of the export or they are different. If they are differ contracts, as they are in the case, they are not different contracts. If their transactions are different, the last purchaser within the State is the M.[445G H] 2 4.1 There cannot be two last purchasers in the sale of same goods within the same State. Similarly, there cannot be both export and import the goods under a separate contract with the appellant 's foreign buyers to the latter will not make the two contracts either inte rally linked or the contract. [442E F]. Serajudul Chand Rungaria vs Bhawalka Bros. Ltd., [1975], Supp. SCR 169, followed.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974. The respondent moved an application for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate in the proceedings. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services was in accordance with the standing orders justifying the removal of the employee on successful probation during the initial or extended period of probation; that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the probationary period, his service was terminated by notice dated 12.10.1974. The appellant filed an appeal before the Labour Court which held that there was no retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and therefore the termination in this case was neither illegal nor improper or unjustified and the claim of the appellant for reinstatement was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of the appel lant was ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits. [532C] 1.2 In order to invoke the fiction enacted in sub section 2 (a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant date i.e. the date of termination of his service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date, if the workman has been given one month 's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the period of notice has expired or the workman had been paid in lieu of such notice wages for the period he has been paid at the time of retrenchment compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days ' average pay (for every completed year of continuous service) or any part thereof, in excess of six months. [525D E] 1:3 The termination is ab initio illegal and inoperative. He must, therefore, be deemed to be In continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in section 25B(1). [526E F] 2.1 It is not necessary for the purposes of sub section (2) (a), that the workman should be in continuous service within one year or six months, as the case may be, if he satisfies the conditions in clause (a). The condition is that commencing the date with reference to which calculation is to be made in case of retrenchment the date for the purpose of section 25C and Chapter VA. [500F G] 2:2 In the instant case, admittedly the appellant had rendered service for six more than 240 days within a period Of 12 months and, indisputably, therefore his case falls within section 25FF(1) of the Act. [426B C] 3. The termination was ab facto void and ineffective. There is a catena of decisions which rule that where the termination is illegal especially where there is an ineffective order of retrenchment, there is neither termination nor cessation of service and a mere declaration follows that he continued to be under continuous service with full back wages is not a valid ground for terminating the services. [498F G; 499A] 4. The question whether the termination was in contravention of section 26 or 25B (1) has to be decided first by the Labour court, on the basis of evidence and on principle. In other words, it must be negatived on the ground that it would render sub section 3(2)(a) otiose and socially beneficial legislation would receive a set back by this impermissible assumption. [ 499E F; 500B] 5.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. On his report to the Deputy Commissioner, Bhatinda that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and had demanded Rs. 30/ as bribe from one Ude Singh, the appellant was called upon to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him if the allegations in the charge sheet were proved. The appellant submitted his explanation on February 22, 1955, but the Deputy commissioner by order dt. March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and in lieu thereof he was asked to showcause why disciplinary proceedings should not he taken against the appellant if the allegation in the chargesheet were proved, and if the charges were proved the appellant would be guilty of misconduct. The Deputy Commissioner by his order dated March 17. 1955 ordered the services to be terminated. On February 22 the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of termination on the ground that the order was not passed according to which employment of the appel lant was terminated and that the appellant had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by his impugned order the services were terminated. The High Court held that the Deputy Commis sioner did not act in exercise of this authority, the order being invalid, it was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The protection of article 311(2) of the Constitution applies as much to a temporary public servant as to permanent public servants. By virtue of article 310 of the Constitu tion the appellant is not liable to be dismissed or removed from service until he had been given reasonable opportunity against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The order of dismissal was therefore invalid. [719 D E] (ii) The enquiry against the respondent was for ascertaining whether he was fit to be confirmed, and a termination made pursuant to such an enquiry would not fall within the principle of the rule of law. [ 719 B C] State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das, ; , followed.

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 for selection to the posts of Professors in the colleges. By another notification dated July 25, 1969, the Commission was consulted and it was brought to its notice that the Commission had considered the suitability of candidates for promotion as Professors in accordance with the law. The Commission submitted its report on June 25,1969, which made it quite clear that the State Government referred the selections to the Commission for the appointments. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the impugned notification. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The selection was not vitiated on account of the writ petitioner 's writ petition challenging the validity. [875 B] (ii) The Commission was also consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another, and it had been specifically stated on behalf of the State that it consulted the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, the High court erred in taking a contrary view. [873 E] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. [874 G H] (iv) The State Government had also placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969 which makes it quite obvious that the appellant had not venturing to take any plea to its contrary. Had the Commission de facto abdicated its power in favour of some committee composed of strangers to the commission, the position might have been different.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The petitioner challenged the validity of the proceedings taken by him under article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution on the ground that the speech was published in its entirety without any reference to the contents of the news item in question, and that the publication of the speech, if it had included the portion which had been so directed to be expunged in the eye of law, amounted to a breach of privilege conferred by article 19 (1) (a). Held, that the petitioner was not entitled to succeed. The expression "the right" in article 194(3) of Constitution means the right to freedom of speech guaranteed under article19(1) of that Article and that even if the privilege was not expressly made subject to the provisions of the law, it did not necessarily mean that it was not so subject. The petitioner had the fundamental right under article 194 (3) to freedom from any action in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in the Legislature or in committees thereof and the expression " the House or Houses of such Legislature" in Article 194(1), could not be construed as including a citizen 's right to move the Court for a writ of prohibition. The provisions of article 194 were intended to protect the freedom of expression guaranteed under that Article, and the petitioner had no right to complain against any alleged irregularity of procedure. The fundamental right was preserved despite the provisions in article 19. The Constitution expressly declares that the powers, privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State and of the members and committees thereof shall be such as may from time to time be defined by the legislature by law. The power conferred on the Legislature by article 194 of the constitution is subject to reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19 and cannot be extended beyond those limits. The right conferred on Parliament under article 195(1). Article 194 (2) does not import into India the law made by Parliament in pursuance of the earlier part of article 105(3), but only applies to the laws enacted by Parliament, and is not subject to any other law made in exercise of constituent power like the law which was considered in the previous part of that part of Article 194. The Act of Parliament has not broken any of the rules of procedure prescribed by it nor has it been made subject or to the provision of the Constitu tion. The validity of a law made under article 246(3)(a), read with articles 19 and 20(1 ), cannot be questioned on the grounds of any alleged illegality of the procedure. Article 194 is not made subject only to the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Con stitution, but will also be subject to those provisions of Part III. The contention that the privileges, privileges or immunities of the House of Commons of a Province and of members and Committees thereof are such as are ordered to be removed by the Speaker under article 200(3 ), is not correct. The privileges and privileges of the Houses of Parliament of a state and of its members and committee thereof are those of the Legislative Assembly of a province, and they are not expressly or impliedly made subject, to the provi sions of article 195 (1)(b) of Part 111 of the Consti tution of India. The President of India has not the power to make any law defining the powers and immunities, privileges, immunities and immunities which include the freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property guaranteed by article 31(2). Article 19(6) does no more than make that clause subject to a fundamental right conferred by the Constitution. The words "the Legislative Assembly" in cl.

The appellant State Government took over the management of a College on 5.5.1971 and appointed the respondent as Reader in that college on 7.4.1971.
