The services of the respondent were terminated by the appellant on the ground that he was drawing a salary of more than Rs.600/ per month. The appellant filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the termination orders, which were dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the requisite qualification is eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Service (O.E.S.) for appointment as Reader and not five years ' service, the respondent was entitled to be considered by the Public Service Commission for appointment to the post of Reader. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The requirement of eight years teaching experience is a matter entirely different from that of the requisite qualifications. [777G] 2.1 The condition of draw ing of Rs. 600/ or more on the date of taking over, which has been laid down in the circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment, is arbitrary and discriminatory. This condition has no nexus, whatev er, with the object underlying the qualification test in an educational institution having regard to quality, efficiency and progress in all respects. It is not unknown that private institutions generally have great handicaps in the matter of finance and oftener the teaching staff in a private college has not the same scales of pay and sometimes even has much lower scales than that of Government colleges. [778C D] 2:2 The requirement for eight years of teaching experience as mentioned in the Circular is a serious grim issue. It has to be administered on sound lines having regardto quality, efficient and progress. In view of this Court 's decision in Smt. Juthika Bhattacharya vs State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors., ; , the High Courts were right in allowing the claim in the writ applications. [779D E] 2(a) The requirement is a person eligible for appointment. He must be suitable for selection for the post.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority granted three temporary permits to the appellants. The appellants made applications to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A) consequent upon the scheme being published by the Corporation under section 69 C, the Corporation alone could not grant temporary permits and if such application is made by the corporation and granted no one else is entitled to obtain a temporary permit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court fell into an error by interpreting section 68 G(1) only to mean that even though there are 7 vacancies for temporary permit, once the Corporation made an application for temporary, not for the full strength but something short of it there was no power left in the State Government to grant temporary permit to any one else. [985C D] 2. The correct approach would be that keeping in view the strength of the vehicles fixed by the competent authority, the authority should first examine the application for number of temporary permits made by it and if they are found to be competent, eligible and qualified they may have to be granted permits for the benefit of large travelling public. That is why power to increase strength of fleet operating on the route is conferred and has to be exercised in public interest meaning transport facility to travelling public.[985D E] 3. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public, and it would be squarely attracted. [89F G] 4. The decision of the State Road Transport Corporation is upheld both by the High Courts as well as by the Supreme Court.

The appellant was the son of a Hindu undivided family. He executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of certain properties in favour of his maternal grandfather, the ancestor of respondents Nos. 1 and 2. The said property was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father respondent No. 9. Respondents Nos. I and 2 filed a suit for possession of the said property on the ground that they were not born at the time when the mortgage deed was executed and so they were entitled to challenged it. The trial court held that the property in dispute was ancestral and he had no right to challenge it. On appeal, the High Court reversed this finding holding that the properties in suit did not belong to the appellant 's father and as such it allowed the appeal of respondents 1 and 9. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral or not depends upon the nature of the property which is capable of being partitioned by metes and bounds. [59 E] (ii) The High Court was in error in holding that it had not followed the earlier Full Bench decision in Parlia Ram vs Mst. (1908) L.R. 35 I.A. 129, that the doctrine of stare decisis was applicable because the principle of stare finality is embodied in section 52 of the Punjab Courts Act, 1920, and the said rule of stare settle law has been applied to the present case. [60 C] (iii) The principle of law laid down by this Court in Parsi Ram vs Chela Ram (1909) L R. 35 1. A. 129 is that a decision which has been followed for a long period of time and has been acted upon by persons in the formation of contracts or in the disposition of their property, or in legal procedure or in other ways will generally be followed by courts of higher authority than the court establishing the rule, even though the court before whom the matter arises afterwards might not have given the same decision had the question come before it originally. [61 C D] (iv) The doctrine of law is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the Court and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under sections 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants entered Ebir Ali 's house with the common intention of killing him and caused injuries to him. The Sessions Judge accepted the verdict and convicted them all under sections 448 and 307 read with section 34 of the Code. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted the appellants but convicted the appellants under section 449 and section 307/149 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307 readwith section 34. The appellants contended that there could be no conviction under section 450 read with s.34 of Indian Penal code because the offence committed by a number of persons was actually committed in order to the committing of an offence punishable with death, and that the offence under section 302 read with S. 34 was not sustainable in law. Held, that the words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of the I.P.C., but also in the two succeeding sections, namely, 450, 451 and 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code and section 457 of I. P. C. The word "in" in section 448 of the Cr. P C. is used where house trespass is committed "inorder to the commission of any offence punishable under section 448". In the present case when it was found that the four appellants attacked Haji E brar Ali, the appellants attacked him with dagger while one used the dagger on him, each of them held that he down while one using the dagger was in law considered to have done the entire act of holding Ebber Ali down and applying the dagger. If Matiullah by himself had held Ebris Ali down, and struck him with the dagger, with the intention of causing his death and injury had actually resulted in his death he would have been guilty of murder except in some special circumstances as mentioned in section 300 of the IPC.

The appellant was the nearest male holder of a property in Gurdaspur district. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that he was entitled to succeed to the properties mentioned in the plaint as well as to the sum of Rs. 1,539 odd being the share of the last male holder excluded from inheritance by the collaterals. The appellant contended that the respondent had discharged this initial onus and that the courts below were not justified in holding that the suit was maintainable. Held, that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was cast on her under section 112(2) of the Indian Succession Act. The evidence showed that the collateral had been excluded from succession to the self acquired property of her father. The collaterals were beyond the fourth degree and it was enough for the court to say that irrespective of whether or not the custom, as recorded in Rattigan 's book so as to shift the onus to the daughter who is the res pondent. The fact that the daughter did not contest the succession of the collateral does not affect the presumption arising on the basis of the evidence produced by her. The rule laid down in Mt. Vaishno Ditti vs Mt. Rameshri, (19O8) 43 P.R. 191, approved. Held further, that even if the presumption as to correctness of a Riwaj i am is raised and accepted even though it may be rebuttable, the respondent has not discharged the onus which was thrown on her as a result of the production of the Riwahi am of 1913 and that being so, the appellant must succeed. The question whether or no distinction is to be made between ancestral and self acquired properties has to be decided on principle in each case. Mst. Subhani vs Nawab, (1889) 24 P. R. 191 and Nahab vs Mt., Aimna Bibi, Lah. 364, referred to.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. He applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney in respect of certain properties. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) Of the Indian Stamp Act to the High Court and the reference was heard by a Bench consisting of three Judges. The first two judges held that the instrument in question was a deed of settlement which comprised several matters, but the second one related to distinct matters and must be stamped with the aggregate amount of duty. The second judge held that though the instrument was executed by one person, if he fills several capacities and the authority conferred is general, there would be distinct delegations in respect thereof. The third judge held against the respondent. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the words "distinct matters" used in section 5 Of the Stamp act refer to different classes of instruments which might be executed either by one individual or by another and not by a single individual when he is acting as an executor or administrator. The word "distinguished" in section 4 Of the Act means something more than "categories". It is well settled that when two words are used in a statute in two consecutive provisions, they must be construed as distinct matters. In the present case the instrument did not contain distinct matters but consisted of one matter only and that matter was the execution of a general power of Attorney by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the donee. Chaudhury vs Chaudhury ([1879] A.C. 848), referred to.

The assessee company was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was an Indian State. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of the newly formed State instituted a Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, and the said Ordinance was repealed by the Finance Act, 1950. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the depreciation allowed under the Saurashtra Income Tax Ordinance, being a deductible amount in computing the written down value of the assets of the assessee company could be deducted from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, even though not claimed. Held, that the provisions of the Finance Acts were applicable to the present case and the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was a deductible deduction in computing written down values under the said Act. The words "of a Part B State" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms. The word "of any law relating to tax on profits of business" in para 2 of that order means and includes not only leave no doubt as regards the intention of the authority but also the fact that it is within the competence of the Central Government to make the removal of difficulties. The expression "of such Part B States" in Paragraph 2 of this Removal of difficulties Order must mean that the Income tax Officer, in determining the written off value under section 10(5) (b), has to apply the provisions in computing its written down Value under section I3(5)(b) of the Indian Incometax Act irrespective of whether any difficulty had arisen in giving effect to the provisions. The Commissioner of Income tax vs Kamala Mills Ltd., ; , followed.

The appellant was a contractor of the respondent Corporation. The respondent Corporation invited tenders from registered contractors for laying civil and structural works, including construction of a Main Station Building. Paragraph I of the notifi cation listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" as also the "commit tive minimum qualifica tion" as provided in para I of Part I of Schedule II to the . The appellant 's tender was accepted by the respondent corporation and the contract was terminated on 3rd January, 1989. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award of the contract. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the prequalifying conditions set out in para 1 were only the three conditions set forth in para II and that the details called for in Para I could be supplied at any time before the final award of contract. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the clause requiring the intending tenderers to furnish a tender for the contract, was not mandatory; (ii) the terms and conditions set up by the appellant were only directory and not mandatory and (iii) the supply of certain documents referred to in para V was indispensable to assess whether the applicant fulfilled the pre qualificato ry requirements. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of para I is a note on the tendering system in K.P.C. and the application other than the mini mum qualifying requirement should be prerogative of K. P.C., only. It was not known on what grounds that application was rejected nor had that party come to Court with any such grievance. The acceptance of the tender of the 4th respondents was, therefore, not open to challenge. [239F G] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had no doubt placed a condition precedent for supply of forms of tender by it but was bound to conform to it even in regard to this contract. It is clear from the terms of para V that the conditions called for under Para I were not supplied along with the request for application of tender forms. The clause required the K.C . to furnish the requisite information and particulars regarding these requirements. [240G H] 1:3. The requirement was satisfied by the KP. C.C.; that he fulfilled all the pre qualification conditions setout in para IV. The terms and condi tions of Para V were not complied with; and that it was not possible to read the three essential requirements as stated in para VI. [241H] 1 :4. The contract in Ramana 's case was admittedly "a note on a tender system in the notification dated 23.1.1988" which inter alia provided that the intending tenderer should satisfy the K P. C., by supplying such of the documents called for by it, and that he satisfied the conditions specified in para. V. The reference to "annual output of the works" was obviously a reference to the works of the nature described in para 11. [242H; 243A B] 1 5. The question whether the course adopted by the P.W.I. had caused any real prejudice to the appellant and other parties who had already supplied all the documents in time and sought no extension at all, was a matter for the K .P.c. to assess. [243D E] 1 6. The first respondent was not entitled to act arbitrarily in accepting the tender documents only because it thought it would not be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. But it is not known whether this rule was applicable to the case. [244E] 7.

The appellant was the owner of a house. He had a house in which he had a shop. The house was let out to him for residential purposes and the appellant was put in possession of the land. In pursuance of an agreement between the parties, the appellant made an application before the Additional Custodian under section 5 A of the East Punjab Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, for confirmation of the exchange and other consequential and incidental orders made in connection therewith. The Additional Custodian rejected the application on the ground that the order of confirmation was not appealable under section 27 of the Act. The appellant then filed an appeal to the Custodian General which was dismissed. On a revision petition by the appellant, the High Court held that the decision of the Additional custodian was final and conclusive and that the orders of confirmation were binding on the Additional Controller. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order under appeal was one passed by virtue of section 27(3) of the Central Act of 1950 which purports to indicate the effect of repeal on previous matters. Under section 58(3), the application made by the person affected thereby is subject to the revisional powers of the Custodian. Section 27(4) provides that anything done or any action taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under this Ordinance shall be deemed to have been done or taken in the exercise of the powers conferred by the Ordinance as if this Act were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action was taken. [1137 B C] (ii) The appellant 's contention that the Additional Deputy Custodian had no kind of interest in the land which entitled them to contest the application for confirmation, was without substance and must fail. The order of the Assistant Custodian under appeal is one passed on the basis of a decision of this Court in the case of N. M. Abdullah vs The State of Bombay, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 1137. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the confirmation of transactions relating to such land was opposed to the policy and directives of the Government. [1104 C D] (iii) The orders under appeal were not appealable but only those orders which could be taken into consideration are regulated by section 40(4). Under section 27, the application of the appellant for confirmation pending on the date when the Central Acts of 1950 came into force had to be dealt with and disposed of under the Act and the order was final. [111 E F] (iv) The High Courts were right in taking the view that the power exercisable thereunder by the Custodian under the East Act of 1947 was not subject to appeal and remitted the matter back to him to decide afresh on merits.

The appellant company, a locality in Bombay, was a factory. Its factory consisted of workmen employed in the tiny, but were getting on well in their business and in their relations with their workmen. The dispute between the parties related to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishment before 1965. The Tribunal held that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata as it did not provide for those categories of bonus and confined itself to profit based bonus only, but also included certain other categories of employees in the industrial dispute. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Bonus Act speaks of a whole Code, on the sole subject of profit based wage, to consider whether any festival or festival is called for. It does not provide that the Tribunal should make a claim of customary bonus or those based on custom. [603 D] (2) The object of the Bonus Act is to give relief to persons employed in certain establishments not in all establishments. The Act provides for a complete code and no species of bonus can survive without any other form of bonus, nor can it annihilate by implication, other distinct and different kinds of bonus such as the one oriented on custom or condition of service. [503 G] (3) The Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it. It is not open to the workmen to raise a fresh industrial dispute for the years 1965 and 1966 and so long as that award stood, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be subversive of the rule of res judicata. [403 G H] (4) The Tribunal was right in holding that the Bonus Scheme was not an exhaustive one. It did not apply at all to the case.

The petitioners were appointed directly by the Haryana Superior Judicial Service of Punjab in December, 1976. They were promoted to the Higher Judicial Service on the basis of a competitive examination held for recruitment to the Superior Judicial Services of the State. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana declared that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that the High Court acted upon the amendment made in the Punjab on December 31, 1976 with retrospective effect from April 9, 1976, including the amendment to rule 12. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The seniority of members of service is to be determined with reference to the dates of confirmation without applying the rule of rotation. [1046C] 2.1 The High Courts were not justified in applying the Rule of rotation at the time of confirmation of the promotees. [1147D] Haryana State and Haryana vs State of Haryana, ; , followed. 1.2 In Punjab, the High Courts never consulted on the question whether the Governor in the exercise of power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 has the power to frame rules regulating the conditions of service of judicial officers of the States. [1104E] 2:3 The High courts were not right in applying rule 12 to the seniority list of the Service, because, the rules must now be understood to mean that the decision which is taken by the Governor of Punjab on the recommendation of the Governor for the first time shall be final and conclusive. [111A B] Haryana Government vs State, ; referred to. 2.4 The High court was not justified on the ground that the rule had been amended in consultation with the High court. [112C D] Haryana Public Service Commission vs Punjab Civil Service (Civil Appeal No. 42 of 1977 decided on 31st December, 1977) and Haryana State vs State Civil Service, ; followed.

The respondents were appointed as Junior Assistant to the post of Senior Assistants in the Commercial Taxes Department. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated February 18, 1986 passed by the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad, directing the State Government to examine the legal effect of the Government Order in G.O.Ms. No. 1648 dated November 20, 1982 and to consider the legal consequence of the said order. The Government allowed the representation of the respondents and directed that the order of appointment, seniority, promotion etc., be maintained. The High Court held that the zonal seniority was the criteria. Aggrieved by the decision of the Tribunal, the State filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government has no inherent power in creating a zone or organising local cadre within the zones except in accordance with the provisions made in the Andhra pradesh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation for Direct Recruitment) Order 1975. [574D] 1.2 The State Govern ment has no authority to create a zone, or organising Local Cadre within a zone. [575F] 1:3. The State Govt. has no power to bifurcate or reorganise a zone within a Zone or cadres therein. In exercise of the power under proviso to paragraph 3(1) it is for the President notwithstanding the expiry of the period of twelve months prescribed in sub para (1) of para graph 3, by an order require the State Govt., whenever he considers it expedient so to do to have the power to divide or reorganize a zone into local cadres for different parts of the State. [576F G] 1 :4. The power given to the State Govern ments in sub paragraph (7) of Para graph 3 is only to organise a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts in any department when more than one cadre in relation to such category exists in each department; so that State Government may organise one cadre when morethan one cadre is in respect thereof. [577F G, 578A] 1 5. The expression 'constituted otherwise ' occurring in paragraph 2(e) is of wide amplitude but is only relatable to the power given by the Presi dent to the state government to organise local cadres in respect any class or classes of posts. [578B C] 1 6. The word 'otherwise ' is of widest amplitude and includes all other matters which are included in sub paragraphs (1), (2) and (3). [578F] 7. The words 'constitute ' used in paragraph 3 (7)(a) read with paragraph 3.(7) give ample power to the Government to organise any local cadre for the purpose of recruitment, seniority or promotion etc. as the case may be. [579A B] 8.

The appellant was the owner of Gadi Sirampur in execution of a mortgage decree. The respondent No. 1 obtained a permanent lease of four villages from the appellant for a term of ten years and the appellant purchased the said lands on payment of Rs. 1,10,631/ . The appellant 's father had executed a mortgage deed in favour of the respondent No 2. The appellant was not a party to that suit. The trial court held that the respondent was subrogated to the position of the Bank and that the appellant was entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants. On appeal, the High Court reversed this decision holding that the plaintiff was sub bound to pay the permanent lease in respect of the lands and mesne profits from the date of the mortgage till the date on which the suit was filed. Held, that the question whether a mortgagor in possession has power to lease the mortgaged property depends upon the authority to deal with the property in the usual course of management. The mortgagor in Possession is not liable for destructive waste is acts which are destructive or permanently injurious to the mortgaged properties if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts. The true position has been stated in the following terms by Das, J., in Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar (I.L.R. and Balmukund vs Motilal (A.I.R, , approved. Held further, that it is for the lessee if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagee to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of administration.

The petitioner, a contractor, filed an arbitration suit in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The respondent filed an application before the Calcutta high Court under Sections 5,12 and 33 for setting aside the arbitration agreement dated November 23, 1990 in respect of the first time in July 1979. The learned Single Judge of the Calcutta Division Bench dismissed the application on the ground that the claim was barred by limitation. The Division Bench held that it was not proved that the petitioner had sent any claim in July, 1979 and that the respondent had abandoned the contract, even assuming that any claim was as a fact made in July. 1979 and payment was not made, the petitioner could not take recourse to arbitration under section 8 of the Act for appointment of an arbitrator. The High Court quashed the arbitration clause 68 of the contract in matter Nos. 1326, 1364 and 1365/90 dated November 3, 1990 and held that the claims were barred by limitations. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the petitioner having made the claim for the first lime in July 1978, the arbitration could not be proceeded with; (ii) the respondent having sent the bills on July 12, 1979, and payment being not made there, the respondent could not have taken recourse to the provisions of the facts of this case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Court is entitled to permit a contracting party to rescind the contract or the court can revoke, the authority to refer the disputes or differences to arbitration. [368C] 2.1 In the instant case, the petition was clearly and undoubtedly hopelessly barred claim as the petitioner by his conduct slept over his right for more than 10 years. Statutory arbitrations stand apart. In these circumstances it is an exceptional case and the courts below have justifiably exercised their discretionary power, and jurisdiction under sections5 and 12(2) (b) to permit the respondent to rescind, the contract. [369D E] 2:2.1 The Court has discretion to exercise its discretion in permitting a contracting parties to rescind or rescind the arbitration agreements. In all cases it is not a condition precedent that there should be an order of appointment as to avail the remedy under section 5.

The appellants in the appeal were the estate of a Zamindar. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of section 2(1) and the notification issued under section 3(1), as amended by Act 1 of 1964, provided that where a suit is wholly or partly dismissed under rule 8, the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action. The appellants contended that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred by the principles of res judicata and also on the ground that the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the Act. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the objections were barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. On appeal the High Court held that the plea was barred under the principles laid down by this Court in Raj Kishore Pratap Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh (1962) Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564 and that the bar of resjudicata would not operate as res judicata against a plaintiff in a subsequent suit on the same point. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The contention that the judgment debtor was entitled to get compensation under the Act is unsustainable. The objection of the judgment creditor is unsustainable because it is only a part of the mortgaged property has vested in the State absolutely free from all encumbrances. [914 D] The question whether the decree cannot be executed against the estate or not depends on the plea taken by the parties and the decision of the claims officer or the Board has been made final by the Act, and it is not open to the appellants to proceed with the execution. Their only remedy is to get the compensation under Act. [936 D] In the present case, the decree holder had a right to proceed against the properties of the mortgagor in view Of section 4 (d) and section 4 of the Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1964.

The respondents, who were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ', challenged the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Services Examination Rules (O.As.) on the ground that they had been allocated to any of the Central Services, Group 'B ' and Group 'C ' as no embargo was placed restricting the candidates of Group 'D ' service, as in the case of Group A ' Service, to sit for the main examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS or Central services Group ' A '. The Tribunal dismissed the O.As. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the second Proviso to Rule 17 is violative of Article 14; and (ii) the proviso is not ultra vires Regulation 4 of C.S.(E) Rules, which provides for a candidate who has been allocated from the service to a service shall not be eligible to appear again in the Civil Service Examination unless he has first resigned from the Service. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The second proviso is violative Article 14. [97G] 1.2 The proviso to rule 4 of Rule 4 is not unconstitutional and ultra vires. Regulation 4(iii) of CS.E. (OAs) Rules provides that a candidate, who has already been allocated and appointed to a Service shall not he eligible to be considered for appointment to any service/post on the basis of the result of the previous CSE. The proviso is also violative of article 14. Therefore, the second Explanation to Rule 5 of CSCS (E) is unconstitutional against the appellants. [99H; 100A] 1:3. The second Proviso is not invalid because it makes a discrimination between the candidates who have been allocated for the service and those who on the other hand are appointed to the service. [100B] 1.(4) The proviso cannot be struck down as unconstitutional because the services under Group A and Group B are different services and, therefore, the impugned second proviso has no application. [101C D] 2.1 In view of the decision of this Court in C.A. No. 5470/90 dated 20th August 1990, the first proviso to r. 4 of Central Services Examination (Amendment) Rules 1987 is held to be discriminatory against the candidates appointed to IPS and 16 Group 'E '. [102D] 2.(a) The second Explanation is violative because it does not travel beyond the intent of the main rule putting any unjustifiable embargo on the number of attempts at the examination. [103F] (b) The first proviso is unconstitutional as it makes no discrimination between candidates appointed through the same open competition to appear in the next CSE, and those candidates who are allocated to IPS or Union territory, which is not otherwise eligible in terms of clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). [103G] 2(c) The impugned second Proviso has no rational nexus with the object of the scheme putting any unreasonable embargo on any candidate appointed to IAS, or to sit at the next Civil Service examination. The provision is not violative of Articles 14. It is also discriminatory against candidates appointed in the Indian Police or Central Service Group 'As applicable to the Indian police or Central service Group '. Therefore the second and third proviso is held unconstitutional. [104H; 105A] 2:2. The first Proviso to rs.4 of CSE Rules, 1987 is violative as it does no discrimination against the candidate appointed in any other manner eligible in accordance with the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.P .S.C. and is not valid. [105B] 3.1 It is not discriminatory because the first Proviso is equally applicable to all candidates who were otherwise eligible.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The Advisory Board, after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, rejected the request for assistance of a friend. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court and that application was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the detenu would have been better placed before the Advisory Board. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Advisory Boards had no justification to refuse assistance of the Deputy Collector as a friend was bad and continued detention of the appel lant became vitiated. [790B] 2.1 In the instant case, the detaining author ity has not taken into consideration the allegation that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have be better placed. The Board, therefore, is not justified in refusing assistance of an Advocate. [789D] 2:2 It is true that while section 8(e) disentitles a detenu from claiming the assistance of natural justice as afriend '. But what cannot be permitted directly should not be allowed to be done in an indirect way. Sundararajan, J., speaking for the Court, explained the position and held that if a person was not a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. [788E F] 2 :3 The Advisory board has no justification for refusing assistance to the appellant in such circumstances. The rule in A. K. Roy etc. vs Union of India & Anr., ; applied.

The appellants were the owners of certain premises requisitioned and acquired under the Defence of India Act, 1939. The requisition orders provided that the goods requisitioned and requisitioned were to be delivered by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they related. The appellants contended that the delivery orders did not pass on September 30, 1946, when the goods were actually appropriated to the particular order and therefore there was no acquisition of property under the Act. Held, that the requisition orders did riot apply to the case. The words "the taking over" in r. 75 A (2) of the Defence Of India Rules, 1939, are wide enough to include an order of requisition made by the Government of India on September 29, 1946. The word "acquisition" is not defined in the Act and it includes all property which may be taken in execution of a decree or order passed by the Court. In the present case the requisition order did not apply to any particular property but only to the mills as such. Held further, that under r. 77 of the Rules framed under the Government Of India Act the property in the goods passed to the Government and not to the owners thereof. The delivery orders were valid and binding on the appellants. The provisions of rr. 75A (2), (3) and (4) of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure did not require that the property should be taken over by the owner thereof or that the properties in the present cases had been delivered to the appellants under the orders of the Government.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned was 1963 64. In the assessment relating to the assessment year 1963 64, the assessee claimed that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree with the matter and held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section 23A. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Tribunal. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax under Section23A was made on or before the date relevant to the assess year 1963 63, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision and not a reserve. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessee itself called it a provision. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve for the purpose of the Income Tax Act. [113E] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. In Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , this Court held that the provisions made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision which was a provision, and not an reserve. [114F] In VIrshad Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. vs Commis sioner of Income tax, Andhra pradesh, , this court held that since no order imposing additional tax is made on the anticipated loss and contingency are charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are repre sentable being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. [115E F] Vazir Qasim Sultan Tobacco Cooperative Ltd. & Ors.

The petitioners in the writ petitions, who were working as Assistant Engineers (on a later point of time) in the erstwhile State of Rajasthan joined service in the year 1955 and continued to be on the cadre of Assistant Engineers. They challenged the validity of the seniority list dated December 17, 1965 issued by the Government of India on the ground that officers appointed to temporary posts on the basis of interview alone were subjected to competitive written and personality test and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. The petitioners contended that they were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds so as to obtain the result that all Assistant Engineers formed one class under the Indian Railway Establishment Board. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification of temporary Assistant Officers into those that were recruited on the same day by selection was not discriminatory but violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [1025C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners who were appointed to the cadre posts in Class 1 service and supporting their claim for permanent Assistant Engineers joined service much later than the results of the competitive examinations were placed above those appointed on the date of selection by the Union Public Service Commission. The requisite direction was thus made and carried out. [1125D] 1:3. There is no provision in the Rules which excludes the rule of constructive res judicata. The distinction between the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case (supra) and the important question of equality was once for all settled. To find fault with it, at this juncture again on the touch stone of equality dimension would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprehensible now at this point of times to dig up old issues. [1102E F] Katyni Dayal 'S case (Supra) distinguished. 1:4. The rule of weightage also appears to be reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Similarly when the dispute raised between the Officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented, in KatYani Dayal"s case, still it was a dispute raised before this Court which has already been decided finally. A dispute now sought to be raised under Article 32 of the Constitu tion must be held to be barred by principles of res judicata as also in the rule frown of constructive Res Judicata. [111E F; 112A B] Kattyani Dayal & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.5 The distinction and the classification between the three services was equally well marked. The classification was well found and expanded. It is thus clear that the distinction and classification of the temporary Assistant Engineers and members of the Indian Railways Service of Engineers Class I fell clearly to be identified and marked. [112B C] Katyanani Dayal vs Union Of India, ; , distinguished.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 I.P.C., and section 11 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but on appeal by special leave it was contended that section 11 Of the WestBengal Special Courts (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the offences alleged to have been committed by the appellant within the specified areas were required to be tried by the Special Court under the special procedure. Held, that the provisions of the Ordinance and the rules framed thereunder did not violate article 14 Of the Constitution. The object of which was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State was to prevent disorder and disorder and to ensure public safety. The Act was intended to achieve a social purpose or achieved the same result. It was not necessary that the Legislature should select only such offences or classes of cases as were likely to be committed by persons who were to be proceeded against by the special tribunal. The fact that the deviation from normal procedure prescribed in the Ordinance was not so many or vital as in the Bengal case, did not affect the result, as the defect of absence of a reasonable or rational classification was still there. The Legislature had left it to the State Government to classify offences or class of cases for the purpose of the Act, and the statute was open to challenge of making arbitrary discrimination. The State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, [1952] S.C.R. 284, followed.

The prosecution case was that the appellants along with two others were tried for offences under sections 302, 396 I.P.C. and section 396 I P.C., and convicted by the Sessions Judge, Kanpur, under section 396 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the other four accused but convicted the other five accused under section 302 I. P. C. and the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to them by the learned Sessions Judge was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that having regard to the size of the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased, it is not probable that the assailants armed with various weapons could have been present in that kothas at the time of the occurrence and that the evidence of P.W. 2 and P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 to the extent that their evidence was corroborated by the evidence on record, were not convincing. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The evidence of the eye witnesses is corroborated by their evidence in material particulars. [574 D] (2) There is no reason whatsoever for rejecting the evidence given by P. Ws. 1 and 7. The evidence was that while they went to the eastern side of the village, the deceased and his wife were sleeping in the house and beating the deceased. They were not strangers and there was sufficient light at the place of occurrence. [575 D] In the instant case, the evidence is corroborated from the evidence. There is also no reason for rejecting their evidence on the ground that they are interested witnesses. The fact that some of the accused persons were acquitted by the trial court could not be relied upon because they had intentionally made improvements in their version about the occurrence. They have been believed by not only the learned trial judge but also by the Judges of the High Courts.

The appellant State Road Transport Corporation created under a State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to run its business as an undertaking and the employer terminated the employment of some of the employees during the initial period of probation. The respondent Corporation terminated the services of some employees during that period on the ground of unsuitability. Thereupon, an industrial dispute was raised by the appellant. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance with section 25F. The employer Corporation came up before a Division Bench which held that the termination of service was not retrenchment within the meaning of section 2 (oo) but was retrenchment within its ambit, and that the discharge of the employee was bad for non compliance with section25F. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the services were terminated on the grounds of unsubsity and therefore did not amount to retrenchment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'termination ' in section 25FF of the has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word. It means the discharge or dismissal of the workman by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent Corporation had not terminated the service of the appellants from the date of their initial appointment and there was no order of termination of the services. The High Court has rightly come to the conclusion that in these cases the order terminating the services was bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour Court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. [789D] 1:3. The question whether a discharge or retrenchment is retrenchment within section 2 of the Act does not arise for consideration before this Court. It is the stand of the employer that the employees were probationers at the time of their appointment and that they were terminated after termination of their service. There was no dispute that as a condition precedent to discharge the requirements of section 25 F of the , it had not been complied with, and if the discharge was not based on any misconduct or victimisation, the employer would be liable for dismissal. [788E] 1 :4. The expression "termination" in section2(oo), does not include termination of services by way off punishment. The effect of non compliance of section25 F is that every case of termination has to be decided on its own facts. The stage has come when the view indicated in money 's case has been "break into the consensus" and there is no scope for putting the clock back or for an anti clockwise operation. Once the conclusion is reached that retrenchment as contemplated under section 2, on transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as a "deemed retrenchment", it would be wrong to hold that the expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of employment except those not expressly included in section25G or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the .

The assessee, a dealer in unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration, filed returns of sales effected by it of unclaimed and unrelated goods year after year and paid sales tax pursu ant to the assessment made by the Sales Tax department. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the assessee 's turnover under section 56 of the Indian Railways Act, 1941. The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes rejected the claim on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed or unconnected goods was a regular feature of the assessee"s activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the same. In second appeal, the Tribunal held that the sale effected by the assessee was a "dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1940 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the good. It seems to South Eastern Railway was a 'dealer for the purposes of the Calcutta Finance ( Sales Tax)Act, 1941 and therefore the sale took place. The Board of Revenue, West Bengal and simi larly, it is an act which may he regarded as obviously incidental or subsidiary to its commercial business as carriers of the same goods. It appears to South eastern Railway was the 'dealer ' for the purpose of the said Act. [781E F] 2. In the instant case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423.

The appellant, a Director of the Insurance Company, was appointed as Managing Director on March 1, 1949. He resigned from the office in 1942 and was succeeded by his brother J. Dalmia. The appellant filed a suit against the Union Agencies for recovery of certain sums of money which were due to them from the appellants. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mere fact that the funds of the company were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved that the amount was received in cash and not through transfer which transactions had to be adjusted. [387 G] (ii) The fact that J. was a Director in the appellant 's firm was not conclusive as to whether he had any knowledge of the transaction with respect to the full working of the scheme to provide for the losses of the Union agencies from the funds. [388 C D] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the falsification of the journal vouchers related back to the original diversion of the amount out of the funds and that the fact that it was not shown that J had ever issued instructions regarding the activities of the union Agencies had no bearing on the question whether the appellant had knowledge of these facts. [389 D E] (iv) The evidence on record showed that the money of the appellant company was diverted to the Union Agency by the transaction proved by the prosecution. It could not have been possible for the prosecution to lead direct evidence about the source of the money to the union agencies and to prove that the appellant did so in a position to know the source or knowledge of its source. [390 E F] (v) The appellant had no knowledge of his knowledge with respect of the full operation of the schemes to provide him with the credit standing in the books of the Company. He had also no knowledge about the transactions with the Insurance company and that he had no know about the whole affair. He was not aware of the transactions. [391 G H] (vi) The conduct of J. in dealing with the transactions was not such as to amount to a criminal conspiracy. It was not possible for him to believe that J was misled by the dealings with the Bank and that it had nothing to do with the movement of the securities held by the Insurance Companies or the receipt of cash or the other transactions. The fact, therefore, that J did not know about their business in the relevant accounting period was a mere ruse to show that the transaction was done by J. [392 G H; 393 A B] (vii) The prosecution case was that the moneys were diverted for the Union agency and that they had been paid to the Bank by J, and that there was no evidence to show the diversion of funds and the desirability of falsifying the accounts and papers of the office. [393 C D].

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. The Government of Bombay sanctioned certain rules called the Allocated Government Servants (Absorption, Seniority, Pay and Allowances) Rules, 1957. These rules provided that "the ministerial staff in the Secretariat service shall be deemed to have been allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of a State and were allotted to serving in connection therewith. " The appellants were not absorbed in the Ministerial Service of a Secretariat Service but were transferred to the Secretariat of the Government of Gujarat and assigned duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Kutch. The respondents Nos. 2 to 148 who were holding the permanent posts of the secretariats of the Part B State of Saurashtra and the State Government of Saurashtra were allotted the posts of clerks in the secretaries of the part B State. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of transfer on the ground that it altered the conditions of service of applicants for the Secretariat cadre on and from November 1, 1956. The High Court held that the order violated r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules framed by the Government and quashed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The rules did not violate the proviso to cl. (6) of section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1956 which altered the condition of service applicable immediately before November 1. 1956 to the disadvantageous. [519 D] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the Government had the authority to transfer subject to the Constitution and rules made under article 309 any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do. Transfer of the personnel from the States of Saurashtra to the secretariat could not be challenged, and that because they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts they would not be deprived of their statutory right under section 115(7) proviso. [525 G H] (iii) The order of transferring the appellants to the Secretariats was contrary to the Recruitment rules. It altered the condi tions of service under the orders of the Central Government, and it altered conditions of serv ice. The order did not amount to admission of an officer for the first time in the service. [500 G] (iv) The State had the power to transfer the respondent from the districts and to post and assign them duties in the Secretar ical Department. The power to fix the conditions was reserved exclusively to the Central Govern ment. [511 B C] (v) The Government had no authority to vary the conditions. The rules were made under Article 309 of the Constitution. There was merely "regularisation" of the appointment of those persons for the purpose of performing service in the department and on terms not ceremanted, but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States personnel in the departments.

The Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was passed in 1948. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Haryana General Sales tax (Amendment & Validation) Ordinance, 1967 on the ground that it contravened section 15 of the Central Sales Tax Act, as amended by the Punjab General sales Tax (Second Amendment and Validation), Act, 1969. The High Court dismissed their petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the provisions of the Punjab Amending Act and the Validation Act were not discriminatory and that the levy of tax on sale or purchase of declared goods within a State was violative of article 14 and was also unconstitutional being in violation of articles 14 and 19. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Haryana General sales tax (Second amendment and Validation ) Act, 1968 is valid. [553 B] (2) The provisions of section 15(a) of the Act are not discriminatory as they are violative of Articles 14 and19. [554 C] (3) The Act has been made retrospective but no machinery is provided to discover if the declared goods were assessed to tax more than once. As there was a discrimination between the imported goods and local goods, the stage of tax is the sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay the tax and in the case of purchase tax the stage is purchase by the first dealer liable under section 5(2)(a) (vi). [554 E] (4) The levy of sales tax on declared goods is not discriminatory. The rate of tax same in every case is the price of goods manufactured or produced in the State and similar goods imported in the course of inter state trade or commerce. [555 F G] (5) The fact that the imported raw materials are exempt from taxation altogether, does not make any difference because the levy is on sale of declared articles. It is only when a person is not liable to tax under section 3(2) of Central Sales tax Act, that he can be taxed at one stage in the same way as the dealer who pays the tax.

The appellants who were the mortgagors of a joint family business filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amount due from them on account of mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed that decree holding that the mortgages were not binding on them or on their shares in the joint family property and that the debt was scaled down by the High court in favour of defendants 2 to 7 only and that they would still be entitled to avail himself of the benefit of the scaling down of the decree. The appellants contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and exceptions to this rule were admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage had been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; and that, as the decree holders were bound under the terms of the compromise they could not be allowed to take into court all the documents in their power or possession relating to the mortgage and reconveyor. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that a mortgage decree is one and composite and exceptions are admitted in Special circumstances where there is severance of the interests of the mort gage has been dis disruption at the behest of the mortgagor himself; but where there was severance of interest of the mortgaged property by the mortgagee, he would certainly be enti tled to have his debts scaled under the provisions of the Act in spite of the provision of general law which prevents a mortgagor from denying the liability of the interest which he owns in the mortgaged properties to satisfy the entire mortgage debt. Held further, that in case of a mortgage debt when the loan has been advanced to more than one person, if one of the debtors happens to be an agriculturist while others are not, the agriculturist debtor would certainly have the benefit thereof and would be liable to be sold.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of rent and damages. The respondents contended that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The trial court held that the first plaintiff was entitled to recover possession of the premises as sub tenants, but the High Court in appeal reversed this decision holding that the City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts were not competent to entertain a suit for the recovery of arrears of rent where the relationship of landlord and tenant existed between the parties. HELD : (i) The suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant, but between a sub tenant and a subtenant. The plaint in the present case did not disclose that the appellants were the tenants of the suit premises. [373 B] (ii) The High Court correctly decided that the suit filed by the plaintiffs could not be determined by the City civil court. The suit filed in the City of Bombay was one relating to possession of premises to which the provisions of Part 11 of the Act apply and in that suit claims and questions arising out of the said Act or any of its provisions had to be dealt with. [375 C] (iii) The suits were essentially a suit between a tenant and sub tenants and the suit did not cease to be a suit by virtue of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. [374 D] (iv) The City Civil court could not decree the suit in the High court for trying the title thereto. The suits filed by them were essentially one relating only to possession and not to the sub tenants. [376 G H] (v) The provisions of section 41 of the City Tenants ' Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1944, are applicable to a suit where there is no question of title to the premises let out to the respondents.

The appellant was appointed managing director of a private company in the year 1955. He was appointed as the managing director by an order dated July 7, 1955. The respondent was appointed the managing directors on January 14, 1957. On July 7 the appellant filed a suit against the Company and the respondents for the following reliefs: (a) that the appointment of the appellant should be made after the commencement of the Act; (b) that he had not ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the meetings of the Board of Directors; (c) that his appointment was illegal and inoperative; (d) that in any event, the appointment was void. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant had been validly appointed as managing director and therefore the appointment could not be made by the company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the word "assignment" in section 255 of the new Act, which has reference only to an appointment by a director, does not include appointment; (ii) the words "assign" in the main part of section 86B of the old Act are used in connection with the making provision in this regard. HELD : (i)(a) The word "association" in sub section (1) of section 255 is wide enough to include "appointment". The word 'assignment ' does not mean "appointment", and it means appointment. It is intended that a certain number of directors would be the chosen representatives of the shareholders. [334 B C] (b)(i) The words "as respects" in s. 86B(1) are used to include appointment. The word, therefore, does indicate that there should be no perpetual management. The persons constituting the managing company as such must change their position from time to time and so even if they were appointed directors, there would be no hereditary management. [336 C D] (ii)(a). The word is used in section 86A(1), which has a wide connotation. It means "appointment" or "assigned". The words are not intended to include appointments". The expression "assuming that by virtue of the provisions of section 312, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of the section would have included "appointments". [335 D E] (c)(ii) The proviso to section 86 B does not indicate that it was intended that the word 'revocation ' in the sub section would include " appointment" and thereby making it possible for the directors to continue to be members. [333 F G] (d)(iii). The proviso is intended to make an assignment of a managing director to another person, as the latter has no power to appoint him after the expiry of the period of his office. [332 B C].

The appellants are the tenants of the respondent firm. The respondent filed an eviction petition being H.R.C. No. 641/75 against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the Respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for contravening the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Act. In an appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction petition was filed against the appellant firm and one another partnership firm and that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellant had sublet the premises to M/S. Adeswar Glass Mart and was liable to he evicted for contravention of the provisions. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that it is only by virtue of the provision of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. [420C] Chhotelal Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, ; , relied upon. In the instant case no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise this contention at this stage at all. This contention must fail. Had this contention been raised in the Trial Court or even in the first Appel late Court, it would have been open to them to amend the eviction petitions and join the partners as re spondents. [426D E] Chh landlady Pyarelal, the partnership firm is carried on business at the said premises and that firm was carried on the business in that premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the same business. Moreover, although a notice was given by the respondent to the appellant and M/ S. Adhirajlal, it could not be said that the partnership deed and ledgers were produced. It is also not one which would have shown that rent was received by the appellants from M/ SS. Adarayan Glass Industries, the firm or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in Chhotelals Pyarelal 's case is directly applicable to the case before this Court.

The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under Entry No. 1, List I of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature enacted the Central Act with a view to provide for the imposition of ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling limit. Section 2(n) defines "vacant land" to mean land which is used or is capable of being used for purposes of agriculture, or for purposes ancillary thereto including horticulture, forest land, pasture land, waste land, plantation and topeaking of such plants as may be prescribed by the Rules. The Act was enacted with a purpose to provide that if any land situated within the limits of an urban agglomeration other than land which was mainly used for the purpose of agriculture and agriculture in this connection includes horticulture, but does not include raising of grass, dairy farming, poultry farming, breeding live stock and cultivation or the growing of such crops as may he prescribed by rules, the whole of the Andhra Pradesh shall be deemed to belong to category D in that Schedule. Section 3(j) defines 'vacant lands ' to mean "land which is capable, of being use for purposes Of agriculture, but includes land deemed to be agricultural land under this Act". The Andhra Act was amended by the Andhra Act No. 1151 of 1976 and a new section 2(p)(A)(ii) was introduced in 1976. Section 4 provided that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess or to exceed two acres, he shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of the Act was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Andhra State Legislature had no competence to enact the impugned Act; (ii) the definition of "vacants" in section 2 (n) of the Central Acts was not ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the State, and (iii) the entire Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1976 was ultra vires. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of 'vacants ' in section 3(f) is materially in the same terms as the definition in the Andhra Land Reforms Acts. Section 7 sub section (2) of that Act defines " Vacant land". Sub section (3) provides that if a person or family unit holds land in excess, of the limit specified in column (1) of Schedule I, he would be liable for surrender to the State Government. The entire Andhra State Act is ultra vires the State legislature. [1155D E] 2. The expression "vacancy land" in Section 2 (o) (A)(i) of Central Acts is not defined in the Act but in the definition section 3 (f) of Act No, 1151. Therefore, the definition cannot be extended to land situate within the urban agglomerations referred to in section 1(1). [1156E F] 3. The term "vacation land" has been defined in section 4(a)(i), to mean any land which may be used for purpose of cultivation or for the purposes ancillary to agriculture, and includes horticulture but does no include raising or raising grass, Dairy farming, cattle feed, breeding, poultry, breeding cattle, breeding. poultry farming is not included within the definition. [1256F G] 4. The word "vacate land" means any land used or capable of use for purpose other than agriculture. But if a land is not entered in the revenue or land records before the appointed day as for the pur pose of agriculture it cannot be said that the whole land was within the meaning of the expression " Vacancy land". [1257F G; 1258A] 5.

The appellant company was ordered to be wound up by the Company and the workmen were directed to report for duty. The company terminated the services of the workmen on the ground that they had not been given any notice or opportunity of being heard before terminating their services. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the discharge of the workman was justified but it set aside the order of dismissal and ordered reinstatement with full back wages. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Industrial Tribunal did not act as a court of appeal and substitute its own judgment for that of the management. It had considered the justification for absence without leave and found that the company had decided to terminate the services by giving notice to the workmen. [677 E] The question whether the discharge and/or suspension of the employees was justified or not depended upon the circumstances of each case. In the present case, the Tribunal found that there was no consideration for the condition imposed and the company could change its mind and ignore the condition. It did not consider the effect of the condition on the part of the appellant in terminating the services. [678 F G] The Industrial Tribu nal had considered all the circumstances and came to a conclusion that the respondent workmen failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and that was the reason why they were not taken back. [679 D E] In the instant case, though the Tribunal had found that it had decided that the appellant company had given notice to show cause against the dismissal of the respondent, the Industrial Tribunal found in favour of the company on the basis of its finding that the workmen themselves tried to coerce the Company by theirlow down ' tactics and that the Company was not justified in refusing leave.

The respondent University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 recommended the names of Dr. G.S. Nathawat for the said post. The appellant Dr. Urea Kant was selected and appointed as Professor in the department of Bot any year. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by a common judgment dated March 6, 1991. The Division Bench held that the purpose of preparation of the reserve list was that if the person selected at No. 1 did not join then he would be appointed against a future vacancy. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment of Dr UreaKNK was made in order to curtail the ad hoc appointments and also because the regular selections take place after the post had been filled up on the recommendations of the Selection Committee. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a clear error in restricting the scope of reserve list only against the post for which the selec tion was made and which according to the High court could only be available to the incumbent in the reserve category if the persons selected at the said list did not joining such post. Such interpretation is not borne out from any of the provisions of Section 3(1) of the Act of 1974. [426C D] 1.2 The Selection Commit tee in the present case was constituted for the selection of Professor, in Botsany and such Selection Committee had approved and recommended the name of Dr, Urea KNKKN KNkwat on 20th June, 1989. The Syndicate in its Resolution dated 10th July, 1978 had resolved that the reserve lists be prepared by the Selection Commis sioner for selection of a Professor in a University, there fore, it was held that once a person selected by the selection committee has joined that post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve select list is of no avail and becomes extinct. There was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve List alive for a long period of one year as no person selected for the posts can at all be expected not to join for such a long time of one y year. If we examine the matter from another angle, it would be clear that according to University such a procedure is in vogue in all the universities of Rajasthan that a reserve list is used for the appointment on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserved list and numerous appointments had been made in the last decade from the reserve panel. The university has also submitted that if it is held to be correct, it will create chaotic situation in the University as all appoint ment so far made from the Reserve List will become assail able.

The petitioners challenged the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, on the ground that they had been discriminated against by the provisions of section 9 of the Act in as much as they had applied for permission to change their existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose. The petitioners contended that the provisions Of sections 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the said Act were ultra vires the Constitution of India. The respondents contended that they applied for sanction under section 10 of the aforesaid Act in respect of their land as reserved for industrial purposes and that the permission was not obtained by them within the meaning of section 19(1) of the . The petitioners also contended that section 9 Of the Act did not apply to the area which was not a notified area. Held, that the petitioners had no right to challenge the validity or the notification issued under section 9. The provisions of sections 9 and 10 of Bombay Town planning Act, 1955, were in terms applicable to the land in question and they could not be challenged on the grounds that they contravened the provisions contained in section 14 Of the Bombay City Planning Act. The object of the local authority was to guide itself and to make it obligatory on the local authorities to give permission for development work. The power conferred by section 13 of Bombay Act was not unguided, arbitrary or uncontrolled and as such infringed article 19(i)(f) and (g). The provisions Of section 9 were in essence a matter of no moment for the authority under section 13 is no less than the Municipal Commis sioner himself or the Chief Officer of the Municipal Borough.
