When the power had to be exercised by one of the highest officers of the Local Authority intimately connected with the preparation of the development plan in all its stages, it was difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. The preparation of a development plan for Greater Bombay was an immense task and the authorities proceeded with it in a manner which would have been operative with the result that the acquisition might be delayed for a further period of ten years. The procedure prescribed by section 19 of the City Town Planning Regulation, 1954 was not one of mere formality but one of its preparation and the local authori ty had to proceed on the basis of the tentative plan. The rules framed under section 19 were not ultra vires.

The appellant was a Part B State and had always been so in the territory of India. In 1947, the State of Kutch merged with the Dominion of India and by article 1 of the Agreement of Merger, the Maharao of Kutch became part of the State. The State of Saurashtra merged with that Dominion on August 2, 1948. On May 4, 1948, the Government of Bombay issued a notification under section 290A of the Government Of India Act, 1935, appointing two persons as the Part B States to be the territories which, at the date of the passing of this Act, were included in the State List. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution and that the notification was invalid. Held, that the decision of the Tribunal was correct and must be affirmed. The dispute related to the boundary between the two States and the question whether the territory in this State belonged to the Kutch State or not was a matter which could be decided by arbitration under article 1 read with the First Schedule to the Constitution. The award did not purport to nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. The Government of India had exercised effective administrative control over Sind and the dispute related only to the location of the boundary line, and the operative part of it declared the alignment of the boundaries between the State and Pakistan. The agreement between the parties was reached purely as an executive act and no legislative sanction was obtained by the Government for its implementation. The Union of India could not treat it as part of Indian territory and therefore the notification issued by the Bombay Government under section 2(2) of the Act was invalid, because, in giving effect to the award of the tribunal, cession of India into a Part C State was involved.

The mortgagor 's interest in the mortgaged property was sold by the mortgagor to the auction purchaser on April 7, 1925. The mortgagor 'died a mortgage on June 14, 1922 and after his death the mortgagee became entitled to transfer encumber or sell the whole property including the interest of principal or interest thereafter. On October 2, 1927, the mortgagor purchased from the mortgagor 'the mortgaged property and after the date on which the mortgage amount was payable, sold it in favour of the auction purchasers who were the heirs of the mortgagor and certain alienees of the mortgaged properties. The mortgagee 's right to redeem the mortgaged land was extinguished by the sale of the mortgage property. On August 16, 1934, the appellant obtained assignment of his interest in a portion of the mort gage and assigned his interest therein to one M on April 14, 1925, and on October 2. On September 16, 1945, the mortgagee sold the entire property including some alienees in favour Of the mortgagor. The mortgagees then filed a suit for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of their interest in Mauza Bahaldih. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was partly simple and partly usufructuary and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon it, the mortgage "was partly simple, partly usufructuary" and partly simple. On appeal, the High Court held that the mortgagor had in his plaint not relied on any other part payment of principal and interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The right conferred by section 68 of the Transfer of Property Act is again not a right to enforce the mortgage but a right of sue for the mortgage money on the personal covenant or to claim compensation when the mortgagee is deprived of his security. [642 D] (ii) The suit filed by the plaintiff was within time and had to be filed within twelve years from the date of dispossession. The suit was therefore barred by limitation. [643 E] (iii) The mortgage deed dated June 14. 1922, was a simple document which contained paragraphs 12 and 14 of the mortgages. The words "as security for the realisation of the principal and interests" in section 68(1)(b) of the Act were not intended to extend or restrict the period for enforcement Of the mortgage against the transferee of the equity of redemption. [641 F] (iv) The plaintiff 's claim to enforce a mortgage is barred by the law of limitation. The right granted by section 69 is again subject to the limitation prescribed by the Limitation Act for filing a suit. Section 68 of Transfer of property Act confers a right upon the mortgagee to sue for it in four different classes of cases and no others. These classes are (a) where the mortgagor binds himself to repay the mortgage debt; (b) where, by any cause other than the wrongful act or default of the mortgagee or mortgagee, the mortgaged is wholly or partially destroyed or the security is rendered insufficient within the meaning of section 66(1).

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Vadig and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. The appellants contended that even if a nominal charges were realised from the employee that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, the point has now become more or less academic. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act 1958 is a statute which authorises the levy of passenger tax. This Act has been amended several times right from the year 1960 to 1975. Before analysing the relevant provisions of the said Act it may be necessary to extract the Preamble to the Act. Section 2(7) defines 'stage carriage ' thus: "stage carriages" means a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey and includes such a carriage or other omnibus when used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the . Rule 2(i) of the Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules, 1940 framed under the Bombay Act is a statutory definition. [361 E F] 2. The word 'public ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [362 F G] 3. The words 'public servants ' have got a very wide connotation and mean a carriage by which any members of public can get free access to on payment off the usual charge. It could not by any processes of reasoning be deemed as to include employee of a Private Company who are giving facilities notas members of tho public but as held by this Court in the case of the State Transport Corporation vs The appellants, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 878, that the transport provided to the employees by the company would be a public servant in any sense of the term. [363 A B] 4. The definition of 'stages carriage ' as given in section 2(1) of Bombay Motor vehicles (Taxation of Passengers)Act 1958 is not exhaustive and means such carriage to whom any member or member of tho Public can have Free access on paying the usual rates. It may be that the term 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules, but that however does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the statute it is of the opinion that the tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of tho nature of a public serv ice. [360 F G; 361 A B].

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a licence for a "no objection certificate" filed by them under Rule 102 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1952, challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that there was a mosque, a public cinema licence and a temple in the vicinity or the place where the cinema house is to be constructed. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there were two stages through which an application for a license had to be processed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that if before granting a licence, the licensing authority had satisfied himself that there existed no impediment to the granting of such a licence and was therefore perfectly justified in granting the same, and that the order granting a license was not a fit case for interference by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to object is at the initial stage when a no objection certificate is applied for by the intending applicant for such a certificate. But there is nothing in the Act or the rules which requires advertisement of such an application inviting objections and consideration of the objections before grant of licence. [799C D] 2. Rule 102 empowers the licensing author ity to grant a cinema licence on being satisfied that all the relevant rules have been complied with and the licence may be granted on such terms and conditions and subject to such restrictions as the licensing Authority may determine. The power to grant licence is not absolute but is discretionary. [899E F] 3. Rule 103 confers power on the licensing authorities to refuse a cinema license if the cinema is likely to cause obstruction, inconvenience, annoyance, risk or damage to residents, or passers by in the proximity of the cinema. Rule 104 provides that no objection Certificate shall be granted unless it is accompanied by an affidavit stating that any objection certificate has been obtained and that such objection certificate will not be valid for a period of two years from the date of issue in the case of permanent cinemas. [800G H] 4. The appellant did not file any objection at that stage "no objections" certificate was granted to him. He filed an application under Rule 103 which was rejected by the licensing autho rity on the grounds that there is a mosque and a place of entertainment. The Rules envisage issuance of a license for a permanent cinema and quasi permanent cinema as well as a touring cinema. The licence was not renewed. The licensing authority, therefore, granted a licence to the appellant. [900D E] 5. Rule 105 confers power upon the licensing au thority to grant such a license on being satis fied in the prescribed manner. If after taking into consideration the objections a noobjection certificate is granted, there ends the matter subject, of course, to any properly constituted legal proceedings conceivably a writ petition under Article 226. But sub section (3) of Section 5 provides that an application may be made before the expiry of the period for receipt of a notice of hearing and if the authority has reason to refuse such application or to grant the same it shall record its reasons in writing. If the duty to give notice and hear objections is not mandatory, the actual order passed on a matter must be shown to have injuriously affected the interest of the party which was given no notice of the matter. [901E F; 801A B] 6. The appeal is allowed.

The respondent executed a contract in respect of the mining lease. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the transfer of the lease to the respondent. The respondent wrote to the appellant that the lease was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that the appellant had not agreed to purchase the mining leases. The lease deed provided that the lessee would have a possessory right before execution of a conveyance of the mine. The respondents filed an appeal against the decree. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) the respondent had failed to establish the new case; (2) the contract was concluded by an oral application for shares in a mining lease, and (3) the appellant was at liberty to revoke the offer at any tune before its acceptance by the respondent, and that as the Government had not made the offer, the appellant could not get a possessory rights before execution. HELD: The plaint was not an acceptance of the offer but was intended to be an acceptance. [583 D] (a) The letter dated September 2. 1957 written by the appellant to the respondents clearly stated that the contract in question was concluded and that in breach of the contract the respondent failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent of the Central Government. [584 E F] (b) The plea that the respondent made a concluded contract on September, 2,1957 was not accepted by the High Court. The letter written by appellant dated September,2, 1957, did not amount to an acceptance and the appellant 's offer was not supported by any consideration. The pleadings and issues raised the question whether a con tract was made on September. 2, in a suit for specific performance should be decided first. [585 F G] (c) The respondent had not established the new Case. In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded. The offer as well as acceptance should Pr=& the institution of the suit and the approval of the central government to the assignment of the ' mining lease could not be specifically performed and on this ground the High court dismissed the appellant suit.

The appellants were office bearers of a company. A complaint was filed against them under section 3(1) of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1955 alleging that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. The appellants challenged the validity of the investigation in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 3 (1) provides for taking under cultivation any waste or arable land whether appurtenant to a building or not for growing thereon of food crops generally or of specified food crops and section 3 is a specific mandate. HELD : The power conferred on the Government under section 4(2) of Act cannot be challenged as invalid. [655 F] Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , followed. Ch.Tika Ramji and Ors. v The State, ; , referred to. In Ch.tika Ramji 's case the Bihar Act was a pre Constitution Act and it could have continued to be in force only till it was altered, repealed o.r amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [677 G] Chota Ramji & ors. vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Ors., ; referred to, distinguished. Chota Ram & Ors., vs The Sate of U P. and Ors, , referred.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order was issued by the State Government granting concessions to entrepreneurs for starting new industries in Mysore State. The Government of the State issued another order which recited that the reasons for making the said order were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June, 1969 when the order dated 12th January 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given under the said orders. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the basis set out earlier. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concession granted under the order of 30th May, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is not applicable to the instant case because the Government wants to resile from a promise or an assurance given by it on the ground that undue advantage is being taken or misuse was being made of the concession granting the Court may permit the Government to do so but before allowing the Government, would have to be satisfied that allegations by the government about misuse being made or undue advantage being taken. [950C D] 2. The fact that the order passed by the High Courts on 12th February, 1977 did not specify the power under which it was issued will make no difference because such a power is clearly there in Section 8A and where the source of power underwhich it is issued is not stated in an order but can be found on examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. The second submission of the learned counsel for the appellants must also fail. [951D E] 3. In order to test the validity of the order, one has to see the substance of the Concession granted under Order 30, Rule 3 of the said Rules. It is clear that in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of sales Tax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the order. In view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the State Govern ment had no authority to provide for the grant of refund. [961F G] Union of India vs M/s Indo Afghan Agencies Limited, ; , referred to.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. for causing the death of one of the persons belonging to the group of the accused. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 and A 3 but convicted A 2 under Sections 148 and 307 read with section 149 I P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to A 3. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 148 and on applying 149 I .P. C. cannot be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I. P. C., and they were acquitted by the High court. [8B] 2.1 In so far as the presence and partic ipation of the assailants in the attack on the deceased is concerned, it is not the prosecution case that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 1, A 2 and A3 were armed with spears, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with sticks and knives and they had rioting between the two factions. There was no dispute that A 3 were unidentified person who were implicated in the occurrence. The High Court rightly held that it would be safe to accept the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 to the extent it is corroborated by the evidence 6 of the eye witnesses and the number and nature of injuries, which are caused by the accused persons. [88C D] 2:2 In so much as the appellants formed an unlawful com mission with common intention with common object of murdering the de ceased, the prosecution has not established that apart, from the 7 accused there were other unknown persons who had been involved in crime.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam, which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 was completed on 30th December 1966. In the course of proceedings under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1922, the assessee claimed that the value of Rs,. 16, 500 should be included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by him at the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gain accrued or arose to him as a result of the transaction. The Income tax officer issued a notice under section 147 of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for its assessment year 1967 67 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within thirty days of the service of the notice. The assessee submitted a return on 4th April 1968, but it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assessee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. 48 The assessee 's appeal against this order was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. In further appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (1) the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assesses in respect Of the transfer; (2) the assessee had an honest and bonafide transaction where the consideration for the transfer had been correctly disclosed or declared by him, but was intended to deal only with cases where the real consideration received by the asses see was not disclosed and the consideration declared in respect thereof was shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by him; (3) the transaction was not bona fide and in fact in fulfilment of a contractual obligation, the assesses who had sold the property should be liable to pay tax on capital gains which have not accrued or arisen to him. HELD: (1)(a) The assessee could not claim to have discharged this burden which lay outside the legislative power of Parliament and it would not be possible to justify it even as an incidental or ancillary provision or a provision intended to prevent evasion of tax. [655 D] (b) In the present case, the transaction in respect to the transfer by the respondent was a perfectly honest and bona fide transaction where both the conditions were satisfied. The transaction was therefore perfectly honest. [643 C] (c) The High Court erred in holding that the assessee 'was not correctly assessed on the basis of the sale and that the transaction is not bona fides or mala fide. [641 D] In the instant case, it could be said that the respondent had been rightly assessed to tax under section 47(2). [645 E] (d) The order of assessment was based on a true assumption of sub section (2), which was enacted by Parliament not as a separate section but as part of section 52 which, as originally stood, dealt only with transactions of transfer and not of sale. [651 A B] (e) The respondent had no intention to evade tax. There is nothing in the Act which would justify the imposition of the applicability of that provision. [661 D F] (f) The contention that the property was sold for a consideration which was more than the sum of Rs 16,000 shown at the time of transfer was not tenable.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 16(1)(a)(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant had gone to "a shop to make purchases" without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. He was found in possession of the tin plate and a sample of Til seeds was sent for analysis. He admitted that he had purchased the til seeds from the shop. The trial court convicted him under section 7(1) (a)(i) of that Act and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court acquitted him but convicted him on the ground that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the whole purpose of the act was to preventing adulteration, sale or storage or distribution of certain types of food '; and (ii) the use of the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what was stored or sold was "fruit" at all. [329 B] In the instant case, the appellant was not present at the time when the seeds were sold by him to the Food Inspector. He did not even remember who made the cash memo when he sold these Til seeds. Therefore, the conviction of the accused must be set aside. [330 C D] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , applied.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He filed a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. The suit was decreed in his favour on 30.9.1969. On appeal, the Divisional Commissioner confirmed the decree holding that the dismissal was bad and he had continued to remain in service and that the appellant continued to serve. He continued to hold the post till the decision of the State Government on his appeal and beyond three years from the date of the order. The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the respondent. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the order dated 30.10.1969 was not passed in accordance with Article 58 of the First Schedule to the . Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed. [54F] 1.2 In all these three cases after the appellate authority has disposed of the appeal the operative order is the order in accordance therewith. [55G] 1:3. The cause for action first arises when the remedies available to the public servant under the relevant service rules as to re instate are disposed of. The question whether it should be disposal of one appeal or the entire hierarchy of reliefs as may have been provided, is a condition precedent to maintaining of claims under the . [55H] 1 :4. In all such cases only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from the order passed in revision, it is the right to sue shall first accrued. submission of just a memorial or representation to the Head of the establishment shall not be taken into consideration in the matter of fixing limitation. [58H] 2:1. The period of one year for making of the application and power of condonation of delay of a total period of six month has been vested under section 20 of the .

The appellant, who was the owner of an immovable property consisting of himself and his father, instituted a suit for partition in forma pauperis in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittoor. The trial court rejected the contention that the alienations made by his father as well as sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in all the said properties was not affected by them. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether an appellate decree passed by the High court affirmed the decision is one of affirmance or not depends on the nature of the subject matter in controversy in the suit which is intended to be brought to this court under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. If the appeal court makes a variation in the decision, it is not a decree of affirmence and this is not affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant and not against him. [470 E F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the appellate decree must be considered as a whole in relation to the decision in the case of a matter in dispute in the proposed appeal to the Privy Council, and so it should be held that the said finding was binding on the trial Court. [471 G H] Chitturi Subba Rao vs Vela Mankanni Rao, A.I.R. (1955) Mad. 953, approved. (iii) The decision of a High Court in an appeal under article 136 is not final and must be affirmed. It is open to the appellant to urge that the finding of the High Courts on merits was erroneous or vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. [473 C] Chittturi Subba Reddy vs Velavaram, A I.R., (1955), Mad. 853, followed. (iv) The principle of affirmations on which the provision rests postulates either affirmance of the judgment or the decree. In the present case, the High COurt had taken a different view and had taken the same view.

The provisions of section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with the proviso to section 115 of the Code of civil Procedure, are in pari materia with those of the original section 115. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in cases arising out of original suits of a value less than Rs. 20,000/ and in other cases the revisional jurisdiction was concurrently shared between the High Court and the District Court. The provisions of sections 96 to 112 of the Civil Procedure Code read with section 115 are in identical terms. Section 25, in its application to Uttar Pradesh, retrospectively provides that any amendment made or provision inserted in the Code by a State Legislature before the commencement of the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1972, if pending immediately before 1st August, 1978, would continue to be governed by section 115 as it stood before that date. The proviso thereto also provides that in respect of cases arising from original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by a District Court, the High Courts alone shall be competent to make an order under this section. Section 7 of the Act merely embodies the general principle against resort to remedies outside the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act. The language of the successive amendments made in the bifurcation of revisional jurisdiction is clear and unambiguous.

The respondent, a private limited company, was incorporated in the State of Rajasthan under the . The State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, declaring its intention to acquire certain lands belonging to them. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi were not maintainable as the ad interim exparte prohibitory order secured by them had been issued by the State Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under section 51(1 ) of the Act arose within the State 's State of Jaipur i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the State. [602C] 2. The notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by State Government under section 53(1), or the Act, on the basis of which the notification was issued became effective the moment it was published in the official Gazette as thereupon the notified land became vested in the state Government free from all encumbrances. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer under section 54(2) for the grant of an appropriate writ, direction or order under article 32 of the Constitu tion for quashing the notification issued by it under section 50(1). If the respondents felt aggrieved by the acquisition, they could challenge the validity or the issue of the notification. [063D E] 3. The expression ' cause of any territorial jurisdiction ' is a bundle of facts which taken with the law applicable to them gives the plaintiff a right to relief against the defendant. The mere service of the notice under section52(2), on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road, Calcutta i. e., within the geographical limits of the state of West Bengal could not give rise to a cause of ' action within that territory unless the service is an integral part of the cause of the action. The whole cause of actions culminating in acquisition of land under s.52(1 )(a) on the at their Registered office at18 B , brabourna Road, and within the jurisdiction of State of WestBengal could not given rise to the cause 'of action within the territory unless tho service of such notice was an integral parts of the ' cause '. The High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a rule n0oisi on the petition under article226 of the Consti tution or to make the ad interlocutory prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the acquired land acquired. [507E F] 4. The word 'cause of action ' is tersely defined in Mulla 's Code of Civil Procedure: "The cause of a suit wholly or in part arises". It is a composite form of defence and the cause is wide and the Judges must ever be vigilant to protect the citizen against arbitrary executive action. [ 607F G] 5. The power of the High Courts under article 227 of the constitution is not limited by the clemency of self ordained restraint. There has to be in the larger public interest an clement of self order.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in dispute on the ground that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises by a co operative society and that the building was not covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had failed to prove that the spent Rs. 1000 towards repairs of the building, and that he had failed in the payment of rent despite notice dated 24th March 1977. On appeal, the Additional District Judge affirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about arrears of rent. The High Court confirmed the findings. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the building in question had been constructed by a cooperative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the Judge that the buildings were not ten years old on the date of suit and, consequently, the new rent Act had no application to the building; and (ii) the appellant had failed before the trial Court to prove the arrears of the rent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent landlord was in the witness box payment by cheque dated August 16, 1976 but when the plaintiff was in his witness box he was in a witness box for the respondent. In the absence of any such report, record or assessment the date on which it is actually occupied for the first time. [340D] 2. The appellant had not filed any document to prove his rent since April 7, 1976 and, hence, the question assumes importance in the present case. [334E] 3. In a suit under section 20 of the Act there is no reason why the benefit of the new Act be not given to the appellant. Section 20 of that Act stipulates that in any suit for ejectment on the grounds mentioned in cl. (a) to sub section (2), viz., the arrears or years ' old on which rent and damages for use and occupation of the buildings due from him, such damages for using and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the date from which the landlord may, in lieu of passing a decree for eviction on that ground, pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction. [341F G] 4. The question in the instant case is whether by seeking the benefit under section 39 of the old Act there was a change in the cause of action. In A.K. Gupta & Sons vs Damodar Valley Corporation this Court held that a sum of Rs. 1,000/ was paid by the appellant to the landlord through a crossed cheque dated 16th August, 1976 which was received by the landlord on 15th September, 1976. But when the appellant 's suit for recovery of possession on the basis of the said cheque was pending in the High Court, it completed ten years. Then the question arose whether the new Rents Act will be attracted if the building completed within ten years from the date when the construction is completed. The Trial Court held the building to be not ten year old on that date and, accordingly, the appellant cannot get any protection of the newly added section 20. [343G H; 344A] 5. Section 2(f) defines 'tenant ' in the Act to mean a person who has been constructed substantially out of funds obtained by way of loan or advance from the State Government or Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a co cooperative society or the Uttar Pradesh Multipurpose Co operative Society and the period of repayment of such loan or advances exceeds the aforesaid period. The proviso to sub s.(4) enumerates the dates on which the payment by cheques is made. Sub section (5) of section 20 stipulates that the parties are entitled to make necessary amendment in their pleadings and to adduce additional evidence where necessary. [344C D] 6.

The appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The respondents contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that therefore the arbitration clause in the agreement did not apply. Held, that the appellant was entitled to the decree. The agreement dated February 6, 1948, was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor and in consequence there was a valid reference to arbitration. The award was not a certified copy of the order under section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, but was an original instrument. The appellant had been authorised to execute the agreement on behalf of the Governor, and in pursuance thereof he paid the requisite stamp duty under section 35 of the Stamp Act and had it validated. The High Court was right in holding that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and that no decree could be passed thereon. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated by notification in the Official Gazette, but there is nothing in section 175 itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person, and when that is established the requirements of the section must be held to be satisfied. The fact that the arbitrator had been authorized by the Government acting through his Secretary to execute a agreement for reference to an arbitration does not preclude authorisation from being conferred as it was not required by section 175 (3).

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department. On various dates in the State of Punjab, he placed orders for purchase of sign boards and import lincences. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of these orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received against the respondent pertaining to the purchase of the sign boards. Vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau. The respondent filed a complaint before the Special Judge, Punjab, who quashed the First Information Report on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of such sign boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II, and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea taken by the respondent was that he had no right to withhold or withdraw a pension or any part of it whether permanently or for a specified period and that the prosecution as against Mangal Singh Minhas was rightly quashed. On the question whether the order of acquittal passed against him was sustainable in law, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has not gone into the merits of the case and set aside the orders appealed against in this case. [922C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had retired as long as on December 13, 1979. It is true that the Government servants cannot constitute a class by themselves so as to bring their cases within the purview of Article 309 of the Constitution. But it is the third proviso which enjoins that no judicial proceedings shall be commenced against a person referred to therein for prosecution in respect of a cause of action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution. [936F G] 1:3 The High Courts have taken the view that Rule 22.22 of the Rules has been misinterpreted by the High Court in holding that the said rule placed an embargo on prosecution. [981G H; 924A] Des Raj Sing vs State of Haryana, ; , referred to. 1.4 In the present case, it is clear from the facts of the instant cases that the respondent in criminal appeal No. 422 of 1988 was a Government Engineer and was not entitled to any such judicial proceedings if he had become disqualified under the provisions of Article 311(2) of the Constitu tion. [980B] Desraj Singhal vs State, ; ; , followed. 1:5 The High court has rightly quashed the prosecution of Mangal Singh on the view taken by it that a Government servant after his retire ment should not be prosecuted for grave misconduct of action arose or the incident took place several years before he retired from service. [979E] Des Rai Singhal vs The State of U.P., ; , distinguished. 1 :6. In view of the fact that the High Courts had taken the same view on the question of law, it would be a futile exercise to consider the question afresh in the light of the observations made above.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The authorised capital of the company was Rs. 100/ each ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs.100/ each were held by the directors including Ramayamma. On April 1, 1946, the respondent company took over the business conducted by Nageswara Rao Panthulu for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2,500 ordinary shares. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to vote at the meeting of the Company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings for the three years ending March 31, 1948, the Income tax Officer found that for the 3 years ending June 31, 1949, the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent as against the ordinary shares which was considerably less than sixty per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax Officer but the Tribunal held that the undistributed portion of the assessable income of the respondent was not liable to be distributed as dividend within the meaning of section 23A and reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the company in respect thereof. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent Company was one in which the public were substantially interested and there was no person who could hold twenty five per cent or more of the ordinary share issued by the respondent. [17 E] (ii) The expression "twenty five per centum of the voting power" would mean not twenty five percent of the total voting power but power exercisable in respect of shares other than shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. [18 G] (iii) The words "thirty five per curium of the capital of such subsidiary company" in section 23(1) are wide enough to include directors from the remaining members of the 16 company. If a director does not belong to the controlling group, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation to section 23 (A) even though such director was directly entrusted with the management of the affairs of the companies.

The appellants were the sole selling agents of the respondent Mills. The goods were delivered to them by the respondent on behalf of another person, who was a registered firm and carried on business in Bombay. In pursuance of all this delivery was made to Dharsi Moolji. The respondent paid Dwarkadas Khetan and Company as their agent. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of sales tax on the ground that the bales remained in the physical possession of the first appellant at all material times and were not physically delivered to the second appellant. The trial court held that the delivery was not true and correct, but the High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the goods left by the appellants were delivered under the control of Dwarkadis, because, they had reached the quotaholder in the end, or rather his proper agent, and so with a del credere agent, because such a person was the agent of the seller only up to a point. The delivery was without any straining of language as the person to whom the goods were actually delivered. Dharsi Food Products Co., Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 829, followed. Dwarkadasi Mills Ltd. and Dharsi, vs Dwarkadash Khetan, A.I.R (1924) P. C. 1, referred to. The fact that the appellants had delivered the bales at all relevant time did not make any difference because the goods remained in their possession. Dharlia Moolji paid Dwaraklal Bairathi for the goods and the Mills sent them to Dharlia, Moolji refused to accept them. Dwarkamal vs State of Bombay, A I.R., (1925) P & E. 1 and Dharlia Kirpa vs Dwarkalal, A L. R.

The appellant was a Professor of a Government College. He was charged with having accepted gratification of Rs. 500/ as bribe for showing favour to a candidate whose name was not mentioned in the prospectus, practical examination for the first year B.Sc. and his name was included in the Physics practical examination. The Special Judge convicted him under section 165A of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to two years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs., 1,000/ . On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the last part of the Ninth clause as it stood before its amendment in 1964 was applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression "public servant" is not defined in section 21 of the Penal Code but has a wider connotation and if no limitation is placed on it, the words "corrupt", "illegal" and "otherwise" mentioned in section 5(1)(d) are wide enough to include every person who is remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty. [321 B] (2) The word "obtains" has wide connotation and it includes every person in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated for the purpose of any Public duty. It is not necessary that the public servant while misconducting himself should have done so in the discharge of his duty. Section 5(i)(d)(1) provides that a public servant shall be deemed to commit an offence if he is holder of an office. He cannot be said to be holding any office when he is appointed for the purposes of examining certain answer books even though that may fall within the performance or a public duty, and in which capacity alone he could fall within section 21. [320 C D] (3) The use of the word "other wise" in section 6(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, shows that the words 'corrupt ' and 'illegal ' are used in section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But it is not possible to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the High Courts, a reading of section 5 (1)(a) as it stands before its Amendment in 1964 shows that connection with Government was necessary either in respect of the payment of remuneration or in respect Of the performance by the Government. [322 C D; 322 A B] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. (4) The words 'abusing his position as a public officer ' qualify the word 'other wise ' and do not form two clauses. If that is so, the abuse of position as public servant would be essential whether the means are corrupt or illegal or are of the nature covered by the word `corrupt or illegal ' mentioned in clause (a) of section 6. [323 C D]. Dhaneshwar Narayan Saxena vs State of Delhi ; , followed. (5) The definition of "public servants" in the Prevention Of Corruption Act is not confined to public servants but includes a person who has been remunerated with fee orcommission for the work of any office or pay or commission. Therefore, the use of word 'obtains ' on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of a receiver. [324 E F] (6) The abuse of positions as a Public servant would not amount to public servant within the meaning of section 21(1). [327 D] Dhaneswar Narain Saxena v Delhi Administration, ; , applied.

The petitioners, who were casual labour engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 and 16 years in the construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway, challenged the validity of the orders of their absorption. The Court granted interim relief to the petitioners. In the writ petitions filed by them under Article 32 of the Constitution, the Court directed that the scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative, should be implemented. A number of documents and circulars issued by the Administration have been produced in support of their claim. The petitioners have also furnished written submissions. In addition to the directions given by this Court, they have also produced written submissions, particulars of service of each of them, which was the previous requirement. The respondents have filed a counter affidavit stating that the petitioners have put in more than 360 days of service. The affidavits have been placed before this Court to show that the Administration is requiring continuous service for purpose of eligibility, and that the casual labour in open line as well as willing project casual labour are combined for the purpose of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. In view of the submission made by the respondents, this Court directed the petitioners to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued from time to time. The Union of India has filed a rejoinder. It is stated on behalf of the respondents that the Court had not been given any direction to treat them at par as temporary servants and that they were now entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. In this regard, it was also submitted that the claim of the petitioners for equal pay has been considered by this court in the Signals and Telegraphs Association and another vs Union of india. The learned Additional Solicitor General further accepted the position that the respondents should be entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. That would take away inequality which is main grievance of the Petitioners. The Respondents shall have a direction to consider the claims of each petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. For over ten years, litigations of this type have been coming to the Court. about three years back, this court directed a scheme for absorbing in permanent service and granting recovery of rent. The writ petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs.

The appellants, who were members of a Association carrying on business in partnership, entered into an agreement with the Forward Markets Commission for the settlement of certain types of forward contracts. The terms and conditions of forward contract contained in the said agreement were governed by the provisions contained in clauses (3), (4) and (6) of Bye laws of the Association. Clause (a) provided that "the prices at which cotton may be bought or sold are at any time controlled under the provisions of the , if the Forward markets Commission is of opinion that continuation of trading in hedge transactions for any delivery or deliveries is detrimental to the interests of the trade and the public interest or to the larger interests of general public, the Government may by notification in the Official Gazette establish a Commission to be called the Forward Market Committee for the purpose of exercising such functions and discharging such duties as may be assigned to it by or under this Act. " The appellants contended that the Forward Contracts Control Commission could not have conferred any power on the Commission to frame bye laws and that the power of the Central Government under section 12(1) of the Act was not a judicial power but only executive power and that, therefore, the Central Govern ment had no power to make a bye law. Held, that the Central Govt. had no authority under section 11 or 12 as the Forward Marketing Commission had no powers under section 13 of the . The Central Government had no such power in view of section 4(f) of Act No. 52 of 1953 and the Central government had no jurisdiction to frame the bye laws. The Central Governmen ties had no right to make bye law with retrospective effect and therefore the new bye law made on January 21, 1956, was invalid.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The shares were held by the company as dividend, and compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes was paid to it. In appeal before this Court, the question was whether the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to the land acquisition compensation received by the Uka Sugar Mills Ltd., after 31st March 1948 was in the hands of the assessee company. HELD : (i) The High Court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami or premia received by it from the company out of those capital gains, to which the dividend must be deemed to be capital gain, and whether any part of the compensation received for compulsory acquisitions of land was capital gain. [34 C] (ii) The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the case remanded to the High court for disposal according to law. [35 D] (iii) In the instant case, the High Courts had not recorded final answers on all the questions in favour of the assessees. [36 E F] (iv) The question whether any amounts of salamis realised by the assessee from the Company were still income liable to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable for the purposes of section 2(6A) of the Income tax Act, 1922, was not a question of "capital gain" and whether the amount of Salami received for the compulsory acquisition could be considered exempt from liability to tax.

The appellants were charged with offences punishable under the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act. The prosecution case was that Sandalwood oil was not a wood oil as defined in section 2(f) (1) of the Act and therefore it is not a forest produce within the meaning of section 2 (f) of Act. On the basis of the information received by the Forest Department, the High Court convicted the appellants under section 5(1)(a) (i) of Kerala Forest Produce (Regulation of Production, Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for short). The High Court held that Sandals were not 'wood oil ' as defined under section 2. (f ) (i), (ii) and (iii) of that Act. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'agricultural produce ' in section2(f)(i) must be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be restricted in a narrow circum stances to include what was ordinarily and in common parlance be spoken of wood oil. [156F] 1.2 In the interpretation clause, it is stated that an interpretation clause should be used for the purpose of interpreting word which are ambiguous or equivocal, and not so as to disturb the meaning or the meaning which are plain. It is stated therein that the construction of the word 'industry ' in Section 2(j) would require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be gathered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [157G H] 1:3 The dictionary meaning of the term is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary, popular and natural sense whenever that word is used in an interpretation cl. (a) of Section 2 (k). It cannot be interpreted without taking into account the social, economic and political setting in which it is intended to operate. [158A B] 1 :4 In the instant case, the dictionary meaning given to 'agricultural ' is not to be taken as substituting one set of words for another, or as strictly defining what the meaning must be under all circumstances but rather as declaring what may be comprehended within the term where the circumstances require that it should be so construed. [159E F] 2.1 In the context and literal interpretation, the word is generally used as a word of extension. When used in the interpretation cl.(a) it seeks to enlarge the meaning by excluding its ordinary meaning.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code but acquitted. The High Court convicted him on appeal to this Court, Held, that the evidence in the present case was not sufficient to sustain a conviction and the conviction could not be set aside on the ground that it was not "reasonable" for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. The mere fact that the deceased was to be produced as a prosecution witness did not mean that he was guilty of the offence charged. The evidence in this case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn from the evidence of an expert unless it was corroborated in material particulars in his statement made at various stages of the case and which had been pointed out by the High Court. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution were not sufficient for sustaining the conviction. The recovery of the kassi was a wholly neutral circumstance because it had not been proved that it belonged to Bhagwandas. The appellant was therefore guilty of an offence punishable under section 307 I.P.C. and sentenced to transportation for life. The sentence of death passed on him was set aside by the Rajasthan High Court in appeal. Sundarlal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, A.I.R. 1954 S C 28 859, followed. The fact that a facile fluent liar had made two dying declarations did not affect the conviction of the appellant. The first dying declaration was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. The second dying declaration did not relate to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before this Court nor was it proved that the opinion of these authors were given in regard to circumstances precisely similar to that which arose at the time of the trial.

The appellant company was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The workmen employed in the factory were represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers Union. The dispute between the management of the appellant company and its workmen related to the employees of the factory at Jamshedpur. The Tribunal held that the workers of the Company had been given special leave with pay to attend the meetings of the executive committee specially held for the purpose. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the company that the Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at Jamshedpur and that the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal had rejected the demand for special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has not committed any error in holding that the constitution of the union prior to its purported amendment contained amongst other Articles, Articles 1 and 3. [558C] (2) The scheme of the Act is clear and unambiguous. It provides that a trade union would not be entitled to registration under the Act unless the executive thereof is constituted in accordance with the provisions of the . In considering such a demand, the first question which strikes one is as to why the meetings are set out in the said agreement and the statement and no other disparities social or economic. [559E F] (3) The fact that the union had been allowed certain of its workmen to attend without loss of pay proceedings before conciliation officers and industrial tribunals, does not detract from the position that the executive Committee meetings of a registered office shall not be changed except by resolution of the General Body meeting specially held in view of the express terms of that section. [560F G] (4) The statement made by the parties to the dispute that the workmen concerned were at liberty to work beyond 48 hours per week as provided therein, does also show that the company 's intention was validly amended on either January 6, 1963 or that it had not been given any notice of loss of wages proceedings before Conciliation officers and Industrial Tribunals. [561G H] (5) The question whether the meetings were set out by the union in the agreement dated January 6. 1963 or the statement of the parties was erroneous and could not be sustained. [562A B] (6) The reference to the Tribunal under section 10(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is operative in respect of the workmen of the appellants company ' s factory at Ranchi and not the workmen in its other establishments. [563C D] (7) The demand for Special Leave having been made by a union at Jamshedpur, the Tribunal could not in the very nature of things specify or limit the number of such meetings for such an attempt would amount to interference in the administration of the Union and its autonomy. Its order must be indefinite with the result that the appellant 's company would not know before hand on how many occasions and to how many of its employees would be called upon to grant special leave, and the tribunal 's award set aside. [564D E] (8) The award is operative even in respect Of the workmen at Ranchi. The demand of the workers for special Leave comprised in demand No. 3, Factory Staff, in Jamshedpur before the Tribunal showed that if facilities are given to the workmen to conduct the administration, the workmen 's representatives would obviously be working overtime and the company in fairness would be expected to pay them compensation for such overtime work. [565E F; 564A B]. (9) The claim for special leaves having been raised by the appellant at Jamshedpur before conciliation proceedings were started at Jamshedpur the Tribunal fixed the rate of ordinary wages for the workmen.

The assessee was dissolved on March 31, 1939. The timber business of the firm was taken over by two partners of the same family. In 1934 there was a partition between the two families and the firm came into existence. The forest business of M/s. Hakam Mal Tani Mal Tai Mal Toni was taken up by two partner of the assessee firm. An instrument of partnership recording the terms of the partnership and reciting the dissolution of the earlier partnership was executed on June 29, 1939, and the business in timber which was carried on by the undivided family was taken to be carried on in the name of M. Mal Tami Mal Thani Mal Tipper. The assessee was reconstituted in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/S. Hakham Mal Tni Mal Tali Mal Tana Mal Kuthiala, Abdullapur Depot, Simla, had been dissolved on April 1, 1939 and the timber business was taken by two of the partners of M 's firm in 1934. The departmental authorities held that succession to the family firm M was not carrying on business and that it succeeded to the business on April, 1, 1943. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession was not governed by section 25(4) or 25(5) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court in reference held that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25 (4) and the second proviso to section 25 of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had no application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the business of Messrs. Hakum Mal Tan Tani M Mal Tauthial A, Abdulapur Depot Simla, was carried out by two partnerships and that the timber was dissolved in March, 1939 when the assessee 's name was entered into. HELD : The assessee firm was constituted to carry on the timber in the business carried on at the time of dissolution from April 1 , 1939. [648 D] The business of a firm is an old and a running business and an intention to maintain continuity of the business and its transactions may reasonably be attributed to the assessee. It must therefore be held that it was not necessary for the assessee to carry out business on the date of dissolution of that firm in March , 1939, to have the business at the commencement of the Act 7 Of 1939. In the absence of other evidence, it may be held, that the income of the partner had become a separate from April I, 1939 or it may mean that from the end of March 31 , 1939 there had been separation. When a deed recites that the accounts were settled upto March 31 1, 1948, and upto March 30, 1939 the business was brought into operation and was on that account entitled to the benefit of section 25 4 of the Incometax Act.

The appellant was granted stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimogarh. The Secretary to the Regional Authority, respondent No. 29, filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal against the order of the State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal and obtained stay of the order. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the said order was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Secretary to Government, Regional Transport Authori ties, Shmoga, had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963, after a lapse of such a long time from the date of grant of the permit. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The order granting the permit is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of a permit. The appeals before the High court were therefore not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no juris diction to entertain the appeals and interfere with the order passed by the State transport Appellate Tribunal. [189 D] In the instant case, the Regional Trans port Authority granted the permit to the appellant on the same day. The Transport Authority did not have jurisdiction to entertain such appeal and to interfere with it. [190 E F] The High Court was therefore, in error in dismissing the writ application of the appel lant.

The appellant was elected to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in 1967. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur and there was no evidence to show that the respondent was guilty of any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (3A). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the election petition was not signed by the respondent and the news item in the newspaper had been published on 7 February 1967; (2) the meeting was not held at the time of polling; (3) the respondent had not filed any report about the alleged corrupt practice; and (4) the appellant was denied opportunity to meet the respondent. HELD: (i) The High court rightly observed that no notice was given to the respondent before Hapur on 7 2 1967, that he was denied an opportunity to participate in the election. [905 D] (ii) The publication in the newspapers 'Vir Arjun ' Exhibit 22 is a general diary of Thana Hapur bearing the date 7 February, 1967 and the newspaper report shows that the meeting which was held on 7 1 1967 was a meeting organised by the supporters of the Congress Party. The alleged incident at Chhajjupur was unacceptable because, first information report given by the appellant to the Election Commission was not lodged with the police station. Secondly, the news items in the daily newspaper were published on 8 February 1967 and secondly, the newspaper publication said that a constable was sent to the Town Hall Maidan at Hapur on 19 2 1967. [900 G H] (iii) The respondent had filed an affidavit before the High Court stating that he had been informed by him of the news article about the attack on the office of the Republican Party on 7 3 1967, and that he did not know as to what was happening in the village. The evidence on behalf Of the appellant is that he knew the speeches made by the Chief Minister on 7 4 1967 and 14 2 1967 and that people from Ghaziabad would be brought into the field. [ 900 G H; 905 A B] (iv) The newspaper publication stated that a crowd was created and names of various persons were mentioned as having tried to run towards the jeep which carried the leaders of the country. The appellant had also alleged that the speeches were made with the consent of the respondent Prakash Vir Shastri or his election agent.

The respondent filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. The appellant decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tion under Order 21 Rule 90 read with Article 134 of the Constitution of India before the District Judge, Jaipur City, Jaipur, praying for delivery of possession of the property auctioned by him. The application was opposed by the judgment debtor on the ground that as the application was filed more than one year after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under article 134 of . The District Judge held that in view of Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1908, an application for setting off the sale could not be made within three years from the date of decree and as such, Article 134 stood impliedly repealed by section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code. The District judge also held that since the application for delivery was filed beyond one year from the time of confirmation, it should be held that the application under O. XXI Rule 95 of the C.P.C. was barred. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the judgment debtors it was contended that: (1) The auction purchaser having filed an appeal against the order of the District judge, the judgmentdebtor was not entitled to compute the period of one year under Article 134 and as there was no attempt to support the judgment creditor 's contention, he could not have filed the application within a period of 12 years from date of the decree; (2) The application for set aside the order dated 21.1.1979 passed by the District Court confirming the sale was made more than two years after the dismissal of the appeal and (3) The High Court had erred in holding that Article 134 would apply to an application filed under O XXI Rule 92 of the code of Civil procedure, because: (a) the auction purchaser will be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree is passed; (b) all questions relating to delivery of posses sion of the properties shall be referred to the executing court; and (c) all question relating to the delivery of pos session of the immovable property to such purchaser or his representative shall be deemed not to be questions relating

The appellant was the candidate of the first respondent. The first respondent filed an election petition claiming a declaration that the appellant 's election was void and that he was entitled to be declared duly elected from the constituency. In support of the petition, the first Respondent alleged various corrupt practices on the part of the appellant. However, the High Court dismissed the petition holding that both these acts amounted to corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act and were sufficient to void the election. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The publication of a wall poster by the first res pondent was not a valid notice under RSC Order 18 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [732C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had not stated that it was because he was a Marxist leader and was also arrested for harbouring the murderers. The evidence in the petition did not disclose any such fact as to how many facts related to the defec tive poster. It was only when the first respond ent himself knew that the offending poster was affixed prior to the election, that he had reasonably calculated that the voters or at any rate the voters in and about the locality where the theatre was being put up had knowledge of the fact that it is a murderer who was not known to him. [764D E] 1:3 The first Respondent had also deposed that he knew the contents of the wall poster on the day prior to his election. He had also stated that he did not know as to why it would create an impression in the mind of the voters of the said wall that it had happened to be a murder. [774E F] 1 :4 The first responde nt has not stated as to what was the exact words alleged by him. He has also deposed to the fact, that the contents were not mentioned in the pamphlet. In his cross examination he stated that the first appellant had never stated that any of the facts had been stated by him in the election petition. The High Court has rightly pointed out that the writings were at the instance of the second respondent himself and that there was no direct reference to or implication of the words used, no impres sion could be read in the words as against him. It is true that the First Respondent had stated generally that it would be necessary to prove the extrinsic facts to show that the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of the defi cution. But the fact remains that the second Respondent himself has not been examined by the High court as a witness in chief. The Court is therefore, right in saying that by reference to any possible meaning of the word used, the no impec tional facts could be stated to show the suffi cient nature of the expression complained of. [763C D] 1 5. In the present case, it was not shown that the respondent had taken the photographs in question on the said days. The mere fact that the High Courts have insisted that it should be done with the knowledge and consent of the candidate would not make any difference to the facts as to whether the allegations contained in the annexure were reasonably believed or not. [762C D; 733A] In the circumstances, the appeal must fail. [761D E].

The respondent No. 5, a public limited company, was granted the land in question by the State Government under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay, issued a notification under section 20 of the Act on April 30, 1974, declaring the disputed land to be reserved for recreation ground or recreational ground in the interest of general public. The respondent No 2 set aside the said order and directed the appellant to grant sanction of the plan submitted by the respondent No 5 after hearing the petitioners as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the development plan. Being aggrieved, the appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the said resolution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the land was proposed to be allotted for recreation grounds and not to any other purpose. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent had misunderstood the provisions of section 46 of the Maharashtra Municipal Corporation Act, 1976 and having regard to the position that in granting sanction to the plan, the respondent NO. 2 was quite alive to public interest, the High court should have taken into consideration other relevant facts including the contemplated revision of the scheme, apart from those mentioned in section 46. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contention of the petitioners against the validity of resolution dated 14.3.1974 is no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revised development plan has since been published and the plan is submitted by respondent No, 5 and conditioned by the Respondent No. 2 is not inconsistent with the draft revision plan. [928C] 1.2 The contention that the Municipal Corpora tion which is the Planning Authority, had prepared the draft scheme in accordance with the direction of the respondent no. 2, is without any substance and is rejected. [936D] 1:3. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public depends upon the question as to the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the respondent under the Urban Land Ceiling Act. A copy of the draft modified development plan is produced before this Court by the appellants. The Respondent No 2 has acted in public interest by imposing the conditions mentioned therein. [ 925F] 1 :4. The condition would show that considerable area out of the disputed lands had been reserved for recreational ground or green belt. The plan, as sanctioned by the res pondent No.2 with the conditions imposed, has been shown in the draft refixed plan. It was open to the Municipal corporation to accept the verdict of the appellate authority and it has done so by not challenging it in the High Courts or before this court.

The employers contended that they had been guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out which under the law was illegal.
