The employers contended before the Industrial Court that they were guilty of contravening the provisions of section 28 read with Items l(a), l(b) and 2(a) of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 ( 'the Act ' for short). The Industrial Court held that the employers had committed an unfair labour practice. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The findings of the Industrial court are set right. [66D] 1.2 The complaints of the union were that the employer was guilty of imposition and continuing the lock out as resumption of production is gradually expanded and that till all the old workmen who were in service of the employers at the time of alleged closure, that is upto and inclusive of April 8, 1980, will be re inducted in service. There will be a continuous watch by the ministerial officer to be appointed by the Industrial Tribunal till all those old workmen are re inducted into service. [67D E] 1:3 The complaint of the employer that they have committed an illegal lock out is not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, and with a view to set right the matter proceeded to examine the same in this judgment. [68F G] 2.1 In examining whether the employer has imposed a lockout or has closed the industrial establishment, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closure has to be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lock out was necessarily temporary or for a period. The employer may close down industrial activity bonafide on such eventualities as suffering continuous loss, no possibility of revival of business or inability for various other reasons to continue the industrial activity. There may be a closure for any of these reasons though these reasons are not exhaustive but are merely illustrative. To say that the closing down of the industrial undertaking is a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the appellant employer at the stage when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down the industrial undertakings, the Industrial Courts before which the action of the respondent in order to determine whether the closure was a bona fide one or was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the appellants employer.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which were to be considered by the Income tax authorities and to make a fresh statement of its case. The assessee company made a claim for deduction every year being treated as a dealer in investments and properties but this claim was rejected by the Appellate Tribunal on the ground that it was not a 'dealer ' within the meaning of section 2(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the assessee was a dealer and not an investor and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties of the assessee company could be taxed as business profits. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the question whether the assessee 's income was a 'business ' or an investor was itself a question of law; (2) the High Court had no jurisdiction to make the fresh statement under section 66(1) of Income tax, 1922 and (3) the Tribunal had erred in holding that the appellant company could not be treated as an investor. HELD: (i) The questions actually framed by this Court on the last occasion were not appropriate and (ii) the questions actually asked by the assessee were questions of fact. [52 E] (a) It is well settled that a question whether a business involves the application of law to the facts found in the setting of the particular case, must be regarded as conclusive in a proceeding under section ' 66( 1). But it would be open to challenge the conclusion of fact drawn by the Tribunal on such ground. [53 G] (b) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or properties or whether of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law, must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is open to the High Courts to examine whether the Tribunal has applied the relevant legal principles correctly or not in reaching its final conclusion; and in that sense, the scope of enquiry and the extent of the jurisdiction of the High court in dealing with such points is the same as in dealing With pure points of law. [54 G H] (c) The proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and the claim of the asses see that the profit and losses arise from the sales of shares or securities etc. cannot be taxed. If, fog, it is found on examination of the transactions themselves that the essential characteristics of a business of the assesses were of dealing in shares and investments and property, the finding of fact recorded by the appellate Tribunal must be treated final. [55 G H; 56 A] (d) The High Courts must not interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunals on the primary questions of facts. But it is open for the High courts to examine the question as framed at present and to decide whether the tribunal had applied the particular legal principles properly or not, in reaching their final conclusion. [56 B C] (e) The finding of the Tribunal that the question can be properly framed "as to whether there was material to support the said finding" is perverse and cannot be based on any legal evidence or material or that the conclusion arrived at without considering the relevant facts has vitiated the finding.

The appellant was a member of the Madras Provincial Judicial Service, and was officiating as District Munsif in the State of Andhra Pradesh. He was suspended by an order dated January 28, 1954, pending enquiry into certain charges against him. The Government passed an order on January 28. 1954, suspending him until further orders, and the same was communicated to him on January 30, 1954. On April 28, 1953, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the order of suspension. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants was without jurisdiction and that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the High court is not a mere administrative order and does not amount to an order of dismissal or removal from service within article 311. [419 D] (ii) The Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry and decide for itself whether the charges were well founded. No such question was raised in the petition or in the writ petition. It was also contended that the High Courts had no jurisdiction under article 311 to suspend a judicial officer pending final orders of the Government. [420 D] The order passed by the High 'Court on January 29, 1954 was merely one of suspension pending final order by the Government and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor of removal from the service within Article 311 of Constitution. It could not be said that the concluding proviso in Rule 4(1) (a) of the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953 had subsequently been amended by G. 0. No. 938 dated April 11, 1955. The order in fact was passed on October 1, 1953.

The appellant was a registered holder of shares in a company which owned shares of the company. The company had obtained probate of the said letters of trust from the estate of one of its directors, a private limited company and appointed the respondent as the respondent, James Anderson. The respondent claimed that the dividends deemed to have been distributed under the order dated March 26, 1953, were distributed in his individual name by the appellant and pursuant thereto the relevant share certificates were delivered to him. The Income tax Officer included the dividend deemed to be distributed in respect of those shares and no question arose as to whether the dividend was assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the dividend could not be taxed under section 23A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because the company had failed to establish that it was liable to pay income tax on the dividends declared by the respondent. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the expression "shareholder" in section 2(2) of the Income tax (Second Amendment) Act, 1950, means a person by whom income tax is payable and may be enforced against him or his legal representative in the manner and to the extent the statute permits. The expression "assessee" in the said section means a shareholder registered in the books of the Company and such shareholder alone is liable to be taxed in respect thereof if he had not died, but for the death of the legal representative although he was himself not a member of the family. Amarchand Shroff vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, , referred to.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State of Baster. He entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the acquisition of his rights in estates, mahals and alienated villages and alienated certain lands in Madhya Pradesh and to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. The appellant contended that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler and was within the class of persons who were by name specifically included in the definition of "proprietor" and therefore clearly within the scope of the Act. The expression "maufidar" as defined in article 366(22) of the Consti tution means a person who is the holder of land which has been separately assessed to land revenue, whether such land revenue be payable or has been released, compounded for or redeemed in whole or in part; and the word "maui" includes an ex ruler. The definition of 'proprietor ' contained in section 2(j) of Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, does not make him a Ruler for purposes outside the Constitution and his case must be regarded as a whole by virtue of which he was entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. The word "amahal" is used in article 367(22), which states that "mahal" includes any person who for the time being is recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler".

The respondent was working in a Garden Curator in the office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India. He was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh). The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the order of transfer on the following grounds: (i) that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the C.A.T., (ii) that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago, and (iii) that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. The Tribunal quashed the order on the ground that the decision of the Courts establish that the power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued by the Government. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines say that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted at the same place. [431C] 1.2 In the matter of considering transfer of an individual officer, the Office Memorandum dated 3 4 1986 has been issued by a Bench of which one of us (J.S. Verma J.) was a member. On a perusal of the judgment, it is evident that the constraints and norms which the High Court observes while exercising the said jurisdiction apply equally to the Tribunal created under Article 323 A. (ii). The guidelines do not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right. [ 431D E] 1:3. In this case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by the transfer. [ 432E F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; , followed.

The appellants were charged under Section 304 Part I read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of one Jawahar. The Trial Court convicted them under section 304 Part 1 read with section 34 I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1 and A2. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of A3 that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of P.W. 2 was proved beyond doubt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the accused was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34 I PC. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of P,W.2. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while granting special leave to appeal was not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. [635C D] 2.1 A common intention is to cause simple hurt and, as such, the offence punishable under Section 325 I.p.C.[636D] 2:2. It is also held that the intention of appellants was to caused grievous hurt. As such the conviction and sentence of the appellant under Section 302 read with Sections 109, 1.P., C. read with Sec tion 34, I PC are set aside.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of certain amounts due to it on account of loan together with interest. The respondent No. 3, the father of the appellant, was the owner of a motor vehicle which was purchased by the appellant after its nationalisation. The appellant had two partners, one of whom was a partner in another, and the other a firm consisting of three partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, and another section Doraswamy, since died. The suit was decreed by the trial court against the respondent No 3 and its partners. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Bank against the decree of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Bank that (i) in view of section 4(e) of the Act, the provisions of the , were not applicable to the Bank and as such the Bank was entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided under section 13 of the . HELD: (1) The words `special Indian law ' have a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no reason why the expression should be interpreted in the light of the setting out of the same in the words of the provision of section 3(27)(a) of Act. [966 D] (2) The expression `special ' has a clear, and unambiguous connotation and there can be no doubt that the expression ` special Indian law" must be construed in the context of a statute, but that does not mean that even though the words which are to be interpreted convey a clear meaning, still a different interpretation or meaning should be given to them because of the set out setting.

The petitioners, who were sugar factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the notification issued by the Government under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that it contravened article 19(1)(g) of Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned notification was invalid as it violated articles 14, 19(i)(g), 19(6) and 31 (2) of India and was bad as it contravened articles 19(l)(g). Held, that the notification was valid and must be struck down. The object of the Act is to secure essential commodities for the general public, which is the consumer, at a fair price; but it does not follow from this that the Government should fix wholesale or retail prices in any particular area. It is well known that there are three kinds of prices prevalent in the market for a commodity like sugar, namely, ex factory price, wholesale price and retail price. The first class of prices fixed by the impugned Notification is controlled by the Central Government under s.3(1), and the second class of price fixed by cl. (c) of section 3 (2). The third class of rates fixed for factories in the State are controlled by cl.(c) and cl. 13 of the Order which provides that "the maximum price shall be at the rate of Rs. 17 per maund on any factory failing to deliver the cost of production and distribution". The second class is controlled only by cl, (c). The object is to ensure fair prices for the consumer; it is in the interest of general public that the price should be fixed at a reasonable price. In the present case the impugned notifications were not discriminatory but were based on two sets of grounds: (1) factories are being compelled to sell at below the cost price, and (2), the price fixed is arbitrary and unreasonable. The prices fixed are just as compared with other producers in view of the fact that in form prices are fixed for factory buyers only in Punjab. The petitioners have not even alleged that as a matter of fact the wholesalers and retailers are profiteering and making it impossible for them to sell their products, there is no reasonable classification between different regions or between producers and middlemen in view Of what they say. The impugned notification has therefore been discriminatory because it contravenes articles 14 and 19(2) (b), (c), (d) and (e).

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956, referred to the Second Industrial Tribunal certain disputes between the appellant and its employees. The Tribunal held that there was a rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 and that the Tribunal applied wrong criteria. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the award of 1951 was not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act, and therefore the reference was bad in law. Held: (i) The Government made the order of transfer on April 9, 1957, i.e., after section 2 of the Amendment Act, 1956 came into force. Under that section, the appropriate Government may by notification in writing and for reasons to be stated therein, withdraw any proceeding under this Act pending before a Tribunal constituted under the Act before the commencement of the Amending Act, which was deemed to have come into force on the 10th day of March 1957. The provisions of sections 19(1) and 30 of the , were not applicable to the case. (ii)The award of the Tribunal was binding between the parties as it had been made in violation of the principles of natural justice, causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raising an important issue. Pritam Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. (iii)The Tribunal had jurisdiction to make a fresh award on the merits of the case, and that was not a ground for interference with it in this appeal by special leave. Pritam singh vs The Union of India, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, distinguished.

The appellant was the Matadheen of Sri Gavi Mutt, which was a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The predecessor in office of the appellant filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the scheme was valid, but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the actual administration of the Mutt and its properties, it was partly because the appellant had been obstructed by the respondents in courts of law. his property rights had been taken away. [260 B] (ii) The conclusion that the Scheme was valid is correct. The scheme as framed was a whole, and the challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed. [262 C D] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that since the scheme had not been implemented till 1952, it continued to operate as though they were framed under the provisions Of the earlier Act. [263 E F] (iv) The order of the Central Government was valid and did not contravene article 19 (1)(g). [262 D] R.S. Sharma vs Finsbury Borough Council, ; , referred to. (v) The contention that since in the present case the scheme has not been completely implemented till 1953, it is open to the appellant challenging its validity on the grounds that it contravenes the Mathadhip Act, 1947, was without substance and must be rejected.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacations during all these years. The managing committee of the school rejected his claim for regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as English Teacher with effectfrom July 121982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the following reasoning: (i) The appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989; and (ii) The services of the appellant were terminated by the managing committee after 1986. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in denying the benefit to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [995B] 1.2 The High Courts erred in deny the benefit on the grounds that his initially appointment for89 days was con cerned by the stipulations that he will continue until replace by a candidates from the Select List. The State Government is expected to function as a model employer. "We are of the view that the State Government has failed to discharge that duty in these cases. [996C D] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, A.I.R 1987 S.C. 478; Rattan Lal V. State of Punjab, AJ.R. 1987 S C. 478 and Rattan Lal v State of J & K, A J.R., 1987 S .C. 477, referred to. 1.3 The HighCourt erred in denied the benefit by the appellant to the respondent on the plea that his appointment was made otherwise than in accordance with procedure laid down in the Education Act and the Rules and Regulations framed thereunder.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Vidhan Sabha from a constituency in which he was elected. The respondent, who was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti, challenged the election on the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 to 7 of the Rules did not convert the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti into an office or profit, and that the appellant was entitled to draw a monthly consolidated allowance in lieu of travelling allowances. HELD : (i) The payment to a Chairman, Panchayat Sanstha, is described in the rule as 'a monthly consolidated amount in lieu thereof '. Under those earlier Rules of 1961, the Chairman was entitled only to Rs. 4/ per diem when a Member of the Gram Panchayat performs a journey in connection with his official duties outside the district. The appellant was therefore entitled to the allowance under rr. 3 and 7 of that Rules. [427 B C] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the allowances paid under r, 3 were in addition to the payment under r 3. [447 D E] (iii) The expenditure incurred by a member for travelling allowance or daily allowance is in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duty. [ 428 C] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 653 at p. 656 and Ravanna subanna vsG.S Kaggai, A I.R., 1954 S C. 653, referred to. (iv) The appellant had failed to establish that the allowance payable under r .

The appellant tenant filed a suit for eviction on the ground of sub stantial construction. The respondent landlord filed a written statement and pleaded that the appellant had made constructions materially alter ing the accommodation without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tin shed was sub ject to the provisions of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952 (Act 10 of 1952). On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial court 's order and dismissed the respondents ' suit on the findings that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decision of the Trial Court and decreed the eviction petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant tenant that (i) the tin sheds were sub stances which could be removed without causing any damage to the building, and (ii) constructions so made had materially altered the accommodation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The material alterations contemplated in section 3(1)(c) of U. P. Cantonment Act, 1949 do not constitute material alteration as the determination of this question depends on the facts of each case. In S.B. Mathur vs K.P Gupta, ; , this Court held that construction which converted the tenanted premises into two rooms and tin shed marked by letters CDGH on the Eastern side on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion, is not a substantial change in nature and they alter, the form, front and structure of the accommodation, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out to the tenant. The construction so made would furnish ground for eviction only when they bring about substantial change of the building as contemplated by section 3 (1)(C) of the Act. [975G H; 977A] 2. In the instant case, the disputed constructions which the High Court has found to be 'material alteration ' consisted of a partition wall of 6 feet height in a hall converting the same into two room and a tin shed with letters CGDH on a open land adjoining the accommodation adjacent to it. The Trial Court as well as the first appellate court both have recorded finding that the respondent landlord was not material alteration of substantial character either in the form or structure of accommodation. There is no material on record to sustain the findings of fact recorded by the High court that the appel lant had constructed pucca constructions on three sides. instead the Commissioner 's report is contrary to it and therefore, the finding recorded by him is not vitiated by any error of law apparent on the face of the record. [ 977C D] 3. The question whether disputed constructions constitute material alter ments is a mixed question of fact and law. The courts below have recorded concurrent findings that the Respondent landlord was entitled to file suit for ejectment of a tenant without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate, but the High Courts in second appeals interfered with the findings arrived at by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition were temporary in nature which could not be removed within the mischief of material alteration, [977D E] 4.

The appellant company had filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of damages to the tune of Rs. 26,000/ on account of alleged non delivery of certain goods. Summons in the suit was sent to the registered office of the company in Calcutta and was said to have been served on one Shri Navlakha on 17 3 1975 asking the company to appear at Indore on 25 3 1975 for settlement of issues. The respondent firm filed a revision petition against the order of the Trial Court before the High Court under section 115 C.P.C. The High Court allowed the revision and set aside the ex parte decree. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that since the appellant company came to know about the exparte decree for the first time when its constituted attorney Shri Navnakha was sent on 17 4 1975, the summons would be deemed to have duly served on the company within the meaning of the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of C. P.C., and therefore the application filed by the respondent firm under Order 9 Rule 13 C.p.C was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1032G] 2.1 In Rule 17 of Order 5, it has been provided that where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Case that the service of the summons as effected in accordance with the first paragraph (b), of Rule 1, Order 29, was not due to service on the Company. [ 1032A B] 2:2 The High court went wrong in interfering with it. [1133C D] 3.1 The High Courts went wrong that the judgment by the Trial court setting aside the decree was correct. [1103D] 3:2 No error of jurisdiction was committed by it. The order of this Court setting aside a decree was wrong. [1001F] 3(a) The words 'Principal Officer ' in clause(b) have to be understood with reference to the other provisions of the Code. In Rule 2, Order 5 is not an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on a company in the sense as to what is meant by service of summons on the Secretary, Director or Principal Officer in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. and another vs The Union of India and others; , it was held that the words ' Principal Officer ' have to he understood with referential to the different provisions of Order 9, Rule 13 of the C.Ps. [1003C D].

The Magistrate recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of peace existed even in the final order. The Magistrate passed an order under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the said order on the ground that there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the preliminary order that there existed a breach or peace and that there had been apprehension of breach of the peace. The High Court held that as there was an allegation that there were disputes between the parties, the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145 the Magistrate passed the final orders in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that the final Order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of such peace existed, and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to give a finding in the case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the High Courts is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [962C] 2. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach, if any, of the parties. If he is satisfied about the existence or possession of any land etc., once the record of order is passed, the High Curt in revision cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the magistrate is based. [942D] 3. The objection that there is an omission on the part of the Magis trate to mention in his final order that the breach of a peace existed was not raised by any party before the Magistrate or before the High, Court. Further, it is well settled that under section 146 it is open for the magistrate to be satis fied regarding the nature of dispute likely to cause a breach and if there is no clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [952E F] 4. The question whether the Magistrate should be satisfied about a breach has to be decided on the facts of each case and in the circumstances, it can be safely presumed that apprehension of the breach is not necessary at the time when a final order is made nor is there any provision in the Code requiring such a finding to be recorded in the order.

The appellant, a public limited company, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn and yarn. The company sold its yarn to its old customers who paid it as shown in its accounts. The appellant contended that the company had earned more profits than was disclosed in its books of account and that the sales were not liable to tax under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the question whether a particular transaction is a sale or not must be decided on the facts of each case and it is not necessary for the Tribunal to decide it on the evidence adduced before it. The finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal was final and conclusive as to the legal effect of those findings was a question of law which could be reviewed by the High Court under section 11(1). Commissioner of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co., ; , referred to. In the present case, the appellant had been found to have sold its goods to its new customers and received the price therefor. The question as framed by the appellant did not specifically raise this point but it was urged that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to assess the sales in question under section 67(1)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961. It was also contended that there was no need for the intermediaries to purchase from other manufacturers when all their needs were met by the company and that there could be no question as to who found the capital for the intermediary was. Held further, that in the present ease the appellant was not liable as it had not been treated as a dealer under section 14(2) (c), and the Tribunal erred in holding that the intermediaries were benamidars for the appellant. Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Bryan, , referred lo.

The assessee, a manufacturer of blankets and other woollen cloth, was assessed to income tax on the profits of the firm payable after the accounts had been ascertained fully by the Income Tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that Rs. 5,063 as reasonable amount payable as commission to Shri J.P. Vaish, the assessee paid a sum of Rs. 75,465 as commission and Rs. 6,000 as allowance for the accounting year 1947 48. The Tribunal on reference, held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after his death. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) In applying the test of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee, reasonableness of the expenditure has to be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not the assessee in character of a trader or it is not laid out wholly and solely for the purposes of thebusiness of the assesses. (ii) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpo se of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xi) of the Income tax Act has to he decided on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. In the present case both the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and the Appellate Tribunal rejected the view of its own. (iii) The High Court was right in holding that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of Rs 75,467 paid to him was an amount laid out of or expended entirely and exclusively for his purpose of business of assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the income tax authorities.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of which he was a member. On January 13, 1954, the management and the Union filed a joint petition for dismissal of the respondent company on the ground that the appellant had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and prayed for an order directing the company to record compromise or hearing. The Tribunal held that the agreement was collusive and mala fide and that the Secretary of the Union was not competent to enter upon the agreement. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up by the Union of which the workman is a member, as a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, must be decided on the facts of each case. The principle that the party to a dispute should have a fair hearing, is not applicable to an individual dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispute Act unless it is taken by a Union of workmen or by a considerable number of workmen. Central Provinces Transport Service Ltd. vs Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, ; , referred to. The question whether a workman who is a party to the dispute is a necessary party to an industrial dispute under the Act, when the same had not been taken up for hearing, must depend on the circumstances of each individual case. In the present case there were no such exceptional circumstances and it was not unreasonable to think that section 36 of the Act recognises this position by providing that the workman who was a party in a dispute shall be entitled to be represented by an officer of a registered trade union of which him is a members.

The appellants were the tenants in respect of a portion of a house. The respondent No. 1 instituted a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the ground that they had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2 and that he had been assessed to income tax separately and that the property in dispute was not joint family property or even joint property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and were entitled to continue the appeal. On appeal by the respondent No 1, the High Court held that the respondents were competent to continue their appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the provisions of r. 4 of 0. XLI, r. 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not override the provisions Of r. 9 of O. XXII and (2) the High court had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal as the provisions in r. 3 of 0 . XLI were applicable to the case as the nine appellants constituted joint Hindu Family and the surviving appellants could continue their appeals in view of the provisions contained in O. XLI. r. 31 of the code. HELD : (i) The appellate court had not jurisdiction to proceed with the appeal and reversed or vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants under O.XXII, r, 3. [560 F] (ii) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellant when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated as all the appellants had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant No 2 and such decree could have been on a ground common to all of them. [561 G] (iii) The provisions of 0 XLI, rr. 33 and 34 of O XXII were not applicable to it. Rule 3 was therefore inapplicable to the stage when an appeal is filed by all the defendants. [562 D E] (iv) The judgment in the present case was not a case of such a kind. When the legal representatives of the deceased appellant and the remaining appellants were negligent in not taking steps for substitution, the Court was not to exercise its discretion in favour or to reverse or modify the decree passed by it. [563 G H] (v) The appeal by Kedar Nath was not competent in the circumstances of the case and the provisions under O XLI, Rule 33 were not attracted to it.[564 D E].

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Delhi. The respondent landlord filed a petition for eviction against the appellant on the ground of bona fide requirement under section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The appellant contended that no notice to quit had been given nor any notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could not be justified as there was a statutory presumption in favour of the respondent landlord that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the Act. The Rent Controller held that no such notice was necessary because the lease was created prior to the extension of the lease and therefore, the forfeiture was not valid. On appeal, the High Court held that the notice in writing by the landlord was a condition precedent to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease under section 108(1) of Transfer of Property Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the lease stood determined by forfeiture and (ii) the forfeiture could not have been made in terms of section 111 (g); and (iii) the notice terminating tenancy was valid as it did not comply with the requirements of the terms and conditions of the Deed of demise. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The requirement of a notice in the lease deed for a specified period even though it expressed itself as for a term less than one year and under section III(a) has expired by lapse of time. [918C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had all along staked his case on the application of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience. The High Court was right in its view that the provisions of the P.T. Act were not applicable to the lease in question and therefore a forfeiture giving rise to a determination of the lessee under section 11(g). [919D] 1:3. The requirement as to written notice provided in the section is not based on any principle of equity. It is not so in express terms it cannot be said that a notice as contemplated by section 111 has been given in writing. [936F] 1 :4. In the present case, there was no specific statutory provision which required the notice to be given in the notice. The notice did not indicate any statutory requirement of law. It was merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the Section by the legislature and was not based upon any well established principles of equity and natural justice. [981F] In the circumstances, the mere institution of the legal proceeding for eviction does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right if he so chooses, to determine the lease. Once it is held that a valid notice was issued by forfeiture under section 112(g), the appellant cannot be allowed to contend that the document in question did not amount to a statutory provision requiring notice in law for determination of lease. [980B C] 1 5. The provisions of section III (g) and (h) are intended to protect the interest of the tenant and to secure the interests of his lessor with a right, if he is so chooses. [979E F] 1 6. The provision of section 11 (g), as it now stands, requires notice to show cause within 15 days from the date of service of the notice on the tenant. What is required is that notice should be given by the lessee in the present suit for recovery of the building. [978C D] 1 7. The proviso to section 111 provides that where a landlord has terminated the tenancy by giving notice in that behalf, he shall not evict the tenant unless he satisfies any one of the grounds set out in section 3.

The appellant was a Superintendent in the State of Assam. He was dismissed from service with immediate effect on charges under section 5(1) (a), 5(2) and 6(3). The Governor passed an order dismissing him from service. On appeal, the High Court held that the order was not justified as the Governor had acted mala fide in passing the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Governor when acting under sub clause (c) of article 311 of the Constitution was satisfied that in the interest of security of the State it was not expedient to give him an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above. HELD : The order of dismissal from service was passed in violation of article 310(2). [488 B] (i) The words used in the Article are "shall not apply" and, therefore, the consultation with the Public Service Commission is mandatory and that this Article does not confer any right on a public servant so that the absence of consultation or any irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law. [488 C] (ii) The satisfaction recorded by the Governor under sub cl. (c), therefore, that the appellant had to arrive at was that it was "not expedient to do so" and the Governor 's satisfaction was recorded on the language which was used earlier in the unamended Article 311(2), as it stood before amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963. [489 D] Khem Chand vs The Union of India & Ors., ; , followed. (iii) The consultation with Public Service Commis sioner is not mandatory and the consultation must be consulted before an order is passed by the Government. [490 E] (iv) The opinion recorded by a Governor under article 311(3)(c) was binding on the President, as he had been satisfied that it could not be expedient to provide him with the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity of showing cause against his action proposed as stated in the amended Article 311. [497 G] (v) The Governor ' s satisfaction is recorded by him in the language used earlier and in the light of the interpretation placed on that unamended article by this Court. [492 A B] Khemchand vs State of U.P., ; referred to.

The petitioners and the Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, were alleged to have formed serious infraction and/or infringement of their fundamental rights under articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution in the matter of enjoying their religious faith and performance of religious ceremonies. The petitioners and Shia Community of Mohalla Darbar, Varanasi had filed a representative suit for declaration that the said Shia Muslim community was not entitled to perform their religious ceremonies and functions on the plots and structures thereon as also an appropriate writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus commanding respondents 1 to 4 not to prohibit or restrain the Shias from performing their religious duties and practices. The Court passed a preliminary decree for declaration of rights in favour of Shia sect and for restraining the ShiAS community from performing its religious ceremonies, practices, observances and functions. In appeal by the Shira Community against the said decree, the High Court held that the petitioners were not entitled under O.XXI, r.8 C.P.C., to institute the suit in question on the assumption that they had made any ground for challenging title either to the plots or to the structures thereon or even the Shiasi community of the structure on those plots and the rights exercisable by the Sunni community over the plots were not justiciable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned order passed by a District Magistrate under O .XXI. r. 8 C. P.C. was a judicial order and it must be pointed out that all the decisions including those of this Court in Haji Mohammed Ismail vs Munshi Barkat Ali & Ors., ; , relied upon, were not applicable to the facts of the case as the petitioners had also claimed that the plots of land and structures on these plots and structure thereon had been registered as Shia Waqfs for purposes of performing their religion, practices and observances. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the order passed under OXXI r. 54 C.p.C was a Judicial Order or quasi judicial order, the function thereunder being essential an executive (police) function. Having come to the conclusion that the orders under section 144 Cr. P C. were amenable to writ jurisdiction under article 32 of the Consti tution, it is not correct to say that the High Courts had acted in the exercise of their powers under OXl r.54 C. p.C.[1135D E] 2. The power to issue writs under O Xl r, 8 C P.P., C. is conferred on a District Magis trate, a Chief Presidency Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the State Government in that behalf. [1134E F] 3. The jurisdiction of a Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P C. has to be exercised with great care and caution and not as an appellate court. It is well settled that the power to act in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger to public tranquility has been conferred on "a District Magistrate, a chief Presidency Magistrate, or any Executive Magistrate specifically empowered by him". The powers under section 146 Cr.pc. are exercisable only when the District Magistrate or Executive Magistrate is satisfied that the circumstances of the alleged case disclosed such existence and there is no real basis for exercising jurisdiction in aid of his power. [1104G H] 4. The powers to issue writ, order or direction under O XII r. 55 C.I.P.(C.) are not confined to orders passed by courts in urgent matters of nuisance and apprehended danger. [111A B] 5. The Supreme Court has power to grant relief only when there is a clear and unambiguous declaration that a particular case is neither a grave one nor a mere possibility of a serious nature. [112B C] 6. The fact remains that the notification under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act was issued by the respondent No.

The assessee, a limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off on the ground that when in the assessment years 1957 58, the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computation of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had held that there was no genuine loss. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that the loss could not be said to have been determined for the purpose of assessment year 1958 66. The High Court found that the Income Tax officer had wrongly disallowed the assessee 's claim. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had no justification to hold that the claim was not genuine while disposing of the appeal for the earlier years, and that the Tribunal had rightly disallowed the loss claimed by the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 24(3) regarding intimation of losses as notional when he really meant that it was an estimate. It agreed with the conclusion of the Tribunal and found against the Revenue. Section 24(2)(a) provides that where in respect of any assessment year, the net result of the assessee has such as is referred to in sub section (2A), and the loss cannot be wholly set off in accordance with the provisions of that sub section, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on. however, that no loss shall be carry forward for more than eight years. it shall not be carried over to the aforesaid assessment year. [1162E F] 2.1 The High Courts were in error in holding that the provisions in section 24 (3) of 1922 Act regarding intimation by Income Tax Officers do not apply to the loss falling under the head 'capital gains '. [1102G] 2(a) The benefit conferred under section 24 of 1922 act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding the claim for set off was admissible in the view that it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. [1063B] 2.(b) The High court reached the correct conclusion and there is no merit in the appeal. [1014C] 2 (c) The claim of setting off was allowable in the present case. on a bare analysis of these provisions, and without reference to anything more, this appeal can be disposed of.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Research & Development dated 24.12.1985. On his retirement he was re instated as Senior Scientific officer on 30.4.86. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal by way of a writ petition challenging the order of premature retirement which was dismissed by the Central Administrative Tribunal holding that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years, and that he was not entitled to any amount so paid to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the DRDS was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz. DAQAS, was entitled to the said benefit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid, and there is no substance in the present appeal. [316B] 2. The question involved in the instant case is not whether the Government has such power. The fact that the superannuationage of the Members of theDRDS was enhanced, it can not be said that the Respondent who belonged tO the said unit, namely DAQas, was enti tled to the benefit. There is no dispute that the Govern ment had power to vary the service conditions of the member of the service from time to time. The service rules which applied to all the three units were also common, viz., Defence Science Services Rules. [333C D] 3. The High Court has rightly held that there was a right of the Government to prescribe separate conditions of serv ice for the Members belonging to different units and merely on the basis of the superannuation of the Member of the RTA, the service rules would have to run parallel and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by the Tribunal. [332D] 4. The contention that the State Government had power under Rule 12 of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972 to vary its service conditions is not tenable because the rule which applied for the benefit of the President and the members was also granted to the members. [33E F] 5. The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to vary or modify the service condition of the employees belonging to one of the units. Merely because the superannu nation age of members of that unit is increased, the same could not he held that they were entitled to such benefit.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election petition filed by him was dismissed on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice under section 123(2) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The first respondent challenged the election of the appellant before the High Court on various grounds. The High Court held that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the trial judge was satisfied that the appellant had been personally responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as such found him guilty of corrupt practice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High court was not justified in quashing the order of the trial court under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The election petitioner had been rightly convicted by the High 'Court. [975 D] (ii) The first question was whether the appellant proved guilty of a corrupt practice and if so, what punishment should be imposed on him. It is not necessary to decide that question in this case because the trial Judge had jurisdiction to call these two persons as witnesses under the provisions of the Act. [936 G H] (iii) The High ' Court was not called upon to go into this question. There was no evidence on which the judge could have come to the conclusion he did, The first point therefore fails. [981 C D] In the present case, the appellant knew exactly what points he had to meet and evidence was adduced about the publication and distribution of pamphlet by the respondent.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute. In exercise of its powers under section 3 of the Act, the Governor of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification dated March 31, 1956, imposing a tax of six pies in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute to be taxed at such rate not exceeding one anna per rupee as may be specified by the Government. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 286(2) of the Constitution and that the validation Act was beyond the competence of the legislature. Held, that the Validation Act was intra vires the State legislature and was not ultra vires. The impugned notification was valid as it was issued before section 3 Of the Act came into force. The effect of the validating Act was to validate the impugned notification in relation to the amended section. The validation Act could not be challenged on the grounds, inter alia, that it imposed a tax retrospectively and that it did not affect the competence or the power of the Legislature under Entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The State Legislature had no power to enact a law with retrospective operation. The fact that the impugned Act was passed after the amendment of section 3 did not alter the real nature of the tax which by express provisions of the law was imposed upon the seller and the legislature could not impose it retrospectively, unless there can be found in the Constitution itself a limitation on that power. The expression "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of the Amending Act" in section 3 must be read as qualifying the word "notifications". The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted for the offence of theft and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the sentence imposed on him was not a "habitual" and had no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, barbaricisation, criminal companionship, versatile vices through bio environmental pollution, dehumanised cell drill under 'zoological ' conditions and emergence, at the time of release, of an embittered enemy of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully" processed into a hardened delinquent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The sentence imposed by the Sessions Court and confirmed by the High Court is not excessive. [591F] 2.2 In the instant case, the offence committed by the appellant was beyond doubt and he had no sinful antecedents except that of this furillance. He has a young wife and a farm to look after. Given correctional courses through meditational therapy and other measures, his erotic aberration may wither away. A man like the appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. [592G H] 2:3. The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. The respondent assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the , certain plots of land were requisitioned by the Government for public purpose and the compensation payable to the assessee was enhanced by Rs.5,13,624 on March 31, 1956. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable in respect of the said plots. The respondent challenged before the Arbitrator the award on the ground that the income accrued to him on the date of the award. The arbitrator held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesses and therefore, the amount could not be said to have accrued to it as income during the previous year ended March 31. 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. The Arbitrator held that compensation received was not a receipt of a revenue nature. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Arbitrator. In second appeal by the respondent, the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the amount did not accrue to the appellant as its income during that previous year ending March 31 1956 relevant for assessment year in question on the basis that the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum exceeding Rs.7272/10/4 per mensem was in dispute in the appeal filed by the State Government. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sum of compensation received under the Land Acquisition Act was not taxable in the assessment years 1956 57 and therefore the income arising or accruing to the asses see during the relevant previous year stood excluded from the assessment for that year on the principle of law laid down by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding otherwise would be contrary to the provisions of law. [395G] 2. The legal position was explained in Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, ; and Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner Of Income tax Gujarat, , approved. 3. The question whether income could be said tO have accrued or arose to an assessee for the purpose of the Indian Income Tax Act was a matter which must be distinguished from that decided by this court in Kent 's case. [396A] 4. In view of the fact that the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount of compensation payable by the appellant to the respondent assessee, the entire amount was in controversy in the present appeal filed before the High court and therefore there could be no justification for such a proposition. [397C] 5. The interpretation given by this Courts does not affect the interests of revenue. At the same time it safeguards the assessee 's interest and prevents harassment. To hold otherwise would he contrary to law. It is sufficient to point out that there is a clear distinction between cases such as the present one where the right to receive payment is in dispute and it is not a question of merely quantifying the amount to be received, and cases where the rights to receive payments are admitted and the quantification only of the amount payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles. [398D E] 6. The law was explained by this decision. In a case which must fall under section 4(1)(b)(i) of Income Tax, read with Section 19 of Income Topilal Act, it safeguards, the assessee, and prevents harassed harassment. to the extent of the additional amount of compensa tion claimed by the owner of the land.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the appellants on the ground that they had been in possession of the shop as tenants. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal was also dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The language of section 12(1) says that where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise, the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit. If the agreement or the compromise for the eviction of a tenant is found, on the facts of a particular case, to be in violation of a specified Rent Restriction Act, the court would refuse to record the compromise as it will not be a lawful agreement. [882 D E] (2) The words "in any other suit" occurring in section 12 (1)(f) are clear and definite especially in the background of the pleadings of the parties and in our opinion, it squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of section 13(11). [883 F G] (3) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the context of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances, is entitled to have such a decree under the law. It is too late in the day to contend that the provisions Of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [888 F G; 883 A] (4) The expression "in respect of the first part" in section 2(1)(g) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 means that where a tenant has been found to have been in violation thereof, he is entitled under the general law or a statute.

The assessee was a limited company doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56, the Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs. 11,88,000/ out of this loss on the ground that it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the Elphinstone Mills Ltd., and that the company suffered a net loss of Rs 11,63,874/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that under the circumstances the Directors were justified in not declaring any dividend in respect of those years. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss and that it could not be taken into consideration in computing the net income. In reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The loss any reasonable body of Directors of a company would have done just what the Directors of the company did. [8 4 C] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co., , referred to. (ii) In view of the fact that the Directors are naturally more interested in the stability of their concern rather than in increasing the tax payable to the Government, the provisions must be worked not from the standpoint of the tax collector but from that of a businessman. [864 D] Commissioner Of Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., , applied. (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the assessee had suffered a capital losses of Rs 12 lakhs and that therefore, cancelled the orders of the Income Tax Officer under section 23A(1).

The Consolidation Officer acting under section 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, referred the question of title to the Civil Judge for determination. The Civil Judge overruled the objection and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the award. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 37 of the Act does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15 of the , which provides for appeals against orders of the civil judge. Section 12(6) of that Act does provide for a statutory arbitration and section 37 is not applicable to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. The effect of section 46 and section 47 of the is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations. Section 37 of that act does not provide anything inconsistent with this. In the present case, the effect of s.46 and section 49 of the was inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of the U.P. Consolidation of 1954 Act. Section 18 of the Consolidation Act does no make any difference between provisions under the , and section 46 of the . The effect is that the proceedings under the Act are not covered by the provisions mentioned in s.37 of the and section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Section 36 of the provides for a special arbitration and s. 37 of Act does so. Section 38 of the applies to arbitrations as well as to suits referred to in section 37. Section 39 of that is not inconsistent with the . In the instant case, there was no question of considering the effect Of sections 46 and 47 of , or considering whether section 39 of Act 4 of 1954 would apply to arbitration under the consolidation of Holdings.

The petitioner, a diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation, was appointed as Executive Engineer by the respondent corporation. Till 1974 he was holding the post for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, the corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner challenged the said regulations on the ground that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent Corporation is a mere resolution or an executive instruction could not effect such discrimination. [782C] 1.2 In the absence of rules or regulations, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till 1988 by the impugned resolution. The proposition that in the absence Of the rules and regulations, it can be made only a statutory rule or regulation framed under section 64 of the said Act, cannot be accepted since the creation of selection grade in the same category on the strength of their qualification is permissible. [781E F] 1:3. In the instant case, the respondent Board was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. However, since respondent No. 2 was a Degree holder, his promotion was not in accordance with law and was also sought to be done since 1988 by virtue of the resolution. [780F G] 1 :4. The principle that for the purposes of promotion, a valid classification can made among members holding the same post on the date of their qualifications is well known and permissible. The respondent Board, therefore, cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was meant till the year 1988 and was further considered to be a statutory Rule or regulation.

The first petitioner, a practising advocate, filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution for a mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies in the Bombay High Court. The Union of india, on being satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not making the applications within time, filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the same. The High Court dismissed the petition and held that the ratio laid down by this Court in S.P. Gupta 's case was applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The Chief Justice of India is a matter for immediate attention of all concerned and of Government in particular that the need is recognised and administration of justice is ensured. [448C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Chief Justice has quite often both before the Parliament and outside has stated that it has, as matter of policy, not made any appointments to the superior judiciary without the name being cleared by the Chief Minister through the Governor of the State. This is to be done by a judicial recognition of the standard with a concomitant legal and constitutional obligation for the executive to adopt and apply the standard. [459D] 1:3. The Chief justice of India, the chief Justice of the States and the Chief Justices of the High Courts are both in position. In view of what is stated above, it is clear that the primacy of the Chief justice in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. The primacy of a Chief Justice in the exercise of his functions under the Constitution is an over simplification of a sensitive and subtle constitutional sentence and if allowed foul play, would be subversive of the doctrine of judicial independence. [460E F] 1 :4. The judiciary has been given the status and importance of the executive Government. There are unanimity amongst the members of the Executive in the Council of Ministers of the Union and the States. It is, therefore, necessary to have a look at the matter only if the Chief Secretary of the concerned High Court has recommended and recommended that the case be referred to a Chief Minister for initial appointment. [461E F; 462A] 1 5. The executive power of the Central Government is vested in the President of India under Article 239(1) of the constitution. It would therefore, be open to the Central Govern ment to over ride the opinion given by the constitutional function aries required to be consulted and to arrive at its own decision in regard to the appointment of a Judge in the High Court or the Supreme Court. [463B C] 1 6. The responsibility of the administration of the judiciary is that of the highest executive authority. There is no doubt that the Chief Ministers of a State are the head of the Indian Judiciary and they have a constitutional duty to adopt the standard of selection as laid down in the constitutional scheme and context. [464D] 7. It cannot be said that the executive has been giving any position of primacy amongst the three persons who have to be consult ed under Article 217(1). The Chief Ministers are expected to exercise their independent role in the matter of appointments to a High Court and the High court of the states would be at liberty to take such decision as it may think fit in the matters of appointments. [465E F, G] 8. It was not correct to say that the opinion of the majority of the Judges of the Supreme Bench of the Court is binding on the Chief Secretaries of the respective States and that the views expressed by them are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govt. [467B] 9. The independence of the Judiciary is an integral part of the constitutional process and the judiciary has to be given a decisive import unless the executive had some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment is otherwise undesirable. [468C D] 10.

The respondent was serving as a Reve nue Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the appellant Bank. He was served with a memo dated August 1, 1978 by the Divisional Office of the Bank calling for his explanation and thereafter, on March 27, 1979, he was served a letter dated January 23, 1979 asking him to furnish details of persons who traveled and the amounts received by him from various sources including the appellant. The respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found satisfactory. Thereupon, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his dismissal. A Single Judge of the High court allowed the writ petition holding that on retirement of the respondent, he had no right to impose punishment on him and hence the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent and without jurisdiction. The Division Bench also held that since the appellant had submitted to the jurisdiction of Shri U.B. Menon, the initial defect, if any, stood removed and without juris diction. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said enquiry conducted by the said Enquiry Officer. [204C] 1.2 In the facts and circumstances of this case, the course suggested by Shri Shetye could be usefully adopted. The appellant 's attitude was not a mere official but a bank employee for that matter an ex employee. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of punishment but it should not have ordered payment of all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders were bad in law. [205E] 1:3. In the instant case, there is no merit in this contention. The order of removal got merged in the appellate order, and the appellant was informed about his retirement. It is only after he had retired from service that he proceeded with the enquiry. Therefore, the High Courts were right in holding that the order passed by the disciplinary authority was not valid. [206F] 1st Respondent 's appointment as an Enquiry Officer de facto was valid. The re spondent did not deny any bias and mala fides against the Enquiry officer nor did it appear to be in any way prejudiced on the ground of his alleged misconduct. [207G] 2.1 In the circumstances, the ends of justice would be met if instead of directing all consequen tial benefits ' flowing from declaration that a decision of dismissal got merged into the appellate authority 's order, the appellant could have taken steps to remedy the situation by appointing a competent officer to enquire into the charges before the respondent 's retirement from service. It was equally true that the penalty has not been quashed on mer its. [208B C] 2:2 The High Courts should not interfere with the impugned orde r of punishment unless it is shown that the merits of the case so demand but because the technical plea of incompetence, prejudice or mala fide is of no consequence so far as the question of competence is concerned.

The respondents were owners of a building in the mainkhadabad, Delhi. The appellant Corporation had taken on lease for its construction of a new construction and required urgent and extensive repairs.
