A dispute arose as to whether the proposal was under acquisition and also affected by road widening. The respondents submitted their applications to the Commissioner for approval of the plan. The Commissioner rejected the application. The High Court, however, allowed the appellant 's writ petition and issued a mandamus directing the appellant to accord sanction to the plan for execution of work in respect of the building. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Master Plan prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Act 1957 had statutory force, and that the Commissioner could not refuse to accord the sanction asked for by the respondents. HELD: (i) The High court was right in issuing a writ of mandamus directing that the appellant should obtain sanction for the erection of a build ing building or execution of a work unless such building or work would contravene any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 337 or the provisions Of section 340. [172E] (ii) The Commissioner has to give sanction for erection of the buildings or the execution of works, unless such sanction is obtained before it is finalised and sent to the Central Government for approval. There is no dispute that the building operations are allowed to be carried on in the zone otherwise than in conformity with the Master plan. [173G] (iii) The provisions of section 7 do not apply to the construction of buildings or constructions made in a zone where the Master plans have been prepared under Section 7. Section 8(2)(a) provides for the approval of a development plan by the Commissioner. The Development Act is an Act to provide for the development of Delhi according to plan and for matters ancillary thereto. Section 3, sub section 4 and section 5 deal with the procedure for the preparation of Master Plan and the Zonal Development Plan. Section 7(2) provides that after the commencement of the Act no development of land shall be undertaken or carried out in any area by any person or body (including a department of Government). The provisions contained in section 8(1) are applicable to the building or works which have been constructed, with the sanction of the Central Govern ment. [174H; 175A B] (iv) Section 3 of the Development Act provides for a detailed outline of Deeds and modifications of the Master Plans and the two maps relied on by the appellant do not give any indication that any part of the land belonging to the respondents will be covered by a road, or portion of a road. [175G H] (v) The respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part or definite use of the site. The provisions under section 8 do not indicate and indicate that is borne out by the various matters mentioned in the Master Development Plan that the master plan will only give a very broad outline of the Deeds referred to in sub section(2). [175A B, D] (vi) The Master Plan has been prepared for the area which are reserved for roads. The Master plan and the three maps relied upon by the appel lant do not mention that any portion of the property belonging to respondents will he covered by the proposed road. The Respondents ' lands were not in the nature of a public building, but were in any way indicated as having been taken up for the purpose of the development. [176F G] (vii) The appellant 'S 's lands are neither in any kind nor in any other manner indicated. The plan and two maps referred to by the respondent do not show that any parts of the proposed land belonging either to the Respondents will be mentioned in conformity therewith.

The appellant No. 1 was charged with having committed an offence under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and the appellant No 2 was charged under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for having committed offences under section 165A, 165A and 165B of the Penal Code. The Additional District Magistrate acquitted both the appellants but convicted them under section 5(1) (d) read with section 5 (2) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On appeal by the appellant no. 1 the Judicial Commissioner set aside his conviction and sentence on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and that there was no evidence in support of the prosecution case against him. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellants No. 2 and convicted them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant No 1 was asked by the police authorities to make the statements to these two witnesses not with a view to avoid the bar of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code or by way of colourable device but by way Of greater caution particularly having regard to the fact that the appellant NO. 2 was asked to make his statement to those two witnesses in their defence, the appellant Nos. 1 and 2 were not in a position to provide this sum of money for payment of the bribe or illegal gratification to the appellant. [1114 D E] (ii) The evidence of these witnesses being so strong that they could not be allowed to take the whole Affair to its culmination, the High Court was right in holding that the statements made by them were inadmissible in evidence and that their statements were not hit by section 164 Of the Code. [1215 F G] (iii) The statement made by the appellants to the two witnesses was admissible under section 164 as it was not a confessional statement and was therefore inadmissible in nature. [1316 C D] (iv) The High court was right that the evidence of the two eye witnesses being highly unsatisfactory, the statements were inadmissible. [1517 F G].

The respondent was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable, and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge against the appellant was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was acquitted by the trial court but the suit was decreed in his favour. In appeal, the High Court set aside the decree of the first appellate court and remitted the case to it for fresh disposal according to law. On remand, the suit filed by the respondent was allowed. The appellant appealed against the decision of the High court which dismissed the same on the ground that the second respondent had failed to prove the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Courts in limine. It has been argued on behalf of the appellants that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the grounds that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [825E F] 1.2 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the Court is permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. The defendant appellants filed a regular second appeal before the High COurt against the decree passed by the first Appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage by merely saving the order of the trial Court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and not the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heating the learned counsel for the parties, it is clear that the question raised in this appeal should not be lightly brushed down by the Court. [826F G] 2.1 The question involved was whether the suit is barred by limitation. It was asserted on oath before the Court not compe tent in this regard and that later he was again dismissed. It had been further urged that Rule16.2 (2) was not applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. [827F G; 828A] 2:2 In view of the fact that the HighCourt should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself, it would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment provided such a punishment has been awarded to the other police officials tried and con victed along with him.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The respondent entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee entered into a contract with the mills for purchase of coal from various parties after paying full price of the goods covered by the delivery orders and transferred those P.D.Os. to buyers after receiving the price fixed for the sale of those goods. The assessee had no godown for keeping the goods and had not handled them. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery order addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to M/s. Lachhminarain Kenia Mills was credited to the price of goods covered under the delivery Orders and transferred these P. D.Os to buyers. The appellant claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was only one sale and the delivery was appropriated to the contract so that there could be no completed sale since no property passed but only an agreement for sale. The High Court held that this case came within the scope of section 24(1) read with Explanation 2 and restored the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have correctly stated in their judgment that the property in the goods passed to the ultimate endorsee of the delivery Order went to feed their previously defective titles and ensured to their benefit. His Lordship further observed that this was a correct statement of law. [184 D] Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; , followed. (ii) The question whether on the facts of the case there were two separate transactions of sale so as to bring them to charge under section 3 of the Act was not relevant for the purpose of this explanation. A transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the meaning of Explanation 2 if actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips has taken place; on the other hand, a transaction which was not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery meaning to that expressing for purposes of income tax only.

The appellant was declared elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had not been validly nominated and that he was unable to contest the election. The Election Tribunal decided in his favour by a majority, but it held that without "attestation" they were invalid and so rejected them. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the word "subscribe" used in section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is not defined in the General Clauses Act and therefore the word 'subscribes ' has to be given its ordinary meaning. The word " substitutes" is not used in various senses to indicate different modes of signing and that it includes the placing of a mark. The general words are used in the general sense of the word, but they are not defined. In the General clauses Act, the word is defined as including all names or marks which may be written by an elector in any one of the four nomination papers. The General Clauses Acts also provide for the attestation of certain signatures and the making of a marking. The words "subscribers" have to be read ejusdem generis with the word ,and they are used only in the sense of making a signature and as the Act tells us quite clearly how the different types of " signatures" are to be made, it is clear that the words "sign" and "subscribed" are not used. The use of the words 'sign ' and 'subscribe ' in the case of proposers and seconders who are not able to write their names does not make them technical and unsubs tantial.

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. During the pendency of the dispute relating to the re instatement of three of the union leaders who had been dismissed by the Company, the company put up a notice stating that the strike embarked upon by the workmen was illegal and those participating in the strike were liable to disciplinary action for misconduct as per company 's certified standing orders Nos. 22(b) and 24(a). The appellants submitted their explanations and thereafter filed a complaint before the Industrial Tribunal alleging that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal, and that they had not abandoned their service and that there were interested parties to the dispute. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned their services and therefore, their names had been struck off from the muster rolls of the company. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the act of the management in removing them from its roll was illegal as they had failed to resume duty and that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the Board 's standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, the appellants were entitled to relief. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The action of respondent No. 2 in removing those names from its records was illegal. [616D] 2.1 The period stretches over six years and Shri Sachine Chaudhary brings to our notice that back wages have to be computed if ordered in full, on a much higher scale because of two settlements which had raised the scales of wages substantially. While there is no case specifically put forward that the workmen concerned have been employed elsewhere during this period, still we take a total view that their being no provision in the certified standing order by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services of the appel lants in the aforesaid circumstances, the impugned action on the part of the Respondent No. 1 clearly amounted to a change in the condition of service of the Appellants during the admitted pendency of industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. [625E F] 2:2. The period stretch over six year and Shri S.D. Majumdar brings to your notice that the back wages has to be determined if ordered by the Tribunal in full. [716B C] 3.1 In the instant case, the period stretching over six months and Shri Sahoo went on indefinite strike which ended on October 22, 1972 in response to the strike notice given by the union to the Company to press its demand for re instatedment of its three dismissed leaders and had not only by their letters dated September 21, 1972 and September 26, 1972 unequivocally intimated to the company that they did not intend to abandon the service but had also returned the cheques sent to them by the company on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The appellants ' contention that the letter of the said company dated September 7, 1972 was received by them on September 20, 1972 is not correct. [613E F; 614A] 3:2 It may be recalled that the Company did not refute the averment made by the appellants in their letter dated September 26. 1972 that passed between the parties. The Company 's action was manifestly illegal and invalid. [512C D] 4.1 There is no substance in the contention of the respondents that the failure to perform the duties pertaining to the office must be with actual or imputed intention, on the face of the surrounding circumstances of each case. [641D] Gopal Chandra Misra vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees executed a trust deed in March 1950, in favour of the appellant for securing repayment of certain sums which were due to him from the trustees. The appellant filed an application under 0. 21 r. 89 C.P.C., for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 as security for payment to the appellant. The trial court passed a decree against the trustees directing them to pay Rs. 3,910/ . The High Court in revision set aside the order of the District Court and directed that Rs.250/ be paid over to the appellants. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the provisions of 0.21 r.89 C. P.C. were not complied with, and (ii) that in view of the decision of this Court in Bai Shri Bhagwan & Anr. vs Shri Ram Chand & Anr., ; , the executing court had no jurisdiction to set aside a sale held in execution of a decree. HELD: (i). The High Courts have inherited the jurisdiction of the Bombay High Court which originally extended over the territory now forming part of the State of Gujarat, ceased when a new High Court was set up in the State. [459 E] (ii).The High Court had inherited the jurisdic tion of the City Civil Court under 0, 21 r 89 C., P. C. and had therefore no jurisdiction. The High court was right in holding that the requirements of 0,21 r 89 were complied with. [460 G] (iii) The High 'Court was not justified in setting aside a decree passed by the District Judge on execution of the decree. [461 B] (iv).The provisions of O. 21 R. 89, C.p. 462 and C.I.D. C., J. in Bai Smt. Indira vs Gordhandas, A.I .R. , referred to. (v) The order passed by a Single Judge of the High Court under O.21 R.89, C.,P. C, was binding on the appellant and not on the decree holder. [463 D] (vi).The appeal is allowed and the order passed in the execution of decree is set aside.

The appellant, who was a clerk in the Post Office of the Director Postal Services, was compulsorily retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of retirement on the ground that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) and as such the appellant was not entitled to retire at any time after he had completed 30 years of qualifying service. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that there is no in Firmity in rule 2(1) of Pension Rules, 1950 which permits compulsory retirement of a Government servant in public interest after he has completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 2 of the pension Rules on the other hand provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government to retire a government servant at anytime after he was in completed 30 yew years of service. [802C] 2. The object of Rule 2 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 1(2), however, provides no guidelines for compulsory retirement. A bare reading of the memorandum shows that there has been an obvious fallacy in the argument of the appellant that it does not contain anything to Rule 2. (802D) 3. The Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 is in the nature of executive instructions and is identical with Fundamental Rule 56(j). [803E F] 4. The words "weed out unsuit able employees" can only be read qua the power to retire under para 6 and not under Rule 1 (2). There is thus no force in the contention that the Government of India has issued instruc tions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule. 2(3) of pension Rules can only he exercised to weed out unsuitable employees. [800F G] 5. The instructions being supplementary to the Rule, according to him, the order is not ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. [900G H] 6. The Government has issued instructions dated July II, 1955 which laid down that retirement under rule 2 (1) shall be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interests. The instruction being supplementary must be understood in the sense of a sufficient safeguard against the arbitrary exercise of power by the Government. [902C D] 7. Rule 2046 is a statutory rule and is similar to Fundamental Rule, 56(J). Para 620 of the Manual being executive instructions cannot be supplemented by the execu tive instructions but a statutory provision which is inconsistent with it. The Instructions can only supplement and not supplant the rule. [702D E] 8. The rules are consistent with the Rules. [ 801E F].

The assessee firm was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The income tax authorities held that the assessee was entitled to set off in respect of the deficiency in the year 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting period from 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but the Tribunal held that there was no profit attributable to the said chargeable accounting periods and therefore the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting years. On a reference made by the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act, the High court held that it was not disputed before them that the business carried on in Nepal on or about 23rd November 1942 and that the sales took place in the next year. The High Court also held that since the chargeable assessment period was the same as in 1940 41, the profits of the year preceding the year of charge were taken into consideration if the manufacturing activity leading to the production of finished article which was subsequently sold contributed to the profits realised, according to the High Courts ' decision in Haji Rahmat Ullah and Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., , that the profit and losses of each year must be computed on yearly basis in terms of the definition of "accounting period" under section 2(1)(a) of that Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The concept of " accountsing period", is a legislation intended to tax the profits and gains tax. It is an integral part of the right to impose a tax of 50% of the excess of the profit made in any accounting period after the 1st day of April, 1939 was given. Section 4 defines "chargeable accounting period" as follows: " chargeable accounting periods". "charge able accounting period " means any accounting periods falling wholly within the term beginning on the 1 st day of September, 1939 and ending on 31st day Of March, 1946 and ending with 31stday of March, 1943. " In the case of Haji Rahmatullah and Co., vs Commissioner , the High COurt held that a payment received in any year subsequently to a chargeable accounting Period was not liable to be treated as the profits in that year for the purpose of computing the excess profits for that year under section 7 of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee firm had been carrying on the same business from 28th October, 1942 to 31th March, 1945 and it was paying the entire accounting period ending 31st April 1944. In the facts of the case it was held that though chargeable accountingperiod was the period beginning from 1 st September 1939 till 31st of March 1946, the assessee 's profits accrued or arisen subsequently, and that such profits were not liable for tax under the third proviso to section 5 of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1946. The question must be answered in the negative and in favour of the revenue. [655 H; 614 A B] Haji Rahmatulla & Co. V. Commissioner of Inland Revenue, at 780, distinguished.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification dated 16th May 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the State Government (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, among others, the names of candidates who had qualified in Civil engineering or Mechanical engineering of the K University or their equivalent as provided by the Special Rules of the Government of Kerala. The applicants were also interviewed in the same manner. The Public Service Commis sioner and the K PSC selected the candidates holding civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees. The respondents, who were qualified in civil engineering, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the judgment of the Division Bench of the High court. The learned Single Judge allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare two separate lists for Civil and Mechanical Engineers. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the K.PSC had advised candidates according to the separate list for Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engi nees and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had obtained civil engineering degree. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Kerala Public Services Commission is not directed to prepare a common list. Common List was referred to in the earlier orders in this Court through certain misapprehensions. The KP SC has stated in its counter affidavit that there were directions to the KPsSC to prepare separate lists. But facing difficulties, in view of the observations of this Court in its order dated 23rd April 1980, the State of Kerala filed a petition before this Court for clarification. This Court by its order dt. 23rd March, 1979 dismissed all the S.L.P. with directions. [747G H; 748A] 1.2 The K P.SC has advised candidates in the Kerala Engineering Service (Mechanical Branch) to prepare three separate rank lists one for Civil Judge and the Mechanical Engineer candidates. The name of Gopa Kumar appears in the latter list. The rank list for Engineering (Civil) contains names of 152 candidates and the other (Mechanical) contains 204 candidates. All the Civil Engineering selected have already been appointed. [750H; 749A B] 1:3. The Kerala Government or the KpSC was not directed, to prepare the common list, but facing difficulties in giving effect to the directions given by the High Courts. The State of Karnataka filed a writ petition before the Division bench of the Public Service Tribunal challenging the order of the learned Single judge and directing the Government and the Public Services Commis tions to prepare one separate rank list on the basis of examination already conducted. The High Court dismissed all these petitions. [751C D] 1 :4. The special leave petitions are dismissed.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. The appellant defendant No. 1 contested the suit on the ground that the correct value of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no interest in the firm. In appeal, the High Court held that the valuation of the business was beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff respondent No. 2 is a partner of a partnership firm along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiff has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under estimates the relief the court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation given by the plaintiff and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. [511B C] 1.2 The High Court while repelling the argument that the suit is governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the court Fees Act, and not by section 8(iv) (f). The plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. In such a case it is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. [512C D] 1:3. There is no doubt that in a suit of accounts, the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is neither possible nor manifestly inadequate for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1936 Bombay 166, relied on. 1.4 The plaintiff non applicant before the High court filed a civil revision application before the Calcutta High Court which was dis missed by the High COurt. The defendant No 2 has not challenged the valuation made by the appellant before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1932 Bombay 166 and Ishwarappa vs Dhanji, AIR 1929 Bombay 166. [ 512C D].

The respondents in these appeals were manufacturers of various products in the State. The respondents in the other two cases were manufacturing and selling industrial units. In the writ petitions filed by them before the High Court, the High Courts held that the exemption sought for was originally granted but subsequently revoked. However, the State Government issued a notification dated 1 9 1983 exempting certain categories of dealers from payment of sales tax. The High Court took the view that these rules and instructions had no relevance to the claim for exemption put forward under the notifica tion of 23 10 1981. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that the High court had refused to grant the benefit of the notification on the ground that the industries run by them were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the industries running in any of the two categories specified in column (1) or in column 2 of the said Notification are entitled to exemption under it only some of those units which do not fall under rule 14 of the defer ment notification would be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. [610C D] 1.2 The High Courts have rightly pointed out that the question of grant of eligibility certificate by the Industries Department is not an empty formality but before granting the certificate, the Industries department has to see whether all the requirements as laid down in the notification are fulfilled and complied with or not. But, it is open to the State Govern ment particularly in view of section 22D of the Act to frame such scheme for the purpose as it may deem fit. [625E F] 1:3. The State intended the exemption to be availed of by certain categories only some other non traditional units operating in certain situations. In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding the exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect of the industries mentioned by it. Section 12 is clear that while a notification under it can be prospective or retrospective, only prospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. [510G H] 1 :4. The expression "as is being urged" in the first part of the Notification has not been defined in the Act. Secondly, even granting that the notification may be inter preted having regard to its past history and the possible intention of the Government while issuing the notification, the position of the assesses here is much stronger for, while in the reported case the State was trying only to effectuate the clear object of the exemption and, therefore, could operate only prospec tively. [613H; 614A B] 1 5. The second proviso to section 12(1) of the 1981 notific ation can be treated as one merely clarifying an ambiguity in the earlier one and hence capable of being retrospective. It enacts the rescission of the earlier exemption and is not necessary for the rules of deferment to specifically provide that they will not be available to the industries listed in rule 14 particularly when rule 4 has incorporated the requirement of an eligibility certificate in accordance with the previous instructions for the said purpose. [712B C] 1 6. The proviso to Rule 12(2) of 1981 notifi cation can be read as follows: "Provided that the Government may exempt any class of dealers or any goods or class of goods from the payment of tax under the Act in whole or in part but only for a definite period to be specified in the Notification". [612C D; 614D] 7.

The petitioners were Judicial Officers of Delhi. They were promoted to the service in consultation with the High Court. The seniority list was prepared on the basis that the rule of "quota and rota" had been applied to them by Rule 7(a) of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1954. The petitioners challenged the validity of the seniority list on the ground that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District and Sessions Judges and that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined according to the respective date of their actual officiating service, that the direct recruits appointed to the Service in consultationwith the High Courts were not senior to direct recruits and that direct recruits who were appointed as Additional district and Sessions judges after the promotees were so appointed cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that seniority has to be determined by the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the date from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which they are appointed in a temporary capacity. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The inter se seniority of members of Delhi Judicial Service promoted to service shall be the same as in the Delhi Judicial Services. [395F] 2.1 Rule 7 of the Rules and the Constitution is not intended to apply when appointments are made under Rules 16 and 17. It is only when they are appointment in a substantive capacity to a post in the service that they become members of the Service. The rule of 'quota ' does not use the negative language as the proviso to Rule 7. [397F G] 2:2 In the instant case, the members of tho Judicial Service were appointed by promotion on the recommendation of the High court and the seniority must be governed by the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e.

The appellant was a partner in a trading venture conducted by the respondent. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills to income tax and taxed it under section 3 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. During the pendency of the suit, the Income tax Appellate Tribunal restored the order of assessment of the assessee in respect of the business carried on by Debi Parshad. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The expression 'any person ' in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. "In the present case, the income earned by the assessee was assessed to tax as income of an association of persons. The Tribunal set aside the order assessing the income in the status of 'a firm of individuals and directed that the Income Tax Officer should assess the members individually. [392 D E] Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed. Commissioner of Incometax, U P. vs Lucknow Coal syndi ners, , referred to. The expression "any person" in the set off of section 31(3) proviso 2 at p. 346 : "Theexpression 'any ' person in its widest connotation may take in any person, whether connected or not with the assessee whose income for any year has escaped assessment but this construction cannot be accepted for the said expression is necessarily circum scribed by the scope of the subject matter of the appeal or revision as the case may be. [394 E F] Commissioner off Income tax U. P. v Kanpur Coal systi cates, , followed and applied.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share and the respondent claimed to have purchased the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the ground that the memorandum of appeal should be treated as an order under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The question about the levy of fees in a suit falling under section7(iv) of Act is governed by section 7 of the Madras Court Fees Act and not by section 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court was right in holding that the Memorandum of appeal must be treated to be the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction dependent upon the value as determinable for computation of court fees and that is natural enough. (ii)The question about adequacy of court fee leviable on the appellant 's memorandum of appeals was properly referred by the High Courts under section 5 of the Indian Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1940, to the trial court. The proper court fees were paid on the memorandum and the memorandum was treated as a whole. (iii)The High Court had no power to direct the appellant to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the Memorandum. The question whether the memorandum should be taxed for purposes of court Fees under section 8(iv), is a matter which has to be decided solely by reference to the Act, and it is open to the Division Bench to consider the correctness of the view taken by the Chamber Judge. (iv)The appeal must fail.

The respondent No. 1, a publisher of Newspapers, had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of the NDMC to accord sanction for construction of certain areas in the State of Delhi. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC not to enforce the revised plans on the ground that they were not in accordance with the mandatory requirements of the statutory provisions. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the planning providing for refuge areas in each floor is violative of the Bye laws framed under the Punjab Municipal Act 1911 and that the proposed building plan is over 15m in height and attracts bye law 16.4.8.1 which provides for a better and more reliable fire safety measures than those envisaged by the bye laws 16. 4.8, and that if the fire fighting and rescue equipment cannot have access to such inner vacant space, then, in the context of the specific objectives of bye laws, it is not possible to accept them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The approval by the Chief Fire Officer under the Act is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the council to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety measure in accordance therewith. [608C] 1.2 The clearance from the Chief fire officer envisaged by Bye law 17.4, 8.1, 8, 2.3, 8 4.6, 8 7 and 16.5.8 are not inflexible and wherever more liberal and better standards of fire safety are incor porated in the designs, the bye law does not prevent such better measures being adopted by the NDMC. [625D] 1:4. The clearance by the chief Fire Officer envisaged by bye law 17,1 is an addition to the requirements of bye law16.4 and 16 4.7. The approval of the Chief Executive Fire Officer is an essential condition for eligibility for sanction, however, such clear ance, by itself is not conclusive of the matter nor binding on the NDMC [609E F] 1 :5. The Authority has to bestow serious re consideration on its insistence to have such a pedestrian walk way for the building, if such walk ways do not already obtain in other buildings on the Road. The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal development requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and proba tion inherent in the insistence upon construction of such pedestrian passengers are considered to be one which abuts a vacant space to which fighting and rehabilitation equipment can have access and from which rescue operations are feasible. [613H; 614A] 1 .6. The authorities have to bestows serious re consid eration on the question independently of the chief fire officer 's clearance. [512B C] 1.(a) The Authority is not final or conclusive on the point and, at all events, not binding on it, which can and is entitled to examine the question independently of such clearance from its Chief Fire Officers. [600D E] (b) The approval given by the Central Government under Bye laws 17.1 is not in consonance with the requirements for eligibility of the plan to be considered for accord ing to the plans in the light of the observations in this order and without insisting upon any fresh clearance from DUAC or the Chief Elec tricity Officer within 3 weeks thereafter and report to this Court the decision taken upon such re construction. [599F G] (c) The clearance of the Superintending Engineer is an integral part of the planning, which has treated such provisions as a whole. [596G H] (d) The permission by the Executive Fire Officers envisaged by a bye law, which had treated such provision as an inflexible, rigid standard and whether the location and distribution of the refuge areas therein was violative of Bye laws, is not a condition precedent to eligibility for sanctioning the plan.

The joint family carried on business of a grocery shop, liquor shops and other premises. The parties were living separately in the same house. In 1946, the parties entered into an agreement with the appellant for the purchase of liquor shops, and the parties agreed to have arbitrators appointed by the Court for examining the accounts from 1942 up to March 31, 1946. On June 29, 1945, the appellant filed a suit for partition against the respondent on the ground that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that the parties omitted to provide in the compromise about the future conduct of the motor business and that they stood in the position of co owners and as contemplated by section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act. The trial court held that though the motor bus service was still a joint family business, it had been carried on by some members of a family whose names were not entered in the partnership list. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree holding that the dispute between the parties was different from the cause of action in the previous suit and that the suit was barred under section 90. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent did not want his brothers to interfere with his exclusive running of the liquor business after March 31 1946, and he had no real grievance in the matter. [106 E] (ii) The cause of actions in the subsequent suit was different than the cause for action in that earlier suit. The cause was different and the suit must be barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure. [107 B C] (iii) The appellant 's claim is barred by the provisions of Order II Rule 2(1). [108 E F] (iv) The plaintiff had himself to thank for preventing the natural course of events and for forbidding the accounts to be taken after March 1, 1946, but he did not care to ask that accounts of other businesses including the motor transport business. He was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree following upon it. [108 F G] (v) The suit was therefore barred under O. II, r. 2(2)(3), C.P.C., as amended by Act No. 1 of 1946.

The appellant was working as a "manufacturing process" under the Factories Act, 1948. The salt works were carried on in the open and not in the factory. The appellant 's salt works had been covered by the Factory Act of 1948. Under section 2 of the Act, " manufacturing process " includes any process incidental to any kind of work done or done for purposes of gain. Section 3(1) defines "factory" to mean a factory as defined in section 2 and includes a mine subject to the operation of the , or a railway running shed. The factory was not a factory within the meaning of the Factories (Act, 1948). The appellant contended that the salt works did not come within the definition of " manufacturing processes " as no process for making, altering, packing, cleaning or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal was carried on. Held, that the expression " premises" in section 3(2) of the includes not only buildings and that it does not include factories as defined by section 2 Of the Act but also includes mine subject ing to the provisions of the Mines (Regulation and Development) Act, 1952. The process of converting sea water into salt was carried out in the Salt Works and described as "manufactured" by the respondent. The expression "factory " in the definition is used only in relation to buildings and not to buildings. The word " factory" in the Factories Acts includes a building which is referred to in section 93 of the . The process involves the carrying on of an activity on open land, and the use of such land or building for purposes ancillary thereto is incidental to its user, sale or letting. The definition of the word "factory ' in section 4 of the is not restricted to buildings as defined under the Act. The term " factory " in section 5 Of the Factories Works would include factories which are covered by section 3 Of the , and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within the description of " factory ". The process carried out at the Salt works was the process of treating the sea water as a distinct commodity and not as a manufacturing process. The processes carried out by the appellant were not for making or carrying out any manufacturing process but only for feeding the stock from the farm. The use of the salt in the salt water did amount to manufacture within the term "factory". The process was not an "manufacture" within the terms of section 2(1)(f) and would therefore be a " factory if it was used in the appellant ' s manufacturing process".

The respondent was a Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Technical Education and was working as Instructor in the Polytechnics. In 1949, he was promoted to the post of Instructor in May, 1949. He joined duty there on December 1, 1949, and continued to work there till November 28, 1949 when he was again posted as Instructor. On June 11, 1956, the respondent was reverted to his parent department. The respondent filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of reversion. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant 's services were not justified and directed the absorption of the respondent in the department of Technical education from the date of his initial appointment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that he was not similarly situated as K. N. Chetty. He was a junior to him in the parent Department and was identically situated. [259 D] (2) It is well settled that in the matter of absorption of an employee, the State Government has evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department, of Technical Educational Education from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he was initially sent. [260 D E] (3) The grant of relief prayed for by the respondent would have unsettled and caused wholesale alterations of the seniority list with regard to the entire cadre of Engineers thus affecting persons who were not before the Court and who would have been r condemned unheard. Further, acceptance of the petitioners ' contentions would have no relevance in the case of the respondents.

The appellant, a foreign national and the Indian Council of Social Welfare, was recognised as an international agency under the Foreigner 's (Regulation) Act, 1986. The respondent No. 1, a resident of India, filed an application before the Court of Small Causes, Calcutta for appointment of a foreigner as a guardian of a child in adoption. The appellant contended that he had been selected by a recognised social or child welfare agency and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to him since he was a citizen of India under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the Act did not apply to the case as it was enacted directly without the intervention of any court in India, and that it was not open to the foreign parents to make an application for appointment as guardian of the child with a view to its eventual adoption. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The Act does not apply in India. It is only if no Indian family comes forward to take a child on adoption within a maximum period of two months that the child may be regarded as available for inter country adoption subject only to one exception namely that if the child is handicapped or is in bad state of health needing urgent medical attention, which is not possible for the social or children welfare agency looking after the child to provide, the recognised social and child welfare agencies will have to approach a recognised Social or child Welfare Organisation. [842C D] 2. The recognised social, or child interest agency through which an application of a foreign parent for taking a child is made directly without its intervention would be illegal if it wants such child to be given in inter country Adoption. Every recognised social/ child welfare organisation must maintain a proper and satisfactory home study report on which the court can rely. [829D] 3. The recognition of foreign parents by foreign parents need not wait until social or Child welfare agencies are recognised by the Government as directed in this order but pending recognition of social or family welfare agencies for the purpose of inter country appointment of an Indian child may he made to the Court only through such recognised social Or child welfare Agency. [827E] 4. The provisions of Act do not apply even to a foreigner who wishes to take the child in adopt, and the recognised Social/ Child Welfare agency must prepare a child study report for the child so as to help the foreigner to come to a decision whether it will be for the welfare of the children to be provided in adoption to the foreigner desiring to take her in adoption, or to adopt any other person. [826F] 5. The recognized social or the child welfare authority should, on receiving an application from the foreign parent, make sure that the said social or a child education agency will provide moral and material stability and security and whether it would be in the interest of the minor child to serve the child and would be able to handle trans portal problems likely to arise from such adoption. [825F] 6. The Central Government should, with the assistance of the foreign mother, make an order appointing the foreign guardian of such a child as guardian for the minor by the foreign father in which the foreigner resides. [828A B] 7.

The appellant company was a factory in Bombay. It had branches in Bombay, Ahmedabad and Bangalore. The gross profits of the company were Rs. 48,65,450. The Company claimed that it had kept proper accounts which had been audited by a reputed firm of auditors and that the balance 6% should be deducted from its gross profits as per the profit and loss account. The Tribunal held that the computation of allocable surplus was not properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit & loss account were depreciation and therefore, the amount of Rs. 21,06,576 was not deductible from the gross profits. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was justified in adding back the sum of Rs, 2,65.706 to the gross profit. [114D] (ii) The claim of the appellant that it has been paid back is not sustainable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. The claim for deduction of certain items was postponed by the Tribunal on the ground that the company had not furnished the requisite particulars. The company had produced figures for depreciation and there was no evidence to show that the amount in question was more than Rs. 20,000. [115E] (iii) The appellant could not raise any objection in law to the payment of such amount. The appellant had produced a figures for depre profits and renewals. The respondent had produced the figures for the depreciation and the Tribunal had rejected this claim on the basis that the appellant had not submitted the requisite details. The workmen would be entitled to bonus at 14,76,706 and not Rs.20% as awarded by the Industrial Tribunal. [116G H] (iv) The company has already declared and paid Rs. 10,000 as bonus for the accounting year 1965 66 on the footing that after distribution of bonus at 20% for the year 1964 65 there must have been a surplus and it should have been set on for the next year, namely, 1965 66. [117A] (v) The workmen will be entitled only to bonus in an accounting year bonus as per section 32(1).

The appellant was a member of the Tamil Nadu General Service officer in 1954. He was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1957 and then as Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1957. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member, Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the order of November 29, 1974 of the Government was to grant absolution to the appellant from the repercussions of the note of the Deputy Commissioner, of Commercial Tax, made in 1969. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Government had no power to extend the absolution beyond the period of one year on the ground of administrative exigencies and that the said order was not passed in accordance with the rules framed under the Tamil Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1959. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Govern ment retiring the appellant after he has attained the age of superannuation is bound to perplex any right thinking man and make him wonder whether the right hand knows what the left hand has done. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appel lant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But, with nothing of the sort, it is indeed odd to retire a government servant a few months after promoting him to a Selection post. [771 F G] 2. The appellant was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion. He had already retired as Joint Tax Officer and posted as member, Sales tax Appellate Tribunal, a prestigious post. It has to be mentioned here that the post of Deputy Commissioner in 1954 is a Selection Post. Under Rule 36(b) (i) of the Rules for the State and Subordinate Services: "Promotions in a service or class to a selection category or to a selected grade shall be made on grounds of merit and ability, seniority being considered only where merit and suitability are approximately equal". So, what do we have ? There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of the appellanant in 1969 which said: "He is sincere and hard working. He manages his office very well. He exercises adequate control over subordinates. He maintains a cordial relationship with public. Because of his stiff attitude some of the assessees complain about him stating that he is rude in his behaviour. His reputation is not at all good. There were complaints that he used to threaten dealers and take money. The entire matter is under investigation by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department. He has earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him during the period from May to June 1966 and his service book shows that he had an excellent record of service. He also earned several valuable properties and reports. The several promotions gained on his behaviour are not considered in the personal file of his appellant. One wonders whether the failure to note the result of the enquiry in the individual file led to the impugned order of September 29, 1975 of the government was a dropped ground. [781 F H; 782 A B] 3. The Government is entitled to taking into consideration all history of his including that portion of it, which said that he has been promoted as Deputy Commissioned Selection post or selection grade shall he made on ground of merit. If the enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appellant, the ultimate result of his enquiry which was that the charges should be dropped was nowhere noted in the Personal file of appellant. [791 F] 4. The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored once he is promoted. Sometimes past events may help to assess present conduct.

The appellants who were the owners of certain routes in the Kumool District of Andhra Pradesh challenged the validity of the schemes framed under Ch. IV A of the , on the ground that they had been issued without complying with the statutory requirements of section 68 C and rule 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Transport Corporation (General) Rules, 1962. The High Court dismissed their petitions holding that the scheme was not in conformity with the requirements of s. 68 C but it was open to the State Government to issue a notification under section 68 D(1) of the Act prohibiting the transport operators from plying their transport vehicles on routes which were liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The appellants contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue the impugned schemes and the validity thereof was also challenged by way of a writ petition. The contentions were: (1) That the scheme framed by the Corporation was not a law which could have been made applicable to them under Ch, IV A; (2) That it was not the Corporation that formed the opinion indicated in section 68C but really the Chief Minister who had signed the scheme and approved it; (3) That even assuming that the Chief Secretary directed the order in which districts were to be taken up for nationalisation, still the scheme under Ch., IV A could not be assailed as invalid on the grounds of violation of r. 4 of Chapter IV A. HELD: (i) The scheme was valid and did not contravene section 68F(1). [353 B] (ii) The contention that the Corporation had published the schemes in the Gazette for nationalisation of transport services in the western half of the Kurnool District, was without substance because the scheme itself contemplated by section 68E was a violation of section 69 E. [354 C D] (iii) The words "any scheme published under section68C" occurring in Ch. I have to be read as a flexible one which is capable of and was intended to be used for the purpose of making a provision for the regulation of road transport services. [353 G] (iv) The word "provides" in Ch, 1 means the authority to whom the application has to be made, but as the authority is directed to issue it, notwithstanding anything in Ch No. I, it would be comprehended by section 69F(I). [354 D E] (v) The power conferred on the Government under Ch . IV A was not unguided or uncanalised and was meant only to enable the Corporation to compensate the appellants for the loss incurred by them during the period that the appeals were pending in this Court.

The appellant was a dealer under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellant purchased certain goods from its dealers in respect of which sales were made to them by it. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry the Commercial Tax Officer made an order disallowing the assessee 's claim for exemption under two heads namely, (i) under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act, Rs. 1,33,730 6 6 and (ii) under Section 5(1) (iii) thereof Rs. 69,65,979 9 6. The Commercial Tax officer made an assessment disallowing the appellant 's claimed exemption under both heads. The Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order but the revision filed to the Board of Revenue was dismissed. On appeal by the assessee the High Court held that the department was not responsible for preventing the assessee from furnishing the true particulars of the declaration forms and that the Department went wrong in not summoning the dealers to produce the relevant documents to establish that they had issued the declaration form. The High Court also rejected the contention of the appellant that a dealer could claim exemption under the said sub clause, but held that it was not obligatory on the assessing authority to give the selling dealer a true declaration in respect Of the goods received from it and that there was no proviso to section 5 (2) (a)(i). In appeal by certificate, HELD : The expression "on demand" only fixes the point of time when the declaration Forms are to be produced. It does not enable the selling dealers to either directly apply or to compel the purchasing dealer to apply for duplicate forms; nor does it empower the sellingdealer to either direct him to obtain and on the purchasing dealers not to give a declaration except in the form prescribed. [629 D] The expression 'on demand ' only fixes that point of limitation when the form is produced, otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with section 5. Section 5 (1) provides for exemption from tax if the sales are made to a registered dealer for the purposes mentioned therein. But the said provision does not empower the Commissioner or any person appointed to assist him under sub section (1), of section 3 to take evidence on oath etc. It is only when the intention of the Legislature was to give exemption, if the terms of the substantive part of sub cl. (ii), alone are complied with, that would be within it 'smerited discretion. [625 E F] The State of Orissa vs M.A. Tulloch & Co. Ltd., ; , followed.

The Bihar State Legislature enacted the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 3 of the said Act provided that no person shall be deprived of his life or liberty except in accordance with the procedure established by law. The State Government issued a notification on 26th February, 1979 under section 3 of which the provisions of sections 5 to 7 were deemed to have been complied with. The petitioners challenged the validity of the aforesaid notifications on the ground that they had been repeatedly detained from time to time and as such could not be prevented from being released by the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was valid and that the provisions thereof did not apply to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) there were several undertrial prisoners who had been in jail for periods longer than six months, and (2) there was no justification for keeping the under trial prisoners in custody beyond a reasonable period of time. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the state. It is an essential ingredient of 'reasonable, fair and just procedure ' guaranteed by Article 21 and it is the constitutional obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trials to the accused. [541C D] 2. The law does not permit any Government to deprive its citizens of constitutional rights on the plea that the State has no adequate financial resources to incur the necessary expenditure needed for improving the administrative and judicial apparatus with a view to ensuring speedy trial. The power of the Court is, therefore, clearly an essential element of reasonable, fair or just procedure guaranteed by article 21 and is not an essential part of any reasonable, just and just. [530D E] 3. In order to enable the court to discharge this constitutional obligation it is necessary that the Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. The Court should be having records from which these particulars can be easily gathered. [540F G] 4. It would be the constitutional duty of the state to device a procedure which would ensure expeditious trial to the appellant by pleading financial or administrative inabili ty and fairness in expenditure, but as it is not only a mandate of equal justice implicit in Article 14 and right to life and liberty conferred by Article 22, but also the compulsion of the constitutional directive embodied in Article 39A. [542F G; 542B] 5. The Constitution has a constitutional obligation to ensure expeditious trials and adequate judicial apparatus for a person accused of an offence and it must be held implicit in the guarantee of Article 21. [543E F] 6. It will be the duty of this Court as a guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to ensure that defendants are not deprived of their life or freedom from exploitation by private parties. The right to speedy trial is, however, clearly and unequivocally an essential constituent of the Eighth Amendment. [544F G]. 7. It has been the duty cast upon the State of Bihar to device the said a procedure for speedy trial to be followed in the case of cases where bail, in proper exercise of discretion, is refused, the accused persons have not to remain in jail longer than is absolutely necessary.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he was entitled to the protection of the Act. The trial court held that the provisions of section 34 (2 A) should have been taken into consideration by the Revenue Courts in deciding the application of the landlord under section 29(2). On appeal, the High Court allowed the application and set aside the order of eviction passed against the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 34 was not applicable to proceedings where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Act came into force, the period of notice had expired and therefore the landlord could not claim relief from the court. HELD : (i) The provisions of the amending Act which came into operation before the tenancy stood terminated by the notice will have to be taken into account in determining the right of the respondent in the matter of the termination of the tenancy, for the Amending Acts put certain fetters on the right to terminate the tenancy and did not speak of any notice at all. Therefore when there is a dispute about the meaning of sub section (2A) that doubt should be resolved in favour of the tenant, for whose benefit the Amending act was passed. [573 D E] (ii) The legislature could not have intended that the benefit of this beneficent measure should not be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy has not yet terminated but where there is any doubt about the interpretation of sub s.(2 A), that doubt must be resolved and the tenant would be entitled to possession. [574 D] (iii) The notice under section34(1)(a) was merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlords to terminate tenancy, and no further proceedings could be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof. [575 E F] Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai, ; , referred to.

The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan. The property of the petitioners was evacuee property and they had no right to it. They claimed that their interest in the houses, as evacuee property, could not be declared evacuee property unless they were declared to be evacuees. Held, that the petitioners were entitled to claim the properties on the ground that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the house. The order was without jurisdiction so far as it affected the rights of the evacueers and was therefore invalid. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, ; , applied. Efrahim Abhimaker vsustral Co operative Society Ltd., ; , referred to. The petitioners were not entitled to any interest in their houses. They had been rightly declared to have been displaced persons under the Act and they could not claim any right of property on the basis of the order made under section 7 of the Act. E brahim Abubaker vs Mussammatunnissa Begum, ; referred to, Per Sarkar, J. The orders of January 10, 1952, were without jurisdiction as the properties in dispute had been acquired under the , and therefore they could be declared evacueies. EBrahim Abbi vsustrial Co operative Bank Ltd., , applied, and Ebman Ali 's share in the property was not evacuee property. Egrahim Abimanaker vs Quanwani, A.I.R. 1952 Cal. 971, approved. Ezrahim Abiqaker vs Tholnissa Begum ; , distinguished.

The assessee company was running a factory at a constant loss as a result of which it had to raise a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The assessee Company paid two instalments in respect of the advances to be made by the agents and also agreed to pay interest on the advances. The commission was paid by the agent and further agreed to be paid at the rate of 15% on the net profits of the business. The Income tax officer disallowed the deduction claimed by the assessee under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922, in respect Of the amount paid as advance to the selling agents. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim and held that the payments were not legal deductions as contemplated under section I3(xv) and that the agreement was a contract of agency and not a joint venture for the distribution of profit. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that though the commission paid to the agents was at a result Of which it was not liable to tax, the amount was not legally deductible under section 1 3(xv). The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The agreement clearly provided for the consent of the agents not only at the beginning of the manufacture of the yarn by the plant to be installed by the assesses company but at every stage in the pro gramme of manufacture. On the loan advanced to the assessee, and a percentage in the profits of business would be quite consistent with the payment in lieu of services lent and would certainly amount to an expenditure incurred by the assesee wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the 'business which was conducted by the appellant. [200 C D] (2) The question whether or not the agreement amounted to a joint contract or a joint enterprise or a transaction between two or more persons contribute to a Joint venture or a contract for the purposes of business, profession or vocation is irrelevant in order to determine whether the transaction amount ted to a jointly venture in the garb of a contract or an agreement is wholly and solely for the pur pose of the carrying on of the trade. [201 D E] (3) The fact that the assessee company had agreed to share the profits and the losses would not take the case of the asses see from the point of view of the businessman and not from the department or Tribunal 's point of opinion. [202 G H] (4) In order to fall within section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax, 1922 the deduction must be made in respect to a sole selling agent and not in the case where there is an agreement between the assessee Company and its agents. [203 B C] (5) The amount in question was deductible under s.10(2) (xv). [202 E F] (6) In the instant case, the assessee had paid the commission out of profits and conditional on profits being earned cannot accurately be described as a payment made to earn profits by the employee. [204 C D].

The assessee, a private limited company, was assessed for the assessment year 1959 60 (the relevant previous year being the year ended March 31, 1959) on a total income of Rs. 43,407/ . The Income Tax Officer held that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only and directed the Income Tax officer to reopen the assessment by virtue of section 147(b)(e) of the Income tax Act, 1961. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee was entitled to a reference to the High Court under section 256(1) of Income Tax Act, 1922. The Revenue preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which held that Rs. 18,950/ were not liable to be included in the accumulated profit of the Company. The Tribunal referred the following question to the Full Bench of the High court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, the Tribunal was legally correct in holding that Rs 10,000/ constituted a 'accumulated profits ' within the meaning of section 2(6A)(e), Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939?" The High Court answered the first question in favour of the assessee. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the words "accumulation" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not take in current profits and therefore, the expression 'accusation ' in section 6(2)(e). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in answering the first questions in favour. [950C] 2. The words "acumulated profit" in Section 2 (p) (c) of Indian Income Tax are wide enough to include current profits. [ 951D] 3. The expression "accusated profits" occurring in section 4(6)(e)(e ) cannot take in closed profits. The word "accu larly" is used in the sense of 'actually ' and not in a technical sense. It has long since been recognised as an application in that behalf by a party desiring a reference under section 254 operates entirely in favour by one party, although in the course of making the order the Appellate Tribunal may have negatived some points of law raised by that party. [951F G] 4. The statute expressly contemplates an application to the extent that it covers the second question and, therefore, relates to the question whether accumulated profits can take in Current profits. If the application is rejected by the Appellate Tribu nal, it is open to the non applicant, in the event of the Appellate 'Tribunal agreeing to refer the case to the Calcutta High Court, to ask for a reference of those questions of law also which arise on its submissions negatived in appeal by the appellate Tribunal. [952C D] 5. The question whether the provision of Rs 11,000 for tax and Rs. 6,900 for dividend can be taken into account when computing the accumulated income as on March 31.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the respondents were the Mahant. The appellant claimed that he had been in possession of certain lands for over 200 years under a Lakheraj grant made prior to the permanent settlement, that they had been granted in permanent settlement by the Maharaja of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that the respondents had been holding under a Jakheraj Grant made prior before the permanent Settlement, and that they were entitled to fair rent. The District Munsif held that the lands were not Mal lands within the Zamindari of Burdwan but were granted as Lakhe Rajgun jhair in 1841, and decreed the suits. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court agreed with the District Judge on both the points. Held, that a presumption of lost grant could be made only when there was no person capable of making a grant; and if there was any legal impediment to the making of it, the inference to be drawn from that word cannot outweigh the effect of the non exclusion of the lands from the Mal or regularly assessed estate. The fact that the defendants had been dispossessed of land for a long time without payment of rent, could not affect their title. The suit properties formed part of a permanently settled estate and if a grant had been made in favour of the predecessors of the defendants, it must have been made by the Maharaj of Burdwan or by the Rajgun Jhair. It was only in 1931 that the appellants were entitled, to assessment of fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their possession. The respondents could not be said to have asserted a hostile title and the suit properties had been settled on them.

The appellant was the owner of certain agricultural land in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State. The Tenancy Act, 1948 came into force on 15th December 1965. Section 63(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the Tenancy Act provided that when upon a reference a decision is recorded by the competent authority under the Tenancy act, the Civil Court shall decide the issue whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist or not. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th April 1966. The trial court held that the certificate granted by the Mamlatdar certifying that the plaintiff was an agricultural labourer and the bar imposed by section 63(c) of the Act would not operate, and decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court agreed with the trial court holding that in such a situation the civil court had undoubtedly jurisdiction to decide the question whether the appellant is an agricultural labourers or not and, therefore, the civil Court will have jurisdiction to determine the issue. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the jurisdiction of the Civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the tenancy Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by a competent authority is totally ousted; (ii) the civil courts will have no jurisdiction to try and decide the suit in accordance with the decision recorded by them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of Civil Court to settle a dispute under section 70(a), is limited to the Civil Courts only. It does not ipso facto oust the jurisdiction, of the civil Courts to decide that issue even though they arise for decision in a suit properly constituted civil suit before a civil court having jurisdiction to entertain it. [596D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that if an issue arises in a properly constituted suit which the Civil Judge is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the tenancy law, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arose in a civil suit, the jurisdiction will have to be determined by the Revenue Court and not by the High court. [597F] 3. The expression "any issues which are required to he settled, decide, decided, or dealt With by any authority competent under the Act, is totally ousting the jurisdiction conferred upon the Civil courts. Therefore, if a person intending to purchase agricultural land files a suit, for enforcing a con tract entered into by him and if the suit is resisted on the ground that the land is an agriculturists within the meaning of the provisions of section 70A, he will have a locus standi to file such suit.
