[598B C] 4. The civil court has no jurisdiction under section 71 to settle the dispute as it does not fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of a civil Court to decide or dispose of the same. [599F G] 5. If a person intends to purchase the agricultural land, files a claim to purchase such land, he is not an agriculturist and, consequently, ineligible to purchase it, not for his other reason except that it is prohibited by section 70. Therefore if a suit is filed against the tenant for enforcing the contract entered into between him and the landlord, he would be entitled to raise the question as to whether the defendant is an ' agriculturist ' within the definition of the word 'agricultural ' in section 70 or not, and if section 85A imposes an obligation on the civil authorities to refer such issue to the competent authori ty under the provisions contained in the Tenancy Acts, then, notwithstanding the finding that it will be a subsidiary issue, as such, was within the competence of the Revenue Authorities. [600D E] 6. The suit is remanded to the trial Court for disposal according to law in accordance therewith. [698F G; 600A] 7.

The assessee, a heavy engineering concern manufacturing boilers, wagons, etc., was carrying on the business of manufacturing steam parts and for that purpose the assessee was purchasing spare parts. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the steel Foundry Division was an industrial undertaking to which section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 applied. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee and accepted the claim of the asses see. In reference the High Court held that both the Steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division were new industrial undertakings and therefore the assessee could not be said to be an industrial unit within section 15 C. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The two new undertakings are independent producing arti cles which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business of the assesses. Use by the assessee of the articles produced in its existing business or the concept of expansion are not decisive tests in construing section 15A. (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the two new undertaking were formed by reconstruction of the old business of a new industrial undertaking which he certainly does, would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section 15(C). Commissioner of Income tax vs Gangs Sugar Corpora tion Ltd., ; , referred to. (iii) The assessee continued to be the same for the purpose of assessment. manufacture or production of articles and there was no transfer of any assets of the new business to the new undertaking which takes place when there is reconstruction of a business. The fact that the articles are produced in the existing, business or, it may produce some other distinct marketable products, even commodities which may feed the oldbusiness cannot be ignored. (iv) The new industrial Undertakings were independently producing articles which might be of help to the main business but nevertheless the undertakings were distinct and separate from the existing ones.

The inam lands were granted to the appellants for performance of services connected therewith. The inamdars were granted Inam rights in the land. The Inamdars were not inams burdened with services and were not resumable under section 44 B(2)(a)(i) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. The lands were resumed by the Inamdars on the ground that they had been in possession of the inamdars for over 80 years. The appellants filed a suit against the alienees for recovery of the arrears of inam due to them. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the inams comprised both melwaram and melwarnam and the lands were not personal inams burdened by the inamdar or tenants in respect of their services. On appeal, the District Judge held that the Inam Abolition Act was applicable to the inam lands and that the inam was a permanent lease and the inam granted to all the inamholders was for the performance of service connected therewith and was therefore illegal and a nullity. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that section 44B(2) of Madras Hindu religious Endowments Act 1926, which was in force at the time of confirmation of the inams by the Inams Commissioner in 1863 and the subsequent confirmation of grants of the Inam in favour of hereditary office holders then rendered invalid under section 43 B(1), did not apply to a personal inam burdened with service and (2) that the lands in question were not private inams burdened for services and therefore, the appellants could not be evicted. HELD: (i) The inamdar was entitled to resume the inam land made under section 45 B(ii). [549 E] (a) Section 44B of Madras Act XXII of 1927 is applicable only where there has been any alienation at any time the first ground or other grounds mentioned therein. The object of section 44A is to define and enlarge the grounds on which the inams could be resumed and to devise a proper procedure for the resumption. On general grounds of public policy, the legislature has declared that the grant of land in inam where there have been an alienation of the lands either before or after 1934, is not a lease for a term exceeding 5 years. [549 F] (b) The inams were granted by the appellant to the holders of hereditary offices as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the purview of section 43B(1). [598 B C] (c) The lands in dispute were resumables under the inam fair register prepared at the instance of the Inams commissioner in 1863, and the Inam Fair Register prepared at that time was not in force. The inams in question are resumments granted to office holders as remuneration.

The respondent Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. Under section 2(c) of the Act, the Municipality had imposed a tax on houses or buildings and the trustees duly paid such tax were required to take inspection thereof and make extracts therefrom. The appellant Corporation levied house tax on the basis of gross annual letting value at the rate of 7% of such value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The respondent contended that under section 79(1) of Act, 1951, the tax could be assessed on the annual letting values less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 76(6) of a Municipality is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the same basis as the valuation based on capital or annual lettingvalue is obviously inconsistent with section 73 under which the annual tenancy value would be the gross annual rent less 10%. [131 E] (ii) The appellant was entitled to levy the house tax at 7% on the gross yearly letting value. Under sections 75 and 76 when a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year, it can be done subject to the provisions of sections 75, 77 and 78. In order to prevent such a result the legislature has provided by sub section 2 of section 79 that where a Municipality adopts a previous prepared list in an earlier year is adopted it becomes the list for such subsequent year subject to its procedure laid down in section 76( 6) after disposing of the objections if any and it is then only that it becomes conclusive evidence of the valuation and the tax assessed thereon for that particular official years. If it were otherwise, the annual rent or value estimated on a particular building or house would be static for 4 years during which the Corporation can go on adopting the assessment lists prepared in an later year provided however, that it prepares a fresh list oncein every 4 years and can adopt an earlier assessment list such as a new assessment has been completed at the commencement of that particular officer. [132 G H] (iii) The word "if" appearing in sub section (1) is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if" because the word "on" standing by itself makes no sense at all. 79 therefore has to be construed to mean that though a Municipality need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year and need prepare such list once in every 4 year, subject to a procedure laid prescribed by section 76 (6) after dispose of the objection if any, and it was then only the basis for the assessment.

The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1944. During that period, there was a sale of chemicals and raw materials for manufacture. The assessee company sold these chemicals to various persons who were in charge of the chemicals and also to others who were selling the chemicals at a profit. In a confidential report made by the Income tax Officer, the assessee company stated that the price obtained from the purchasers was much more than the trading profits and that the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after the company had been wound up. The Income tax authorities held that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the trade, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business and that therefore the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court held that there could be no such sale in the ordinary course of business or that the excess was liable to tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee Company was wound up at least in so far as its match manufacture was concerned. That the business was sold as a going concern and was in fact worked by the appellant company on behalf of the buyer till the entire consideration was paid, makes no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the assessee Company had kept the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf Of the buyer. One cannot fairly say, therefore, that a sale is something more than a winding up sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and manufacturing chemicals. [968 D E] (ii) The fact that the clause in the Memorandum of Association gave power to the company to Bell chemicals could not make it a business transaction which if profit resulted. In the present case, the company was woundup at least, in so much far as the match manufacture is concerned. The sale of the chemical and raw material for match manufacture did not amount to a trading from which alone profits can arise in business. [948 D] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that there was no profit other than what results from the appreciation of capital. The essence of the matter however, is not that an extra amount has been gained by the selling out or the exchange but whether it can fairly be said that there is a profit other then. [949 F] Doughty vs Commissioner of Taxes, ; , referred to. (iv) The mere fact that in the present transaction the assessee was wounded at least for the reason that the business had been carried on by the buyer, till the whole consideration was not paid, make no difference, because the assessee 's profits and raw goods were too petty in themselves to afford evidence of a continued or sustained trading in chemical chemicals. In such a case it is impossible to infer that the chemicals & raw materials were sold in the normal way of business operations which alone would have attracted tax, if profit resulting.
